title: The Great British Bake Off review – Nigella is wise, generous … and perfect for this national treasure of a show | Nigella Lawson | The Guardian
description: The newest judge on the culinary competition is a soothing presence who is the ideal complement to Paul Hollywood. Long may the show continue with her on it
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The newest judge on the culinary competition is a soothing presence who is the ideal complement to Paul Hollywood. Long may the show continue with her on it
Content: From right to left: Alison Hammond, Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood are custodians of one of British TV’s great treasures.Photograph: Channel 4/PAView image in fullscreenFrom right to left: Alison Hammond, Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood are custodians of one of British TV’s great treasures.Photograph: Channel 4/PATV reviewNigella LawsonReviewThe Great British Bake Off review – Nigella is wise, generous … and perfect for this national treasure of a showThe newest judge on the culinary competition is a soothing presence who is the ideal complement to Paul Hollywood. Long may the show continue with her on itLucy ManganTue 22 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a very good argument to be made for requiring a national referendum on whether presenters of shows that are part of our cultural identity should be allowed to leave, followed by – if necessary – a vote on who should replace them. At the very least, this would avoid the parlous state of affairs we face right now: at the very moment the public is grappling with thenew-look Strictly Come Dancing(Tess and Claudia replaced by Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe, three whole different people!) we are asked to cope with a change to the order of the tented universe too.ForThe Great British Bake Offlineup has replaced Prue Leith (who stepped down after deciding that, at 86, she would quite like to go back to having holidays instead of filming the series all summer) with – the one! The only! – Nigella Lawson.It is, in TV terms, a big “get” and has been much heralded. And if there had been a public vote, Lawson would probably have won it. So is change always synonymous with destruction, or can Nigella buck thetrend for modern enshittificationof all things and give us the sanctuary we crave?Yes, my friends. Yes, she can. She moves through Bake Off dispensing words of wisdom, generous praise and gentle criticism, just as confident as Leith but a much quieter, more soothing presence that works perfectly with Alison Hammond’s ebullience and Paul Hollywood’s teacher-ish vibe. She has a streak of romance that complements Hollywood’s ever-practical approach too, which enables her to enjoy contestants’ flourishes (the mirror, for example, that drag performer Gabe makes to decorate the “self-portrait” showstopper challenge behind which hides his alternative persona) in a way that Paul – a man without whimsy – does not.View image in fullscreenNigella goes Hollywood? The pair have teamed up at last to evaluate some competitive baking.Photograph: Channel 4/PAThe producers wisely do not give Lawson a big introduction on the show itself. Hammond welcomes her, she is lightly ribbed over “sumptuous” (attached to the chocolate stout cake that presents the first challenge) being a very Nigella word (though “ferrous tang” a bit later on has got to be up there too) and then we’re straight into business.The key to a successful stout cake is slow cooking on a low heat and leaving enough time for it to cool before decoration. The contestants all understand this, which reminds you that the greatest attraction of Bake Off was, is and (God willing) always shall be the opportunity to watch competent people do things well and be celebrated – instead of seeing foolish people get humiliated on screen, then destroyed on social media.Accordingly, the tent soon fills with cherry compotes, Swiss meringue and ambition. We move with the presenters, Hammond andNoel Fielding, round the work stations to get our first look at the cakes and contestants. Is everything going OK, Noel asks young Danni. “Indeedaroonie!” Danni replies. “You’re already my favourite,” says a grinning Noel.View image in fullscreenBake Off baker Danni mixes it up in the tent.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4Everywhere you look, people are doing clever things with buttercream, cardamom and something called malt mascarpone because people are amazing. Clara, from Portugal, who began baking two years ago, is trying and failing to make a sugar dome, but true disaster befalls Molly when her perfectly baked cake is taken out of the oven and drops in truly irrecoverable fashion to the floor. She takes a moment, then starts again, this time in sandwich rather than bundt tins so the new bake time will be shorter. Molly, our hearts are with you.‘Eating is my superpower’: Nigella turns up the heat on Bake OffRead moreJudgment time. Connie, who runs a music centre and brings cakes in for her students, has provided “fascinating flavours” but overbaked. “The fear of unmoulding seizes one,” says Nigella, sympathetically. Hairdresser Tom has gone too heavy on the bicarb. But law student and calisthenics fan (this is the other great feature of Bake Off – everyone hints at multitudes) Mo’s peanut and caramel creation is “sensational – I’m in heaven” (Nigella) and “spot on – I love it” (Paul).The technical bake hinges on replacing the right amount of flour with the right amount of crushed walnut and providing a strong enough coffee hit. Tom redeems himself (“My dream cake,” says Nigella), Gabe and Gary (smallholder, took up baking five years ago) make good showings, but Molly’s is deemed lacking. We fear for Molly, until … showstopper challenge triumph! Oh yes. Roaring back she comes, with a “light, tart beautiful bake” replete with mango and lemon curd and honour is restored.My screener contained the star baker reveal but not who was sent home. Assuming it was the contestant who deserved it (although none of them deserves it – they are all magicians to me, conjuring this edible art from nowhere) I pronounce the good ship Bake Off fully seaworthy. Long may she sail with Nigella and crew at the helm.The Great British Bake Off is on Channel 4 in the UK, with an Australian airdate yet to be announcedExplore more on these topicsNigella LawsonTV reviewThe Great British Bake OffTelevisionPaul HollywoodNoel FieldingAlison HammondreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I read 163 novels and these are the six best: Mary Beard on judging the Booker prize | Books | The Guardian
description: I found being a Booker judge hugely rewarding. All the works on our shortlist will change how you see the world
Author: Mary Beard
Headline: I found being a Booker judge hugely rewarding. All the works on our shortlist will change how you see the world
Content: The finalists … the Booker prize 2026 shortlist: L to r, Elizabeth Strout (The Things We Never Say), Marlon James (The Disappearers), M John Harrison (The End of Everything), Douglas Stuart (John of John), Luke Kennard (Black Bag), Rebecca Perry (May We Feed the King).Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/Booker prize foundationView image in fullscreenThe finalists … the Booker prize 2026 shortlist: L to r, Elizabeth Strout (The Things We Never Say), Marlon James (The Disappearers), M John Harrison (The End of Everything), Douglas Stuart (John of John), Luke Kennard (Black Bag), Rebecca Perry (May We Feed the King).Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/Booker prize foundationBooksI read 163 novels and these are the six best: Mary Beard on judging the Booker prizeMary BeardI found being a Booker judge hugely rewarding. All the works on our shortlist will change how you see the worldThis year’s Booker prize shortlistTue 22 Sep 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTShareAs a Booker judge, I think I have worked harder than I have ever done before. Reading 163 novels in six months, making careful assessments, being ready to argue for your judgment, going back to check you haven’t got it wrong … in some ways it took more energy than actuallywritinga book. But it was also hugely rewarding and fun. I shall never forget the discussions in our regular judging meetings, and the pleasure of discovering how we had sometimes reached almost exactly the same view of a book, and sometimes dramatically diverged. There were no big newsworthy squabbles, but a lot of discussion, a lot of listening and re-reading.When each new batch of 30 or so novels arrived at home, through the spring, I plunged in and picked them out at random (only occasionally cheating by selecting a slim volume when I felt I needed to get my total up!) But so thatyouhave more to go on, here is a quick guide to each of the books on the shortlist – in strictly alphabetical order.In M John Harrison’sThe End of Everything, we enter the dystopian world of Kent, sometime in the near future. There’s been a catastrophe of some undefined sort and the survivors have been reduced to scavenging and “making do” after most of the rules of social order have collapsed. Expect an unexpected random shooting or two, and an alien visitor to be managed. But the book is not (just) weird. It is also about us and about now – a gripping read and often funny in the most surprising places. If you can’t always make outexactlywhat is going on, that’s part of the point.Also with the hallmarks of dystopia, but inspired by a rumoured real-life violent incident in Jamaica in the 1980s, Marlon James’sThe Disappearersexplores a vicious killing and its long, unsettling aftermath. While rehearsing for a play, some gay men are attacked by homophobic thugs: one actor is left dead; another has both eyes gouged out; all are scarred in different ways. Later one of the survivors sets out to find the others and reckon with what happened. A hugely ambitious novel, it is told over different times, in different voices and registers (diary extracts, media interviews etc). The characters stick in your head, the wit is sharp, the rawness unforgettable.In contrast, Luke Kennard’sBlack Bagstarts from an hilarious premise. A struggling actor takes a job in a university psychology department, where he must attend classes dressed in a black leather bag. This is based on a real-life experiment from the 1960s, which aimed to discover how the other students would react to the “bag man” in their midst. Beyond its surreal humour, which will have you laughing out loud even on a second read, Black Bag raises big questions about identity, ambition and human frailty, as well as conjuring up some truly absurd sex scenes (in the bag, of course).May We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry has its surreal aspects, too. The narrator, a self-effacing museum curator, specialises in re-creating historical tableaux, with horribly accurate fake fruit and plastic joints of meat. During one assignment, the curator uncovers the story of a forgotten medieval king, trapped in a treacherous court – a reluctant and unsuitable occupant of the throne who came to power as the last option after the death of his brothers. Perry elegantly intertwines present and past to question the boundary between history and fiction, and to ask whether the past can ever be a safe refuge from the here-and-now.Artie Dam, in Elizabeth Strout’sThe Things We Never Say, has no safe refuge anywhere. A much-loved, fiftysomething history teacher in an American high school, who likes messing about in boats, Dam sees his apparently comfortable world gradually collapse. We find him with thoughts of suicide, trying out shoplifting in a bout of madness, facing a new US president – and weighed down by the discovery of an almost unbearable family secret. This is a seductively understated book, which unpicks the silences and shame of family life, while also unpicking the new world of Trump’s America, without ever once haranguing the reader.Silences and shame also underlieJohn of Johnby Douglas Stuart. Here a student – at the end of his course and with no job – returns “home” to the tiny Hebridean island of Harris. Stuart paints the island landscape vividly, but it’s far from the romantic, untouched world of the tourist brochures and it’s a disconcerting sort of home. This is a world of violence, feuds, discontent, hypocrisy, secret sex and isolation that is not only geographic. Yet there is a rough tenderness in the story that Stuart weaves, as well as tremendous emotional depth, and in the end, almost unbelievably, a sense of hope.Each of these books can change how you see the world. So, plunge in and enjoy the ride.Explore the shortlist for this year’s Booker prize and, for a limited time, get all six books for only £79 atguardianbookshop.com. title: ‘I’m afraid they’ll bomb the cafe where I work, or bomb me’: a day in the life of a 12-year-old boy in Gaza | Global development | The Guardian
description: Ramadan, 12, works in a cafe on the beach. He remembers enjoying school, playing and family barbecues before life became about survival
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: Ramadan, 12, works in a cafe on the beach. He remembers enjoying school, playing and family barbecues before life became about survival
Content: Ramadan. Art direction by Guardian DesignGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal development‘I’m afraid they’ll bomb the cafe where I work, or bomb me’: a day in the life of a 12-year-old boy in GazaThis week, as the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. Ramadan lives in a tent on the beach and works to support his familySupported byAbout this contentSeham Tanteshin Gaza andTess McClureTue 22 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTShareAs the war inGazaapproaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.The tent is pitched on a platform set in the sloping sand dunes, above a long expanse of golden coastline. Rats have chewed holes in its canvas sides, and tendrils of pale sand blow in through the gaps. Inside, on the torn mattress he shares with his siblings, 12-year-old Ramadan Ghaban blinks the sleep from his eyes. The sun has just risen but it is already hot.This is a day in the life of a boy in Gaza.Daybreakdouble quotation markI wake up every morning at 6.30am. Sometimes, the heat wakes me up, and sometimes it is the sound of the birds, which are everywhere because we live near the sea.I wash my faceand brush my teeth. We do not have gas, so I gather small pieces of wood and plastic to light the fire so we can boil water for tea.My name is Ramadan Yaqoub Ghaban. I am 12 years old, from Beit Lahia. I now live in al-Nuwairi, in the coastal area of Nuseirat. I have three sisters and one brother.Ramadan’s family was displaced to the coastal area of NuseiratMorningRamadan picks his way over the dunes and between the tents, looking for any wood for a fire to boil the family’s kettle. There are few trees left here, so there’s little to be found, but he finds some scraps of plastic and a piece of driftwood, and crouches to break branches off a thorn bush. With his brother Adi, he builds a small fire to warm the kettle and make tea.Then he sets off down the beach to work, the wind whipping up sand as he walks.In the morning, Ramadan looks for wood to burn to boil the kettledouble quotation markAfter breakfast, I go to work by the sea, at a cafe. The cafe is about 300 metres from our tent, and it takes me only a few minutes to get there.I usually walk along the beach. On the way, I seefishermencatching fish and crabs and selling what they catch. Sometimes, I stop to watch them bringing the fish out of the sea. Usually I work for 12 hours – from about 7am until the evening. Sometimes, people stay up eating until 10pm, and so I work until late. When I walk home it is dark, and large rats come out of the darkness and brush against my legs.I move tables, arrange chairs, take tables out and at night bring them back, clean and arrange them,rake the sand around the tables to keep it smoothand collect the trash. Yesterday, some people were grilling food. They were having a barbecue, and the smell of it was everywhere! I was telling myself, “If we were at our home, we might have been having a barbecue.” Then those people went and left a bag of chips behind. I was hungry, so I took it and ate it.My work is very tiring, but I do it because I have to support my siblings. I see the neighbour’s kids hanging around and playing, living with their father, and he brings them food and drink, but I have to work to get food and drink. Otherwise my younger sisters cry without money to buy food.Ramadan rakes the sand around the beach cafe where he worksBefore the war, my father used to work harvesting strawberries in Beit Lahia and gathering recycling, but he doesn’t work any more. He was killed when he was at my aunt and uncle’s house, when he went there to help them evacuate. We heard the Israelis had bombed a nearby house. We wondered, “Which house?” Then a woman came to the school where we were sheltering, saying, “Your father is dead. Your father is dead.” We didn’t believe her, but when we went to the house, it had been destroyed. We rushed to move the rubble and find him, but the Israelis were firing shells, so we couldn’t reach him and we fled.My father remained under the rubble for four months. After four months, we returned to Beit Lahia, and pulled him out from under the rubble. We buried my father in the cemetery.LunchtimeAt about 1.30pm, a water truck comes, and Ramadan takes a break from his work to dash up the hill and fill the family’s empty bottles. He and his younger sisters take them to the truck and fill about 15 bottles for drinking and washing. When they are all full, he loads them into a trolley made from a plastic crate. Its mismatched wheels spin and wobble on the stick that forms the axel, as he drags it over the sand dunes and back down the hill.Ramadan fills his cart with as many bottles of water as he candouble quotation markWhen the water trucks arrive, I fill as many containers as I can. Sometimes, they arrive at six in the morning, and sometimes in the afternoon.In our tent, rats have eaten everything,even gnawed the water containers. We don’t have any good ones left – they’re all leaking, so we fill up plastic bottles instead.Before the war, we had a home. We lived in a house with two bedrooms, a living room, a bathroom and a kitchen.I used to go to school in the morning, sit with my classmates, have breakfastand play during the break. Now we live in tents, and rodents have chewed the whole tent – they’ve torn it all apart. Soon winter will come, and our tents will fly away in the winds – we will have water seeping inwhile we’re sleeping, or we’ll get flooded. In winter there are strong winds and storms, and all the cafes get shut because the sea rises and gets closer.The thing I’m most afraid of is that the war will return, or that they’ll bomb the cafewhere I work, or bomb me if I’m walking, or they’ll bomb a house, or a hall or something – because we have a hall nearby here where people dance. I’m worried that the war and famine will return, and we won’t find food and water. During the famine we’d go hungry for three or four days. I used to go to the aid point at Zikim to get bread, and I saw people pushing and fighting over a kilo of flour. I saw it with my own eyes, and I saw people being killed. The Israelis would fire bullets right next to us: we’d be lying down, and bullets would come from above. If someone raised their head, they’d die instantly – their heads were torn apart. I hope those days do not return.Eveningdouble quotation markI finish my work between7pm and 10pm, and the people at the cafeteria give me 10 shekels[£2.45].Before the war, 10 shekels could buy a lot of things – but now it buys some cheese and a loaf of bread.What I like about my work is that it is close to the sea. I like breathing the sea air and swimming when I get the chance. I taught myself how to swim, and if there is a break in between my tasks, I will run into the sea to cool off.In the future, I want to be a lifeguard to rescue people – so if someone is drowning, I’ll save them. Or I want to be a doctor or a lawyer. My other hope for the future is that the war will end, that we’ll rebuild our homesand the Israelis will withdraw and go back to their borders, and life can be like it used to be. I would not have to work and I could go back tostudy in classrooms. I have not been to school since the beginning of the war, since the very first day. I really loved reading. Arabic was my favourite subject.Ramadan cools off in the sea. He has taught himself to swimI don’t have much time to play during the day. In the evening, afterthe customers leave, I go out to see my friends. Sometimes, we used to make kites and fly them,butthey started bombing children who flew them. The other day, they bombed three children’s kites, so I stopped making them.I walk home along the beach. When I return to the tent, I wash, change my clothes, pray, have dinner and go to sleep.CreditsVideo: Tantesh Media ServicesArt direction: Harry Fischer, Anaïs Mims, Barry Ainslie and Alessia AmitrianoVideo editor/producer: Joshua JacobVideo executive producers: Temujin Doran and Augusta AnthonyAdditional research: Harriet Barber

title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
Author: John Crace
Headline: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
Content: Andy Burnham joked about Donald Trump calling Manchester ‘some town’ in their first meeting, while Trump called Burnham a ‘great businessperson’.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham joked about Donald Trump calling Manchester ‘some town’ in their first meeting, while Trump called Burnham a ‘great businessperson’.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamCall it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King BabyJohn CraceMeeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President TrumpUS politics live – latest updatesTue 22 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTShareHow do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby.Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guessDonald Trumpis a fool’s errand.So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover.The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at theUnited Nationsgeneral assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident.All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed?And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”?View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham met Donald Trump while in the US to attend the United Nations general assembly.Photograph: Toby Melville/PATaking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water.It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that.Burnham then bigged up thedeal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual.Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old.Then a question on thesanctions imposed on illegal settlementsin the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal.There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting?Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchDonald TrumpUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: Swan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brother | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stage
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stage
Content: Charles Spencer's book in a London bookshop.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenCharles Spencer's book in a London bookshop.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersAutobiography and memoirReviewSwan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brotherAmid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stageEmma BrockesTue 22 Sep 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the lateDiana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer – perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400 pages of score settling, chest thumping, wild indiscretion and some truly touching passages about his late sister, the reader is left with a head-spinning story of the world that created Diana and a certain sourness at the manner in which it is told.Let’s start with the headlines in last week’s Daily Mail, the newspaper to whom Spencer sold serialisation of a book which includes a line describing tabloid journalists as “those who inhabit the murky swamps of malevolence, and who need to suck their victims dry of their souls”. Perhaps he meant a different set of hacks. Anyway the top line in the Mail was that, shortly after Diana’s death, King Charles insulted her in a phone call to Spencer: “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” Your take on this quote will likely dictate how you receive the book, and here’s mine: I’m willing to believe the king behaved badly, but “hissed” is a red flag, one of those embellishments, like “snarled” or “flounced”, that writers tend to use to make those they’re writing about appear worse. Spencer, always the injured party, has so many axes grinding away in this book that at times it’s impossible to hear what he’s saying.Before we get to that, the question on everyone’s lips is: why write this book now? Spencer maintains it’s because, as the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death drew near, he kept being asked to contribute to other people’s projects. Rather than allow the narrative to be guided by “some TV producer” from a network “I will never watch” he promptly got on with his own. Likely that’s not the sole reason; elsewhere in the book he writes about how, back in the day, his father was always at risk of running out of cash to run Althorp, the family’s Northamptonshire estate, and one wonders if the present earl is having similar difficulties.Never mind. For fans of petty grievances, among whom I count myself, the book is an absolute corker of resentment, and in Spencer we have a hero who, decades after the fact, is still harping on about a great many things involving a large cast of characters who he has absolutely not forgiven for any of it. While telling the story of his and Diana’s relationship, there are drive-bys on Peter Carter-Ruck, Princess Michael of Kent, Princess Margaret, his three ex-wives, whom he describes in an amazing parenthetical take down as “all double divorcees”, and members of a police protection squad who, in 1986, let sniffer dogs jump all over his furniture.double quotation markSpencer writes that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtshipIf too many words are spent on, for example, the perfidiousness of Martin Bashir, I could read an entire book on the subject of Spencer’s horror at what his stepmother, Raine, did to the interiors at Althorp, including installing “exceptionally ugly double glazing”, “shiny velveteen” upholstery, and “unsightly wall-to-wall carpeting”. (This is before we get to the scene in which Raine, standing at the top of the staircase in search of breakfast, bellows to staff below, “where’s my fucking egg?”)Interspersed with these delights is a portrait of Diana that is affectionate, sad, and lovely in places. Spencer suffers the pain of the less famous sibling who doesn’t want to give up his own version of their childhood and there’s a stiffness to some passages as Spencer insists it was all less unhappy than the record implies. His portrait of their mother, Frances, feels like a useful corrective to a figure who has been publicly maligned, and who comes across in the book as the parent most responsible for Diana’s gifts: spirited, mildly eccentric, a more interesting character than the plodding males in the Spencer line. (Charles, winningly, allows that this is the case, pointing out that the men in his family have always been outclassed by the women.)And of course there is the devastating account of the coldness and aggression of the then Prince of Wales. Spencer tells us that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtship, during which he commented on her weight, ignored her at parties and told her he didn’t love her, to the extent that, Spencer writes, Diana tried to get out of the engagement. Their father told her it was too late. This all chimes with other accounts of the doomed marriage, albeit in gorier detail, and explains the fury of Spencer’s finest hour, the speech he gave at Diana’s funeral in which he lambasted not only the press but the royals, reclaiming the young princes William and Harry for their mother’s “blood family”.At his best, in these passages, Spencer acts as a proxy for the rest of us by registering the absolute lunacy of those days after Diana’s death – by which I mean not the public outpouring, but the behaviour of the royal family, who remained deaf to the nation’s needs until they were forced to change course.“What was Prince Charles actually doing there?” writes Spencer, incredulously, in relation to his former brother-in-law’s prominent role at the funeral, pointing out to some comic effect that no one wants their “ex” at their funeral? Diana’s former husband was there because the young princes were there, walking for two miles behind their mother’s coffin while mourners wailed and shouted out at them, an outcome Spencer had vigorously argued against. Now, he writes flatly, “It all seemed mad to me – the more so as I began to appreciate the extent of the ordeal we had embarked on.”To be honest, at times in this book, they all seem quite mad. “That’s it ... it’s curtains ... Duch is dead,” Spencer reports his sister Jane as saying to him on the phone when news of Diana’s death was confirmed. Before the funeral, per Spencer’s account, Prince Charles wanted to walk behind the coffin in the middle, centre stage, until brought up short by his father, Prince Philip, who said words to the effect of don’t be so bloody silly, and put Charles Spencer in the centre, with the boys either side and Diana’s ex-husband and ex-father in law on the outside. There was a split second, writes Spencer, when it seemed as if the pall-bearers might buckle under the weight of Diana’s reinforced, lead-lined coffin. All of this is fascinating and Spencer tells it well.Still, the book suffers from problems of self pity and self regard (I won’t get into the passages about Spencer’s ADHD or the weasily justifications he gives for telling Diana, in her hour of need, that she couldn’t move into a property on the Althorp estate; the main house has 90 rooms). Every few chapters we return to the unfolding play-by-play of how he wrote his speech – the decision he made to substitute the word “power” for the word “strength”; how his oratory gathered, his greatness formed, and look, it was a fantastic speech, but at some point in the book you start to think, alright Alexander Hamilton, give it a rest. Before the funeral, Spencer visits Diana lying in her casket and reads out his speech to her, sensing that his dead sister is “applauding my words, with soft insistence”. Even here, Spencer manages to take centre stage.After the book’s litany of bitter grievances I came away wondering whether Spencer has been in the ear of his nephew Prince Harry these last few years. Mostly, however, I felt sadness for the insurmountable difficulties his sister faced marrying into that family. The king is peevish all the way through and Spencer is peevish right back at him. You come away feeling the pair thoroughly deserved each other. And in the middle Diana, 30 years dead, frozen in time and – as she ever was – at the mercy of other people’s interpretations.Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer is published by Michael Joseph (£28).
