title: Why you should quit and not look back: ‘Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters’ | Well actually | The Guardian
description: In her new book, The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, Lindsay Crouse discusses the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: In her new book, The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, Lindsay Crouse discusses the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesDeep diveWell actuallyInterviewWhy you should quit and not look back: ‘Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters’Elle HuntIn her new book, The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, Lindsay Crouse discusses the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself freeTue 22 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLindsay Crouse used to define herself as not a quitter.She went to Harvard University, where she learned to become even more high-achieving and ambitious, then landed an assistant job at the New York Times and worked her way up to become an opinion writer and producer. On the weekends, Crouse ran marathons and did endurance sports, clocking new personal bests throughout her thirties.“My entire life was really guided by only one question: how can I go harder, and do more?” she says now over Zoom.Over time, though, that mentality began to backfire. After having two children, Crouse started falling behind, dropping balls and losing her passion for running and writing. Something needed to change.Like Crouse, many of us are conditioned to persevere. In her new book The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, she reckons with the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free.View image in fullscreenLindsay Crouse’s book the Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out.Photograph: HarperCollins PublishersNow Crouse argues quitting is essential for a satisfying, successful life. She herself left her prestigious job to chase unknown risks and rewards. “We need to start viewing quitting as a tool of perseverance, rather than the enemy of it,” she said. “If we find ourselves in a hole, often we dig harder when we should just stop digging.”Our conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.What is the biggest misconception we have about quitting?In the moment, not quitting in some ways feels heroic, like you’re martyring yourself to your own capacity or grit. In fact, you’re actually limiting yourself, because you’re not walking away from things that are failing. In the long run, if we want to do our best, we need to get better at quitting. It could be a pivot or a break, but ultimately I think that can help us do better and go further.Quitting involves entertaining uncertainty and oftentimes risk, but focusing on that means we don’t ask ourselves: are we continuing because we love what we’re doing or because we’re afraid of confronting what might happen if we stop?What do we stand to gain from quitting?This is about priorities: if we commit to everything, we commit to nothing. A lot of this book was me talking to myself: I really thought it was so impressive that I was saying yes to everything, like “Wow, look at all you can do!” Writing it, I realised that attitude was a lot more narrow-minded and even timid than I was willing to admit.Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters. By quitting things that don’t, we can better commit to what’s meaningful and build our lives around that.Sometimes, you hit a roadblock when you’re working towards something. How do we know when to quit, and when to push through?I’m not encouraging people not to engage with struggle or develop resilience. This book is for people who are almost so good at enduring that they don’t realise the costs that come with it. It’s like they’ve confused their ability to persevere with a mandate that they should.I talk about “quitting intelligence”, which is learning to separate temporary setbacks from fundamental futility: how are we thinking about continuing? Are we rationalising it, feeling desperate to salvage something that we’ve already invested in, veering into self-sabotage?With longer-term goals, we can think about progress: are we getting closer to what we want over time, or moving further away? Are we working hard productively, or pointlessly? Those two things help us to assess whether it’s time to quit or invest.If you start working harder or change your approach, and still don’t see the results you want, maybe you’re in the wrong arena and your efforts might be better suited somewhere. If you’re enjoying what you’re doing, that is valuable enough. But if you’re frustrated that it’s not working out, you can just stop and do something else. That sounds obvious, but I think sometimes we tell ourselves we don’t have that choice.Why do we persevere with things that we know, deep down, we would be better off giving up?We’ve learned to ignore very instinctive cues. I realised that I’d done the same, writing about a study done on zebrafish at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. At first, when zebrafish encounter a strong current, they will respond with a surge of effort, but if that doesn’t work, they will give up. This is judged by specialised cells in their brains, which scientists call “futility counters”. Zebrafish know to listen to these cues because it factors into their survival, but humans have learned to override them.A lot of it comes down to the idea of control: where we really want something to happen, we convince ourselves that we have the power to achieve it through hard work, but sometimes we’re denying futility. We equate the idea of being a quitter with being a failure, but often we fail to see that the failure has already happened. We just throw more into it, investing more in a lost cause, and that’s the greatest failure of all.You interviewed dozens of people about their quitting stories. Did any of them change your thinking?I interviewed a woman who was going through devastating rounds of IVF. Having a child was central to what she wanted from life, and she sacrificed an entire decade to that cause, putting all these wonderful things on hold for this goal that simply wasn’t happening. Meanwhile, it was making her miserable.Eventually, she quit IVF and moved on with her life. When I reached out to her a year or two later for fact-checking, she had a baby, having become pregnant naturally at 41 – she didn’t know how. It just confirmed that she never had control in the first place.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLindsay CrousePhotograph: Sophie Sahara CompressedThat made me think about what isn’t working in my life that I might be refusing to acknowledge. A lot of us just push harder, letting the work itself convince us and stand in for the results or success we’re seeking. We can control how hard we work, but we can’t always control the outcome.How can we navigate “hope-selling industries” like IVF and dating apps, while protecting our wellbeing?We need to be mindful, moderate our engagement and create checkpoints for ourselves. The decision scientist Annie Duke calls these “kill criteria”: clear, specific conditions for quitting that we establish before we even start, and before our emotional investment can cloud our judgement.To some extent, these industries are disincentivised from getting us what we want: they want us to keep coming back, to keep swiping and grinding. That’s not to say don’t use them, but perseverance can become a compulsion, even pathological, and these industries don’t help.Of course, the flipside is that a lot of people persevere and do end up with a child or a relationship, but that can also make us feel that we’re failing if we don’t. Sometimes we need to realise what actually can work and focus on that instead.What would you tell someone who talks endlessly about leaving their partner, or quitting their job, but doesn’t act?Staying is a decision, too. I’ve heard people say “I really want to quit, but I can’t.” I think you have to ask yourself: why can’t you? If you think you can’t quit your job because you need money, have you actually run those numbers? Maybe you have, and you don’t like them. That’s fine, but you need to own that choice to stay.If you want to leave your relationship, but are afraid of starting over, own that. Maybe you just want to get married. Down the line, tell yourself that was a decision you made, and you knew what you were getting into. Otherwise, you can quit and do your future self a favour – your partner, too. Who wants to be in a relationship without investment?Being only one foot in is a very passive and kind of cowardly way to live your life. You need to ask yourself: “Am I hoping that this doubt, or deliberation, is just going to abate?” That question helps you reframe the situation – and the answer is no. You have to act: either own it or leave, but don’t think that these problems will just disappear. Maybe you can put up with them, but is that the life you want?Often we dither over these decisions because we fear making the wrong one. In quitting, do we risk future regret?In the long course of our lives, we tend to regret inaction a lot more than action. We’re so focused on tomorrow or next week, but we need to think in the long-term: what is the gift that we can give ourselves in five or ten years’ time? It’s often acting now, so that our future selves don’t have to make this choice.The more that we quit, the better we get at it: we’re less fearful and more able to cope with uncertainty. We have more confidence in ourselves that we’ll make it work. If we don’t develop that muscle, quitting will continue to be understandably scary, and that feeling may keep us stuck in place. Isn’t life all about growth?What if we’re not in a position to make a big change?Thinking about what you really want to do and how you want to spend your time can help you move forward more intentionally than just feeling like “I can’t.” For example, if your job isn’t a source of meaning and purpose for you, maybe you can get that somewhere else. Instead of a career change, maybe you need a different work environment.Otherwise, when we want to solve a problem, often we try to add more when the solution is actually to take something away. Instead of quitting a job or ending a relationship, we can overhaul our lives significantly by eliminating clutter.That was the case for me. I had so much digital clutter, calendar clutter, physical clutter, and routines that I’d almost slid into, like going to bed with my phone. Eliminating those smaller things helped me build the muscle for making bigger changes.You quit your job at the New York Times early this year, after 15 years. What part did your book play in that decision?I realised I was living decisions that I made when I was 20, and they weren’t working for me anymore. I wasn’t happy, and I wasn’t doing the kind of work I wanted to be doing. I wanted to follow my own advice and live in the uncertainty for a bit.I didn’t write this book to convince myself to quit my job at the Times, but I would still be working there if I hadn’t, for sure. I’ve always been the kind of person to wade slowly in, rather than cannonball. I strongly believe in building an off-ramp, and this book was that for me. I am the kind of cautious person who never quits anything; I wanted to be bolder and take more risks, and I’m at a point in my life where I can.I’m 42 now. I have a chance to take a swing and bet on myself. If I don’t, I know that’s what I’ll regret when I’m looking back at 60. That made the decision a lot easier.For me, this book is not about quitting your job or getting a divorce; it’s about questioning the tendency to convince yourself that you can’t or shouldn’t. I felt that was essential for myself, independent of my employment status. It was this idea that Icanstop – and so, sometimes, perhaps, I should.The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Outby Lindsay Crouse is out nowExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyDeep diveHealth & wellbeingHealth, mind and body booksinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump praises relations with Burnham despite tensions over AI and Iran | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York
Content: Andy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump praises relations with Burnham despite tensions over AI and IranUS president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New YorkPippa Crerarin New York andKiran Staceyin LondonTue 22 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” withAndy Burnhamthan under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos islands and the war in Iran.At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister.Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered overIran.UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead.On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure.Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US.1:29Guardian political editor asks Trump about Iran war economic consequences – videoAsked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”.Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops.In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year.But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology.“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said.“Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.”Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks.In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of theChagos Islandsto Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia.“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said.But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”.However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK.UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial.But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.“I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.”Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade.“Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said.Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamUnited NationsChagos IslandsForeign policyAI (artificial intelligence)IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap grows | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London
Author: Will Parman
Headline: Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London
Content: Food banks say many more people will be forced to rely on charity unless local housing allowance is more closely linked to rents.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenFood banks say many more people will be forced to rely on charity unless local housing allowance is more closely linked to rents.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverUK cost of living crisisPay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap growsWirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in LondonPatrick ButlerandWill ParmanTue 22 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you prioritise paying the rent, putting food on the table or keeping the house warm in winter? In practice, says Laura Braddock, a single mum from Wirral, Merseyside, you always pay the rent first and improvise the rest. “If I’ve got a roof over our head, then everything else I can muddle through.”The pressing problem for Braddock, 39, is that muddling through is getting harder. The monthly rent for her two-bedroom flat far outstrips the local housing allowance (LHA) she receives – and the gap may widen.She pays her landlord £550 a month, but receives £425 in housing allowance, leaving her to make up a £125 “rent gap” out of her grocery and heating budgets.The former shop worker has a range of tried and tested strategies to cope, and to shield her son as far as possible from cost of living pressures. She may pay half the gas bill. She’ll eat cheap pasta and beans – or skip her own meals altogether.In January, however, these strategies, and the constant juggling with ever tighter budgets, failed. She was forced to go to a food bank for the first time in years to make end meet.It’s hard, she reflects, and the stress can affect her mental health. “When I’m tired or hungry or whatever, that then has an impact on me, the way I parent. I’ve got no energy sometimes … It’s difficult.”View image in fullscreenLetting sign in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month.Photograph: William Barton/AlamyView image in fullscreenLetting signs in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyHundreds of thousands of low-income households are feeling the same pressures, said Trussell, the food bank network. Unless the government links LHA more closely to actual rents, it added, many more will be forced to turn to charity food.The growing gap between LHA rates and local rents means more than half (62%) of private renters receiving housing support have gone without food and heating in the past six months because they could not afford them, Trussell estimated.The gap is expected to reach record levels this autumn. According to the Resolution Foundation thinktank, theaverage difference between rent and LHAfaced by a low-income household renting a two-bedroom home in the private sector is £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 a month in parts of London.Trussell wants the government to relink LHA to the cheapest 30% of local rents. It estimates this would lift 105,000 peopleout of severe hardship by 2028-29, including 40,000 children. TheResolution Foundationestimates this would cost £2bn a year.Campaigners will focus on the LHA gap– the consequence of years of austerity and rising private rents – in the run-up to next month’s budget, arguing it is an effective way to give low-income families “breathing space” from cost of living pressures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeatrice Orchard, the head of policy at Trussell, said: “Nobody should be forced to choose between paying the rent and putting food on the table. But for increasing numbers of UK renters, this is already a bleak reality. Keeping LHA frozen while rents rise is driving people to food banks.”Governments have often been reluctant to match rents and housing support, fearing landlords will simply put up rents, or that tenants will move to plusher rented homes.Braddock, who fears that her landlord is preparing to put up her rent, tightening her budget even further, disagrees: “If the local housing allowance matched the going rate for a two-bedroom or a one-bedroom [place] then people don’t need to move. It’ll just mean they don’t struggle to get through the month, because the rent’s being paid.“I don’t think the government understands … From a parent’s point of view, you’ve got to think about keeping your kids safe and your kids warm. And they wonder why there’s an epidemic of mental health [concerns]”.A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “We’re tackling the impact of rising rents and the housing shortage with our commitment to build 1.5m homes – including the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation.“Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisHousingHousing benefitBenefitsRenting propertyCommunitiesFood banksnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank says | Devolution | The Guardian
description: IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding
Content: Andy Burnham plans to give England’s mayors significantly greater control over funding and public services.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham plans to give England’s mayors significantly greater control over funding and public services.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Pool AFP/APDevolutionEngland’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank saysIPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in fundingJosh HallidayNorth of England editorTue 22 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda being “derailed by one bad decision”, a thinktank has said.Ministers will set out plans next month to give regional leaders control over potentially billions of pounds of additional funding under a “transformational” shift of power outside Whitehall.From 2028, mayors will be able tokeep a share of income taxgenerated in their areas – giving them greater scope to borrow for major infrastructure projects – as well as retain business rates from 2027 and raise further funds through a “tourist tax”.IPPR North, whose researchers have worked closely with Burnham’s government, welcomed the “bold and ambitious” plans as a step towards “reversing decades of damaging over-centralisation that has held the country back”.It called for mayors to be allowed to keep a 5% share of income tax, which would move an extra £3.8bn a year out of Whitehall and roughly double the funding under their control.However, the thinktank said increasingly powerful mayors should be subject to much tougher oversight.In its 30-page report, IPPR North warned: “A bad decision or mismanaged funding from any one authority risks turning public opinion against devolution and undoing progress.”Its proposals include establishing new regional audit offices to scrutinise how money is spent and what it delivers. It is also proposed that each region should be overseen by a senior accounting officer, similar to the model of permanent secretaries running government departments.Larger mayoral authorities, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, should be overseen by beefed-up accountability committees to guard against any “misuse of funds, corruption and elite capture by lobbying interests”, the thinktank said.Burnham, a former Greater Manchester mayor, has placed the transfer of power outside Whitehall at the heart of his government, establishing No 10 North in Manchester to act as the engine room of rapid devolution.Proposals outlined in aCabinet Office paperin July, weeks after Burnham became prime minister, would represent the most dramatic shift of authority to the English regions in modern times.There are concerns, however, about the capacity of newer and smaller combined authorities to take on these expanded powers, which include employment support, local transport, housing, innovation, local energy and cultural investment.View image in fullscreenRegional mayors at Downing Street for a devolution meeting in July 2024.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyWhile some mayoral authorities are well established, others, such as the Reform UK-led bodies in Hull and East Yorkshire and Greater Lincolnshire, were only founded last year. Several other planned mayoral authorities, spanning millions of people along the south coast and in north-westEngland, have not yet been established.Ministers are due to set out a timeline for fiscal devolution to the English regions in a white paper to be published alongside the autumn budget on 28 October.Aditi Sriram, the lead author of the IPPR North report, said Britain was at a “defining moment” in how it is governed and that accountability was essential to the success of devolution.“For too long, mayors have been expected to drive growth with one hand tied behind their backs, reliant on Whitehall for the money and permission to get things done,” she said. “Critics are loud, political trust is faltering, and the public wants to see action, so the devolution agenda cannot afford to fail.”Jim O’Neill, the former Treasury minister who advised Burnham before he became prime minister, said in a foreword to the report that critics would dismiss devolution as an “irrelevance and a probable source of wasted taxpayers’ money”.But he said the best answer to those “cynics” would be to hand mayors of the most populated areas the greatest powers. “This is assuming they have the capacity to cope, the desire to be accountable and, of course, just like Greater Manchester has had, the aspiration to be bold,” he said.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionMayoral electionsTax and spendingAndy BurnhamLabourLocal politicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish community | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom Kippur
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Counter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom Kippur
Content: Police patrol outside the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester as the Jewish community marks Yom Kippur on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice patrol outside the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester as the Jewish community marks Yom Kippur on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesUK security and counter-terrorismPolice believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish communityCounter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom KippurVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentTue 22 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice believe they have stopped an imminent plot to attack Jewish communities in theManchesterarea.The announcement on Tuesday follows the arrest of two men on Sunday at 2.45pm in Manchester and comes during the Jewish holy month.Counter-terrorism investigators were unusually explicit about the alleged attack plot, which was halted after an operation lasting several months. Police believe they have detained the main suspects and any materials they may have been planning to use.Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.”The arrests and official confirmation of a suspected attack plot comes almosta year after an Islamist-incited attack on a Manchester synagogueon Yom Kippur left two people dead, with the attacker shot dead by police.Arrests were made hours before this year’s Yom Kippur started, with police fearing any plot might be “imminent”. The Jewish festival of Sukkot falls on Friday, with other holy days to follow.Evans added: “We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy Day period.“I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.”The two men in their 30s were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act, meaning police suspected they were terrorists. Police will not officially say what the motive was, nor the nationality or ethnicity of those detained.The Guardian understands that a far-right motive is thought to be unlikely. Sources stress the investigation is at an early stage. Islamist extremism is among possible motives under consideration, and given a spate of recent attacks against Jewish targets, investigators are searching for any sign of a state link. Investigators are increasingly finding it difficult to determine motive until much later in an investigation, if at all.The UK’s terrorism threat level is now at its second highest level of severe.The investigation was led by CTP in London and the two men arrested have been taken to a police station in the capital for questioning.Warrants for their further detention have been granted, meaning they can be held until Sunday.The arrests led to searches in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, which police say have now been completed. Examination of electronic devices such as mobile phones is under way.Evans added: “Counter Terrorism Policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.“As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action.“We are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues.“Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.”The Community Security Trust (CST), which works to keep Jewish communities in the UK safe from attack, said: “This is utterly chilling, coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year, and is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time.“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and alert, and to report any suspicious activity to police on 999 and then to CST.”Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismManchesterReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Children as young as 13 being referred to UK hospital suffering from ‘ketamine bladder’ | Drugs | The Guardian
description: County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysis
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysis
Content: Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnalysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty ImagesDrugsChildren as young as 13 being referred to UK hospital suffering from ‘ketamine bladder’County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysisAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 22 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren as young as 13 in the UK have been referred to a specialist clinic for a “devastating” bladder condition linked to sustained use of ketamine.Medics at Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool opened the first ketamine clinic in the UK for young people amid a surge in urology problems linked to addiction of the drug.Now analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Excessive use of ketamine can cause serious health problems as the drug and its breakdown products sit in the bladder for a long time, where they can damage the lining and muscle tissue.Ketamine-induced uropathy – also known as ketamine bladder – is a severe and painful condition caused by the drug damaging the bladder, urinary tubes and kidneys. Symptoms include frequent urination, loss of bladder control and blood in the urine.View image in fullscreenKetamine use can damage the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, say experts.Photograph: Joe Bird/AlamySome of the children affected are using incontinence pads and urinating in buckets next to their bed at night due to bladder problems caused by addiction to ketamine.“The damage caused by ketamine can be devastating,” said Harriet Corbett, a consultant paediatric urologist at Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust.“It can affect the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, and the effects can be irreversible.Young peoplecan experience chronic bladder pain and incontinence and, in the most severe cases, may go on to require major surgery or dialysis.”Doctors were being referred to a rising number of children with bladder symptoms caused by non-prescribed ketamine use, Corbett added.“What this first year of analysis has highlighted is the importance of understanding the young person behind the diagnosis.”Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.“By looking at factors such as age, where they live, their background and their life experiences, we can start to build a much clearer picture of who is being affected and how we can best support them.“This problem is preventable. Understanding more about the young people who are presenting to us is an important step towards preventing further harm,” Corbett said.View image in fullscreenAlder Hey children’s hospital has opened the UK’s first ketamine clinic for young people.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyAnalysis of the clinic’s first 60 patients by researchers at Alder Hey and Lancaster University showed their average age was 14, ranging from 13 to 15.About two-thirds were girls, and roughly the same proportion lived in the most deprived areas, according to the analysis published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood medical journal.Of the 60, 16 had autism or ADHD, or both. One in five had experience of the care system. Almost three-quarters (72%) had experienced emotional trauma during childhood.The agony of ketamine addiction: ‘I felt like I was peeing glass’Read moreProf Rachel Isba, a consultant in paediatric public health medicine at Alder Hey and professor emerita of children and young people’s health at Lancaster University, said: “One of the most important things about this work is that we are trying to understand the wider picture.“Ketamine use does not happen in isolation, and our analysis is helping us explore the different factors that may be associated with young people developing serious health problems.”The clinic at Alder Hey takes a “non-judgmental” approach, Isba said. “We want to give young people a safe space to talk about what is happening in their lives and work with them to develop a plan to stop using ketamine and prevent further damage.”Explore more on these topicsDrugsChildrenHealthYoung peoplePovertyHospitalsAutismnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies
Content: The new test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer for rapid diagnosis.Photograph: andrei_r/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe new test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer for rapid diagnosis.Photograph: andrei_r/Getty Images/iStockphotoWomen's healthUK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopauseTest using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopiesAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 22 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause.The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems.Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer.Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly.The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester UniversityNHSfoundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive.Thousands of women could be spared painful cancer exam by new NHS AI blood testRead moreIn a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests.Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer.The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’sHealth.Researchers said the test was not accurate enough to rule cancer out on its own but could fast-track women at the highest risk for urgent investigation while sparing lower-risk women immediate invasive testing, with repeat sampling or full assessment if symptoms continued.They cautioned that the samples in the study were assessed by highly trained specialist cytologists, so it was not known whether the same accuracy could be reproduced in other settings, and that the test had not been studied in women without symptoms.Researchers said the test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer, to “support rapid diagnosis, provide quick reassurance and reduce the burden of invasive testing for women with postmenopausal bleeding”.‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?Read moreProf Emma Davidson, of the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, said: “Bleeding after the menopause is understandably alarming for women because it can be a sign of cancer, but the vast majority of those investigated will not have the disease.“At the moment, many women face invasive, uncomfortable tests that can be stressful as well as costly for health services before cancer can be ruled out. Our study shows that a simple test using urine and vaginal samples could help identify the women most likely to have cancer while safely reassuring many others much earlier in the diagnostic pathway.“If further studies confirm these findings in routine practice, this approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women every year.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthCancerMenopauseNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prize | Books | The Guardian
description: The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist
Content: Next on your reading pile … the 2026 Booker shortlist.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/Booker prize foundationView image in fullscreenNext on your reading pile … the 2026 Booker shortlist.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/Booker prize foundationBooksPrevious winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prizeThe two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelistBooker judge Mary Beard on this year’s shortlistElla CreamerTue 22 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winnerElizabeth Stroutand prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison.Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November.James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time forThe Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list.Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in aGuardian review.Quick GuideThe Booker prize 2026 shortlistShowThe End of Everythingby M John Harrison (Serpent's Tail)The Disappearersby Marlon James (Hamish Hamilton)Black Bagby Luke Kennard (John Murray)May We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry (Granta)The Things We Never Sayby Elizabeth Strout (Viking)John of Johnby Douglas Stuart (Picador)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US.Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faberin the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.”The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu.Kennard made the list forBlack Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment.Completing the shortlist is Perry, the sole debut novelist, withMay We Feed the King. The book – which won this year’sWaterstones debut prize– is about a modern-day curator tasked with dressing rooms in historic houses, who becomes increasingly obsessed with the life of a medieval king.Four of the shortlisted titles are by men, and three of them – Black Bag, The Disappearers, and John of John – explore masculinity and male sexuality. That the shortlisted authors are predominantly male is “quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”, said Cocker. The masculinity theme may come down to men “having to rethink their role”, he added. Beard said she doesn’t think it’s a “very masculine” shortlist, while Lockwood half-joked that “all these books are gay”.Among the surprises on the shortlist was the absence of American author Emma Cline, whose novel Switzy, which follows a man suffering from dementia travelling to a euthanasia clinic, receivedpositive reviewsacross the board, amidpredictionsthat it could win the overall award. British author Gwendoline Riley also failed to make the cut with her longlisted novel The Palm House.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe judges said the shortlisting meeting lasted approximately three hours. The five other books that didn’t make the shortlist were The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis, Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman, The Renovation by Kenan Orhan, All Them Dogs by Djamel White, and The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams.This year’s prize was open to books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.Last year’s prize was awarded to David Szalay for his novelFlesh. Recent winners include Samantha Harvey forOrbital, Paul Lynch forProphet Song, and Shehan Karunatilaka forThe Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.Explore the shortlist for this year’s Booker prize and, for a limited time, get all six books for only £79 atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksBooker prizeAwards and prizesFictionMarlon JamesElizabeth StroutnewsShareReuse this content

title: From paleo to intermittent fasting: are any diets actually good for us? | Diets and dieting | The Guardian
description: As diet trends proliferate on social media, it can be hard to work out which are backed by science and which should be ignored. From paleo to keto, raw food to intermittent fasting, each attracts a tribe of ardent followers. Now Daniel Lieberman, professor of biological sciences at Harvard University, has written a book to try to cut through the noise. In Fed Up, he uses his background as an evolutionary anthropologist to scrutinise the evidence, turning himself into a guinea pig in the process and trying various diets. In this podcast, he tells Ian Sample which one has remained part of his routine

title: The truth about UK prisons and organised crime: ‘They’re your good lads. Respectful. Keep their noses clean’ | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: In more than two decades in the Prison Service, Pia Sinha gained a reputation as a fixer. Now, as head of the Prison Reform Trust, she’s sounding the alarm about overcrowding and other problems
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: In more than two decades in the Prison Service, Pia Sinha gained a reputation as a fixer. Now, as head of the Prison Reform Trust, she’s sounding the alarm about overcrowding and other problems
Content: ‘You want a peaceful life as a human being, no matter where you are’ ... Pia Sinha.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You want a peaceful life as a human being, no matter where you are’ ... Pia Sinha.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianPrisons and probationThe truth about UK prisons and organised crime: ‘They’re your good lads. Respectful. Keep their noses clean’In more than two decades in the Prison Service, Pia Sinha gained a reputation as a fixer. Now, as head of the Prison Reform Trust, she’s sounding the alarm about overcrowding and other problemsZoe WilliamsTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePia Sinha has led the Prison Reform Trust since 2023. In that time, she has seen a Conservative government finally admit to an overcrowding crisis that had tipped over the edge. (It was in October 2023 that the early release scheme was devised; by May 2024, the Tories had alsolaunched Operation Safeguard, using police cells as temporary housing.) She’s watched a change of government, then a change of prime minister, then Andy Burnham instantly assailed by negative headlines as the consequences of that early release scheme unfolded: prisoners had to actually be released early. “We’re a bit concerned about how [Burnham] has handled it,” she says, in the trust’s scruffy, un-corporate offices in central London, “but that’s in the knowledge that he had a bit of a hospital pass.”To recap on Burnham’s handling: when he came in in July, he paused the scheme for an urgent review; in August he announced a series of exclusions, further crimes for which people couldn’t be released early, including manslaughter and death by dangerous driving. That solved an immediate problem, that the killers of PC Andrew Harper would otherwise have been released, but had the knock-on effect ofreducing the numbers expected to be releasedby about a quarter. The conversation Sinha wants to have is what prison overcrowding looks like, what it does to prisoners and staff – and what it means for society.Now 53, Sinha arrived in the UK from India with her parents, aged 14. “I think that’s part of the reason I can adapt from one prison to another: I had to learn how to survive and cope, you become very good at reading your environment,” she says, smiling at the implication that the teenagers of north Harrow, circa 1987, were not unlike a prison population. She studied psychology and economics, went on to do a masters in counselling psychology, and was running a pub in north London when she got a job at Holloway, the now defunct women’s prison. When she got her first prison governorship 14 years later, of the open prison Thorn Cross, she was very unusual – not just because she was the first Asian female prison governor, but also for her manner, which is sunny, personable, enquiring and receptive.Prison governors – the women as well as the men – often construct a quasi-military persona to indicate that their word is final, and it’s easy to assume that is how it has to be done, since someone’s word has to be. That’s not Sinha’s style at all. But she was unusual from the start, since she came into prison work as a counselling psychologist, to support the prisoners themselves.Traditionally psychologists were forensic: they saw their job as addressing the offending behaviour, with the aim of protecting the public. In 1999, aftera spate of self-harm incidentsand suicides, the service had started to ask: “How do you get these women out of their crises? How do you get them to not be so suicidal?”View image in fullscreen‘I can adapt from one prison to another’ ... Sinha at HMP Wandsworth in 2007.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianShe stayed at Holloway for five years, and it was rewarding work. The forensic and the counselling strands of psychology turned out to be complementary because – who could have foreseen? – it turned out: “You can’t actually do any meaningful work with people unless they are stable.”A lot of people argue that incarceration per se is unjust to women, since they’re often victims of crimes that are worse than anything they’ve committed, and the stress of it on mothers, unable to care for their children and not necessarily trusting whoever is caring for them, is unbearable. But Sinha isn’t someone who thinks that women don’t belong in prison at all. “I don’t want to slip into describing all women as victims, because that’s often not the case. Women are capable of causing serious harm. Being in prison is an opportunity to look at the harm they’ve caused and get the insight that they need. I’ve seen it work. There are many women who will say that prison was the best thing that happened to them.”The problem with prisons is that, whatever improvements are made, they’re still part of society and change with it. Nowhere is this more clearly demonstrated than in the women’s estate, where things really did get a lot better at the turn of this century, only to get a lot worse after austerity.The use of force in the women’s estate has increased dramatically, which seems absolutely extraordinary. And more extraordinary still, as Sinha explains it, this is partly because prisons are often seen as a place of refuge: “Women go through the court process, presenting as really complex, with multiple unmet needs, and they need somewhere they can be safe. Whatever crime they’ve committed, there would need to be somewhere in the community that gives the judiciary some assurance that if they go back home, they won’t be going into more abuse; that their mental health or addictions can be addressed. The default position in many minds is that prison is safer. Prisons have become really good at coping with complexity.”However, she says, “Women end up in prison and then get hugely triggered by the environment, which creates strong urges to self-harm or commit suicide. Staff are completely overwhelmed by the depth of complexity, so force is often used to try to stop women from harming themselves, which feels crazy.”View image in fullscreen‘It made me cry’ ... Liverpool prison.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/Corbis/Getty ImagesWhat about transgender prisoners? There has been much debate over where they should be held, but Sinha is quite reserved on the issue. “It’s a pressing issue only when it goes wrong, and this is just what happens in prisons. Everything trundles along fine, and then something really horrendous happens and then you have to take a policy position. Prisons are fundamentally all shades of grey. But policy has to be black and white.”After Holloway, Sinha went to Wandsworth in 2004, during which time governor Ian Mulholland was trying to turn it around, from one of the most degraded prisons in Britain (a huge population, dilapidated, vermin-infested buildings, a febrile, lawless atmosphere) to one of the country’s success stories (though by 2024, per that point about prisons mirroring society, it was a story of yet more failure, with the high-profileescape of Daniel Khalifetriggering an inspection that revealed conditionsso appallingthat the governor, Katie Price, resigned).After leaving Wandsworth in 2009, Sinha did stints at Wormwood Scrubs, Send and Downview, among others. She arrived at Thorn Cross in Cheshire in 2013, just as the scandal broke that armed robber Michael Wheatley (AKA the Skullcracker) had absconded from a different open prison and immediately raided a building society. “Then there was another high-profile abscond,” she remembers. You can hear her 27 years in the service when she uses the jargon: “abscond” as a noun; “ROTL” for release on temporary licence. “The public didn’t realise, really, that open prisons existed, and that even quite notorious criminals might be ending their sentence in one.” This was where she got her reputation as a fixer, someone who could turn a crisis around, and that’s how she arrived at Liverpool prison.double quotation markA prisoner would  be asked: ‘Do you want a cell with lights or one with windows?’This was 2017, and what was happening at Liverpool was “symptomatic of what was happening in prisons up and down the country,” she says. “It just got hit first.” It was a crumbling Victorian local prison, that was falling apart. “The estate contract had just been privatised, and grossly underfunded. They weren’t getting to any of the repair jobs, so it was literally breaking. The overcrowding wasn’t quite at the scale and magnitude of the crisis now, but every space mattered. And people were being put in cells that were disgusting. Every window broken. No plumbing, no heating, mould. Dickensian. It became a bit of a joke to staff. A prisoner would come in through reception, and officers would say: ‘Do you want a cell with lights or do you want a cell with windows? Do you want a cell that’s got mould or do you want a cell that has electricity?’ As ajoke.”She is still audibly enraged.“It was full of rats and cockroaches. Honestly, it made me cry when I went there. The inspector had written about a prisoner sitting with this vacant look, in a dark room without electricity, with the smell of mould, a broken window – mentally unwell. And the nail in the coffin was that when the inspector asked senior leaders, ‘How are you presiding over this? What do you think of the state of it?’ they said: ‘It’s going quite well.’”The story of how Sinha remade Liverpool prison – getting prisoners involved in the refurbishment, fixing the electricity so that everyone could have a kettle, building partnerships with charities, universities, businesses, everyone she could find outside the jail – is a painstaking one, but it all started because the crisis was so bad that the head of the Prison Service, Michael Spurr, let Sinha cut capacity. Not every problem in a prison is down to overcrowding, but there’s almost nothing you can fix until you’ve fixed that.Certain activities, such as 45 minutes’ exercise a day, are mandated, but an overcrowded prison is understaffed by definition, so it could take the prison officers the full day just to get everyone into the yard, one wing at a time, which means prisoners spend the other 23 hours locked in a cell. It wrecks morale, Sinha says, because “whether you go in as a prison officer or a psychologist, if you’re public spirited, you want to do a good job. But if really all you’re doing is banging people up, you start thinking: ‘I don’t want this job. This is shit.’”View image in fullscreen‘The public didn’t realise that open prisons existed and notorious criminals might be ending their sentence in one’ … Michael Wheatley arrives at court in 2014.Photograph: PA Video/PAWhen the right people leave the service and the wrong people stay, you get a lot of corruption. The range and scale ofcrimes committed by staff last yearwas staggering: one prison governor was convicted of having a relationship with an inmate; one prison health worker smuggled in drugs with a value of £1m to a single jail. You also get areas and corridors where prison officers won’t go. In Liverpool, Sinha asked an academic to see if there were any no-go areas, and she said: “Not yet, but there’s a risk, especially on the fives.” She meant the fifth floor of each wing, the reason being that overstretched officers don’t have time to go up five flights of stairs. “Nobody wants that. Prisoners don’t want their jails to be like that. In the end, you want a peaceful life as a human being, no matter where you are.“The real underbelly of it,” Sinha continues, “is that if you lose control of the prison it falls into the hands of really sophisticated organised criminals, running quite successful, profitable businesses.” Phones and drugs are dropped in by drone; there’s a large captive market of bored, impulsive people (some of these conditions are modern, some timeless). And the prisoners running these empires? “They’re your good lads. They’re respectful. They keep their noses clean. They’re not really in trouble, and they are in plain sight. I don’t want to mince my words. This situation is very dangerous. When prisoners are controlling the prison as opposed to the staff, who protects the vast majority of prisoners? There are vulnerable prisoners whose only source of security is another prisoner. Staff are scared as well. I’m not saying this is everywhere, but it is a lot of places.”Regularly, now, HMIP (his majesty’s inspectorate of prisons) warns ofserious failings, “and HMIP is good – it’s independent,” Sinha says. But it can’t magic away the reality, “which is that standards are irrelevant if there are too many prisoners and not enough staff. The whole legitimacy of the inspectorate pivots on their standards being attainable.”In this era, “the noise in the political system is all that prisoners need to be punished. When you’re saying, ‘Prisons should be decent’, you’re screaming into the void,” Sinha says. But she can’t stop making the case for reform, because the situation as it stands is absurd. It’s not just that overcrowded prisons can’t rehabilitate prisoners. It’s not even solely a humanitarian case, that conditions in many prisons aren’t defensible. It’s simply a fact that some prisons are in such chaos that they’ve become temples and academies of further crime. “So what’s the outcome for future victims?” Sinha asks. “You might be able to satisfy current victims with harsh policies, but what happens to the victims of the future?”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
