title: Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle  | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him
Content: Gianni Infantino has reasserted his intention to stand for re-election as Fifa president.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Getty Images for Fanatics; BSR Agency/Getty Images; Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has reasserted his intention to stand for re-election as Fifa president.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Getty Images for Fanatics; BSR Agency/Getty Images; Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesSoccerWill anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacleFifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge himMatt HughesTue 22 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForGianni Infantinothere is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year.Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifaabandoned its World Cup sell-off planlast month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body.Infantino proposes an ‘independent external review’ of Fifa governanceRead moreFrom his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence.Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimateFifapresidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March. That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him.Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him.A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight.“As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team.“If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.”Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter.The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’sWorld Cupin Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team.As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared.The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino.View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani (right), president of Concacaf, is reluctant to walk away from his current role but would be the most credible challenger to Infantino.Photograph: Elizabeth Ruiz Ruiz/Getty ImagesThe AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on.To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE.Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing.Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate.“While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.”Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward.An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome.“The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.”Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues.Thrive subsequentlybought 20% of the LA Lakerslast month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda.A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there.“All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.”Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino before the World Cup final.Photograph: Pablo Morano/BSR Agency/Getty Images“I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.”There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal.Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal.Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino.“It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.”Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition,revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additionalpayment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associationsduring the next four-year cycle.Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it.Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since.Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership.Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation.For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said.“The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”Explore more on these topicsFootballGianni InfantinoFifaWorld CupFootball politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How I Shop with Tom Daley: ‘I am obsessed with my knitting machine!’ | Tom Daley | The Guardian
description: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The retired diver talks scrapbooking, cheap chargers, and trouser fails with the Filter
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The retired diver talks scrapbooking, cheap chargers, and trouser fails with the Filter
Content: Composite: Jordan Carter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Jordan Carter/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterTom DaleyInterviewHow I Shop with Tom Daley: ‘I am obsessed with my knitting machine!’As told toLily SmithAlways wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food, and the basic they scrimp on? The retired diver talks scrapbooking, cheap chargers, and trouser fails with the FilterHow I Shop with Laura JacksonTue 22 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Daley OBE is a retired professional diver who has won five Olympic medals, including gold at Tokyo 2020. Since retiring from competitivediving, he has hosted Channel 4’s Game of Wool: Britain’s Best Knitter, while continuing to share his passion for knitting and crafts through hisMade With Lovebrand andYouTube channel. He is married to US screenwriter Dustin Lance Black, and the pair have two children.What’s the last treat you bought for yourself?Small treat: vanilla and chocolate soft-serve ice-cream swirl; slightly larger treat: a little getaway we just booked for Halloween with the kids and some friends.Where do you buy your food?In LA, Trader Joe’s or Ralphs, but in London, it tends to be M&S.View image in fullscreenStateside staples: Trader Joe’s is a go-to for groceries in LA.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/GettyShop Trader Joe’s at AmazonWhat’s the best present you’ve given?I always make a scrapbook of our year for my husband at Christmas, so we now have 14 scrapbooks of tickets, photos, room keys, memories and things to show the kids when they grow up.… and the best present you’ve received?Some ChiaoGoo interchangeable needles.View image in fullscreenChiaoGoo twist lace interchangeable knitting needlesFrom £119.99 at WoolstackFrom £95.38 at AmazonWhat’s your favourite online store?The Selfridges gift section has saved me many times as they always have great ideas!Shop SelfridgesWhat’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?I love craft stores, the colour and creativity of it all. But there is a shop called Trove 167 (previously Bermondsey 167) in London where I would always buy my gifts from.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tessa Barnes Photography/Trove 167Shop Trove 167What’s the gadget you use most often?I am obsessed with my LK150 knitting machine at the moment. I have made a couple of jumpers using it, and it makes things so much faster, but I am not as good at machine knitting as I am at hand knitting. I also probably use my portable phone charger a lot.View image in fullscreenSilver Reed LK150 knitting machine£430 at Hobbycraft£430 at WoolBoxWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?I don’t tend to regret many things, but I will say it is always the cheap chargers that end up breaking first.View image in fullscreenFrayed nerves: Tom Daley says cheap chargers are always regrettable.Photograph: Catherine McQueen/GettyWhat’s the thing(s) you get delivered?There is something about buying loo roll in person … I just think it should always be delivered, lol, from somewhere like Ralphs (the US version of Tesco) or Amazon.Where do you buy your underwear?I usually ask for underwear as a Christmas and birthday gift, so I have a very random collection.What would you buy with £20 – and £200?For £20, a reusable water bottle; for £200, a nice massage or spa day.View image in fullscreenTom would soak it all in at a relaxing spa day.Photograph: Aire Images/Getty ImagesWhat’s your ‘saved search’ on eBay/Vinted?I often use it as inspiration for things I want to make. I like to think of online shopping now as one big knitting and crochet moodboard.What item do you buy on repeat?Yarn! I have an unhealthy obsession with going to yarn shops and feeling it, buying it, and imagining what I could make with it.View image in fullscreenHooked on yarn: half the fun is imagining what to make next.Photograph: Kostikova/GettyShop yarn at WoolBoxHow do you make your coffee at home?I’m a black coffee guy. I make an americano using my concrete AnZa coffee machine.View image in fullscreenBreeze-y (block) does it for black coffee at homeWhat’s your biggest splurge?I tend to splurge on experiences. I like doing things with friends and family, such as going to theme parks or new places.And what everyday item do you scrimp on?I don’t spend money on plain T-shirts, especially white ones, because the kids get them mucky so quickly.And what’s your greatest vintage find?When I was in Calgary, I was obsessed with some vintage shops near me, where the prices of items would go down week by week: it was always a gamble whether something would still be there the next week. I found an amazing cropped floral jacket that I wore to death, including to an after party at the Met Gala in 2021, where I ripped my trousers.For more, read How I Shop withFred SirieixandLaura JacksonView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterExplore more on these topicsTom DaleyThe FilterKnittingCelebrityCraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The great iced coffee debate: is it wrong to take a beverage into a job interview? | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: It might seem a perfectly natural thing to do. But, on TikTok, a recruiter has expressed her dismay at gen Zs showing up with a takeout drink – and it’s caused a ruckus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It might seem a perfectly natural thing to do. But, on TikTok, a recruiter has expressed her dismay at gen Zs showing up with a takeout drink – and it’s caused a ruckus
Content: Time and place …Photograph: Dimitar Gorgev/AlamyView image in fullscreenTime and place …Photograph: Dimitar Gorgev/AlamyPass notesSocial etiquetteThe great iced coffee debate: is it wrong to take a beverage into a job interview?It might seem a perfectly natural thing to do. But, on TikTok, a recruiter has expressed her dismay at gen Zs showing up with a takeout drink – and it’s caused a ruckusTue 22 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Iced coffee.Age:Colonial troops in Algeria invented a sweetened cold coffee beverage known as Mazagran in around about 1840. However, in Japan, a cold brew was popular among sailors even earlier, in the 17th century.Fascinating.Isn’t it? But actually this is less about the age of the drink, more about the age of the drinkers. Plus, when it is and isn’t appropriate to drink it.Go on.It started witha TikTok…Obviously!From @caitlinrecruiter.Who I’m guessing has something to do with recruitment?Correct: 16 years’ experience, mostly with Fortune 500 corporations.Impressive.Where does iced coffee come in?With a candidate at a job interview. This is what Caitlin has noted among some of her gen Z job-hunters. She’s not a fan.Is it the ice that’s the problem?No, iced coffee is just popular with that generation. The issue is around bringing a beverage to an interview and the casual impression it gives. “It just looks like you didn’t have time to finish your coffee beforehand,” says Caitlin.Maybe you didn’t.Well, maybe you should have made time! Time management is important. WhenLinkedIn surveyed more than 1,000 managersabout interview no-nos, showing up late came out top.What else?Using foul language.You can shove your effing job up your …Yes! Also, dressing inappropriately, looking at your phone, appearing disinterested or disengaged, not asking questions about the job or company.So act like you care?Yes. Back to Caitlin’s TikTok, she says bringing a coffee to an interview makes it look like “a stop on your list of errands for the day. It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks, now you’re stopping by your interview, then you’re onto the next thing.”I’m guessing it went viral?371k at time of writing. She’s calling it the great iced coffee debate.Comments on both sides of the argument?And across a generational divide. For example: “Professional millennial here. I would never show up with a drink in my hand.” And: “This comment section proves that generation has lost the art of professionalism.”And some examples from the other (possibly younger) side?“But an interview IS just a stop on my day. It’s not my whole day.” (13k likes) And: “Do you guys need employees or not.” (19.7k likes).Do say:“Yes, I’d like to know what success would look like in the position.”Don’t say:“Can we wrap this up, I’ve got things to do. Am I hired or what?”Explore more on these topicsSocial etiquettePass notesYoung peopleWork & careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The viral Hyrox horror: is the ‘go hard or go home’ attitude to exercise finally over? | Fitness | The Guardian
description: When an athlete soiled herself at a hybrid fitness event, it sparked a debate about a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real cost
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: When an athlete soiled herself at a hybrid fitness event, it sparked a debate about a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real cost
Content: Viral moment … Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenViral moment … Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesFitnessThe viral Hyrox horror: is the ‘go hard or go home’ attitude to exercise finally over?When an athlete soiled herself at a hybrid fitness event, it sparked a debate about a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real costLeah HarperTue 22 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow far would you go to secure an impressive marathon time, or a Hyrox personal best? Maybe you’d turn down a boozy night out in favour of eight hours’ kip the night before? Or perhaps you’d swap sugary treats for protein shakes, and commit to a gruelling training plan in the run-up? It’s not uncommon for athletes to want to give it their all come race day – but few of us would go as far as the Australian Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk, who continued to take part in the hybrid fitness event a little over a week ago, despite having noticeably soiled herself.Wietrzyk’s immediate response appeared to be one of defiance. “Go hard or go home … a win is a win,”she said in a now-deleted Instagram post, having been allowed to finish and win the event in Beijing. Hyrox organisers initially seemed to back her position,posting a statement(also now deleted) which said: “We ask our athletes to push themselves to the highest levels. At times, they will go beyond what even we thought was possible.”But as images of faecal matter dripping down Wietrzyk’s legs – while she continued to use communal equipment – circulated online, few appeared to admire her commitment. Rather, some raised concerns that her bowel incontinence posed a health risk to other competitors.Both parties quickly pivotedto apologies, with Wietrzyk admitting that she should have “stepped off the track” and that there was “more to life than racing”. Hyrox co-founderMoritz Fürste statedthat “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race”, before going on to confirm that, “there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again”.View image in fullscreenTo the limit … Joanna Wietrzyk in action in the Hyrox event in Beijing.Photograph: Fred Lee/Getty ImagesBut could the viral moment mark a turning point in what is considered aspirational or acceptable when it comes to fitness goals? Hybrid training, which combines cardio with strength exercises, has beengrowing in popularity over recent years, alongside associated competitions such as Hyrox,ATHXand the CrossFit Games. But among the fitness community, attitudes towards the benefits of an unrelentingly competitive mindset may be starting to shift.“Recently I have noticed individuals showing more consideration for their wellbeing,” explainsHarvey Smith, a sport and exercise psychologistwhose work focuses on supporting athletes with the psychological demands of performance, training and competition. A number of his clients take part in endurance and hybrid events such as Hyrox, as well as other sports. “There is a growing awareness that chasing extreme performance markers does not always align with long-term physical or mental health, and more people are actively reflecting on that trade-off rather than assuming harder is always better,” he says.Even so, he acknowledges that competitive culture can be slow to change, and extreme effort is still often celebrated, “so I would say we are in a transition rather than a complete shift”. He believes the incident in Beijing has opened up an important conversation about where the line sits between admirable resilience and a culture that pushes people to ignore their body’s signals at real cost.“I think it should be obvious that doing Hyrox is not about health, it’s about competition,” saysDaniel Lieberman, a paleoanthropologist at Harvard University and author of books includingExercised: Why Something We Never Evolved to Do is Healthy and Rewarding. “While we have capacities to do extreme things, we never evolved to stand on one line and run as fast as possible to another line 26.2 miles away, or – even more bizarrely – to eight times over run a kilometre and then push sleds, carry weights, do burpees, and so on” – as athletes do as part of Hyrox competitions.double quotation markIt’s important for people to challenge themselves ... but extreme competition can also be toxicMatteo Massaini, fitness coach“We now have hundreds of studies which show that you don’t need a lot of physical activity to promote health,” Lieberman adds. “More can bring greater benefits but only up to a point, at which the benefits tail off and possibly reverse.” It is easy to see why even the most devoted gym-goer might question the merits of pushing themselves to the limit – especially if in doing so they have been plagued by injury.For the sport and performance coachMatteo Massaini, there’s no one size fits all approach. “I think it’s really important for people to challenge themselves and strive to be better – and I think Hyrox has actually really helped with that,” he says. “But extreme competition can also be toxic.”Massaini has taken part in Hyrox himself, as well as numerous running competitions, and stresses the importance of not prioritising personal achievements over the wellbeing of others – although he can see how it’s easy to get tunnel vision on race day. “The beautiful thing about humanity is that we’re all very different: not everyone needs to have the attitude of ‘go hard or go home’,” he says. “Some people have different goals.”There’s a long history of athletes pooing themselves mid-race – why, and how can you avoid it?Read moreLikewise, Chloe White, co-owner of small group personal training facilityRaw Inc Training, agrees that competitive events can provide “a positive, performance-based goal and shift the focus away from appearance towards what the body can achieve”. She has competed in Hyrox, ATHX,Turf GamesandButterfly Effectevents, and has found there is now a “greater awareness of recovery, injury management and longevity, although a ‘more is better’ culture still exists within parts of the industry”.Is it possible to achieve your fitness dreams without getting caught up in a competitive culture? Smith says that grounding your determination “in process, self-compassion, and realistic support structures” is the key to success – rather than simply fixating on a win or a PB. Meanwhile, he’s seen more coaches, event organisers, and athletes talking openly about sustainable performance and the risks of overtraining. “A more useful question for people to sit with is often: ‘How do you stay determined without the result controlling your sense of self-worth?’”Explore more on these topicsFitnessHealth & wellbeingRunningTraining programmesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We didn’t set out to make a show for animals!’ The Netflix seal cartoon that’s a huge hit … with pets | Television | The Guardian
description: Videos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdict
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Videos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdict
Content: Seal of approval? Ozzy gets up close to watch the Netflix show Sealook.Photograph: Courtesy Rich PelleyView image in fullscreenSeal of approval? Ozzy gets up close to watch the Netflix show Sealook.Photograph: Courtesy Rich PelleyTelevision‘We didn’t set out to make a show for animals!’ The Netflix seal cartoon that’s a huge hit … with petsVideos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdictRich PelleyTue 22 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOzzy the four-month-old goldendoodle isn’t normally allowed on the sofa. But today he has been granted special privileges because I’ve come round specifically to watch TV with him. We’re not watching Paw Patrol, Scooby-Doo, or even Crufts. We’re watching Sealook, the Netflix kids’ cartoon about a colony of seals that dogs and cats online are supposedly obsessed with. But is this really a thing? And will Ozzy care?I hit play. A gang of wide-eyed pastel-coloured seals are in a slapstick scrape. There’s no dialogue: they mostly lie around on the ice, and try to annoy each other by doing silly things like making funny noises, throwing snowballs or keeping each other awake. Ozzy seems more interested in chewing his pizzle stick – which I discover, slightly too late, is the dried penis of a bull. Then again, perhaps this is just canine second-screening: Sealook on the telly, bull penis in the mouth.View image in fullscreen‘They mostly lie around on the ice’ … Sealook, NetflixPhotograph: NetflixOzzy may be playing hard to impress, but he’s in the minority. Search #sealook and there are loads of dogs pawing at the TV and cats batting at the characters. “They do watch television, but not this intently,” says Jessica Blumen from Oregon, who has had nearly 10m views for an Instagram video of her two goldendoodles’ reaction. Benny, nearly one, and five-month-old Myrtle, certainly seem to be converts, judging by their reaction to watching a group of animated seals banging on the ice. “The minute the seals started drumming, Benny sat up and Myrtle had these subtle head tilts.”It’s even become a sort of doggy mindfulness regime. “Last night Benny was getting a little wild – goldendoodles get zoomies at night – so I turned it on and he immediately settled. Even when an episode ends and flashes up a yellow bar saying ‘fin’, that still keeps his attention.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueŠvepsė, a one-and-a-half-year-old rescue cat in Lithuania, is already a TV fan, enjoying animal documentaries and having previously been fascinated by a Lithuanian strongman competition. But Sealookproduced an even stronger reaction. “She became very focused on the screen and tried to catch the characters with her paws. Sometimes, she simply sat there watching very carefully without taking her eyes off the screen,” says owner Erika. “We’re used to her watching animal documentaries, but seeing her try to catch the characters in Sealook was something we hadn’t seen before.”Rio, a six-month-old golden retriever owned by Melly Roman in Houston, Texas, is another fan. “We have the TV on for background noise and he never normally watches,” she says. “But he started barking when one of the seals came really close to the screen. We tried again later and he sat and watched a couple of episodes.” The clip helped take Rio’s Instagram following from about 115 to nearly 4,000.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThis, I tell Ozzy, is exactly the sort of behaviour that could help boost his own Instagram following of 137. Watching television is a far better party trick than barking at his own reflection or stealing hair scrunchies from his human mum. I’d offer to become his social media manager, but I don’t have any interest in freebies from Bonio.Still, before I write off Ozzy as a hopeless influencer, what are cats and dogs seeing when they watch Sealook? One possible reason is the colour palette: it’s all white snow, pale-blue ice and brightly coloured seals. Cats and dogs see blues and yellows particularly well, which perhaps makes Sealook about as easy to ignore as a bowl of Whiskas or Pedigree Chum.Dr David Williams, an associate lecturer in veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Cambridge, thinks movement may be just as important as colour. “Cats and dogs are particularly interested in movement because they’re interested in chasing a mouse or another prey item,” he says. “They’re also crepuscular – most active around dawn and dusk – so movement in low light matters particularly to them.”Sound may matter too. Dr Emily Blackwell, a companion animal behaviour expert at Bristol Veterinary School, says the seals’ “high-pitched squeaking noises may mimic the sounds of prey species – rodents – and also sound very similar to the squeaky toys that many of our pets have”.View image in fullscreenRich Pelley and Ozzy settle down to watch Sealook.Photograph: courtesy Rich PelleyDr Freya Mowat, an associate professor of veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how dogs watch television, says dogs seem particularly drawn to animal-like movement. “My own research has shown that dogs prefer watching dogs to humans,” she says. “Seals? I don’t know, but they are closer to dogs than people! Cartoons are great content for dogs: high contrast, lots of movement, nice fun music – it’s the whole package.”Was any of this deliberate? Apparently not, says Leah Yeon, communications lead at The Pinkfong Company, the South Korean co-producer of Sealook. “Seeing cats and now dogs as well becoming so absorbed in Sealook has been a fun and unexpected surprise.”The show’s simple snowy landscapes, vivid colours and short, repetitive movements were designed for audiences of children, although the team suspects the same ingredients may help explain its appeal to pets. The trend began with cats, then dogs jumped on the bandwagon. “We didn’t set out to make a show for animals,” says Yeon, “but it continues to be fascinating – and very amusing – to see it connect with this new audience.”Which leaves one final experiment. Williams suggested turning the sound off to see whether Ozzy’s interest changes. Right then, Ozzy. Volume down.Nothing. I turn the sound back on and, finally, Ozzy looks up. A seal slides across the ice; his ears prick up. Another squeaks and he edges towards the screen. At last! I grab my phone, visions of 4,000 followers dancing before me. But seconds later, Ozzy wanders off in search of a hair scrunchie or bull penis. Sealook, it seems, has yet to earn his seal of approval. Doggy stardom will have to wait.Sealook is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAnimation on TVfeaturesShareReuse this content
