title: A tale of two trap houses: being cuckooed ruined my friend’s life – but did it then help save him? | Drugs | The Guardian
description: The long read: Drug gangs have moved off Britain’s streets and into vulnerable people’s homes. Addicts like my friend are easy targets, but the reality can be more complicated than it seems
Author: Max Daly
Headline: The long read: Drug gangs have moved off Britain’s streets and into vulnerable people’s homes. Addicts like my friend are easy targets, but the reality can be more complicated than it seems
Content: Cuckooing Night Scene FinalIllustration: Callum Rowland/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCuckooing Night Scene FinalIllustration: Callum Rowland/The GuardianThe long readDrugsA tale of two trap houses: being cuckooed ruined my friend’s life – but did it then help save him?Drug gangs have moved off Britain’s streets and into vulnerable people’s homes. Addicts like my friend are easy targets, but the reality can be more complicated than it seemsMax DalyTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.11 EDTShareDuncan is a good friend of mine. He looks like a Dickensian rock’n’roller: tall and skinny, long hair, retro clothes. He’s read the Flashman novels three times. We met in secondary school in westLondonin the early 1980s. We got drunk, smoked Rothmans and banana skin spliffs and played Dungeons & Dragons. At 14, we got into punk together and spent our teens playing music and seeing live bands. As we moved into our 20s, I trained as a journalist and Duncan, a talented songwriter and guitarist, carried on with music.At the age of 23 he got involved in heroin. He found the lifestyle immediately seductive, his partner at the time, Lucy, told me. He would often befriend his dealers. “I remember more than once waiting in his car as he’d gone up some tower block to score, thinking where on earth is he?” Lucy said. “He’d be hanging out chatting. There were some genuinely fascinating characters with incredible stories to tell.”We kept in touch. By the 2000s, after a few near fatal overdoses, it became obvious he had a long-term drug problem. But at the end of the decade, when Duncan was in his late 30s, his life changed when his then-partner gave birth to a boy. He was a natural father, becoming a full-time dad when his partner returned to work after maternity leave. Love and dedication to his son reduced Duncan’s drug use, but did not entirely dislodge it.In 2013, he swapped the west London council flat he had been subletting for a nicer, ground floor studio apartment in a council estate in north-east London, near where his partner and young son now lived. By this time, Duncan was what drug experts call a “functioning” heroin user, managing his addiction with methadone while living a relatively stable life. He was working as a painter and decorator, played in a band that toured the US, and remained a dedicated dad. He got a job as a teaching assistant, helping some of the most troubled kids in the borough, which he loved.His friends regularly spent time at his flat, which he had turned into his own, homely space. He had repainted his bedroom-lounge, and filled it with his collection of trinkets, retro furniture, artwork, vinyl records and a huge plant. His mother visited, his son regularly stayed the night and I crashed on the couch a few times.By 2015, even while house prices were rocketing in trendy areas a few streets away, Duncan’s estate became neglected and scary at night. Families moved out and were replaced by single tenants leaving prison and care. Eventually, the estate was officially condemned by the council, which planned to decant tenants into a new estate being built a mile away. Duncan had watched as a group of noisy local kids had grown up into a gang of aggressive teenage drug dealers. They were made up of about a dozen boys and young men from the estate and the surrounding area, most aged around 15 to 17, and some as young as 12.Coming home in the evening, Duncan would find the gang, dressed in black joggers and puffer jackets, hanging around the stairwell selling crack and heroin. “Sometimes, something, or somebody, would get thrown against my window,” said Duncan. “A couple of times I heard someone who got a really bad kicking from them, whimpering outside and I phoned an ambulance. They were horrible cunts.”Within a year, Duncan’s home would be doubling up as the gang’s drug dealing base.Over the past 30 years, the British “trap house”, slang for a place used as a drug dealing base, has evolved. Rather than derelict crack houses, drug gangs now prefer to operate from a hidden countrywide network of vulnerable people’s homes that they have taken over in a process known as “cuckooing”.The origins of this shift go back to the 1990s, when a new wave of professionalised drug dealing crews spread out across the country. Their growth was fuelled by two products that were transforming Britain’s drug trade: crack and mobile phones. Blackberries and Nokias had enabled buyers and sellers to arrange transactions in less visible locations, and dealers now started to expand their operations, using a system of young runners who would call in orders and deliver the drugs.In Brighton, a gang called the Londoners moved their drug sales teams off the streets and into the homes of local people, where they could more easily operate away from the prying eyes of police and rival gangs. When 10 of the Londoners were jailed in 2000, along with a man whose home they had taken over, a fresh gang from south London arrived to fill the gap. “I was buying crack and heroin from 15- and 16-year-old south London boys on BMXs in 2001,” Pete, a former Brighton street drug user told me in 2018. “I thought, fuck, you’re young. They would come down on the train and set up flats with heroin users.”Over the 2000s and 2010s, wave after wave of gangs fanned out from Britain’s drug supply hubs – London, Liverpool and Birmingham – to set up shop in smaller towns and cities across the country. They took over the homes of drug users and young women who had been groomed by older male gang members. As early as 2008 Suffolk constabulary reported that more than a third of Class A drug dealers arrested in Suffolk were under 21, and the majority were from London. (Before this period, most crack and heroin dealers in towns and smaller cities were “user-dealers”, addicted heroin users in their 30s or older, who were not as “professionalised” as the big city drug gangs.) Gangs often used sex workers, who targeted male tenants and moved in, bringing the young dealers with them. Community safety teams,who rescued 80 tenants in London in 2005, were the first to call the tactic “cuckooing”.In 2015, the NationalCrimeAgency published an intelligence assessment that belatedly acknowledged “cuckooing” was part of “an emerging criminal business model”, whereby young people were being sent by drug gangs to sell out of town, which they dubbed “county lines”. By 2018, children who were described as “missing” in their local papers could now sometimes be found on Snapchat waving wads of notes, boasting to their classmates about their out-of-town moneymaking adventures “going country”. Rap lyrics, particularly drill music – where victims of cuckooing were denigrated as “fiends”, “cats” or “nitties” – soundtracked and glamourised the rise of the British trap house.The reality was far more bleak: children hanging out in dingy flats with ageing drug injectors, earning far less than they had hoped and living in daily fear of being jumped by police, or worse, rival gangs. The whole system was reliant on grooming and exploitation. Over the years, reporting on Britain’s drug trade, I’ve spoken to several young drug dealers and cuckooed tenants about what it was like for them. One boy from Liverpool sold drugs from cuckooed homes in Devon, staying in a middle-aged crack user’s flat when he was 14. There was mould, “a plant growing out the wall” and the place was so dirty he ended up cleaning it himself. He smoked weed “to take the smell of crack away”. Another teenager from London, from a strict religious Nigerian family, worked 15-hour days from cuckooed flats in the east of England for three years. He told his parents he was on football trips or staying with friends; in reality he was holed up with drug users and armed with a machete.A former sex worker and crack user I spoke to, whose home in Southend was cuckooed, actually felt sorry for the young dealers camped out in her flat. “They used to lie on my settee and sleep with the phone by their head, working 22 hours a day. They were putting on an act, trying to pretend they were the big boys, but they were young kids getting exploited.”Cuckooing can involve sexual and financial grooming, the targeting of disabled and mentally ill people, people in private rented properties in affluent neighbourhoods, and even relatives and carers of gang members. In one case, said Insp Andrew Cameron of Operation Pantera, which was aimed at tackling the problem in London, a nephew cuckooed his aunt’s house for a south London drug gang. In another, a care worker cuckooed the home of a patient, who was tortured with cigarette burns and beaten by drug dealers. One particularly grim case involved William Algar, a 53-year-old jazz trumpeter from Barnes, south-west London, who had mental health and drug problems. In 2019, his home was cuckooed by a gang of drug dealers. He fell out with one of them over money, and the dealer threatened to kill his cat. After Algar’s sister reported him missing, police found his severed head and torso in the flat, and the rest of his body in a park. He had been stabbed to death with a zombie knife and dismembered in his own bath.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Callum Rowland/The GuardianJack Spicer, a lecturer in criminology at the University of Bath and author of Cuckoo Land, has interviewed many victims of cuckooing. What makes the practice so insidious, he says, is that for many victims there is nowhere to run. Yet Spicer also notes that in some cases, cuckooing can be a more complex scenario than is commonly understood: “From the perspective of an outsider looking in, cuckooing can take on a seductively simplistic appearance: the ‘evil’ drug dealer duping the vulnerable user of drugs, the naive local resident opening their door to the dangerous outsider. At best these tell only a partial story.”That helps explain why Duncan, a musician, artist and father, ended up opening his doors to drug gangs – not once but twice – and why his two experiences turned out to be so different. The first brought him only misery; the second, in his telling at least, brought him a strange kind of friendship.Life started unravelling for Duncan in 2016. His girlfriend left him and his close friend, the band’s singer, died of cancer. He was fired from his teaching job after his drug treatment service informed the school that he was in rehab. Losing his job made him particularly bitter. His drug use increased. He stopped returning his friends’ calls and saw less of his son.Before, he had no reason to interact with the estate’s teenage gang. He bought his drugs – methadone, with a bit of heroin and crack on the side as a treat – from a trusted seller back west. But in January 2017, during a cold snap, Duncan offered shelter in his flat to two heroin users who had been sleeping rough in a tent in a nearby snow-covered graveyard. Patrick, a beggar from Bristol, took the kitchen floor and Josef, an unemployed Polish stonemason, took the living room sofa. “The estate was feeling more and more threatening during that time,” said Duncan. “I felt safer with those two around.” But his two lodgers bought drugs from the gang on Duncan’s estate, and he became a regular buyer, too.Around this time, Chloe, a school teacher and friend of Duncan’s, began to worry about him. The two of them had been in a relationship for a period, and after they split, they remained friends. To her, he was “the loveliest person in the world – caring, kind and creative”. When they were together, she never saw him taking heroin, but she knew he did. So when he stopped returning her calls, she went round to check on him. The door was answered by a man she recognised as Patrick, the train station beggar, who nervously told her Duncan was out. When she later saw Duncan in the street, he ran off. “I was thinking, what is going on here?” she recalled.One day, in the summer of 2017, one of the boys from the estate gang knocked and asked if his pregnant girlfriend could use Duncan’s toilet. From then on, said Duncan, the gang’s presence in the flat “escalated”. First it was repeated visits to charge phones or use the toilet. Then, as autumn approached and the weather got worse, the gang made Duncan an offer: £30 worth of crack and heroin a day for the use of his flat as a drug dealing base. He found himself agreeing.“They had something to offer,” said Duncan, who had developed a debilitating leg wound from years injecting in his groin. “I’d wrecked my health and couldn’t work much so I needed the freebies. Heroin makes you quite fearless. It makes you feel as though you can cope with anything, but it also imbues a certain amount of recklessness. The strangest situations start to seem normal very quickly.”The gang – a mix of Asian, black and white teenagers – was in and out of his home from about 10.30 in the morning, when one of the senior members would drop off the drugs stash, until late at night. A trio of slightly older gang members, aged about 16 and 17, made him feel particularly uneasy. The younger dealers would all be paid at his flat by a senior gang member in the afternoon. Usually there were only one or two of them there at once, but sometimes his home was packed. They used the flat as a base for dealing crack and heroin, to relax, prepare drugs for sale and to stash their zombie knives.Duncan said some of the younger dealers were respectful, and that “three or four of the little soldiers were alright to chat to”. He would shoot up while the young gang members were in his flat, trying to find a vein in his groin or his leg. “All that stuff frightened those kids and probably disgusted them, so it kept them at a distance,” he told me. One of the gang would use the bathroom after dropping off the stash in the morning, always leaving the toilet seat covered in carefully laid out layers of tissue.Without work, and with a constant supply of free crack and heroin, Duncan’s life became dominated by getting high and waiting to get high. And as time passed, the cuckooing turned nastier. “Some of the younger ones were fascinated with knives, they liked to pretend to stab me. They thought it was funny,” he recalled. “Sometimes they poked me with the tips. They didn’t mean it, I don’t think. I got lots of small cuts, it wasn’t too bad. One time they were playing and one of them stabbed me quite deep in the leg. I don’t know why.”One of the gang’s associates forced Duncan to register a car in his name that was then used to sell drugs. The car accrued a string of fines and was written off in an accident. The debts fell on Duncan.After a string of complaints from other residents, in early 2018 the police warned Duncan that if he continued to let the gang use his flat he could lose his tenancy. By this time, he was too scared to stop them. According to internal local authority case notes, one housing officer messaged colleagues in February 2018 to say that council staff were themselves scared to visit Duncan’s flat: “Attended flat and went in for short while only … didn’t feel it was very safe. Duncan said he is desperate to move out as soon as possible as drug gang is using his flat whenever they want.” (The council later launched an investigation into its management of Duncan’s tenancy.)In April, the police emailed the council to say that it was no longer safe for Duncan to stay in the flat because he was being cuckooed. “We are getting inundated with complaints from neighbours. He needs moving urgently in my opinion,” one email reported. “I’ll try and keep an eye on the address although it’s difficult to visit Duncan as he doesn’t like police being seen walking into his property, which I can totally understand. The gang in question seem to have eyes everywhere on that estate.”That month, Duncan was talking to a housing officer at his front door about how he wanted to move off the estate because he was scared of the gang. Some of the gang were listening from the stairwell and wrongly presumed Duncan was talking to a police officer. They put the word out that they would kill Duncan. Later that week he was cycling near his home when someone jumped out of a car and shouted: “You fucking grass we’re going to kill you.” “I knew I had to get out of that flat,” said Duncan.A few days later, a place in an emergency homeless hostel was found for him in the east of the borough. Duncan packed what possessions he could into one of his key worker’s cars and left the place he’d made home for six years. His flat, which contained the rest of his belongings, was secured with heavy duty steel panels.The relief of escaping the gang did not last long. In the dingy, crowded hostel, Duncan’s mental health was already deteriorating, when one day he received a call from the council. They told him that, owing to a communication error, they had accidentally sent all the possessions he had left in his flat for incineration. This was not just furniture, but smaller things of great sentimental value, such as his son’s childhood drawings, his own artwork, treasured LPs and keepsakes. Duncan was heartbroken. He told his housing officer it was one of the worst things that had ever happened to him.Duncan’s friends had no idea where he had fled to. “This cuckooing thing had obliterated his life, but he totally disengaged with us all during that period,” said Billie, a fellow punk musician who’d known Duncan since the early 1990s. It took her six months to trace him to the hostel. After hearing snippets of information about his perilous health, she left him messages there, but heard nothing. “That was the first time since I’ve known him where I thought: ‘Oh my God, the wheels have completely come off.’ I really think we could have actually lost him then,” she told me.After 10 months in the hostel, in 2019 he was eventually rehoused in a decent one-bedroom flat in a low-rise estate in a quieter, more suburban part of the borough. But he found it hard to start anew. Debt collectors were chasing him for fines and damage to the cars the gang rented out in his name, and because of the threats to his life, he was scared to go to the part of the borough where his son lived, and where his drug treatment service was.Worried about him, in March 2019, a friend and I drove to his flat to see how he was. Inside, it was a mess. A bowl filled with stinking, mouldy fruit sat on the table. Duncan seemed to be living on a diet of Shreddies and milk with jam mixed in. He was convinced he had parasites under his skin, in his hair, and in his blood, a feeling that can be triggered by long-term crack use. We took him to hospital for some check-ups, particularly on the large injecting wound on his leg, for which he started to receive treatment.In between Covid lockdowns he was able to move more freely around the borough, after most of the teenage gang that cuckooed him were arrested. We met a couple of times as he started taking action against the council, with the help of a lawyer, for destroying his possessions. After several months of legal wrangling, he was awarded a good chunk of money, which he mainly spent on an array of beautiful guitars and drugs. He drifted away from his friends again.Then, in November 2024, I got a call from Duncan. He told me he felt really lonely and he wanted to meet up. He explained that over the past three years, he’d built a close bond with someone, but that person had just been sent to prison. Anyone I know, I asked? No, he replied, it was a drug dealer who had been using his house as a base for his business for the previous three years. I couldn’t believe it. But this time, as Duncan explained over a fry-up in a local cafe, wasn’t like the last one.View image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/PACompared with the teenagers on Duncan’s old estate, the second gang, which I’ll call the T-Line, was a more professional outfit. It ran a sizeable chunk of the heroin and crack trade in this part of north-east London. It was led by an experienced dealer in his early 40s. A confident, charming east Londoner, Tony was a well-known figure in the borough’s drug trade. Duncan had bought drugs from him while he was living in the homeless hostel. “He’s a personable kind of bloke,” Duncan told me. “He’s ingratiating. He liked sharing recipes and he liked my artwork. We just clicked, I guess.”The first time Tony had visited him at home, he noticed portraits Duncan had painted of his own family. Tony said he liked them, and paid Duncan to paint a picture of his own two young sons. There was another thing Tony liked about Duncan’s flat: it would make an ideal trap house. The estate was low key, plus Duncan was one of his calmer, more reliable customers. He could be counted upon to keep quiet. The few times Tony’s crew had been round Duncan’s flat, he had seemed unfazed.Tony suggested a deal: free daily crack and heroin in return for the flat being used as the gang’s secret weighing and stash house. So in 2021, for the second time in the space of three years, Duncan opened his home to a drug dealing gang. And when Tony asked him if he wanted to help prepare the drugs for sale, in return for more crack. Duncan knew that, legally speaking, doing so would change him from a passive victim to a willing offender. If he was caught he could be kicked out of his council flat and sent to prison. Even so, he said yes.Duncan’s coffee table was repurposed as a drug processing station. Every day Tony, who now had keys to the flat, arrived at about 11.30am on his scooter with kilo bricks of heroin and crack, usually leaving around midnight. They worked long days together at the flat. It was Duncan’s job to weigh out and line up hundreds of 0.1 gram “shots” of each drug, ready to be wrapped into bags for street sale. Duncan estimates he helped cut and weigh about 5,000 “shots” of heroin and crack every week. Surrounded by enough narcotics to get the whole neighbourhood high, Duncan would have a regular puff on his crack pipe, part of his daily drug wage. “It was therapeutic for me,” he said. “I’d do 100 shots and have a pipe and do another 100 and so on.” As Duncan sorted out the drugs, Tony would be shouting via speakerphone, bossing his underlings.Members of Tony’s crew came and went throughout the day. The longer the T-Line was camped out at his flat, the more Duncan found himself involved in its day-to-day business. “I did quite a lot of stuff for him like you would do with a friend,” said Duncan. “I tested his gear for him, I opened bank accounts he could use.”Tony’s world was full of risk and violence, yet amid this dark backdrop, grew a friendship “built through a kind of domesticity”, according to Duncan. Tony brought a packed lunch, usually Jamaican food made by his sister or mother, which he put in the fridge. Sometimes while Tony coordinated drug deals over the phone, and after Duncan had finished dividing up the crack and smack, Duncan painted pictures for Tony.“I used to tidy the house for him,” recalled Duncan. “I felt privileged to be accepted, and proud he was friends with me. He would make me look after myself. On my own, I couldn’t be bothered, but he got me together.” Even though he provided Duncan with a constant supply of class A drugs, Duncan said Tony “tried to discourage me from using drugs so much”, and “encouraged me to eat better – he was always feeding me his mum’s food”.As they weighed and bagged drug deals, with Duncan sat at the coffee table and Tony at the small dining table, they talked about everything from conspiracy theories and the causes of poverty in Britain’s black community to their hopes for the future, and their pasts. Tony liked to get involved in every conversation. “He would never shut up, so I went out of the room to make calls.”Tony told Duncan he grew up in poverty with a “wasteman” dad and had been selling drugs since he was a teenager. His chief motivation was to give his children, who he said were both in private school and the only two black kids in their class, a life different from his own. “He told me he was always going to go a bit further, take more risks, than the police chasing him because he was doing it for his kids, and the cops didn’t have as much to lose as he did.”But Tony had a plan. By Christmas 2024, he said, he would call time on his drug dealing career. He had prepared the ground by setting up a catering truck and a semi-legitimate transport business. Come the following year, he would start anew.The problem was that in 2023, things had started to unravel for the T-Line. A rival drug crew started ramming T-Line scooter riders off the road. They responded by squirting their attackers with ammonia. The beef was halted only after Tony contacted a criminal associate who warned the rival gang that there would be lethal consequences unless they backed down. Then Kane, Tony’s lieutenant who distributed the T-Line’s drugs to street dealers, was arrested for running a drug network in Norwich. Tony took on more responsibility, including doing more of the “road work”, moving drugs around the neighbourhood himself by scooter.“It made him more exposed,” said Duncan. “He was getting more abrasive, more anxious, shouting at people more on the phone. He was very stressed. I told him not to bring bad energy into my place. He said he would try to keep calm, but he couldn’t.” When Duncan discovered that Tony had been hiding bricks of crack and heroin in his flat, he started stealing bits for himself, reasoning it was in his house after all. When Tony found out, they had fierce rows. “I said, if you don’t like it, don’t come back. But he would come back because it was the perfect house.”Within the space of a few months in mid-2024, both of them came within inches of death. Duncan collapsed at his flat. He had contracted septicaemia after his injection wound became infected, and doctors told him he was lucky to survive. Not long after, Tony confronted a gang of teenagers trying to steal his scooter and was stabbed four times. Lying in the street, bleeding heavily, Tony managed to call a friend, who came to the scene, lifted him into a car and took him to casualty. “When I saw him a few weeks later we hugged. I was really happy to see him,” said Duncan.Tony was getting increasingly nervous about being caught. He had been in prison three times for dealing. He was getting too old for jail, he told Duncan. He “didn’t have the energy for it” and dreaded being separated from his boys. His retirement date was coming closer.One day in November 2024, Tony didn’t turn up at his usual time. Later that day Duncan got a phone call from one of the gang to say he’d been arrested after a police helicopter pursuit. Duncan was gutted for him. He was also thinking that, if the police had been keeping Tony under surveillance, his flat would be next. Yet as the days went by, alone at home, it wasn’t fear that he felt, but an intense loneliness.Before Tony’s arrest, Duncan had ended his “love affair” with crack. It no longer agreed with his body, he felt. He also cut down from two grams of heroin a day to half a gram. “For the first time, it felt like it was holding me back,” he said.Today, a year and a half later, it seems like Duncan has never been better. He’s eating well and looking after his health. He’s ditched his sometimes curmudgeonly attitude, he has his addiction under control, and he’s seeing his family and friends more than he has done for a decade.Duncan believes his friendship with Tony helped him turn his life around. “The most obvious way he helped me was by bringing food from home,” he said. “Good home-cooked food. So my diet improved and I got a taste for Caribbean food. Music too. We listened to a lot of music and he turned me on to stuff I’d not heard before. Having a guest come to my home made me look after the place and myself more, and the work, although pretty tedious, was something to try to be good at, so that was positive too. I felt part of something, and part of a team.”It’s hard to comprehend how Duncan, who had helpful, open-minded friends with money in their bank accounts, would be aided most by someone most people considered his biggest threat. But, in Duncan’s telling, this is exactly what happened. Tony “helped me to pull my socks up, so to speak”, he said. Behind his day job as a drug dealer, according to Duncan, Tony was essentially a businessman, a family man, a nice guy. “Well, it’s an odd person who only has one side to their character, wouldn’t you say?” said Duncan.There are indeed nice drug dealers, I’ve met many myself. I’ve met some nasty ones too. People do not like to see themselves as being exploited, and Duncan denies he was manipulated. He said the two of them had a genuine friendship, and that if he had wanted Tony to stop using his home, he would have complied. But some of Duncan’s friends have a different take.Chloe, the teacher, met Tony by accident one day in 2024. After hearing that Duncan had been in hospital and having not seen him in two years, she called round to his flat to check he was OK. As they chatted over tea, the front door opened and Tony let himself in. Chloe was surprised, and so was Tony. She was scared, not because of Tony himself, but because she knew it was drug business. “Duncan really likes Tony,” said Chloe, “but if you’re storing your illegal drugs in someone else’s house, if you’re asking them to do something in return for a thing they cannot resist. There’s a power imbalance; you are definitely the boss”.Cuckooing is now a specific criminal offence, after the Crime and Policing Act took effect this year. But experts say it will not be stopped so simply. A rise in “deep poverty”, tracked in the Joseph Rowntree Foundation’s2026 report, has led to more people living highly precarious, marginalised lives in deprived areas. These people are easy targets for cuckooing.Drug gangs are increasingly targeting people’s homes in cities such as London, Bristol and Leeds. Operation Pantera recorded 1,539 cases of cuckooing in the capital between May 2025 and April 2026. Two years earlier, cuckooing had been flagged by the Met in just 380 investigations. In Leeds, cuckooing is now a major cause of vulnerable people being evicted from their homes.Tony was sentenced to three years in prison in early 2025, but he and Duncan still chat on the phone, mainly about local gossip. Now and then Duncan buys things online on Tony’s behalf, which a friend of Tony’s will pick up and deliver to him. Sometimes Tony sounds downbeat, says Duncan, but he also talks about his kids, and plans for a future outside the drug business. During a day release in August, Tony paid Duncan a brief visit. “He’d obviously been working out inside, he was huge,” said Duncan. “He told me I looked really skinny and to put on some weight. It was really lovely to see him, he was smiling and we hugged.”Tony is due to be released in a year or so. I asked Duncan what he would do if Tony wanted to use his home again as a drug dealing base. “I’d say no. I’ve got other things to do in my life now,” he replied. “I couldn’t give him the time he’d need off me.”Their friendship was partly a matter of timing. “What [Tony] gave me at that time was a purpose,” Duncan said. “There seemed to be more regard for me as an artist and musician within his community than I’d ever felt before and my experience and knowledge of drugs was valued too. It was flattering to be respected like that and to be accepted into that world. And it was exciting.”From low-level drug dealer to human trafficker: are modern slavery laws catching the wrong people?Read moreLike many of his friends, Billie the guitarist is delighted that Duncan is doing so well. She thinks that his turnaround was more to do with his wound finally healing in 2024 than his friendship with a drug dealer. And she’s scared. “He’s very positive about this person, and they probably saw it as a mutually beneficial relationship, but to me this was complete parasiticism. Hearing that he’s going to come out soon actually worries me a lot. I want to just keep on telling him, think about your son.”I asked Duncan if he and Tony would still be friends when Tony gets out of prison. He said yes, but only to a point. “As close as we were, there was always a distance he kept between us,” said Duncan. “He never acknowledged his real name, he never told me it or allowed me to call him it. He kept up this pretence that we never actually knew each other well, a bit like people having an affair.”All names have been changedListen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead
Content: ‘The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations.’Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations.’Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionUS newsTrump invades the UN with a brutish speechTed WidmerGone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years aheadTue 22 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 21.45 EDTShareExpectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has madeno secretof his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the USdecided to withdrawfrom in July 2025).His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peacein January(just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the presidentwonderedif his new creation might simply replace.Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon.Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for himRead moreBut even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s.In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader.A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect.In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it.Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree to work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks).Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly beingdepleted.There was a lengthy assault on climate crisis, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied arecordfor the hottest month ever recorded, and several importantsciencereports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, thetemperatureon the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when hebraggedthat the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his2025 speechto the UN.Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick.On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US andChinamight cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized.Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speechRead moreOther topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship withCanada, once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now. It will take years to repair the damage to a vital strategic relationship to the North.Instead, more attention was paid toGreenland. The president claimed the US would now be enjoying basing rights – which we already enjoy – and he also suggested that foreign adversaries would not be allowed on their bases. That is hardly news – they have never been allowed bases on Greenland.While discussing his own vision of sovereignty, including his claims to Venezuelan oil, Trump drew from a sordid page of US history, and quoted a corrupt New York politician, William M “Boss” Tweed, to say “to the victor belong the spoils”. Tweed, the leader of Tammany Hall, was later convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars from the public, and died in jail.Perhaps the saddest aspect of this speech was its utter lack of American idealism – the very force that led to the UN’s creation. In the 250th year of the United States, there were plenty of themes that might have won over a skeptical audience, but there were no inspiring words about fighting poverty, or reducing nuclear tests or keeping weapons out of space (asJohn F Kennedypromised in 1963).Or human rights (introduced as a major theme by JimmyCarterin 1977), or about reducing tensions with Russia (which RonaldReaganspoke about in 1988), or the end of the cold war (which George HWBushcelebrated in 1990), or the need to fight terrorism while avoiding Islamophobia (as BillClintonexplained carefully in 1998).It was just raw power; and a power that is likely to diminish in the years ahead. The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations. But the United States is now at historically low levels of approval around the world, as measured by the Pew GlobalAttitudesproject, with only 23% of people (across 36 nations) expressing confidence in Trump’s leadership. The number is unlikely to go up after today’s performance.Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of AmericaExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicsUnited NationsDonald TrumpUS foreign policyClimate crisisChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Logan and Jake Paul.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenLogan and Jake Paul.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicOpinionUS politicsThe Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencersArwa MahdawiJake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policyTue 22 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTShareWe’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in amatter of weeks. Prices are rising, troopmorale is plummeting, and there is little evidence things will improve.The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recentlythreatenedto “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doingidiotic stuntson YouTube and gettinghit in the faceduring boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department ofWar Crimes?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech.In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzingerwrote, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.” That about sums it up.The Paul brothers, to be fair, rose to the occasion as best they could. In a speech which channelled Churchill, if Churchill had suffered several major blows to the head, Logansaidthat touring the Pentagon had been “a cool experience”. Albeit not quite as cool as being deployed to fight and possiblydiein an illegal bombing campaign started by president Trump, a convicted felon, on the advice of Benjamin Netanyahu, an accused war criminal. “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country,” Logan said. Which is why you won’t see him doing it; easier to pocket millionsfighting on TV.As well as giving a pep talk to the military, Jake met up withtreasury secretaryScott Bessent and the US treasurer todiscusshow “to get more young Americans financially empowered.” That must have been an interesting chat considering how, back in 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the YouTuber with unlawfully promoting crypto assets without disclosing that he was being paid to do so; he eventuallysettledwithout admitting or denying the charges. (Logan has also faced a lawsuit linked to a dodgycrypto venture, although the case was eventually dismissed). Exactly the sort of person you want the treasury secretary expending energy talking to when US debt recentlytopped $40tnfor the first time ever and a financial crisis seems to bearound the corner.Just how Jake Paul and Bessent hope to financially empower young Americans is unclear. But it is unlikely to be via the traditional method of working hard at school and then going to university. Jake very much shares the Trump administration’s contempt for education. In 2020 hetweetedthat he’s “sick of our education system and how it’s teaching kids 0 real life skills for them to secure there [sic.] own future.” He also oncedescribedhigh school as “kids sitting in Geography to learn where Timbuktu is for no reason.” The reason you learn where Timbuktu is, Jake, is so the US can overthrow it after they’re done with Iran and Greenland.There has always been a strong vein of anti-intellectualism in US politics. “[T]he subordination of men of ideas to men of emotional power or manipulative skill are hardly innovations of the twentieth century,” Richard Hofstadter wrote in his 1963 book Anti-intellectualism in American Life. “[T]hey are inheritances from American Protestantism.” But while this may not be a new impulse, the Trump administration’s embrace of ignorance is doing damage that can’t be easily undone. The US is stuck in a vicious vacuousness cycle: the Trump administration has slashed research funding and disruptedthousandsof grants, leading many promising young academics toflee the US. As expertise is eliminated and critical thinkingpurgedfrom government institutes, chancers like the Paul brothers are elevated.Still, I suppose we should count our blessings, before even they are affected byIran-induced inflation. At least the boneheaded Paul brothers are simply having meetings with high-level Trump administration officials. At least they’re not directly involved with military or economic policy. Although, the way things are going it’s only a matter of time. “I’m going to make a prediction that you will be, in the not-too-distant future, running for political office,” Trump told Jake, who has been a vocal Maga supporter, on stage at arally earlier this year. “You have my complete and total endorsement.” Could another blond buffoon with zero qualifications become president of the US? Tune in to find out in the next season of America: the Empire ImplodesArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Great to see what Tom Cruise’s belly button looks like, but it’s the stuff he is never asked about that interests me  | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Most stars, and especially women, are endlessly expected to explain the past, with lessons learned and all the regrets. But not Tom – it’s Hollywood’s free pass, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Most stars, and especially women, are endlessly expected to explain the past, with lessons learned and all the regrets. But not Tom – it’s Hollywood’s free pass, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Tom Cruise poses for a selfie before the World Cup final at the MetLife Stadium, New Jersey, on 19 July 2026.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTom Cruise poses for a selfie before the World Cup final at the MetLife Stadium, New Jersey, on 19 July 2026.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionTom CruiseGreat to see what Tom Cruise’s belly button looks like, but it’s the stuff he is never asked about that interests meMarina HydeMost stars, and especially women, are endlessly expected to explain the past: the lessons learned and all the regrets. But not Tom – it’s Hollywood’s free passTue 22 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTShareThere really is no press tour like aTom Cruisepress tour – which is why there have not really been any Tom Cruise press tours for a very long time indeed. We’re now at the stage of this one where even the interviewers have been forced on to the interview circuit to defend their interviews.Anyway: Cruise. The guy has one childwith ex-wife Katie Holmeswho dropped his surname as soon as she was legally allowed, and two Scientologist children widely reported to be effectively estrangedfrom their mother, Nicole Kidman. The divorces from Kidman and Holmes were clearly deeply strange and traumatic events for both women, and have remained shrouded in unusually watertight and presumably contractual secrecy. Yet you can currently find Tom Cruise promoting his latest movie not being asked about any of this stuff, or indeed any of his other extensive “stuff” – as always – but instead doing things like giving Travis and Jason Kelce’s podcast a lecture on thebenefits of VistaVision. Hate to say it, but a woman could never.At some level, you have to admire the mad image-industrial complex that labours to keep “the last movie star” from having to talk about the things all the other movie stars are required to lay on the line in order to promote their wares. Only a few weeks ago, Kidman wason the cover of Voguebeing required to pick over her two marriages in what was otherwise the most saccharine of interviews.Meanwhile, the world is obliged on pain of death to regard the 64-year-old Tom Cruise as ageless (and probably deathless). A few years ago, his Top Gun co-star Kelly McGillis – 62 at the time –explainedwhy she had not been approached to return for the sequel, Top Gun Maverick. “I’m old and I’m fat, and I look age-appropriate for what my age is,” she replied with deadly affectlessness, “and that is not what that whole scene is about.”View image in fullscreenTom Cruise on the cover of GQ magazine.Photograph: Mario SorrentiCruise, in contrast, has chosen to coverthis month’s GQmagazine with his shirt flung open, pulling down the waistband of his jeans – a choice we’d probably have to describe as wholly mesmerising rather than directly appealing. Hand on heart, Tom Cruise feels like someone you’d like to have sex with about as much as you’d like him to explain VistaVision to you. Wait, what am I talking about? Let me adjust: I strongly suspect most women would rather have 87 hours’ worth of defensive questions about image grain and aspect ratio lined up just in case.Even less enticing is the sheer guffawing prickliness with which Cruise responds to GQ’s question about what it meant to recently turn 64. “It means I’m 64.” Okaaaaay. Does it change anything about the way you think about anything, the interviewer, Zach Baron, wonders with desperate vagueness. “It’s just like, No!” scoffs Cruise. “Zach’s like,Does it change anything? When you’re looking at this, does it, like…Man, I’m just saying: it doesn’t at all. What changes things is I love seeing people do well.”Even Cruise’s yesteryear PR anecdotes have been written over in the service of making him seem like Hollywood’s apex benefactor. Back in the day, Tom always used to explain how he struggled with reading scripts because he was dyslexic. These days, the story has changed to reflect his unique position in, and contribution to, the cinematic culture. On the Kelces’ podcast, he took the time to explain how he makes writers and directors read their scripts out loud to him: “I don’t read the scripts. I have them read it to me. I have them read it to me because I don’t want my ideas to invade it yet. I want to understand what is their communication. They’ve been working on it. They have things that are just there. So they come to me, and I just sit there, and I’m like, I want you to read it to me.”As mentioned, perhaps the most meta element of this press tour is that the GQ interviewer now feels he has to get himself out there on the circuit to do interviews about his strange interview. He wasn’t instructed not to ask about Scientology,Baron told the Washington Post, but just decided not to do it because it has been done before. Then again, you sense that even if Baron had asked, he could have been re-hit with an answer like “What changes things is I love seeing people do well”. The good news for those who ordered this word salad is that there are an entire 10 days to go before Digger, the film Cruise is promoting, finally makes landfall. Expect plenty more to be served up by then.Perhaps most ironically, a report from a Bafta event where Cruise was interviewed this week describes the audience as “otherwise low-key”, until Tom launched into a six-minute monologueabout the primacy of human art over AI. “What you put attention on, you give life,” he freestyled. “People wanna see real things.” As he had it: “There is nothing like human.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd yet, is he anything like human? More and more, the real-life Tom Cruise feels like something sprung from the pages of fiction. He’s a sort of Peter Pan’s shadow who leads a largely disconnected existence from the Cruise of the screen – the only Cruise that makes sense. Strange that for decades now, one of the most obviously bizarre people in public life has still been allowed – required, really – to be routinely hailed as his medium’s one remaining superstar. Perhaps that and his medium’s steady decline are not altogether unconnected.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist. Her new book is What a Time to Be Alive! title: Never mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American people | Leslie Vinjamuri | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear, says Leslie Vinjamuri, CEO of Chicago Council on Global Affairs
Author: Leslie Vinjamuri
Headline: Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear, says Leslie Vinjamuri, CEO of Chicago Council on Global Affairs
Content: Nato leaders including Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni and French president Emmanuel Macron meet Donald Trump at The Hague, June 2025.Photograph: Haiyun Jiang/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNato leaders including Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni and French president Emmanuel Macron meet Donald Trump at The Hague, June 2025.Photograph: Haiyun Jiang/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNatoNever mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American peopleLeslie VinjamuriMark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing earTue 22 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareAt a moment when Europe is focused on persuading Donald Trump to remain committed to Nato, it needs to convince Americans, too. So the presence this evening of the Nato secretary general,Mark Rutte, in front of a public audience in Des Moines, Iowa, is significant. This is the home town of Trump’s ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker, and the visit brings the debate over Nato’s future directly to a midwestern audience in a red state that operates far from elite foreign-policy circles in Washington. Rutte’s appearance is long overdue.Russia’s war in Ukraine and uncertainty over the US commitment to European security have forced European leaders toconfront their dependence on Washington. While some are pressing for building European capabilities as a means to separate from the US, others see greater European defence spending as essential to keeping the US engaged. Either way, European governments can’t rely solely on meetings with Trump to secure the alliance’s future.Instead, Europe’s leaders need to look beyond Washington and take a tip from Rutte. Making the public case for Nato, the transatlantic partnership, and shared security across the middle of the country, is essential, not optional. This case should begin with the American people.For decades, Americans have supported the transatlantic relationship because they understood that Europe’s security is closely connected to their own.Natoand the transatlantic partnership were part of a wider ambition, designed to make the world safe for democracy, not least for the growth and prosperity this created. Public support has been essential to this undertaking.For many Americans, democracy is now failing to deliver on the promise of prosperity, and in some key areas the contrast with Europe is stark. In the Commonwealth Fund’s2023 survey, 46% of US adults with lower or average incomes reported skipping or delaying needed healthcare because of cost, compared with 16% in each of the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. Populists have been quick to highlight the shortcomings of America’s democracy, and this message has resonated across swaths of the population, particularly rural voters and Americans without a university degree – both central to Trump’s electoral coalition.When it comes to the American public, there is plenty of room for optimism, but in a political context that is ripe for populists to cultivate antagonism toward spending on foreign causes, there is little room for complacency. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ polling consistently shows that Americans support Nato and the transatlantic partnership.Its recent survey with Ipsosfound that 68% of Americans supported maintaining or increasing the US commitment to Nato. Yet only 47% were confident that European allies would come to America’s defence if it were attacked, down from 62% in 2025. Public support for Ukraine has also remained substantial, even as Americans debate the scale and duration of US assistance; a2024 surveyfound that 58% supported sending additional arms and military supplies to Ukraine, and the same number supported economic assistance.European leaders would be wise to invest in a public diplomacy strategy in order to cultivate understanding among Americans outside Washington’s foreign-policy establishment. The secretary general’s decision to travel to Iowa should be seen as a crucial part of Europe’s midwest strategy. Other leading foreign policy organisations have sought to do the same. Over the summer, the Ditchley Foundation used the occasion ofAmerica’s 250thto deepen its partnerships across the US, convening roundtables in South Carolina and Illinois.This outreach is essential to counter the persistent myth that Europeans are free-riding on America’s coattails. Europe’s renewed commitment to defence is significant, with a 20% increase in 2025 compared with 2024 among the EU’s 27 member states. This remains poorly understood in the US. Nato’sAnnual 2025 reportnotes that all of Nato’s 32 members met or exceeded the 2% of GDP expenditure target for that year. Allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP annuallyby 2035in defence and related security. The precise figures matter, but so does the broader message: that Europe is investing in the capacity to defend itself and contribute to shared security.It would also be smart to highlight the opportunities created by this investment for American companies. Defence cooperation supports jobs and growth opportunities. It also boosts transatlantic supply chains and research partnerships. But the ties that bind Europe and America reach deeper than military procurement. The case for the alliance should ultimately be made in terms that people recognise in their own lives: the security of their jobs, the price and availability of energy, the resilience of the technology they rely on and, above all, the prospect of their families living without the threat of a wider war.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe transatlantic partnership cannot be secured through presidential diplomacy alone. European leaders should continue engaging the White House, but they must also make their case to the American public. The long-term future of Nato will depend not only on what presidents decide, but on whether citizens on both sides of the Atlantic continue to see the alliance as essential to their security, democracy and prosperity.Leslie Vinjamuri is president and CEO of Chicago Council on Global AffairsExplore more on these topicsNatoOpinionUS politicsEuropeMark RuttecommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage? | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solution, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solution, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘[The issue is] making fools of MPs, who will say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable, but have to keep pretending otherwise in public.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘[The issue is] making fools of MPs, who will say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable, but have to keep pretending otherwise in public.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionPensionsBritain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?Gaby HinsliffThe issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solutionTue 22 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTShareThere is always something oddly unreal about party conference season. In theory, everyone is getting away from Westminster to better reflect on the state of the nation. In practice, the whole circus just briefly relocates to the coast, to live off warm white wine and gossip for three days, before coming back with a streaming cold. But this year, reality seems more elusive than usual.Everyone knows hard choices loom, but everyone is frightened to make them. Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock, whose future will be vigorously debated on the fringes and in private conversation this autumn, but less so on the stage.George Osborne’sshameless 2011 bid for pensioner votes– under which the state pension rises, come rain or shine, by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth for working people, or 2.5% – has alreadycost around three times as muchas the Treasury originally expected.TheOffice for Budget Responsibility reckons that by 2030 it will be swallowing more than £15bn a year – almost enough to fund the cause over which chancellor John Healey was recently willingto resign, namely raising defence spending to 3% of GDP in time to prevent a Russian attack on Nato.But even if you’re willing to roll the dice on another war, there’s no shortage of alternative proposals for spending the money.The British Chambers of Commerce wants it diverted intotackling youth unemploymentvia cuts to national insurance, while the rightwing thinktank Centre for Social Justice argues for spending it on boostingthe life chancesof working-class boys. But perhaps more fittingly, it could pay forAndy Burnham’s dreamof free social care for the very age group that is liable to lose out from breaking the lock. Would pensioners rather have a3.9% rise next year– though it could be higher, if inflation really rockets this autumn – or relief from the fear of having to sell family homes to fund nursing care? Because right now, it’s difficult to see how they can have both. Yet the failure to be honest about these tradeoffs is bending British politics out of shape.It’s making fools of MPs, who will readily say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable but have to keep pretending otherwise in public, even as they’re being asked to nod throughpainful cuts to disability benefits. It’s sending young and painfully squeezed people a message that nobody cares about them, fuelling intergenerational resentment. And it’s encouraging a phoney debate about tax and spend, in which parties of the left pretend they can find serious money from unicorn taxes – the magical kind that raise billions but somehow without hitting anyone likely to vote for them, or driving the highly mobile rich to Monaco – while parties of the right pretend they can make huge welfare savings they somehow missed during 14 years in power.Breaking the triple lock is becoming enough of a no-brainer to attract genuine cross-party consensus, stumped only by the cross-party conviction that the public will hate them for it.That fear is not unfounded. According to YouGov, two-thirds of Britons – and 70% of over-65s –want to keep the lock. Labour remains terrified of repeatingRachel Reeves’ 2024 gambit,when she tried to take winter fuel allowance away from better-off pensioners in a hurry, but couldn’t bring herself to make the political case for doing so, and was eventually forced into retreat.For the Tories, going after pensioners would be suicidal, and the same goes for the Liberal Democrats, so long as they’re trying to hold on to the formerly true-blue shire seats they captured two years ago.Only the Greensseem to be keeping their options open, and they’re not going to win the next election. Fear of a pensioner backlash is distorting everything, like a dam in a river that forces the water to find other ways around it, eroding the banks until they eventually collapse.Nobody is arguing that pensioner poverty has ceased to be a problem. (If anything, retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers did, which means this conversation may get harder the longer it’s deferred.) And even for those who aren’t on the breadline, the prospect of losing money at an age when you can no longer try to earn your way out of trouble is genuinely frightening.But there are better ways of helping older people who genuinely need it than a triple lock that benefits both rich and poor, and working-age poverty is real too. Choosing to shield pensioners from the harsh economic realities of the last few years has hit some of their children and grandchildren unfairly hard: while pensioner benefits rose in real terms by£900 between 2010-11 and 2024-25, benefits for children and working-age people fell by £1,400, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank.Yet anyone daring to make that case at the next election for breaking the lock can expect to be mercilessly shelled by rivals, including those who deep down agree with them.What is focusing minds now is the realisation that for the first time, next spring, the state pensionmay rise high enough to attract tax(though ministers say anyone poor enough to rely solely on it would be exempt). The stealth option would be to keep the triple lock nominally in place, but tax away the increase for wealthier pensioners – essentially giving with one hand and taking with the other, a bit like the Tories did overchild benefit for higher-rate taxpayers. It avoids an outright confrontation, but plenty of pensioners will notice the money being clawed back and resent it nonetheless.Better, surely, to break the lock as part of a new and much broader deal on generational fairness, which protects vulnerable elderly people but recognises that the young are also struggling – while lifting the burden of social care andsettling arguments around pension tax reliefinto the bargain.Smart spending in an era of shrinking resources ought to mean working out how to use the same money differently to meet new challenges, not just clinging to the past because you can’t face talking about the future. But for now, it seems, that’s just a little too much reality to bear.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPensionsOpinionFamily financesAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyLabourState pensionsWelfarecommentShareReuse this content

title: My son has left home – and I feel full of complicated joy | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: I took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your mother, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: I took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your mother, writes Zoe Williams
Content: ‘As a parent, it’s time to manage your own disappointment …’Photograph: Terry Vine/Getty Images (Posed by models)View image in fullscreen‘As a parent, it’s time to manage your own disappointment …’Photograph: Terry Vine/Getty Images (Posed by models)OpinionFamilyMy son has left home – and I feel full of complicated joyZoe WilliamsI took him to university this weekend, and it reminded me of the exhilaration of suddenly having your own space, absolutely separate from your motherTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareWhen kids are small, and their expectations of an event diverge from yours in some important way, you feel terrible about it. You might be taking them to a play, and they thought that meant they’d be allowed to play, but actually it meant they had to sit still while strangers shouted things. You experience their disappointment as much as your own physical pain.Then when they’re “adults”, your expectations diverge again. They thought you’d drop them at university and immediately leave, while you thought you’d unpack, and meet their flatmates, explore the city, and spin round a supermarket, then have a Nando’s, and maybe read a bedtime story, get chatting to the other parents and maybe all do karaoke? Well, then it’s time to manage your own disappointment, and the only thing to be said for that is that it’s way less bad than managing theirs.When I went to university, my mum’s boyfriend drove me and there wasn’t room for her in the car, so it was a beautifully symmetrical event: I wanted him to leave and he wanted to leave. Then when she came to see me, I would count down the hours until she had to leave, and I used to love it when other people’s mums came to see them, because often they were nice, but, also, the schadenfreude was intense.Mothers out of context are appalling. I don’t think there’s a feeling I’ve ever had that I remember with more clarity. Tugging on that memory unspooled the whole Technicolor exhilaration of suddenly having your own context, that your mother is absolutely not in. So there was more joy in being rejected by my son after dropping him off than you’d think, plus I went to KFC with his out-of-context dad on the way home and they gave us some free chicken selects. Don’t know why, maybe because we looked so complicatedly overjoyed.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Lib Dems: Ed Davey wants Tory voters without losing the left | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The party leader offers social liberalism and lower taxes, hoping opposition to Reform UK will hold together voters with competing economic interests
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The party leader offers social liberalism and lower taxes, hoping opposition to Reform UK will hold together voters with competing economic interests
Content: Ed Davey after delivering his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat party conference on 22 September.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEd Davey after delivering his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat party conference on 22 September.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionLiberal Democrat conferenceThe Guardian view on the Lib Dems: Ed Davey wants Tory voters without losing the leftEditorialThe party leader offers social liberalism and lower taxes, hoping opposition to Reform UK will hold together voters with competing economic interestsTue 22 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTShareSir Ed Davey’s speech at the Liberal Democrat party conference was a calculated appeal to voters who recoil from a rightwing bloc associated with Brexit, nationalism and reactionary politics. That’s not a bad place to start. But he wants this message not to be lost in the headlines about his party’s£17bn tax giveawayaimed at disillusioned Conservative voters. To walk that line, his address sought to present Reform UK’s politics as an existential threat to Britain, appealing directly to left-leaning tactical voters. At the same time, he told moderate Tories that only a vote for the Lib Dems can reliably block both Reform and a Conservative-supported Nigel Farage premiership.It’s a clever strategy. Too clever,thinksome in his party, who yearn for clearer dividing lines. Yet the Lib Dem leader is nothing if notambitious. He claims that his party could have more MPs than the Conservatives after the next election. In 2024, the Lib Dems won 60 of their 72 seats from the Tories; they were also second in a score of Conservative-held seats. That electoral geography pushes the Lib Dems as replacing the Conservatives as the respectable, pro-market opposition, while Reform occupies the space of the nationalist right. The logic is that in a multiparty system under first past the post, it may no longer be necessary to be a national party. Sir Ed might become kingmaker as the parliamentary expression of a liberal southern tendency.View image in fullscreenPaula Surridge.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianRejoining the single market would be in Britain’s interests. But presenting the move as a frictionless growth policy obscures the major change involved in accepting common rules and institutions. Sir Ed’s tax cuts may be smart politics, parking Lib Dem tanks on Tory territory. But they are a world away from his 2024 election image as thechampionof carer’s allowance, NHS funding and local sewage protests. That leftwing stance importantly allowed him then to tap into tactical anti-Conservative voting.Raising the personal allowance to£15,000allows Sir Ed to speak to almost every taxpayer in a cost of living crisis, while increasing the higher-rate threshold to £56,000 targets professionals in the south on whom his electoral strategy depends. The trouble is that the tax cuts are a promise, but the growth – from closer ties to Europe – that “pays” for them is a forecast. Choosing tax cuts over public investment leaves the Lib Dems exposed to competition from the left, from Labour and the Greens.Sir Ed is trying to detach economic liberalism from the socially conservative nationalists and link it to a pro-European and socially liberal party. He’s right to say that “people feel powerless”, but the examples that Sir Ed uses to demonstrate their lack of agency – unsafe maternity care, inadequate disability provision and polluted rivers – largely arise from failures of collective provision or state regulation. Their solutions require capable public institutions and more resources.The political scientist Paula Surridgewrotethat continued Lib Dem success depends on them being seen as a safe alternative for liberal-left voters. The cultural and social liberalism he sells would reassure this group. But tax cuts might disquiet them. Sir Ed is betting that these tactical voters care more about defeating the nationalist right than the Lib Dems’ economic programme. That was the case in 2024. After years of the public dealing with high prices, it may be harder to land that message next time.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
