title: The Guardian view on Keynes in the West End: James Graham’s latest play captures the zeitgeist | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As the chancellor, John Healey, ponders options ahead of his first budget, the playwright’s new work offers lessons from the past
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: As the chancellor, John Healey, ponders options ahead of his first budget, the playwright’s new work offers lessons from the past
Content: Pip Carter, Natalia Osipova and Rory Kinnear in rehearsals for The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenPip Carter, Natalia Osipova and Rory Kinnear in rehearsals for The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanOpinionTheatreThe Guardian view on Keynes in the West End: James Graham’s latest play captures the zeitgeistEditorialAs the chancellor, John Healey, ponders options ahead of his first budget, the playwright’s new work offers lessons from the pastTue 22 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTShareStill only 44, James Graham has become a formidable chronicler of our national story. On themes such as the rise ofRupert Murdoch, social upheaval in post-industrial Britain and theneurosesof the England men’s football team, the playwright and screenwriter has made it his vocation to read the signs of our times and write them up for the stage.Graham’s new play goes a bit further back in history, but its subject matter is characteristically of the moment. Opening this week in the West End,The Standard of Livingoffers a portrait of the sentimental and intellectual passions of John Maynard Keynes (played by Rory Kinnear), as the great economist makes his name between the first and second world wars. As Keynes rails against the laissez-faire ethos of the age, he seeks to devise a theory of growth that justifies state intervention on people’s behalf in the wake of the Great Depression.A month out from the first budget to be delivered by Andy Burnham’s government, the contemporary relevance is not hard to spot. Ever since the prime ministerpledgedto bring an “end to 40 years of neoliberalism” and launch a new era of public investment to bring about growth, his opponents havesoughtto characterise that project as a reckless Labour version of Trussism. Discussion of the nation’s political direction has been reduced to a numbers game relentlessly focused on bond yields, debt levels and what markets will or will not countenance.View image in fullscreenJohn Maynard Keynes in 1940.Photograph: Tim Gidal/Getty ImagesJohn Healey may or may not take a seat in the stalls during the play’s scheduled run. But just as Graham’s Labour of Love prescientlyaddressedthe Labour party’s problems in its red wall heartlands, and Dear England explored a nation’s insecurities through sporting anxiety, his latest offering captures the zeitgeist in a way that goes beyond the contents of the chancellor’s budget briefcase.The economic historian Robert Skidelsky, who died this year,observedthat “our age has eerily come to rhyme with Keynes’s”. In the aftermath of the 2008 crash, nationalist threats to the global order have multiplied and the far right has been able to mobilise popular discontent at declining living standards. Whether progressive governments can negotiate the fiscal room for manoeuvre to allow them to respond effectively is a key issue of our time. Meanwhile, the existentialthreatposed by unregulated artificial intelligence has taken the laissez-faire debate on to new and alarming territory.Graham and Nicholas Hytner, the director of The Standard of Living, are too skilled to allow such echoes to add up to a sombre night out. Keynes’s marriage to the Russian ballerinaLydia Lopukhova, for example, is deftly exploited to make dance a metaphor for what a graceful balance of economic forces might look like. Perhaps the highlight of the evening thus becomes a vigorouspasde deuxacross the stage involving Keynes and his free-marketeering rival, Friedrich Hayek, choreographed to the rhythm of an argument about interest rates.Ideas, art, love affairs and the bohemian excesses of theBloomsbury setall compete for audience attention. At a time when the common good risks being undermined by market imperatives, algorithmic abstractions and rogue AI agents, Graham has once again produced a play that poses the right question at the right time: how can humans take back control?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Sex-based discrimination in medicine costs lives  | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article on women being less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article on women being less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditions
Content: ‘Women are not asking for preferential treatment; they need equitable access to timely diagnosis, appropriate investigation and effective care.’Photograph: Daria Artemenko/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Women are not asking for preferential treatment; they need equitable access to timely diagnosis, appropriate investigation and effective care.’Photograph: Daria Artemenko/AlamyWomen's healthLettersSex-based discrimination in medicine costs livesReaders respond to an article on women being less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditionsTue 22 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTShareAs head of pharmacovigilance at a clinical trials technology company, I was not surprised that a review of global research found that women are less likely than men to be offered active treatment for the same conditions (Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’, 16 September).This inequality costs lives. A British Heart Foundation-funded study found thatwomen were less likely than mento receive recommended care after a heart attack. Research in 2018 estimated thatmore than 8,000 women’s deaths may have been preventedover 10 years had they received the same standard of care as men.The problem starts long before a patient reaches the hospital, however. For years, women have been woefully underrepresented in clinical trials, initially because policy excluded women who might become pregnant. However, women also have busy lives, typically managing home and work, which makes taking time off a challenge that many find impossible.Yet without representation in the trials that give us safer, more effective medication, women’s specific needs are sidelined – which is unacceptable given that women experience50%-70% more side-effects from drugsthan men. Including women in more trials would go a long way towards addressing the health inequality between women and men.Claire WilliamsNorthWest EHealthSex-based discrimination is not new, but the fact that women with the same health conditions as men – from kidney to heart to liver problems – are less likely to be offered treatment continues to shock us. These are not just men’s issues, as they have historically been treated, but conditions that significantly affect women.Thisnew researchis significant because it goes beyond gynaecological conditions. It illustrates that medical misogyny is not just rife in “women’s specialities”, where conditions are dismissed as “women’s problems”, but across fields, contributing to women receiving less treatment and less help for their health problems.A fundamental shift in attitude is needed. Addressing this requires mandatory education in women’s health and in sex- and gender-sensitive medicine to eliminate bias throughout the training and continuing professional development of all healthcare professionals. Education must also begin in schools, with stronger sex and health education to challenge stereotypes and improve understanding of women’s health.The renewedwomen’s health strategyand the10-year health plan for Englandprovide an opportunity to act. Women are not asking for preferential treatment; they need equal access to timely diagnosis, appropriate investigation and effective care.Prof Geeta NargundHealth Equality FoundationI was delighted to see more discussion of endometriosis and other women’s health issues (‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosis, 15 September). However, there remains a woeful disregard of many of the issues women face.Pelvic pain is experienced by many women, as the article pointed out. In my case, as extreme pain came to dominate my life, I saw several top (male) professors of gynaecology and urinary disease before – thanks toa Guardian article– I saw a female gynaecologist who pointed me to a solution. This was physiotherapy specifically directed to dealing with women’s health issues, and pain in particular. These techniques need to be far more widely available and known.Prof Sophie WatsonThe Open UniversityHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Minority ethnic NHS staff pay a heavy price for speaking up about patient safety | NHS | The Guardian
description: Letter: Providing psychological safety to Black, Asian and ethnic minority staff so they can raise concerns about patient care without fear would save lives, write Dr Jennifer Creese, Dr Joy Spiliopoulos and Prof Carolyn Tarrant
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Providing psychological safety to Black, Asian and ethnic minority staff so they can raise concerns about patient care without fear would save lives, write Dr Jennifer Creese, Dr Joy Spiliopoulos and Prof Carolyn Tarrant
Content: Black, Asian and ethnic minority staff make up more than 40% of the medical and dental workforce.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenBlack, Asian and ethnic minority staff make up more than 40% of the medical and dental workforce.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PANHSLettersMinority ethnic NHS staff pay a heavy price for speaking up about patient safetyProviding psychological safety to Black, Asian and ethnic minority staff so they can raise concerns about patient care without fear would save lives, writeDr Jennifer Creese, Dr Joy SpiliopoulosandProf Carolyn TarrantTue 22 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTShareYour report (One in five black, Asian and minority ethnic NHS managers in England plan to quit amid racism, report finds, 15 September) rightly highlights racism, exclusion and blocked career progression in the NHS. But it also points to a wider risk: patient safety. Care mistakes already cost the NHS£14.7bn a year.A March 2025reportby the NHS Race & Health Observatory notes that Black, Asian and minority ethnic (BAME) staff, who make up more than 40% of the medical and dental workforce, still face harassment and discrimination in promotion, everyday work and disciplinary processes. This fuels stress, burnout and poorer mental health. Bullying and harassment are estimated to cost NHS England£2bn a yearthrough staff turnover, sickness and lost productivity. In such environments,BAME staffare less likely than white colleagues to speak up about patient safety, fearing that their concerns will not be understood or taken seriously.In recent research funded by the National Institute forHealthand Care Research, BAME NHS staff told us that racism, exclusion and barriers to progression affected not only their wellbeing but also whether they felt able to speak up when they saw patient safety issues. Staff in medical, nursing, midwifery, psychological therapy and patient safety roles described not being heard, unclear routes for raising concerns, fear of backlash, exclusion and bullying. Visa-dependent staff described particular anxieties. The result was reduced trust in organisations, diminished professional fulfilment and, in some cases, staff leaving.NHS England’s pledge that new staff standards will require trusts to tackle racism and ensure equal representation, equal opportunities and fair treatment is welcome. But the standards must also require trusts to create psychological safety for BAME staff: workplaces where staff can raise concerns about safety and racism without fear of repercussions. This would support retention and progression, reduce avoidable costs and, most importantly, protect patients’ lives.Dr Joy Spiliopoulos, Dr Jennifer Creese and Prof Carolyn TarrantUniversity of LeicesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Russians have a pragmatic approach to politics  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Letter: There has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch, writes Mergen Mongush
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: There has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch, writes Mergen Mongush
Content: Screens in Moscow showing live feeds from polling stations across Russia on the first day of parliamentary elections on 18 September.Photograph: Shamil Zhumatov/ReutersView image in fullscreenScreens in Moscow showing live feeds from polling stations across Russia on the first day of parliamentary elections on 18 September.Photograph: Shamil Zhumatov/ReutersRussiaLettersRussians have a pragmatic approach to politicsThere has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch, writesMergen MongushTue 22 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTShareTo an old Russian like me, Rafael Behr is as wrong as sin, because he is watching (and describing) the smoke without seeing the fire (To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one, 16 September).In their unqualified admiration for your democracy, our leaders have done a lot to emulate it: in 1861, Alexander II abolished serfdom; in 1905, Nicholas II allowed the creation of our elected parliament; in 1917, Kerensky allowed women to vote; in 1990, Gorbachev reintroduced a multiparty system; he, Yeltsin and Medvedev resigned in 1991, 1999 and 2020 respectively (like your Wilson, Thatcher, Blair, Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and Starmer in 1976, 1990, 2007, 2016, 2019, 2022, again 2022, and 2026 respectively).But ordinary Russians are up to their ears in their age-longque será, seráapproach to politics. So there has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch. Had Mr Behr lived in our provincial towns instead of Moscow in the 1990s, he would have produced a very different article.Mergen MongushMoscow, RussiaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Keeping billionaires and the taxman happy | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Letters: Stephen Gillian says the super-rich could help guarantee a decent wage for low-paid people in return for some tax benefits. Plus letters from Les Bright and Steve Brown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Stephen Gillian says the super-rich could help guarantee a decent wage for low-paid people in return for some tax benefits. Plus letters from Les Bright and Steve Brown
Content: ‘Jim Ratcliffe has some gall, living as he does in a tax-free monarchical haven in the south of France.’Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Jim Ratcliffe has some gall, living as he does in a tax-free monarchical haven in the south of France.’Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAThe super-richLettersKeeping billionaires and the taxman happyStephen Gilliansays the super-rich could help guarantee a decent wage for low-paid people in return for some tax benefits. Plus letters fromLes BrightandSteve BrownTue 22 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTShareI have a simple solution to help keep the super-rich happy with their tax bills while keeping their enormous wealth safely stored offshore and allowing them possibly to spend more time in the UK (Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit, 19 September). They could insist that any company they earn their wealth from commits to paying all UK staff a decent living wage.For this small compromise from the billionaires (who will still play the money markets and profit from others’ hard labour), the government could offer to reduce employers’ taxation costs by increasing the point at which low-paid people pay tax. Perhaps it could reduce national insurance payments for low-paid people, both employee and employer, thereby stopping the farce of the government paying income support to those on low incomes and then increasing taxation to fund it.You might even argue that reducing taxation would steal the thunder from the shortsighted and status quo-enthused rightwing – possibly proving that the Labour party doesn’t have to tax to spend. What’s not to like?Stephen GillianShrewsbury, ShropshireWhat is the BBC up to, giving its Big Boss interview slot toJim Ratcliffe, a man who loves his country so much that he moved his affairs to Monaco six years ago to avoid paying his fair share of tax? He thinks that immigration and benefits are at the heart of our problems, but I’m inclined to think that his noxious views contribute to the division that is scarring the nation.Les BrightExeterJim Ratcliffehas some gall, living as he does in a tax-free monarchical haven in the south of France. Does he ever connect with the ordinary people – some of whom still work at the football club he purports to support – who don’t have the luxury of being a multibillionaire paying less income tax than the working poor of Manchester do? Where is his sense of responsibility or awareness of the national interest? Words can hurt both individuals and nations, and for one so powerful, should be chosen with great care.Steve BrownFontenay-sous-Bois, FranceHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: First blood to England in ODI series after Will Jacks helps see off Sri Lanka | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: England won a slow-burn first ODI against Sri Lanka by 89 runs at Chester-le-Street, with Will Jacks starring with five wickets and 46 not out
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: England won a slow-burn first ODI against Sri Lanka by 89 runs at Chester-le-Street, with Will Jacks starring with five wickets and 46 not out
Content: England's Harry Brook and Will Jacks celebrate taking the wicket of Sri Lanka's Dilshan Madushanka to complete a comfortable win.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenEngland's Harry Brook and Will Jacks celebrate taking the wicket of Sri Lanka's Dilshan Madushanka to complete a comfortable win.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAEngland cricket teamFirst blood to England in ODI series after Will Jacks helps see off Sri LankaAll-rounder takes five wickets after vital 46 not outHarry Brook top-scores with 67 in comfortable winAli Martinat Banks Homes RiversideTue 22 Sep 2026 15.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Brook had called on his ­England players to continue the “high-octane” cricket witnessed during their clean sweep in the Twenty20s but this latest victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international was more of a slow-burn affair.Gone was the neck-arching carnage of the previous week and in its place, on a tired end-of-season surface, England were bowled out for 265 in 48.1 overs. Brook top-scored with 67 under a warm September sun, before his bowlers rolled the tourists for 176 to take a 1-0 lead into Thursday’s second match at Headingley.Familiarity with conditions doubtless played its part and Sri Lanka, on the wrong side of the toss, never truly felt in the hunt. For Brook it was an 11th victory as England’s ODI captain, nudging him into credit after 10 defeats and continuing what has been a quiet resurgence in the format this year.Cricket in the 21st century: 25 ways the game has changed | Phil WalkerRead moreThe volume will need to increase over the next 12 months as England build towards the next 50-over World Cup. But while hugely relevant lessons were never going to be learned in Chester-le-Street, the role played by Will Jacks was significant on the day and, as the new vice-captain, underlined his centrality more broadly.Without Jacks’s unbeaten 46 in the first innings, including 18 runs taken off the 48th over, Sri Lanka might well have had a sniff here. Indeed, since returning in a lower middle-order role last year – one that has taken adjustment given his preference to bat in the top three – Jacks has averaged 43 and struck at over 100.His off-breaks are also developing into a handy tool for Brook, returning five for 22 from seven overs here – including the top-scorer, Dunith Wellalage for 45 – as he mixed up his pace and angles. Only Vic Marks, five for 20 against New Zealand in Wellington way back in 1984, boasts better ODI figures by an England spinner – not that the man himself would ever boast about such things.“[Jacks] is not a part-timer, he’s a very good off-spinner,” said Brook. “He can spin the ball big and contain. He could have moaned and groaned about playing as an all-rounder but he’s accepted that and become a very vital player for us over the past 18 months. He’s a very good leader, with bat, ball and in the field.”Save for Jofra Archer, who took a bit of tap at the end of his all-format summer, Brook’s attack suppressed their opponents to defend a sub-300 total for the first time since 2022. Jamie Overton picked up two wickets bowling cross-seamers, while the loss of Adil Rashid – out of the series with a hand injury – was not felt.Quick GuideMark Wood retires from international cricketShowEngland bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket. The 36-year-old paceman played 38 Test matches over an 11-year England career, taking 119 wickets.“My stats won’t read I was the best bowler ever – but I hope my teammates think I was someone who tried my best every time,” he said.Wood last played for England in an eight-wicket defeat to Australia in the first Test of the 2025/26 Ashes series. He made 70 one-day international appearances and was part of England’s 50-over World Cup-winning squad in 2019.The Northumberland-born bowler played 38 T20s and was in the England squad which won the World Cup in 2022, although injury ruled him out of the semi-final and the final.Injuries ultimately cost Wood more caps, and a knee problem has prompted him to call time on his international career.“When you speak to other people, they say it hits you in the face, there’s a big feeling around that being it, ‘you’re done’,” he told Sky Sports.“I’ve never really had that, I love playing cricket, I love playing for England, that’s been something I’ve felt really strongly about and proud to do. But I’ve had a lot of injuries.“I’ve always found a way where I’ve believed I’d come back and had that resilience where I’m going to come back again, or I’ll be better, or I’ll prove somebody wrong again, but this time it’s just ground me down really.“I never really wanted to give up England, but the lads that are coming through are doing a fantastic job and the news should be about the lads going to get their contracts and I can just focus on other things.”Arguably England’s fastest-ever bowler, Wood clocked 97.7mph in the 2021/22 Ashes series. He took the final wicket at Trent Bridge when England regained the urn in 2015.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.WinViz actually had Sri Lanka as marginal favourites at the halfway stage but looking on, there was a nagging sense England had plenty. After an initial 10-over power-play in which the hosts reached 61 for one – Tom Banton the man out, bowled by a beauty from Asitha Fernando – batting had started to become trickier.Although just as relevant to England falling short of 300 was a sparkling debut from Sachindu Colombage, a 28-year-old wrist-spinner with a jerky, quirky action who claimed three for 44. Colombage was playing for Downham Stow in the East Anglian Premier League last summer and has an unremarkable domestic record. But Gary Kirsten, Sri Lanka’s head coach, looked beyond the numbers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHarry Brook continued his rich vein of form for England with 67.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersWhat Kirsten saw was the drift and dip that can trouble the best and in Joe Root and Jos Buttler, Colombage undid a couple of them here. Both were trapped on the back foot, Root hearing his off-stump rattled for 44 and Buttler pinned lbw for 31 by one that straightened. The less heralded Overton was later bowled by a leg-break that went above the eyeline and spun sharply.Root’s removal in the 23rd over was the first time he had been dismissed in ODI cricket for some 416 deliveries – a streak of 404 runs that goes back to England’s 2-1 win in Sri Lanka last winter. The key wicket was Brook, however, having looked pretty much immovable until he went to charge the seamer Dushmantha Chameera for one of his inside-out scythes and skewed the ball to deep point.It was one of the rare times that ­England had looked to clear the rope in what became their first ODI innings for more than seven years without a six. Brook’s demise also triggered the loss of four wickets for 29 runs in 46 balls, as a promising 182 for three became 211 for seven and tempered ambitions with it.As well as the end of Buttler, this mini-collapse included Rehan Ahmed run out by a direct hit from Charith Asalanka in the ring. England’s new mentor, Kevin Pietersen, had stressed the need for better strike rotation before this match. But there was never a single as Ahmed set off, realised his error, and then pretty much gave up.Watching all this unfold was Jacks, who with a bit of support from Gus Atkinson steered England to a defendable total. His work had only just begun, however, repeatedly punching holes in Sri Lanka’s lineup before sealing a comfortable win – and his first five-fer – with a ripper to bowl the No 11, Dilshan Madushanka.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Mikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030 | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Mikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season
Content: Mikel Arteta celebrates with the Premier League trophy in May, ending Arsenal’s 22-year wait to be champions.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta celebrates with the Premier League trophy in May, ending Arsenal’s 22-year wait to be champions.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianArsenalMikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030Manager’s current deal to expire at end of the seasonSpaniard can expect big increase on £10m-a-year salaryEd AaronsTue 22 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season and could take his reign as the manager beyond a decade.The three-year deal he signed in September 2024 expires at the end of this season and talks have been ongoing since May whenArsenal ended their long wait to be champions. Negotiations were put on hold during the summer transfer window but the Spaniard has reached a ­verbal agreement to extend his stay for a second time.Football Daily | Brighton’s organised chaos viciously pecks Arsenal into submissionRead moreThe length of the contract is unknown but it is understood Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, will commit his future for at least another three years. The 44-year-old is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City at the end of last season.Arsenal have been keen to reward Arteta for transforming the club. His current contract is believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal will cement his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world.As well as leading Arsenal to a first Premier League title since 2004, Arteta last season guided them to the Champions League final, which theylost to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootoutin Budapest. The club started this season with seven straight wins in all competitions before Saturday’s surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton.Arteta reiterated before that game that he was relaxed about his contract situation. “I think we are all very much aligned,” he said. “Whenever the time is right, we’ll get that done. There is nothing to be concerned about. I think we both have the same ambition and the same will.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal are also keen to extend Declan Rice’s contract, the England midfielder having entered the final two years of his deal. It is understood the club have an option to extend it by 12 months but would like to agree new terms in line with their policy of securing Arteta’s most important players on long-term contracts.Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Mariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against Køge | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Mariona Caldentey scored a penalty in injury time in Arsenal’s 1-0 win against HB Køge, after a Chloe Kelly goal in the 13th minute was disallowed by VAR
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Mariona Caldentey scored a penalty in injury time in Arsenal’s 1-0 win against HB Køge, after a Chloe Kelly goal in the 13th minute was disallowed by VAR
Content: Mariona Caldentey celebrates scoring from the spot after after Selina Cerci was brought down in injury time.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMariona Caldentey celebrates scoring from the spot after after Selina Cerci was brought down in injury time.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Champions LeagueMariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against KøgeSuzanne Wrackat Mangata Developments StadiumTue 22 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMariona Caldentey’s 93rd-minute penalty delivered a win and a hefty dose of relief to fans bouncing behind the goal in the North Bank after the ball hit the back of the net, but ­Arsenal’s narrow defeat of HB Køge in their Champions League opener left more questions unanswered than answered for the struggling Gunners.The puffed cheeks of the manager, Renée Slegers, said it all when the full-time whistle went. If it had been revealed after the final whistle that a force field surrounded the opposition goal at Meadow Park, many would have believed it, such was the extent of Arsenal’s ridiculous profligacy in front of goal in their league-phase opener.“It was a mentality and resilience win today,” said Slegers. “The football didn’t give us the win … but we get the goal as a squad.”Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern MunichRead moreExactly what is stopping Arsenal from getting the ball in the back of the net with a swagger reflective of their talent-laden squad is hard to pinpoint.Yes, teams are defending excellently against them, as a battling Køge and their goalkeeper Alberte Vingum did on Tuesday night, but this feels like an Arsenal problem: a mentality one, a training ground one, a ruthlessness one.Practically solving the issue is a multifaceted undertaking, but “making things simple and easy to understand and easy to execute are probably the main two” focuses for Slegers.“Then it’s also about involving the players as much as possible. Getting their input: ‘What do you see? What do you feel on the pitch? What’s your perception in the moment and your analysis afterwards?’”The shadow of Sunday’s trip to Stamford Bridge loomed large at Meadow Park with eight changes made to the team thatsalvaged a point against Manchester Uniteddeep into added time on Saturday.The hope, without being ­disrespectful to their Danish opposition, was that this game would alleviate the frustration the Gunners are experiencing in front of goal, breaking the mental block several players seem to be suffering from. ­Unfortunately, the A-Liga leaders had other ideas.The Gunners’ pressure in the opening 20 minutes, which the Køge manager, Kristian Mørch, described as “like plunging into ice-cold water” that they just had to “try to survive, calm the panic, calm the fear, and then act our way out of it”, seemed to have yielded the breakthrough in the 13th minute, when Caitlin Foord kept an attack alive before sending the ball to Taylor Hinds. The full-back fed Kyra Cooney-Cross and the Australian midfielder’s neat flick was turned in by Chloe Kelly on the volley with the outside of her leg. It was a fine finish but the video assistant referee intervened to penalise an offside Stina Blackstenius for straying into the line of sight of Vingum. Had the hosts got an early goal, the game may have opened up for them a little.View image in fullscreenChloe Kelly scores in the 13th minute before the goal was disallowed with Stina Blackstenius ruled offside.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesThat the match reached half-time still goalless was somewhat inexplicable, but also symbolic of Arsenal’s stuttering start to the season, with just five points from their three Women’s Super League games after consecutive draws, against Crystal Palace and Manchester United.The scale of the achievement for the visiting team was demonstrated by the buoyant celebrations of their coaching staff as soon as the half-time whistle was blown. Mørch bellowed “good job in here”, before tripping on a railing and receiving a chorus of boos from the home fans behind the opposition dugout. He walked across the pitch towards the dressing room with a smile on his face and a finger to his lips shushing the crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTheir decision to celebrate every positive action was a conscious one. “We agreed before the game that we’re going to celebrate every possible win, even just the goalkeeper sometimes catching the ball, that’s a win,” said Mørch. “I could see that some of the Arsenal players got a bit annoyed by it, but we had to try and do whatever we could.”“We noticed it,” said Slegers with a smile. “And I understand it from their perspective. It’s a good tactic, I guess, to keep morale in the team high and maybe intimidate the opposition.”Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG peg back Real MadridShowParis Saint-Germaincame from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw atReal Madridin their Women's Champions League opener.Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – asBenficadispatchedJuventus2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game forInterwith a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish sideBK Häckento a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack.Press AssociationPhotograph: Alberto Gardin/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.As the clock edged towards full time, every effort placed high, wide or cut out was wildly celebrated by the Køge substitutes. They were silenced eventually, when Yukina Sakabe upended Selina Cerci in a rare blip from the visiting team and Caldentey converted from the spot.It was crushing for the visiting team, but Mørch was delighted with his team. “Around minute 80, I came to terms with the idea that if something happens, something happens,” he said. “We were so pressed at that point that these things will sometimes happen. So, for me, I’m not going to say the game ended there, but my judgment of the overall ­performance kind of ended there. I’ve seen what I could dream of from the team.”Relief filled the stands packed with red and white after the goal, but with Chelsea up next, nerves of another wasteful season will not settle.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueArsenal WomenHB Køge WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern Munich | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Carlotta Wamser scored a late equaliser as Manchester City battled back from a two-goal deficit to draw 2-2 with Bayern Munich in the Women’s Champions League
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Carlotta Wamser scored a late equaliser as Manchester City battled back from a two-goal deficit to draw 2-2 with Bayern Munich in the Women’s Champions League
Content: Manchester City's Carlotta Wamser (left) is embraced by Laura Blindkilde Brown after her late equaliser for Manchester City.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenManchester City's Carlotta Wamser (left) is embraced by Laura Blindkilde Brown after her late equaliser for Manchester City.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APWomen's Champions LeagueWamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern MunichSophie Downeyat Uhlsport ParkTue 22 Sep 2026 14.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City produced a gutsy performance to fight back and earn a valuable 2-2 draw away at Bayern Munich on their return to the Champions League. José Barcala’s side took the lead through Giulia Gwinn and an unfortunate Kerstin Casparij own goal but Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser earned the visitors a hard-earned point.City’s head coach, Andrée Jeglertz, was pleased with the resolve of his side after a difficult first half. “It [a comeback] has happened before because we know the quality is there,” he said. “The mentality of ­winning and the belief is there. It shows ­something about this group again.Mariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against KøgeRead more“There were definitely two phases of this game. In the first half, Bayern were very good. I think we were a bit slow on the ball … It was almost like we were surprised by the tempo. I know we weren’t but it looked like that. At the end of the first half, we got a little bit back. The trust and the belief at half-time was good so I felt that this is still possible.”It was always going to be a challenging start for the English champions against a Bayern team who have historically thrived in the league phase of this competition. They came into this unbeaten in their last 15 home group-stage matches and on the back of a semi-final run last ­season that, according to Gwinn, had left them “even hungrier and eager for more”. Not only that but the German team have kicked off the defence of their Frauen-Bundesliga title in stunning fashion with five wins from five.City also arrived in Germany full of confidence after an equally impressive start to the season. Their4-2 win over Liverpoolon Friday had been a further sign of their mettle, finding a way to win despite not being at their best.Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG peg back Real MadridShowParis Saint-Germaincame from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw atReal Madridin their Women's Champions League opener.Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – asBenficadispatchedJuventus2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game forInterwith a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish sideBK Häckento a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack.Press AssociationPhotograph: Alberto Gardin/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.European football, however, presents a different test altogether and they came into this game with plenty of unknowns. How would they measure up after a year out of the competition? Could their injury-hit squad juggle the load of European football and domestic challenges?Reality hit in a first half during which a refreshed Bayern took control of proceedings. Barcala had been able to make five changes to his starting XI, having completely rested Klara Bühl and Gwinn against Köln on Saturday, and they looked full of energy.Bühl immediately stretched every sinew of City’s fragile-looking defence with her pace and guile. The 25-year-old was at the heart of everything Bayern created early on, firing a volley wide before setting up the equally prolific Pernille Harder for a half chance.It did not come as a surprise, therefore, that the hosts broke the deadlock with 11 minutes on the clock. It was a move that cut through the heart of Manchester City as Linda Dallmann broke clear to send Gwinn on her way. The full-back saw the pitch open up in front of her, dispatching a cool finish past Ayaka Yamashita in the City goal.View image in fullscreenGiulia Gwinn reacts after opening the scoring.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APIt was moment when the 4,291-strong crowd raised the decibel level, buoyed by their team’s domination and, perhaps also, the Oktoberfest celebrations. This was Bayern’s first outing at Sportpark Unterhaching and the raucous crowd seemed to settle in straight away at their new home.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe pressure on City continued. Struggling to find space in possession, they were guilty of playing into Bayern’s hands, channelling their attack centrally rather than trying to exploit the wide areas. Things got worse when an unwitting Casparij diverted a dangerous Harder cross into her own net to double the score.This City side are made of stern stuff, however, and Jeglertz’s ­players were handed a lifeline just before the break, albeit in controversial fashion. As a blue smoke flare blazed on the pitch, the referee allowed play to continue while Casparij burst forward. Her cross was met by Khadija Shaw, whose shot was deflected into the path of Mead, who tapped home.View image in fullscreenBayern Munich and Manchester City try to stay focused despite a flare on the pitch.Photograph: Michaela Stache/AFP/Getty ImagesThe second half was a much more even affair as the pendulum of momentum swung between the teams. City should have had an equaliser when Aoba Fujino was brought down by Ena Mahmutovic only for the goalkeeper to step up and save Shaw’s penalty.Despite the hosts still looking potent going forward, City could sense that the tide was shifting and found an equaliser with four minutes to play. Wamser, signed from Bayer Leverkusen this summer, arrived unmarked on the edge of the box to rifle home a finish on her return to Germany.The substitute Edna Imade had two big chances to win it for Bayern late on but the visitors held strong. With one of their most difficult games out of the way, they face Real Madrid next week in Manchester with a chance of making another statement on the European stage.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueBayern Munich WomenManchester City WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Giants’ Jaxson Dart could reportedly miss rest of season with knee injury | New York Giants | The Guardian
description: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Content: Jaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APView image in fullscreenJaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APNew York GiantsGiants’ Jaxson Dart could reportedly miss rest of season with knee injuryTesting said to reveal injury is worse than anticipatedQuarterback was hurt against Rams on MondayGuardian sportTue 22 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart will be out for an extended period of time and could miss the rest of the NFL season aftersuffering a knee injuryin Monday night’s loss to the Los Angeles Rams, according to reports Tuesday.ESPNreportedthat the injury to Dart’s left knee was more severe than initially anticipated. Adam Scheftersaidfurther testing has left the Giants and Dart facing the possibility of season-ending surgery.Rams crush Giants but Jaxson Dart escapes ‘devastating outcome’ after knee injuryRead moreThe second-year quarterback was hurt on the opening possession of the Giants’ 28-6 defeat to the Rams. Initial reports said that Dart sprained his MCL and avoided broken bones, with an MRI set for Tuesday. Head coach John Harbaugh said Monday that he believed a “devastating outcome” had been avoided and that he did not expect Dart to be out long-term without giving a further recovery timeline.The 23-year-old started the season strong in New York’s Week 1 win over Dallas but left the field after taking a huge hit from Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart on the Giants’ seventh play Monday night. Dart watched the second half in a track suit on the sidelines. Jameis Winston could not get much going after Dart’s exit, throwing an end-zone interception as New York got all of their points from field goals.Dart was one of several quarterbacks injured around the league in Week 2.Caleb Williamsof the Chicago Bears is week-to-week and will miss some time with a hamstring injury suffered against the Vikings, while the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow in a defeat to the Cowboys and has no timeline for return.Explore more on these topicsNew York GiantsUS sportsNFLnewsShareReuse this content

title: Great Britain exit Billie Jean King Cup after Czechia triumph in quarter-finals | Billie Jean King Cup | The Guardian
description: Great Britain’s stay at the Billie Jean King Cup finals lasted only one match as they lost against Czechia in the last eight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Great Britain’s stay at the Billie Jean King Cup finals lasted only one match as they lost against Czechia in the last eight
Content: Katie Boulter of Great Britain and Linda Noskova of Czechia leave the court after their match in the Billie Jean King Cup.Photograph: Wang He/Getty Images for LTAView image in fullscreenKatie Boulter of Great Britain and Linda Noskova of Czechia leave the court after their match in the Billie Jean King Cup.Photograph: Wang He/Getty Images for LTABillie Jean King CupGreat Britain exit Billie Jean King Cup after Czechia triumph in quarter-finalsDefeats for Kartal and Boulter condemn Britain to lossMen will play Germany in quarter-finals of Davis CupPress AssociationTue 22 Sep 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreat Britain’s stay at theBillie Jean King Cupfinals lasted only one match as they lost against Czechia in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen. Anne Keothavong’s side were bidding to reach the last four for the fourth time in five years but were considerable underdogs and defeats for Sonay Kartal and Katie Boulter sealed their fate.Led by the Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, the entire Czech team is ranked higher than any of Britain’s players, and it was Noskova who sealed victory with a 6-2, 7-6 (3) win against Boulter. That followed a lengthy struggle between Marie Bouzkova and Kartal lasting a minute short of three hours, which the Czech eventually won 7-6 (2), 4-6, 6-4.Patten and Skupski take Great Britain past Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Final 8Read moreIt was a fine effort from Kartal, who was playing her first match in six months after sustaining a stress fracture in her back in Indian Wells in March and she will now hope to finish the season strongly. The Czechs will bid for their seventh title in the competition since 2011, while Britain’s hopes of lifting the trophy for the first time are over for another year.Keothavong’s team have overperformed in the Billie Jean King Cup of late and did so again by reaching the finals, with an understrength team upsetting Australia in April. Neither Kartal nor Boulter were available for that tie, with the former in the early stages of an injury break that led to her missing the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open.Kartal found her range immediately against the 26th-ranked Bouzkova, who has had a very good season, but could not convert a 40-0 lead in the third game to make it 3-0 and was edged out in a first-set tie-break. She fought back well in the second set, often dictating the play against Bouzkova, who was preferred to the Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova.When Kartal broke to lead 2-1 in the deciding set she appeared to be in the ascendancy, but fatigue seemed to catch up with the 24-year-old as Bouzkova reeled off four games in a row. Kartal, now ranked down at 127, hung on grimly, saving three match points and breaking Bouzkova’s serve, but she could not quite get back on level terms.View image in fullscreenAnne Keothavong, captain of Great Britain, shows support for Sonay Kartal during her match against Marie Bouzkova.Photograph: Wang He/Getty Images for LTAThat left Boulter with the formidable task of trying to beat the world No 6 Noskova, who claimed her first grand slam title at SW19 in July. Boulter struggled with her serve in losing the opening four games but she has a very good record playing for her country and thereafter there was little to choose between the players.But Noskova served brilliantly in the tie-break to lead the Czechs into the semi-finals for the first time since 2023.Great Britain’s men, meanwhile, will play Alexander Zverev’s Germany in the quarter-finals of the Davis Cup in November. Britain booked their return to the eight-team finals, held this year in Bologna, over the weekend witha 4-0 victory against Ecuadorat London’s Copper Box.The Davis Cup finals take place at the SuperTennis Arena from 24 to 29 November, with Britain lined up to play either Spain or Austria if they prevail against Germany.Explore more on these topicsBillie Jean King CupTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Henry Pollock triples salary after signing ‘multi-year’ deal to stay at Northampton | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: England back row Henry Pollock has signed a bumper new contract with Northampton
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: England back row Henry Pollock has signed a bumper new contract with Northampton
Content: Fin Smith of Northampton Saints and Henry Pollock of Northampton Saints celebrate after winning the Prem final in June.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFin Smith of Northampton Saints and Henry Pollock of Northampton Saints celebrate after winning the Prem final in June.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianRugby unionHenry Pollock triples salary after signing ‘multi-year’ deal to stay at Northampton‘I’m happy. It’s an exciting place to be right now’Prem champions have moved to tie down huge assetGerard MeagherTue 22 Sep 2026 05.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry Pollock has signed a newNorthamptoncontract worth in excess of £400,000 a year, ensuring he will remain available for England beyond the 2027 World Cup.The 21-year-old has roughly tripled his salary in a “multi-year” deal thought to extend until 2029. Pollock’s future at the club had come into question when his representative, Eddie Hearn, suggested he deserved a seven-figure salary but while the new deal is a long way short of that, he ends up as one of the best paid back-row forwards in England.Shaun Edwards finally lands England coaching role after joining Red RosesRead moreThe Northampton director of rugby, Phil Dowson, had insisted that a “happy medium” had to be reached for the Saints starlet, who has 13 England caps to his name, having already tied down Tommy Freeman to a new deal at Franklin’s Gardens.Pollock, who also earns about £150,000 a year as one of the 25 England players with an enhanced contract, last week said he would like to play abroad one day and try his hand at other sports. But for now his future lies with Northampton, with Hearn insisting there were a number of other lucrative offers turned down. “He left a lot of money on the table to stay with Northampton,” Hearn said. “But it wasn’t even a tough decision for him.”Pollock said: “I’m massively happy to re-sign with Saints, my boyhood club. It’s an exciting place to be right now. We’re in a great spot as a team, but it feels like there’s still so much more growth in us. I’m still young, and we’ve got a young squad with a brilliant group of lads. Some of my best mates are here, and every day everyone pushes each other to improve and be the best players and team we can be. … For where I am in my career, this is exactly where I want to be.”Dowson, who guided Northampton to their second Prem title in three years last summer, added: “Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he’s a young man of outstanding character. Keeping someone with both his talent and mindset is hugely important for the club.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“What’s most exciting is that there’s still so much more to come from him. Henry is incredibly ambitious and constantly looking for ways to improve. He understands that individual success comes from contributing to a successful team, and he’s already taken on leadership responsibilities within the squad despite his age. Physically, he’s an exceptional athlete. He’s explosive, powerful and highly skilful, with the ability to influence a game in a number of different ways. But there are still areas of his game he can develop, and one of Henry’s greatest strengths is how quickly he learns and adapts.”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionNorthamptonEngland rugby union teamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to evade Taliban wins Asian Games silver | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph ‘something special’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph ‘something special’
Content: Afghanistan’s Fariba Hashimi celebrates with her medal alongside her sister Yuldoz Hashimi and teammate Zahra Rezayee.Photograph: Bryan Foo/ReutersView image in fullscreenAfghanistan’s Fariba Hashimi celebrates with her medal alongside her sister Yuldoz Hashimi and teammate Zahra Rezayee.Photograph: Bryan Foo/ReutersCyclingAfghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to evade Taliban wins Asian Games silverFariba Hashimi fled after Taliban returned to power‘This medal can show resilience from Afghan women’Agence France PresseTue 22 Sep 2026 04.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday, hoping it inspires other women in a country whereTalibanauthorities have sharply curtailed their freedoms.Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second behind China’s Guo Li in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph “something special”.Thirteen-year-old swim sensation sets women’s 200m butterfly record at Asian GamesRead more“I can’t explain my feelings now,” the 23-year-old said, before reflecting on how she was attacked with stones and trained disguised as a man when she started out in the sport as a teenager along with her sister Yulduz, who is also now a pro cyclist.“I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I’m really happy that I have fought against that,” she said. “I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.”The Taliban authoritiesreturned to power in 2021andhave since imposed a series of ruleslimiting women’s access to education and public life, including sport. “They took away our freedom, they took away everything from us,” said Hashimi, who hails from the Faryab province in northern Afghanistan and left the country after the Taliban authorities took over.“This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I’m really happy. I’m not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me.”After fleeingAfghanistanwith the help of the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto, Hashimi relocated to Italy where she now lives and trains. She and her sister competed at the Paris Olympics two years ago, and the 2028 Los Angeles Games are now looming into view. “I never want to give up and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles.”Hashimi reserved a special thanks for the Japanese team for playing a part in her silver medal. “I’m here without a mechanic, without any preparation. We brought one guy with us from the national federation, and he just drove the car. We were fixing the bike ourselves. I was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself. Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingTalibanAfghanistannewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups
Content: Gary Bennett, pictured in 2024, said he was was ‘surprised, shocked and disappointed’ by the council’s decision.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGary Bennett, pictured in 2024, said he was was ‘surprised, shocked and disappointed’ by the council’s decision.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianReform UKReform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red CardCharity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groupsJosh HallidayandRobyn VinterTue 22 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led byReform UKended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card.Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader ofSunderlandcity council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”.Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding.The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”.Bennett, who became only thesecond black player in Sunderland’s historywhen he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996.View image in fullscreenGary Bennett in Sunderland’s stripes in 1994.Photograph: PA/AlamyThe former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years.Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces.He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.”Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”.While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants.“You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight. There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.”Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”.He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”.Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum.Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities.The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”.The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest.In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.”He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.Explore more on these topicsReform UKSunderlandCharitiesLocal politicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceed | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted
Author: Timothy Pratt
Headline: Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted
Content: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers at home in Tunis in February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames ‘Fergie’ Chambers at home in Tunis in February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesUS foreign policySpain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceedLawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecutedTimothy PrattTue 22 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts.Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including theSameer Project,in Gaza.His legal defense team, an array of Spanish parliamentarians, and some celebrity supporters havepublicly opposedthe request, calling it political persecution, which would render it illegitimate under Spanish law.The 22-member council of ministers could have rejected the US petition outright on Tuesday but instead opted to remand the request to the Spanish justice system, beginning a legal process which could now take months.Meanwhile, Chambers has begun the process from prison of applying for asylum inSpain– which by law makes it impossible for the country to extradite him until the process is concluded, according to attorney Aitor Martínez, part of Chambers’ legal team.The attorney also told the Guardian that a third request to allow his client to be released on bond while his situation is resolved awaits a judge’s decision, after previous requests have been denied since Spanish police detained him in Ibiza on 10 July.Elma Saiz, minister of inclusion, social security and migration, devoted less than a minute to announcing Tuesday’s council decision to the Spanish press, calling it “purely procedural”.View image in fullscreenElma Saiz called the government’s decision ‘purely procedural’.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPADetails from the weekly meetings are not public, but sources close to the council told the Guardian: “There was debate, and five ministers from Sumar – including the vice-president – pushed back in the meeting.” Sumar, a leftwing coalition, governs jointly with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party.Sánchez’s government has repeatedly expressed support for the Palestinian people, putting him at odds with the Trump administration.Baltasar Garzón,the international human rights lawyer leading Chambers’ legal team, said that Tuesday’s decision “sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause”.“Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and the protection of those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution by the US government, as it is directed against an individual because of his political activity and solidarity withPalestine.”Ione Belarra, secretary-general of Podemos – a progressive party also vital to Sánchez’s interests – said the government “has chosen to keep [Chambers] imprisoned by giving the green light for Trump’s political persecution to proceed to the courts”. Belarra appeared in Parliament on Tuesday afternoon wearing a T-shirt that said “Free Fergie”.She also noted that Spain must hold a general election by August, and said many of her colleagues in Spain’s Congress “are deeply concerned that by the time Fergie Chambers’ case has gone through the judicial process … Spain could have a more conservative, pro-Israel government”The possibility of Chambers being extradited “risks opening the floodgates to Trump’s repression reaching into Spain and the rest ofEuropeand targeting other progressives”, Belarra said.The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to supportHamas.His partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel, told the Guardianlast monththat the $7.5m went to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, paying off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.View image in fullscreenIone Belarra of Podemos.Photograph: David Canales/Sopa/ShutterstockThe self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s charges of “international money laundering” do not hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means.His money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold them stock worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time and his donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries.Chambers’ views and donations have been extensivelyprofiledin US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.Sealed charges against Chambers were originally filed in New Hampshire.Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have previously brought controversy. A weekafter the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he postedon X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”He has also been a staunch critic of the US, tellinga reporterin 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”“I am heartbroken,” Schnabel told the Guardian. The two have a young son and Schnabel is just over three months pregnant. “Fergie could spend the first year of our baby’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass – even though he has not been convicted of any crime,” she said.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policySpainEuropeHamasPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Outgoing UN chief says polluters have treated atmosphere like an ‘open sewer’ | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastation
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastation
Content: Water forms under Nepal's Khumbu glacier. Guterres said the impacts of the climate crisis were ‘hitting harder and spreading further than many anticipated’.Photograph: Alex Treadway/Icimod/ReutersView image in fullscreenWater forms under Nepal's Khumbu glacier. Guterres said the impacts of the climate crisis were ‘hitting harder and spreading further than many anticipated’.Photograph: Alex Treadway/Icimod/ReutersClimate crisisOutgoing UN chief says polluters have treated atmosphere like an ‘open sewer’António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastationOliver Milmanin New YorkTue 22 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 17.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor one last time,António Guterrestried to fix the world’s gaze upon the dangerously escalating climate crisis. But the departing UN secretary general found world leaders still largely focused on other issues, even after a painful summer of stunning climate-driven disasters.Speaking to assembled dignitaries at the UN on Tuesday, Guterres railed against big oil for treating “the atmosphere as an open sewer” and warned again of the catastrophic effects of the climate crisis.Guterres said: “Three years ago, in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in. Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers.“But as tragic events have shown, impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated.”The UN chief said: “Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay. And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable – you are on the right side of history. Keep going.”View image in fullscreenAntónio Guterres at the UN in New York on Tuesday.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockGuterres has been anunflinching advocatefor climate action in his nine years as UN secretary-general, and his departure from the role is set to leave a void in a geopolitical landscape consumed by wars, inflation fears and other economic concerns rather than our rapidly heating planet.“António Guterres has been the most climate-forward secretary-general in UN history; and this speech shows why,” said Alden Meyer, a veteran climate policy expert at E3G. “He clearly laid out the stakes on the climate emergency – the horrific consequences of inaction and the tremendous opportunities in deploying the available solutions.”This summer has been roiled byrecordheatwaves andwildfiresacross the US and Europe, as well as acatastrophicglacier collapse and landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border. A mounting El Nino event, perhaps the largest in modern human history, is meanwhile set to push global temperatures to new record highs andspur a spike in food insecurity.Yet the climate crisis has slipped from the agenda to the extent it has been little surprise that this week’s UN general assembly is not expected to bear any major new commitments to slash planet-heating emissions or to accelerate the rollout of a clean energy sector that is, while growing,still not on paceto avert further dangerous temperature rises.Even Climate Week, an array of events across New York that overlaps with the UN gathering, is not expected to deliver any major announcements. While a record number of people – more than 100,000 – are set to attend Climate Week events, organizers have lamented an outbreak of “climate hushing” among political and business leaders who have determined the public has tuned out of the planetary emergency.Donald Trump, who has dismantled environmental policies in the US and repeatedly called climate science a “hoax”, has been a major factor in this, even though his UN speech this year dwelled less on the topic than last year’sincendiaryversion.View image in fullscreenThe Lucas fire in California earlier this month.Photograph: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/APBut those who advocate for action said there was broader blame to be cast upon the complacency of other leaders who have failed to ensure the world does notblow past previously agreed temperature thresholds. There is still widespread public alarm about the climate crisis, polling shows, despite the disconnect by political leaders.“We are in a terrible spot. That is the truth, because hypocrisy has won over concrete action,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama, who is pushing for a universal declaration of the rights of nature at the UN this week.“As to the international arena, it’s a terrible situation. Look at the signs. A war in Iran … the other sign that we have is this forthcoming El Nino. So do we need more signs? No, it’s terrible. But what are people doing? Nothing.”While Panama has acted strongly to cut its own emissions, other countries are failing, Navarro argued. “The war in Iran, the El Nino – has it had any impact in terms of countries or political leaders stepping up with bold commitments for real change? Zero,” he said.“All I see around me is hypocrisy, BS, beautiful speeches, zero action. Let’s start telling the truth and start telling the truth to our own citizens. We’re facing climate change and it will have an impact and we’re not doing enough to alter it.”‘It’s my duty to tell the truth’: UN chief on the climate crisis, capitalism and reasons to be hopefulRead moreThe rays of optimism at Climate Week so far have centered on relief over the fact Trump is set to become a lame-duck president and also the continuing growth of renewables such as solar and wind. “Climate” may have become a taboo term for some, but investment in clean energy,particularly in China, isbooming.“The economy is built on batteries and the sun in California, which we know is cheaper,” said Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and potential Democratic candidate for the next presidential election.“You can bottle the sun, you can catch the wind, you don’t have to worry about the sun getting blockaded in the strait of Hormuz. It gets cheaper and cheaper, in the abundance.”Much of this progress is still being overshadowed, Newsom conceded, by Trump. “He’s trying to take us back to the 19th century,” Newsom said of the president. “He’s doubling down on stupid.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisUnited NationsAntónio GuterresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’ | Diana, Princess of Wales | The Guardian
description: Brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, says ‘accuracy is important’ as he responds to broadcaster’s threat to sue over claims made in memoir
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, says ‘accuracy is important’ as he responds to broadcaster’s threat to sue over claims made in memoir
Content: Charles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, my Sister, in the window of a bookshop in London on 22 September 2026.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenCharles Spencer’s memoir, Swan Song: Diana, my Sister, in the window of a bookshop in London on 22 September 2026.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersDiana, Princess of WalesEarl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’Brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, says ‘accuracy is important’ as he responds to broadcaster’s threat to sue over claims made in memoirJamie GriersonandCaroline DaviesTue 22 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarl Spencer has apologised to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book aboutDiana,
