Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s.Morgan had earlierthreatened to sue Spencerover “fabricated inaccuracies” and “examples of brazen falsity” in the book, which was published on Tuesday.In the memoir, the earl claims Morgan was in part responsible for the publication of photographs taken by an allegedly hidden camera in a gym, of Diana working out in a leotard.But the broadcaster told his audience on YouTube on Monday that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror and when he was working at the Sun.Morgan called on Diana’s brother to pulp the remaining copies of his book and said he had instructed his lawyers to demand the work be pulled from sale immediately.Later on Tuesday, Spencer issued a statement apologising to Morgan and admitting he had incorrectly assumed Morgan had been editor of the Mirror at the time.“Earl Spencer’s account of his conversation withPiers Morganis accurate.“Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister’s funeral,” the statement said.“The book then records Earl Spencer’s assumption that Mr Morgan’s response was because he was editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group had published highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym.“The photographs were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. Mr Morgan has pointed out that he did not join the Daily Mirror until October 1995. As an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error.”In his response to Spencer’s apology, Morgan also wrote he was “neither surly nor annoyed” but had been “very respectful” to the earl during their telephone conversation.He wrote: “Earl Spencer’s account of our phone call is also deeply misleading.“I was neither surly nor annoyed, but instead, very respectful to him and his family, as I wrote in my diaries, The Insider. It would seem that Spencer’s recollection of phone calls is very suspect.”Morgan also doubled down on his threat of legal action, writing on social media: “Earl Spencer has apologised to me for his defamatory lies published in his new book, Swan Song, published today.“But I am pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King’s Trust.”The earl has made a series of claims inSwan Song: Diana, My Sister, including that King Charles said “we’ll forget her soon enough” after she died, which has prompted a war of words between him and Buckingham Palace.The book also contains allegations about Morgan, who has rejected the claims.Speaking earlier on his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan said: “Many allies of his majesty have called into question these facts, ever since the most salacious accusations were serialised by the Daily Mail.“Many royal commentators and experts have lined up to say that they simply don’t ring true. The king himself issued a furious rebuke that is almost without precedent. But, in essence, this has all been about opinions. Recollections may vary, after all. Well, until now.“Because I can exclusively reveal on Uncensored that Earl Spencer’s book contains fabricated inaccuracies which will strike to the heart of his credibility. Spencer recounts how he personally called round the tabloid newspaper editors to uninvite them from Princess Diana’s funeral, after they had all been invited. I remember this well, because I was one of them.”Morgan read an extract from Spencer’s book, which claims the editor “snarled with annoyance before he hung up”, as well as the passage concerning the intrusive photographs.He told his audience on YouTube that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror.He said: “Well, this is all pretty extraordinary stuff, isn’t it? And very damning, particularly about me. I come across in the most despicable manner imaginable. There’s just one problem. It’s all bullshit and very, very easy bullshit for me to prove it.“The photographs which he says that I published were printed by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. I joined the Daily Mirror in October in 1995. In fact, at the time of the gym pictures, I was doing a showbiz column on the Mirror’s arch-rival, the Sun. About as far removed from responsibility for the Mirror scoop as I could possibly have been.”Morgan, who was the editor of the Mirror from 1995 to 2004, continued: “Earl Spencer was estranged from Diana and living in South Africa at the time of her death. As editor of the Daily Mirror, I had lunch with her at Kensington Palace with Prince William. After that, it wasn’t uncommon for her to call my office or for me to run stories by her … Ironically, by that time in her life I think I was probably talking to her more often than he was.“My question, though, is this: if Earl Spencer can be so incredibly, defamatorily wrong about such basic facts involving me, well, why should we believe anything else he puts in this book?”He later added: “In the meantime, Earl Spencer, you’ll be hearing – and your publishers – from my lawyers.”Bookshops across London were reported to have appeared quiet on the release day of Spencer’s memoir – with the £28 book marked at half its cover price in some stores.Dozens of copies with red “half price” stickers were stacked in Waterstones flagship Piccadilly store – the largest in Europe. It is also marked as half price on the Waterstones website.Explore more on these topicsDiana, Princess of WalesPiers MorganMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Worse than the scramble for Oasis tickets’: England’s sustainable farming funds run out in just six hours | Farming | The Guardian
description: Entire £233m budget for 2026 allocated in less than a day, leaving thousands of farmers disappointed
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Entire £233m budget for 2026 allocated in less than a day, leaving thousands of farmers disappointed
Content: Farmers have faced a tough year with extreme heat, droughts and soaring fertiliser costs.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFarmers have faced a tough year with extreme heat, droughts and soaring fertiliser costs.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesFarming‘Worse than the scramble for Oasis tickets’: England’s sustainable farming funds run out in just six hoursEntire £233m budget for 2026 allocated in less than a day, leaving thousands of farmers disappointedPippa NeillEnvironment reporterTue 22 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of farmers have been left empty-handed with the government’s 2026 nature funding spent in just six hours.The £233m sustainable farming incentive (SFI) scheme opened for applications from farmers at 10am on Tuesday.SFI is part of a package of payments that replaced the EU’s common agricultural policy, paying farmers to look after nature, soil and other public goods, rather than simply for farming and owning land.But by 4pm on Tuesday – just six hours after it opened – the government confirmed that the 2026 SFI scheme was closed for applications, with all of the budget allocated.For many farmers this was their first opportunity to apply to SFI since thescheme’s sudden closurein March 2025. The next opportunity to apply for funding will be in 2027.“Vicki Hird, the strategic lead on agriculture at The Wildlife Trusts, compared the scramble for SFI funding to “the scramble to get Oasis tickets” and said it was shocking to watch the funding disappear so quickly.“The government really needs to get the budget in order to ensure farmers have the funding they need for nature, food security and national security,” she said.Alice Groom, the head of sustainable land policy at the RSPB, said it was “unprecedented” for the budget to be used up so quickly. “We thought the money would go quickly but not necessarily in one day,” she said.“Defra doesn’t have a way of managing the budget. SFI is supposed to be spent on meeting environmental goals and transitioning to environmental farming, but it’s now first come first served.“There will likely be thousands of farmers who haven’t been able to apply for any funding, which will have implications for their ability to deliver for the environment on their farm,” she said.View image in fullscreenFarmers have suffered the ‘toughest summer in a generation’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesThroughout the day, farmers who had been experiencing problems with their SFI applications had to wait up to five hours to speak to someone to get help. Martin Lines, the CEO of the Nature FriendlyFarmingNetwork, said this will have meant they won’t have spoken to someone until after the scheme had closed.This year has been extremely challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. The SFI funding will have been seen as a way for many farmers to invest in the future of their businesses, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLines said the fact that thousands of farmers would inevitably miss out on funding was “terribly sad” and showed the “desperation” many farmers were experiencing.“If they can’t get access to the funding, how will they remain resilient?” he asked.Groom added that this would “absolutely” affect the government’s ability to meet its legally binding nature targets, including its statutory target to restore 30% of nature by 2030.“Lots of targets will be missed, we’re really worried,” she said.With farmers having suffered through what the NFU has described as the “toughest summer in a generation”, the employers’ association said the government must urgently set out a plan for the 2027 SFI scheme, with increased budget transparency.Andy Burnham, the prime minister, announced in August that there would be an extra £50m in funding for the 2026 SFI; that money was included in this funding round. The NFU said it welcomed this but “remains concerned that the limited SFI budget endangers longstanding environmental delivery and fails to recognise farmers’ desire to deliver greater environmental outcomes”.Explore more on these topicsFarmingRural affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: California and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projects | US politics | The Guardian
description: US officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuels
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuels
Content: Breckenridge, Michigan, Construction of a wind farm. The 133-turbine, 212.8-megawatt project is being constructed by Invenergy Wind LLC and DTE Energy.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBreckenridge, Michigan, Construction of a wind farm. The 133-turbine, 212.8-megawatt project is being constructed by Invenergy Wind LLC and DTE Energy.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesUS politicsCalifornia and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projectsUS officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuelsAssociated PressTue 22 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued theTrump administrationover its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.California attorney general Rob Bonta said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts.New York attorney general Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off theNew Yorkand New Jersey coast.The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country.View image in fullscreenThe Breckenridge wind warm in Michigan.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThe Interior Department started buying back offshore wind leases in March after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action.In exchange for reimbursements of lease fees, companies are investing in fossil fuel projects and geothermal energy. Interior secretary Doug Burgum has said that companies “are shifting investment back toward dependable, secure energy infrastructure that can power our economy and lower utility costs”.James called the deals illegal and said they would ultimately increase Americans’ electricity bills by sabotaging states’ ability to meet growing energy demands.“Americans are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need,” James said in a statement. “These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers’ bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states.”Bonta said that as a national and global leader in the fight against climate change, California finds itself enmeshed in “avoidable and unnecessary battles with our own federal government” to advance climate action and move toward clean energy.Bonta, speaking at a Climate Week event in New York, said climate action needs to match the scope, speed and scale of the problem.“Because we have to go to court and block an unlawful action by the Trump administration each time, it takes time. It slows the process down and we know we are running out of time and we need to be urgent and aggressive,” Bonta said Tuesday in remarks just before Trump addressed the UN general assembly.“We’re still all in, in California,” Bonta said. “No matter what the Trump administration does, we’re going to push to participate in the climate action that is needed to meet this moment and to rise to the occasion.”Later in the day, Bonta was among the California and New York officials participating in a Climate Week panel about state leadership on wind energy. California energy commission chair David Hochschild said at the New York City bar that the power to drive a transition away from fossil fuels still rests primarily with the states.While Trump, who often talks about his hatred of wind power, can slow it down and make it more expensive, Hochschild said, “he can’t put the genie back in the bottle”.Trump has said his goal is to not let any “windmills” be built.New York state energy research and development authority president Doreen Harris said they are all confident they will ultimately succeed in court, however they need energy infrastructure in their states for a reliable grid.“The reality is, even if successful, the question becomes who is going to invest,” Harris said. She added: '“We just want to get back to building.”Attorneys general in Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont joined New York’s suit.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsWest CoastCaliforniaNew YorkTrump administrationDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study finds | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: EVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same age
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: EVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same age
Content: Electric cars with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should not automatically be seen as worn out, the BVRLA chief said.Photograph: Miles Willis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElectric cars with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should not automatically be seen as worn out, the BVRLA chief said.Photograph: Miles Willis/Getty ImagesElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsHigh-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study findsEVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same ageZoe WoodTue 22 Sep 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMotorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find anelectric vehicle(EV) ultimately more reliable than a petrol vehicle, according to a study.An analysis of 47.4m MOT tests found that after cars were driven 90,000 to 120,000 miles, EVs were about 25% less likely to fail than petrol models of the same age (based on a failure rate of 16.5% versus 22.1%).Beyond 120,000 miles, 16% of EVs failed, compared with 23.5% of petrol cars. The study found relatively little difference between the two fuel types at lower mileages.Range Rover launches its first electric vehicle, with starting price of £154,070Read moreThe study by the consultancy New AutoMotive on behalf of the industry group the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA) comes as a growing number of EVs change hands. Many used to belong to company and leasing fleets so have potentially racked up a lot of miles.Toby Poston, the BVRLA chief executive, said that mileage is “one of the first things people look at when buying a used car, and passing 60,000 or 70,000 miles can have a big impact on how a vehicle is perceived”.He added: “What this data shows is that mileage alone should not put consumers off. A well-maintained, higher-mileage electric car can be an extremely durable used vehicle.“That matters because the used market is where the transition to electric becomes accessible to millions more motorists. Giving buyers confidence in these cars will be critical to creating a healthy and affordable secondhand EV market.”Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, which carried out the research, said that high mileage “isn’t a proxy for poor condition in the way buyers have traditionally assumed. The data suggests the mechanical simplicity of an electric drivetrain starts to become increasingly valuable as cars accumulate miles.”The study also identified areas where electric cars performed worse, particularly tyres. EVs recorded nearly twice as many tyre defects as petrol cars and older, low-mileage electric cars showed increased friction-brake defects. Researchers attributed the latter to corrosion associated with the brakes being used less frequently.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMOT tests examine statutory roadworthiness, including brakes, tyres, suspension, steering and lights, but do not measure battery health, degradation or charging performance. This information would therefore need to be considered alongside mechanical roadworthiness when assessing any used EV, the researchers said.“This isn’t an argument for buying a used EV without doing your homework,” Poston said. “Buyers should look at its history, condition, tyres and battery health just as they would scrutinise the engine, gearbox and service history of a petrol or diesel car.“What we can now challenge is the idea that an electric car with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should automatically be regarded as worn out.”Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsMotoring (Money)Motoring (Technology)Automotive industryGreenhouse gas emissionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Patagonia town where Nepal’s deadly glacier flood could be repeated – and what they’ve learned | Argentina | The Guardian
description: The risk to El Chaltén in Argentina has been known for years but recent findings and the Nepal disaster have brought planning for the worst-case scenario into sharp focus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The risk to El Chaltén in Argentina has been known for years but recent findings and the Nepal disaster have brought planning for the worst-case scenario into sharp focus
Content: Laguna Torre at the base of the Torre glacier, which could cause a glacier flood in El Chaltén, Argentina. Photograph: Javier RasettiThe risk to El Chaltén in Argentina has been known for years but recent findings and the Nepal disaster have brought planning for the worst-case scenario into sharp focusByMaría de los Ángeles Orfila in El ChalténSupported byAbout this contentTue 22 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe images from Nepal stopped Daniela Schmidt in her tracks. A geologist at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina, she watchedthe deadly flash floodson 26 August tear through everything in their path, people running for their lives as the water and debris swept over the landscape.“I had never seen anything like it,” she says. “This was one of the most catastrophic events on a global scale related to these glacial floods.”View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the Nepal floods in Nuwakot district, 26 August. Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockThe shock deepened as the first geological figures emerged: the volume of glacier ice and rock that had collapsed and the scale of the resulting flow. Schmidt began comparing them with the cases she had studied during her PhD. Very few glacial lake outburst floods, she realised, had reached anything close to this magnitude.But Nepal also changed the way she saw her own work. Schmidt studies theglacial lake outburst flood (Glof) that could occur at Laguna Torre, in Argentina’s Santa Cruz province, and its potential impact on El Chaltén, a nearby town known as the country’s trekking capital.The disaster already exists on her computer screen: data, models, flood simulations and maps. According to her studies, if the northern slope of Cerro Solo were to collapse into Laguna Torre, at the base of the Torre glacier, a massive volume of water could travel the 5 miles (8km) to El Chaltén in 20 minutes, sweeping along logs, rocks and sediment.Map of the Torre glacier and Torre glacierThe discharge could reach 1,769 cubic metres (62,472 cubic feet) a second, rushing down the Fitz Roy River towards the town and inundating its only access bridge and other critical infrastructure. For anyone in the valley, those 20 minutes would be the window to reach safety. “It is the worst-case flood scenario,” says Schmidt, adding that, in the most conservative analysis, the flow would take between 45 minutes and an hour to reach the town.“You can’t say it will happen on a specific day or at a specific time, but society needs to be prepared,” Schmidt warns. “It is going to happen.”View image in fullscreenSustained melting has created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, which poses a risk to the town below if the glacier collapses. Photograph: Javier RasettiThe threat was already changing how El Chaltén prepared for the future, but the disaster in Nepal has brought these risks to the forefront. Although the scale of that event and the El Chaltén scenario differ, Schmidt sees a similarity in the mechanism: a mass suddenly plunging into a body of water can trigger a flash flood with immense destructive power.Authorities fromLos Glaciares national parkand the municipality of El Chaltén, along with local organisations and various scientific institutions, are working to develop the country’s first Glof early-warning system and draft evacuation protocols.“We are preparing for the worst-case scenario,” says Enrique Rivero, El Chaltén’s secretary of government.The silhouette of Cerro Solo is unmistakable. The vertical granite peak, rising to 2,121 metres (6,959ft) above sea level, is reflected in Laguna Torre amid floating icebergs. That is where the risk begins.View image in fullscreenAs the ice on the Torre glacier retreats, the surrounding slopes can also shift. Photograph: Javier RasettiThe Torre glacier is estimated to have lost 4 sq km (1.5 sq miles) of surface area, while its ice thinned by 60-70 metres between 1952 and 2023. As the ice retreats, the balance of the surrounding slopes also shifts – a process researchers describe as a “release of stress”.This transformation is visible in landslides and rockfalls that leave scars across the mountainside. Between 2002 and 2023, the volume of displaced material increased, while the speed of movement doubled. “It moves slowly, but during heavy rainfall or high temperatures, it accelerates in pulses,” Schmidt says. “As the slopes become unstable, they can slide, dumping a large volume of material into the lake and causing it to overflow. It just needs a trigger.”Her models contemplate landslides involving between 8m and 13m cubic metres of material. If a mass of that size were to collapse into Laguna Torre, it could generate a wave up to 5.8 metres high. The wave would travel across the lake at approximately 20 metres a second, reaching the Fitz Roy River in just one minute and 40 seconds.Under the most conservative and the worst-case scenarios, a flood would eventually reach the bridge and render it unusable. The bridge is the only land access connecting El Chaltén to provincial route 41.The municipality has already ordered the dredging of the river channel and the clearing of the riverbed beneath the bridge. “But now we are being told that the water level could rise by up to 5 metres, which suggests the bridge could be swept away,” Rivero says.View image in fullscreenFitz Roy River in the Laguna Torre valley. The river could rise rapidly by up to 5 metres if a glacial lake outburst flood occurred. Photograph: Javier RasettiThe flood could also affect critical infrastructure located just metres from the riverbanks, including gas and power plants, schools and homes. Discussions have already begun on a contingency plan that considers, among other measures, potential relocation.“Gas supplies coming from Río Gallegos – the capital of Santa Cruz province – would be cut off, leaving us without heating,” says Paula Chaparro, a member of the El Chaltén Mountain Guides Association. “If the power grid fails, El Chaltén relies on generators running on fuel oil; if they run out of fuel, we lose electricity. It’s a problematic chain reaction.”If the event were to occur in summer, peaking in December to February, the town would be cut off, withmore than 27,000 people– locals and tourists alike – stranded in the town. At present, according to residents, there is no signage indicating evacuation routes or instructions, nor do hotels warn guests about the risk.The risk has been known for years, but the available instruments could not precisely determine how quickly the slope was moving or, crucially, how much water could be displaced in a collapse. “We’ll have to wait and see if it happens” was a common reaction among locals, says Sofía Bonangelino, a member ofFriends of Los Glaciares National Park, an association that manages three campsites.View image in fullscreenThe Fitz Roy River bridge, which provides the only access to the town of El Chaltén. Photograph: Javier RasettiEven Horacio Pelozo, the park superintendent, acknowledges this: “The initial studies really weren’t alarming, or anything of the sort.”However, a key new piece of data emerged, Pelozo says, alongside the measurements of the slope’s movement: sustained melting had created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, the depth of which now exceeds 220 metres. Previous estimates had placed the depth at about 80 metres.View image in fullscreenThe remains of Blatten in Switzerland after the collapse of the Birch glacier, 29 May 2025. Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/APThen, in May 2025, an image from the Swiss Alps demonstrated the potential scale of a collapse involving ice and rock:the Birch glacier collapsedon to much of the village of Blatten, burying it in a matter of seconds.Los Glaciares national park has taken steps to address the risk of a Glof, including relocating the De Agostini campsite, rerouting hiking trails, installing warning signs and establishing an evacuation protocol involving at least 25 personnel to manage potential floods during peak visitor seasons.The response has expanded to include coordination with local and national agencies, such as the municipality of El Chaltén, in the Santa Cruz province, the Federal Emergency Agency and the Argentine Geological and Mining Service, though no formal contingency plan has been finalised yet.The El Chaltén city council has passed a resolution to develop an evacuation plan, while a detection system with six monitoring stations – equipped with cameras, sensors and emergency buoys – is in development to trigger alerts via sirens, SMS and email. Yet funding cuts have delayed implementation, with the estimated cost of $220,000 (£163,000) exceeding the park’s current capacity, as noted by Eduardo Marino, a former secretary of government for El Chaltén.“Let’s not talk about Glofs, because it will scare off tourists” – that concern is circulating around town. And it is not hard to understand why – a large part of the community relies on tourism for its livelihood.View image in fullscreenEl Chaltén seen from the beginning of the Laguna Torre trail, which is popular with hikers. Photograph: Javier RasettiMarino owns a hotel; Bonangelino runs a bookstore, rents out a cabin, and works as a ski instructor. For them, as for so many other residents, protecting tourism also means protecting their own livelihoods.View image in fullscreenEduardo Marino who owns a hotel in El Chaltén. Photograph: Javier RasettiMarino was asked to drop the subject until the summer season was over. He refused. He knows a day of heavy rain or exceptionally high temperatures could be enough to trigger an event they are not yet prepared for.For those who work in the mountains, information is key to risk management. “Closing down isn’t the solution,” says Chaparro. The idea, she says, is to offer alternatives: different trails, different activities. “It’s not about being afraid; it’s about staying alert.”High risk yet home to thousands: the makeshift towns at the mercy of landslides and floods in PeruRead moreWhen her colleague Ariel Puntin speaks to local people about the threat he still encounters some who doubt the mountainside could collapse. The problem, he says, is that the gap between “it could happen today” and “it might never happen” is too wide to easily learn how to live with the risk.View image in fullscreenThe Fitz Roy River flooding could affect gas and power plants built near its banks, as well as homes and businesses. Photograph: Javier RasettiFor Schmidt, the events in Nepal should serve as a wake-up call, but also as an opportunity to improve the town’s preparedness. “The community and the tourists must be protected and kept safe in the face of this new reality of constantly changing glacial landscapes,” she says.Bonangelino has noticed a positive shift in recent months. As the studies’ findings have been explained to the community, she says, acceptance has grown that the phenomenon is real and that preparation is necessary.“We are a resilient, responsible community that cares deeply about its environment,” she says. “We rely on tourism, and we aren’t going to neglect it.”Explore more on these topicsSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanArgentinaAmericasFloodingGlaciersIceNatural disastersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Woman and three children killed after ‘intense’ fire ravages Merseyside house | Merseyside | The Guardian
description: One other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in Bootle
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: One other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in Bootle
Content: Emergency personnel at the semi-detached house in Bootle, Sefton, where four people lost their lives.Photograph: Eleanor Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenEmergency personnel at the semi-detached house in Bootle, Sefton, where four people lost their lives.Photograph: Eleanor Barlow/PAMerseysideWoman and three children killed after ‘intense’ fire ravages Merseyside houseOne other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in BootleMark BrownNorth of England correspondentTue 22 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman and three children have died after an overnight fire ripped through a semi-detached house on Merseyside.The Merseyside fire and rescue service (MFRS) said crews arrived at the blaze in Bootle at about 3.45am on Tuesday.Speaking at the scene, the chief fire officer, Nick Searle, said four people inside the house had died and another person, outside the property, had been taken to hospital. He said the fire was “intense” and “spread very rapidly”.Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house, which was alight when they arrived, they added.One local person, who did not want to be named, said: “We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses. The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street.”Another person said: “I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines.”At the scene, Searle said: “Firstly, our thoughts are with everyone who’s been affected by the tragic incident this morning.”He said the MFRS control room received a 999 call at 3.38am and crews from surrounding stations were mobilised, with the first fire engine arriving at 3.45am to find the house “well alight”.“Crews who were wearing breathing apparatus entered the building to search the property for occupants and fighting intense fire, which had spread very rapidly.”Other crews found a casualty outside the property, and he was taken into the care of North West ambulance service and transferred to hospital,” Searle said.“During the course of the search of the property, firefighters discovered four casualties, showing no signs of life, and it’s now been confirmed that all four have tragically lost their lives.”He said MFRS and Merseyside police would carry out a full joint investigation into the cause of the fire. “Our thoughts remain with the loved ones of those lost, and fire crews will maintain a visible and reassuring presence in the community over the coming days.”The MFRS area manager, Kevin Longshaw, said: “This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured.“We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident.”Explore more on these topicsMerseysideFirefightersEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charlotte Church accuses Ed Sheeran of ‘choosing capitalism over doing the right thing’ | Charlotte Church | The Guardian
description: Church, a prominent supporter of Palestinian causes, criticises Sheeran over removal of Macklemore from US tour
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Church, a prominent supporter of Palestinian causes, criticises Sheeran over removal of Macklemore from US tour
Content: Ed Sheeran (left) and Charlotte ChurchComposite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran (left) and Charlotte ChurchComposite: Getty ImagesCharlotte ChurchCharlotte Church accuses Ed Sheeran of ‘choosing capitalism over doing the right thing’Church, a prominent supporter of Palestinian causes, criticises Sheeran over removal of Macklemore from US tourNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentTue 22 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharlotte Church has accused Ed Sheeran of choosing “consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing” over the removal of his friend and support act Macklemore from his US tour.Sheeran’s tour was thrown into crisis afterMacklemore made “free Palestine” declarations on stage. After a significant backlash, including pressure from the owners of stadiums hosting scheduled shows, the rapper was removed from the tour. Shortly afterwards,Sheeran’s other support acts quitin solidarity.Sheeranaddressed the controversy during his concert inPhiladelphia on Saturday, saying what was happening in Gaza was “catastrophic and unjustifiable”. He apologised to fans, saying: “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.” He added that he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics.Church, who has previously been vocal about her support for Palestinians, said: “Ed Sheeran, we’re watching you,” during a gig in Cardiff on Sunday, and urged the audience to chant “free Palestine”.She said: “Whilst he [Sheeran] has made millions and has an enormous following – he has an enormous platform to do real good in the world – he chose consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing.“So we say the same thing to Ed Sheeran because fuck the fact that musicians shouldn’t be involved in politics. Fuck that shit. Politics is life.”She added: “Ed Sheeran, we’re watching you,” and repeated the phrase multiple times with her bandmates.3:09Ed Sheeran sorry for ‘mistakes’ as tour resumes – videoChurch has taken part in pro-Palestinian demonstrations and has been a vocal opponent of thegovernment’s proscription of Palestine Action. She has said the conflict has “massively changed” her.Macklemore claimed that Robert Kraft – the CEO of the Kraft Group, which owns Gillette Stadium – personally called Sheeran to say he would not be allowed to perform at the venue. Sheeran later said he would not be drawn into a public debate about the war in Gaza and that it was “the promoter’s decision” to removeMacklemore.On Saturday, Sheeran became emotional as he said he had been unsure “whether this tour would be carrying on” and “whether I even wanted to be an artist at all” after criticism levelled at him.This included, just hours earlier, a Saturday Night Live UK sketch, which depicted the singer as “sitting on the fence” as war broke out between humans and AI robots.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protesting outside an Ed Sheeran concert in Philadelphia.Photograph: Joe Lamberti/Getty Images“I don’t like to take sides. I don’t want to alienate any of my fans – humans or robots,” cast member Annabel Marlow said, as Sheeran. “A lot of my tickets are bought by scalping bots. Sometimes, when it comes to conflicts, the bravest thing you can do is to say nothing at all.”Meanwhile, The Great British Bake Off star Nadiya Hussain shared a widely circulated video in which the therapist Megan Cooper accused Sheeran of crying “white tears” and playing “the victim”.Sheeran is next due to perform on Friday 25 September at Kraft’s Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts.Explore more on these topicsCharlotte ChurchEd SheeranMacklemoreIsrael-Gaza warPop and rockGazaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jim Ratcliffe halts production at Hull chemical plants over ‘ridiculous’ gas prices | Jim Ratcliffe | The Guardian
description: Billionaire owner of Ineos says company ‘cannot compete’ with global market despite efficiency of Humberside sites
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Billionaire owner of Ineos says company ‘cannot compete’ with global market despite efficiency of Humberside sites
Content: Sir Jim Ratcliffe also claimed that the government’s energy policy was causing ‘economic vandalism’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSir Jim Ratcliffe also claimed that the government’s energy policy was causing ‘economic vandalism’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesJim RatcliffeJim Ratcliffe halts production at Hull chemical plants over ‘ridiculous’ gas pricesBillionaire owner of Ineos says company ‘cannot compete’ with global market despite efficiency of Humberside sitesJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentTue 22 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBillionaire industrialist SirJim Ratcliffeis pausing production at three chemical plants in Hull, blaming the UK’s “ridiculously high” gas prices.Ratcliffe’schemicals conglomerate, Ineos, said on Tuesday it would “mothball” three chemical plants because the cost made it difficult to compete in the global market.Production has already been paused at two of the Humberside plants and the third is due to come offline in a few days, according toIneos. About 240 people are directly employed by the company across the three sites.Ineos said the number of jobs on Humberside that would be affected by a permanent closure would rise to 4,000 including those employed in the sites’ supply chains.“I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. “[W]e just cannot compete.”TheMonaco-based billionaireclaimed that gas prices in the UK were 12 times higher than in the US and eight times more expensive than the coal increasingly used by chemical plants in China.The rising cost of gas in recent years has taken a heavy toll on Europe’s chemicals industry, including the Ineos empire, because it is a vital feedstock used to make the chemical building blocks required to manufacture products ranging from textiles and pharmaceuticals to detergents.Gas prices tend to be higher in the UK than in other parts of Europe due to the country’s reliance on gas for heating and electricity generation. Historically this reliance was met by the UK’s domestic North Sea reserves, but as production declines the UK has become increasingly reliant on imports.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionManchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quitRead moreThe co-owner of Manchester United also said that the UK government’s energy policy was “leading to economic vandalism on an industrial scale” by losing jobs to China and the US “and driving up global CO2emissions at a stroke”.“Not only is the ridiculously high gas price in the UK destroying our manufacturing base and the jobs of hard-working people on Humberside, it is also massively increasing the environmental burden, with replacement products supplied from the USA at double the carbon emissions and from China at eight times the emission level,” Ratcliffe said.A government spokesperson said ministers had taken “bold action” to support the UK’s chemicals industry, including the launch of a £350m co-investment scheme and trade measures on foreign chemicals imports.The spokesperson said the government was preparing to tackle high electricity costs via a pair of discount schemes for manufacturers.The first aims to reduce electricity bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 manufacturing businesses, while a “supercharger” scheme will cut electricity costs for hundreds of the UK’s most electricity-intensive businesses by more than £400m a year.“While this is a commercial decision from Ineos, we know this will be a concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families,” the spokesperson added.Explore more on these topicsJim RatcliffeIneosGasHullCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case was found dead after missing family meal, inquest hears | London | The Guardian
description: Brother-in-law went to check on Nicholas Brandram at his London home and found him unresponsive, coroner says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brother-in-law went to check on Nicholas Brandram at his London home and found him unresponsive, coroner says
Content: There was no evidence of third-party involvement in Nicholas Brandram’s death, the coroner said.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenThere was no evidence of third-party involvement in Nicholas Brandram’s death, the coroner said.Photograph: Family handout/PALondonSuspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case was found dead after missing family meal, inquest hearsBrother-in-law went to check on Nicholas Brandram at his London home and found him unresponsive, coroner saysPress AssociationTue 22 Sep 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man who was arrested on suspicion of being the so-called “Putney pusher” was found dead at his home after missing a family meal, an inquest has heard.Nicholas Brandram, 44, was arrested in June in connection with an incident on Putney Bridge on 5 May 2017 in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus.The former banker was found unresponsive inside his home in Chiswick, westLondon, on 15 September.Melanie Lee, the area coroner, opened and suspended an inquest into his death at west London coroner’s court on Tuesday afternoon.Opening the proceedings, she said: “On the evening of Tuesday 15 September 2026, Nicholas did not attend a family meal as planned.“His brother-in-law attended Nicholas’s home address and gained access using a spare key provided by a neighbour. Upon searching the house, he found Nicholas in an upstairs room.“Paramedics attended and despite resuscitation, he was pronounced deceased at 8.58pm.”The coroner said the death was not considered suspicious and there was “no evidence of third-party involvement”.Lee said provisional results from a postmortem examination indicated his death was “due to ligature compression of the neck”.The Metropolitan police has referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) over its contact with Brandram, who was released under investigation after his arrest.The force said on 17 September that its investigation into the Putney Bridge incident remained ongoing after Brandram’s death.Lee said on Tuesday: “I have been informed this afternoon that a referral has been made to the IOPC. On that basis, I am suspending the inquest.”The coroner added that an inquest was not a trial and “nobody and no organisation is on trial”.Brandram’s sisters, who were present at the inquest opening, have previously accused police of failing him and wider society.The coroner told the family: “I offer my sincere condolences for your loss. I appreciate today will not be an easy day for you.”The family have said they believe Brandram took his own life after“months of immense pressure”caused by the Met’s investigation.In an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Brandram’s sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker said he did not match the description of the attacker.Hicks said there had been “urgency” by the Met to arrest Brandram and to have that reported in the press. “I think he couldn’t understand why there wasn’t urgency to help clear his name,” she added.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms | European Union | The Guardian
description: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc
Content: Alisher Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek businessman, shakes hands with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in 2018.Photograph: SPUTNIK/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlisher Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek businessman, shakes hands with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in 2018.Photograph: SPUTNIK/ReutersEuropean UnionEU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline loomsAlisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the blocJennifer Rankinin BrusselsTue 22 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war onUkrainefor the next three years.With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve theRussiablacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.Ukraine war briefing: Sanctions must continue, EU’s top diplomat stresses, as Russian attacks kill fiveRead moreFrance stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.View image in fullscreenMikhail Fridman was removed from the sanctions list.Photograph: Pavel Golovkin/APUkraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense ‌of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionRussiaUkraineEuropeFranceLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for Senate  | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party
Content: Abdul El-Sayed and former vice-president Kamala Harris in a roundtable discussion on reproductive health in Detroit, Michigan, on 22 September 2026.Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed and former vice-president Kamala Harris in a roundtable discussion on reproductive health in Detroit, Michigan, on 22 September 2026.Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersMichiganKamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for SenateFormer VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured partyJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonTue 22 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending her popularity among Black voters to a progressive Senate nominee still working to unite a party fractured by a bruising primary – and the former vice-president’s loss to Donald Trump in the state.Appearing with El-Sayed at aDetroitbirth center, Harris used a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame that November’s contest against the Republican Mike Rogers as a fight over women’s access to care.“Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America. Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars,” she said, hammering Rogers for his support of the president’s agenda.Harris also criticized the Trumpadministration for halting federal research funding it classified as diversity-related, including studies of fibroids and said the Senate should act as a check on the White House.Arab Americans in Michigan warn centrist Democrats attacking Hasan Piker: ‘They haven’t learned from 2024’Read more“The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, nodding to El-Sayed. The crowd murmured in agreement.El-Sayed, a physician, thanked Harris for “uplifting the issues that we are here to talk about today”, adding his gratitude for her work on them.The senate seat is open following the retirement of the Democratic senator Gary Peters and holding it is a must for the party’s path to a Senate majority. But even with a win in Michigan,Democratswould need to flip at least four Republican-held seats to control the chamber for Trump’s final two years in office.El-Sayed, who backs universal healthcare and sits to the left of his party’s leadership, narrowly defeated the congresswoman Haley Stevens in August, following a bitter primary thatdividedkey constituencies. Black voters in Detroit, the backbone of the Democratic coalition in the state, tended to favor Stevens, and Rogers has also been courting them in the city.The joint appearance also papers over a rift between the Democrats. El-Sayed has called Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide, a sharp break from the Biden-Harris administration’s military support for Israel, but a position that puts him in step with a growing share of the electorate.A Quinnipiac University pollreleased this monthfound 38% of voters more sympathetic to Palestinians and 35% to Israelis, the highest share siding with the Palestinians since the university began asking the question in December 2001.InMichigan, home to a large Arab American community, that shift has already shown up at the ballot box, and El-Sayed was part of it. In 2024, he backed the “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest at US military aid to Israel. He endorsed Harris when she replaced Biden as the nominee later that year. Many of the movement’s supporters did not follow him and the state narrowly went to Trump.The trip also comes amid speculation about Harris’s own political ambitions, as she mulls whether to run again for the White House. Michigan is set to hold the fifth contest on the Democrats’ revised 2028 primary calendar and Harris has further campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia.Closing her remarks, Harris urged the room to remind voters “that they have power and voice in the outcome of this election, which will directly impact their lives in many ways”.Explore more on these topicsMichiganKamala HarrisDetroitDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape and drug offenses | US crime | The Guardian
description: The Massachusetts case is the latest in a series of legal woes for the influencer whose real name is Braden Eric Peters
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: The Massachusetts case is the latest in a series of legal woes for the influencer whose real name is Braden Eric Peters
Content: Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, at an event on 1 May 2026 in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Michele Eve Sandberg/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClavicular, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, at an event on 1 May 2026 in Miami, Florida.Photograph: Michele Eve Sandberg/ShutterstockUS crime‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape and drug offensesThe Massachusetts case is the latest in a series of legal woes for the influencer whose real name is Braden Eric PetersRichard LuscombeTue 22 Sep 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe online influencer known as Clavicular – who has helped to fuel the rise of the extreme male appearance-improvement trend of “looksmaxxing” – has been charged with rape and drug offenses inMassachusetts.The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment on Cape Cod, according to legal documents seen by the Guardian.He faces up to life in prison on felony counts of rape, drugging a person for sexual intercourse, and a misdemeanor charge of providing liquor to a minor.The offenses are alleged to have taken place in Massachusetts in May 2025. It was not immediately clear if they related to aseparate lawsuitfiled in April by a teenager in Florida who said that Peters gave her alcohol during a 2025 party at his parents’ home on Cape Cod, then had sex with her while she was passed out. The girl was 16 at the time of that alleged incident.Peters rose to prominence as a promoter of “looksmaxxing”, which analysts have described as atoxic pursuitby young men of altering or improving their facial looks and physiques, using extreme measures such as bone smashing to achieve more chiseled jawlines, oral and plastic surgeries, and lip enhancement.The trend, which moved into the mainstream from its roots in the misogynistic “incel” (involuntary celibate) community, has an online following of millions. It has also been blamed by mental health experts for worsening issues ofself-esteem, depression, and social anxietyin teenage boys for its messaging that romantic success is tied to physical perfection.The charges against Peters in Massachusetts were filed in Orleans district court on 8 September, the records show, and a summons was issued the same day. A representative of Peters told multiple media outlets that Bulwark, the online news site thatfirst reportedthe charges, was “exaggerating” the status of the case “to boost traffic” because, he said, the influencer had not been physically served.Peters, who has an online following of more than a million, did not respond to the charges directly. But he posted a cryptic messageon Xon Monday night accusing the teenager who filed the Florida lawsuit of “trying to get my attention in anyway possible, a lawsuit?” and calling her “petty”. It was accompanied by a photograph of a letter allegedly written by the teen – who has publicly identified herself – pledging “you have my loyalty 100%”.The lawsuit makes allegations against Peters of battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, fraud, and unauthorized publication of her name and likeness, according toNBC6 South Floridathat reported the developments in April. It stops short of accusing Peters of rape despite the allegations in the lawsuit.According to the lawsuit, Peters initially paid her $1,000 and told her he wanted to make her “the female face of looksmaxxing” – but their relationship soured and went through several highs and lows.When the teen was inMassachusettsin 2025, it said, Peters paid for an Uber to take her to the party at his parents’ home. The age of consent in Massachusetts is 16 – but she alleges that Peters served her vodka despite being under the legal drinking age and “to the point where she was unable to give consent”, then had sex with her anyway.After ignoring her for six months afterwards, the lawsuit said, they rekindled their relationship to a point where Peters was paying her $15,000 a month as a social media promoter. But they fell out again and Peters began an online campaign to discredit her.The teen said Peters also injected her twice against her will with methamphetamine-laced Aqualyx, a substance not approved by the US Food and Drug administration (FDA), to melt fat around her cheeks and jawline.Steven Kramer, Peters’ attorney in that case, said in a statement at the time that his client “denies the claims and disputes the characterization of events”. He said Peters would “vigorously defend himself” through the appropriate legal channels and would not be making any further comment.The Massachusetts rape case is the latest in a series of recent legal woes for Peters, who in February was reported by theNew York Timesto be earning in excess of $100,000 monthly for his livestreams.In March, he was charged in Florida with firearms offenses for allegedlyshootingan already-dead alligator during a livestream. He pleaded no contest in exchange for six months’ probation and 20 hours of unpaid community service.The same month, he and a girlfriend – Violet Marie Lentz, 24 – were arrested andcharged with batterystemming from an alleged assault on a 19-year-old woman at a rented house in Kissimmee, Florida.Explore more on these topicsUS crimeMassachusettsMenSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: UK borrows £18bn in August, putting pressure on Healey before budget | Budget deficit | The Guardian
description: Some economists say it is now ‘inevitable’ that chancellor will need to raise taxes in the budget next month
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Some economists say it is now ‘inevitable’ that chancellor will need to raise taxes in the budget next month
Content: John Healey has promised to stick within the government’s spending limits.Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Healey has promised to stick within the government’s spending limits.Photograph: James Veysey/Rex/ShutterstockBudget deficitUK borrows £18bn in August, putting pressure on Healey before budgetSome economists say it is now ‘inevitable’ that chancellor will need to raise taxes in the budget next monthPhillip InmanTue 22 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government borrowed a higher-than-expected £18.3bn last month, increasing the pressure onJohn Healeyas he attempts to calm jittery bond markets before next month’s budget.Some economists said it was “inevitable” that the chancellor would need to raise taxes on 28 October if he is to meet demands for extra spending on defence without further borrowing from investors on international money markets.Official figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Tuesday said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £2.9bn higher last month than in August 2025.UK government borrowing jumps over forecast to £18.3bn in August as ‘fiscal straightjacket’ tightens – business liveRead moreIt meant that borrowing jumped by £3.5bn above the level expected by the government’s independent forecaster, the Office forBudgetResponsibility (OBR), taking the deficit over the financial year so far to £77.3bn – £8.1bn above forecast.The £18.3bn borrowed in August was also more than the £15.6bn City analysts had forecast.Healey, the chancellor, has promised to stick within the government’s spending limits, which restrict the amount the Treasury can borrow as a proportion of national income.The August figures come after the government ran alarger-than-expected £1.8bn deficit in July, when analysts had expected the figure to be zero.Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the consultancy RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier budget than Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power just a few months ago. Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”The UK has been among the countries hardest hit by the rise in the interest rate on government bonds amidturmoil in financial markets.UK borrowing chartWhile the cost of financing UK bonds has eased in the last week, the Treasury remains under pressure to show it can reduce its reliance on heavy borrowing to maintain welfare spending.On Tuesday, the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds rose three basis points (bps) to 5.232%, while 30-year bond yields were also 3bps higher at 5.729% in early trading.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them. Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts.”The Institute for Fiscal Studies, a thinktank, said that since April, the government had spent £50bn on debt interest, £2bn more than forecast by the OBR in March.“On those forecasts – made before the most recent hikes in government interest rates – debt interest was set to be more than £100bn every year over the next five years,” said Nick Ridpath, an IFS research economist.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCentral government spending on social security benefits and pensions climbed by almost £10bn more than in the same period last year – from £135.3bn to £145bn – mostly in response to rising inflation.The consumer prices indexrose last month to 3.1%and, while the Bank of England held interest rates at its latest meeting last week, the central bank warned that the cost of borrowing may need to rise in the coming months if inflationary pressures persist.Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said: “Today’s public finance figures are another unwelcome setback for the government ahead of next month’s budget.”The International Monetary Fund has urged western governments to gain greater control over their public finances to reassure financial markets that they remain safe havens for lenders.Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was committed to improving the UK’s economic growth, “but we can only deliver that growth with fiscal discipline”.She added: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.”The Conservative party Treasury spokesperson, Andrew Griffith, accused Labour of losing control of the public finances. “They are borrowing so much they’ve overshot the OBR forecast by an extra £8bn of debt,” he said.“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to both have the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”However, the OBR has said estimates of government borrowing published early in the financial year should be considered provisional and they are likely to be revised.Explore more on these topicsBudget deficitBondsEconomicsBudgetEconomic policyJohn HealeyBudget 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: European drugmakers say they are ‘losing ground’ to US and Chinese rivals | Pharmaceuticals industry | The Guardian
description: Some of continent’s biggest pharma firms write to national leaders calling for action to safeguard their futures
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Some of continent’s biggest pharma firms write to national leaders calling for action to safeguard their futures
Content: The letter calls on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness.Photograph: Aleksandr Matveev/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe letter calls on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness.Photograph: Aleksandr Matveev/AlamyPharmaceuticals industryEuropean drugmakers say they are ‘losing ground’ to US and Chinese rivalsSome of continent’s biggest pharma firms write to national leaders calling for action to safeguard their futuresJulia KolleweTue 22 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of Europe’s biggest pharmaceutical companies have said the continent is “losing ground” to rivals including the US and China in developing new drugs and attracting investment.The chairs of nine companies, including Britain’sAstraZeneca, GSK and Denmark’s Novo Nordisk, wrote to Andy Burnham and the national leaders of other European countries on Tuesday to call for action to “safeguard our companies’ future”.The letter, entitled Europe is Losing the Pharma Investment Race – But the Comeback is Within Reach,called on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness.It argued that the pharmaceutical sector is one of Europe’s great postwar achievements that is supporting millions of highly skilled jobs and generating an EU trade surplus of more than €220bn (£188bn). “But this hard-won inheritance is at risk,” the letter said.“In our boardrooms, we see Europe losing ground to global competition. Over $600bn in pharmaceutical investment has been announced in the US andChinain the last two years alone.“European governments must create conditions that attract investment in next-generation medicines before it’s too late,” said the letter, which was also signed by the chairs of Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim, Italy’s Chiesi group, France’s Sanofi and Ipsen, and Novartis and Roche of Switzerland.Europe’sshare of global pharmaceutical research and development has fallen from 43%in 1990 to 31%, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA).The continent’s share of commercial clinical trials – where new medicines are tested for safety and efficacy before they are submitted for regulatory approval –has halved to 9% from 18%a decade ago. Only 4% of clinical trials are focused on cell and gene therapies.China has overtaken Europe inclinical trials, pharmaceuticalpatents, and thedevelopmentof new medicines. The country’s share of global clinical trials rose from less than 10% to almost 30% over the same period.Almost half (49%) of newly approved therapies did not reach European patients last year, up from 46% in 2019; those drugs that do take nearly 600 days on average. This varies hugely from country to country: from a median 56 days in Germany to 1,201 days in Romania,according to datafrom the EFPIA.The industry body has said the root causes of unavailability and delay to accessing new medicines range from the speed of regulatory processes to insufficient budgets in some European countries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClosing the clinical trials gap alone could generate €53bn and create 82,000 jobs in Europe, the nine pharma companies argued in the letter.“We ask national leaders to work with us to reverse Europe’s declining competitiveness, unleash a new era of medical discovery, and secure health sovereignty. We recognise the fiscal pressures many face. But just like defence or energy, modern medicines should be treated as vital infrastructure and not be left to others to provide,” the letter said.It was signed by industry leaders including Michel Demaré, the chair of Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical company, AstraZeneca; Jonathan Symonds, his counterpart atGSK, the country’s second-biggest drugmaker; Lars Rebien Sørensen, the chair of the Wegovy and Ozempic maker, Novo Nordisk; Severin Schwan at the Swiss company Roche; Giovanni Caforio at fellow Swiss firm Novartis, and Frédéric Oudéa at France’s Sanofi.It comes after a public row last year between the industry and the UK government over drug pricing and availability of new treatments to patients. Ministers agreed in December tospend billions of pounds a year extra on medicinessupplied to the NHS after pressure fromDonald Trump, who argued that high drug prices in the US were subsidising lower prices elsewhere.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryEuropeAstraZenecaGSKDrugsMedical researchChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain | George Osborne | The Guardian
description: Former chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI tech
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Former chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI tech
Content: Protests have sprung up across the UK in opposition to the construction of datacentres, including outside the Scottish parliament.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenProtests have sprung up across the UK in opposition to the construction of datacentres, including outside the Scottish parliament.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianGeorge OsborneOpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back BritainFormer chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI techUK politics live – latest updatesHelena HortonTue 22 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacentre nimbys are holding Britain back,George Osbornehas said in reaction to nationwide protests about the giant water- and energy-guzzling structures.The former Tory chancellor is now the head of AI for countries atOpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. His job is to represent the company to governments around the world and he also has a role in enabling the building of datacentres and other infrastructure.Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Somerset on Sunday, Osborne said: “You try and build a datacentre in Britain … I spent my life when I was politician trying to get people to agree to have new roads and railway lines and airport runways, and communities go up in arms – it’s really hard to build a datacentre.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Osborne, who was Britain’s chancellor in David Cameron’s cabinet, now leads OpenAI’s relationship-building with governments around the world.Photograph: Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/APHe said the UK would lose its “sovereignty” over tech to the US if it failed to allow datacentres to be built.He explained: “You can either choose to have these datacentres in Ohio and Georgia and Michigan, which is where they’re all being built … we don’t allow these things to be built. They’re going to be built elsewhere, and you know that’s a loss of some sovereign control over the physical location where these things are.”There have been protests about datacentres across the UK, including incentral London,Devonand outsideHolyrood in Edinburgh. People have said they are a blight on the landscape, questioned whether they will bring jobs to the local area, and argued they will take investment and space that could be used for affordable housing. There are also concerns about the vast water and energy use.The government has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure to get them built more quickly. But the Green party in England hascalled for a moratoriumon building them.Osborne dismissed the concerns over datacentres as nimbyism. He said: “I think a lot of the to opposition datacentres is very much like ‘not in my back yard’. There’s an enormous building boom going on in the United States of datacentres, even as the political opposition undoubtedly is growing.”View image in fullscreenThe protest outside Holyrood.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianVerity Harding, the head of the AI and geopolitics project at Cambridge University’s Bennett School for Public Policy, said people had wider concerns over these centres.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe said: “The reason everyone hates datacentres has nothing to do with datacentres. It’s the only tangible thing to protest against … [people] just don’t like what’s happening and they don’t feel that anybody’s in control or thinking about the impact of it.“It’s exactly because the tech industry execs are talking in this ridiculous way … You know, you cannot go out on the one hand and say this [AI]might kill everybodyone week and then the next week go and appear at a big sales conference saying that you should integrate it into your business.”Bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest AI companies, will be meeting world leaders at the UN general assembly in New York City this week amid debate over the prospect of dangerous, superintelligent AI and whether and how it should be regulated.Osborne said: “The fact that corporate leaders are sitting down with the presidents and prime ministers of the world in the UN security council I would say actually shouldn’t be alarming. It’s actually reassuring that people are beginning to try and use the kind of institutions of the world to think about how we regulate this new technology.”Explore more on these topicsGeorge OsborneDatacentres - UKTechnology policyOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Using AI to ‘talk to animals’ might make us feel clever – but what, if anything, does it do for them? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: As animal behaviorists increasingly use AI in their research, they grapple with how to wield the technology responsibly
Author: Amy Martin
Headline: As animal behaviorists increasingly use AI in their research, they grapple with how to wield the technology responsibly
