Content: Vivek Thakker/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)Using AI to ‘talk to animals’ might make us feel clever – but what, if anything, does it do for them?As animal behaviorists increasingly use AI in their research, they grapple with how to wield the technology responsiblyAmy MartinTue 22 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTShareI’m sitting in a small boat in Shark Bay, Australia, eavesdropping on a conversation between some of Earth’s most intelligent beings. The motor is off, the turquoise sea is glassy, and Stephanie King and I are motionless, transfixed by the whistles, clicks and squeezy, whirring noises made by the dolphins swimming below us.If anyone could tell me what these big-brained social mammals are saying, it would be her. Based at the University of Bristol, she co-leadsShark Bay Dolphin Research, one of the longest-running wild dolphin research projects in the world. She has spent thousands of hours watching and listening to this population.Like most other animal behaviorists, King is increasingly integrating artificial intelligence into her research process. “If it’s used responsibly, AI can transform what we can do with the data we collect,” she says. But when I ask her if AI will someday allow us to “speak dolphin”, she stiffens a little. “I think we’re doing the animals a disservice by focusing on that question,” she says.Dolphins chit-chat in Shark Bay, western AustraliaSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/1_Dolphins_Chit-chat_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp300:00:0000:00:19Dolphins communicate, navigate and find food using buzzes, pops, whistlesand other acoustic signals. These sounds were recorded in Shark Bay,western Australia via an underwater microphone by Amy Martin for the podcastThresholdThe problem, King says, is not AI itself, but the narrative being built around it. She sees her field increasingly framed as a quest for an AI-assisted animal interpreter, with headlines declaring that we’ve almost “cracked the secret language” of various creatures or are about to “decode animals’ speech”. There are even cash prizes for breakthroughs, including theColler Dolittle Challenge, which seeks an algorithm for communicating with non-human organisms.“It’s a sexy topic,” King acknowledges, but in her view, fundamentally misguided. She believes the allure of tech dollars and media attention is priming the pump of research in some unhealthy ways – nudging scientists to make premature claims about AI-assisted findings, and encouraging them to describe their work in sensational terms. “They tend to be biasing themselves towards the most exciting discovery,” says King, which “misleads us to what we know about these animals”.View image in fullscreenBella, a pregnant dolphin at Six Flags Discovery Kingdom, watches trainer Adam Gilbert place a hydrophone into the pool to record her underwater sounds in Vallejo, California. Bella had been observed possibly communicating with her unborn baby and is the focus of new research project.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesWhat we know, in many cases, is in fact very little. Take dolphins. “They’ve been studied for decades, but we’re still scratching the surface with what many of the sounds mean,” King says. Sound itself likely means something different to dolphins than it does to us. They can detect pitches far outside our range of hearing, they process acoustic information much faster than we do, and our sensory systems are wired differently in important ways.For example, both humans and dolphins can echolate – or use sound to navigate – but dolphins process echolocation information in the part of the brainconnected to touch, while for us, it’s more connected to vision. In other words, instead of “seeing” with sound, dolphins might be hear-feeling, or feel-hearing, their way through their watery world. Whatever that experience is, it may be fundamentally inaccessible to us – and it’s not something we can comprehend by plugging their whistles and squeaks into a large language model. “We need to appreciate that they have a complex communication system that we barely understand,” says King. She believes our focus should be learning about that system – piecing together what dolphin behavior and communication means to other dolphins – rather than trying to hack into it, and start a conversation.Dolphins whistle in Shark BaySorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/2_Dolphins_Whistles_Credit_Stephanie_King_-_Shark_Bay_Dolphin_Research.mp300:00:0000:00:33These high-pitched whistles are a very important part of dolphins’ social communication. Mothers use them to keep in contact with their calvesand some whistles are even used as individual identifiers, or name-like calls. Credit: Stephanie King,Shark Bay Dolphin ResearchElephant researcher Joyce Poole agrees. “I get quite exasperated by this goal of being able to talk to the animals,” she says. “I think it’s kind of gimmicky.” One of the world’s leading experts on African savanna elephants, Poole has spent decades observing the animals in the wild, building upa treasure troveof annotated field recordings of their vocalizations, movements and interactions. She’s convinced that there are many layers and nuances of elephant communication that we don’t yet understand, but, like King, she’s skeptical about the concept of inserting ourselves into their dialogues. “Just the basic ability to understand whattheyhave to say and what they are thinking about – that’s enough for me,” she says. “I don’t need to interfere in their lives more than necessary.”Female elephants make noises when a musth male arrives in their groupSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/6_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_1_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp300:00:0000:00:16Joyce Poole has documented female elephants making these overlapping sounds when a musth male arrives in their group, looking to breed. She refers to the sounds as “Female Chorus Rumbles” and they may include snorts, trumpetsand roars, as well aslow-pitched rumbles. Credit: The Elephant Ethogram,ElephantVoicesAt the same time, Poole believes making the inner lives of elephants more legible to humans could transform how we treat them. “I hope that by showing that they’re capable of a more sophisticated kind of communication that we gain them some respect from our fellow humans, and save a place for them in the world, together with their ecosystems and their other fellow travelers,” she says.Poole’s hope is widely shared, and is likely one of the main reasons so many of us are prone to click on stories with headlines about how AI is going to help us talk to animals. As extinction numbers rise and biodiversity declines, we’re desperate for some good news. Humans are also inherently fascinated by other animals; we’ve been telling stories about listening to and learning from them for as long as we’ve walked the Earth. Our technologies have in many ways cut us off from the rest of the living world – could this be a case when a new tool helps us to better tune into and care for our planetmates?double quotation markWe have, as human beings, a very mixed track record, to put it gently, in using technologiesCésar Rodríguez-Garavito“I do see AI as a potentially promising avenue for knowing more, and understanding better, non-human animal lives,” saysCésar Rodríguez-Garavito, founding director of the More Than Human Life (Moth) program at NYU, a leading hub for research and discourse on the rights of nature. He thinks AI could help give animals a voice in the decisions that shape their lives.“More and more researchers and practitioners are asking themselves, ‘Well, how do we bring in the voices of, say, the whales in the regulation of a marine-protected area,’” he says. It may sound far-fetched to us now, but Rodríguez-Garavito says attempts to bring non-human voices into the realms of law and policy are already under way in countries around the world. “I think that this is no longer a science fiction question,” he says. Of course, we don’t need AI to tell us that whales are being negatively impacted by noise, ship strikes, climate disruption and pollution, but perhaps if we heard a direct translation of them expressing pain from underwater seismic testing, or mourning the loss of a calf killed by a ship, we would be more likely to act.“But I cannot speak about potential benefits without speaking about risks,” Rodríguez-Garavito says. “We have, as human beings, a very mixed track record, to put it gently, in using technologies.” That record tells us that we can’t simply deploy AI in the wild and see what happens; we need to think through the risks ahead of time. There’s the possibility of intentional harm, like using AI-powered tools to trick or coerce animals, perhaps moving them into areas where they’re easier to kill (“I mean, think of trophy hunters,” says Poole). But if the past predicts the future, the greatest threats are not a few people using a new technology with malicious intent, but a whole lot of us using it without thinking about – or choosing to care about – the consequences.“The nightmare scenario is one where we interrupt their communications and their lives at will, just for our entertainment,” says Rodríguez-Garavito. It’s not hard to imagine whale-watching companies using AI to lure animals toward boats, for example, or visitors to Yellowstone national park using apps to provoke wolves to howl, elk to bugle, or bison to bellow, exhausting and confusing the animals. Technologies are not beholden to the intentions of their makers. A tool created with the sincere goal of enhancing our respect for animals could end up having the opposite effect by turning them into playthings that we can pester and control.Researchers in the field talk while recording dolphin buzzes and whistlesSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/3_Dolphins_Researchers_in_the_field_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp300:00:0000:00:29Researchers Stephanie King and Laura Palmer document the movements and behaviors of a group of dolphins in Shark Bay. Buzzes and whistles from the dolphins are being picked up by underwater microphones and played through a speaker on the boat. Credit: Amy Martin, ThresholdIn an attempt to help steer the field away from these dark scenarios, the Moth program recently published thePepp framework(prepare, engage, prevent and protect), a set of ethical guidelines for the use of non-human animal communication technologies. But if and how it will actually get put into practice is uncertain. Rodríguez-Garavito says this is a trickle-down effect of the larger absence of legal and ethical boundaries around AI development. “At this point, there is no international agreement on AI,” he says. “It is a free-for-all. I would be much less concerned if we had general principles on what can and cannot be done with AI. There’s nothing like that, and this is why we’re having to develop them from scratch based on what’s been done in other fields of legal practice.”View image in fullscreenAn adult African elephant and a younger calf crossing a dirt track during a game drive in Mikumi, Tanzania.Photograph: Vincenzo Izzo/LightRocket/Getty ImagesFemale elephants rumbleSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/7_Elephants_Female_Chorus_Rumbles_2_Credit_ElephantVoices.mp300:00:0000:00:22Credit: The Elephant Ethogram,ElephantVoicesMickey Pardo, who works with Joyce Poole as a senior scientist atElephantVoices, also sees potential benefits and risks of AI-assisted animal communication tools, but he also wonders if the speculation is a bit overblown on both sides. “Playbacks can be stressful for animals even without AI – when you’re just taking prerecorded sounds and playing them back – especially if you don’t know the context of those sounds,” he says. Maybe a more sophisticated AI version could add to that stress, but Pardo sees it more as turning up the dial on a problem we already have, versus opening an entirely new can of worms.He also questions whether we’re focusing too much on possible harms from AI when there are so many other ways we negatively impact animals’ lives, including in research settings.double quotation markI think you have to use these AI and machine learning approaches alongside careful examination of the animalsStephanie King“The way that animals are treated in biomedical science is so incredibly horrific compared to anything that anybody’s doing in the field of animal communication,” he says. “Not that we shouldn’t be thinking about the ethical implications [of AI] ahead of time. I just worry that perhaps we’re sucking up too much oxygen worrying about a hypothetical ethical problem when there are many very real, present ethical problems that we’re essentially ignoring.”This oxygen-sucking, mesmerizing effect of AI – the attention and money poured toward it, and the almost magical powers we’re willing to ascribe to it – also concerns marine mammal researcherLuke Rendell, based at the University of St Andrews. “There’s been this idea put about that AI is going to find something that we couldn’t,” he says. “It’s something of a confidence trick, I think.”Rendell believes the AI hype has gotten way ahead of the science, and that the public is being led to believe that we know – or are about to know – much more than we actually do about animal communication. For example,Earth Species Projectclaims on their website that “with exponential advances in AI and Large Language Models, decoding animal communication is no longer a question of if – it’s when” and states that they have already found support for their hypothesis that “AI can decode the shared structures of language across the Tree of Life”.Researcher Stephanie King on waiting for the right context to record animalsSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/4_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describing_context_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp300:00:0000:00:47King says AI can be a very helpful tool when used in the right ways, but spending time with the animals in their habitat is essential for understanding what their vocal communication means to them. Credit: Amy Martin, ThresholdThis is the sort of framing that gives Rendell hives. Like Stephanie King, he believes pursuing a quest to reveal the “language” of animals is loaded with humancentric bias that could actually limit our understanding of their unique and wildly diverse ways of getting their messages across. He’s also concerned about long-term damage to his field when theDr Dolittle machinefails to materialize.The study of animal communication has attracted a fair number of charlatans over the years, leading to boom-and-bust cycles of funding and credibility. Rendell says he entered the field of cetacean communication “just as it was recovering from a 15-year hangover” from the work ofJohn Lilly, whose efforts to teach dolphins English using controversial methods – like giving them LSD – brought Lilly a lot of fame, but ultimately led to nothing but a tragic end for one of the dolphins at the center of his experiments. For more than a decade after that, the study of dolphin communication was “the punchline of a joke in scientific circles”. says Rendell, but “we’ve had this flowering in the last 15 to 20 years of understanding and knowledge about cetacean society and communication”, which he says has “taken the whole field on to a new level of credibility. And my main fear is that it is being undermined by these irresponsible claims.”View image in fullscreenA pod of common dolphins surf the bow wake of a boat in the Catalina Channel near Long Beach, California.Photograph: David McNew/Getty ImagesKing says it all comes back to testing any AI findings with the experts: the animals themselves. “I think you have to use these AI and machine learning approaches alongside careful examination of the animals: when they produce calls, and in what context, and how they behave,” she says. This is patient, painstaking work that requires careful studies in the field, often conducted over years – the opposite of Silicon Valley’s “move fast and break things” ethos.King describes how dolphins produce soundSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/09/17/5_Dolphins_Stephanie_King_describes_sound_production_Credit_Amy_Martin.mp300:00:0000:00:26Dolphins detect sound waves through their lower jaws and produce sounds through the top of their heads.King describes how that works as buzzes made by a nearby dolphin are picked up by underwater microphones. Credit: Amy Martin, ThresholdThe days I spent on the water with King involved a lot of quiet waiting, scanning the horizon for the glint of dolphins rising to the surface. When we spotted an animal, King would immediately beginning calling out names – Juicy, Jungle, Piccolo – while the scientists-in-training on the boat with us snapped photographs and took notes. King can identify hundreds of individual dolphins after the briefest glimpse of their dorsal fins, a skill she attributes to the countless hours she has spent in Shark Bay, observing the animals on site. “I come every year, and it’s a really important part of my life,” she says.They’re the sopranos of the forest, so what’s silencing the gibbons’ morning chorus?Read moreShe also believes it’s a really important part of doing good science. When they return from the field, her students will spend time looking through the photographs of the fins, matching them to pictures from previous years in their dolphin “look book”. King says lately some students have been asking her to let AI do that work. It would, of course, be much faster. But she insists they do it manually. “If you really want to understand behavior, then the details matter,” she says. “And the details take time. You can’t rush it.”Meanwhile, a larger question looms for all of us: as exciting as it might be to imagine walking around with an animal translator in our pockets, do we have to wait for new technology to pay more attention to our planetmates? Because whether or not AI ever allows us to talk with animals, there’s nothing stopping us from listening to them, and caring about their lives.Amy Martin is the founder and executive producer ofThreshold, a Peabody award-winning documentary podcast. She is now writing her first book

title: The amazing life of 101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser: ‘We made noise. We closed the streets’  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Sick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a day
Author: Claire Armitstead
Headline: Sick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a day
Content: ‘We were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce’ … Ce Roser in her studio in New York.Photograph: Dario Lasagni/Courtesy VeneKlasenView image in fullscreen‘We were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce’ … Ce Roser in her studio in New York.Photograph: Dario Lasagni/Courtesy VeneKlasenArt and designInterviewThe amazing life of 101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser: ‘We made noise. We closed the streets’Claire ArmitsteadSick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a dayTue 22 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn January of 1971, the American art historian Linda Nochlin published a landmark essay,Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists?It was a provocation and a call to arms that was to send shockwaves through the arts establishment.“It wasn’t just a problem for artists,” says Ce Roser, more than half a century on. “My older friends could not get shows, although they had had brilliant careers before, and that happened also to all of my friends who were poets or writers. Nobody seemed to be able to establish themselves as career artists. So we got together, we complained, and I decided we should have a meeting and really talk seriously about it.”That first meeting at Roser’s home in New York led to the establishment of theWomen in the Arts Foundation, which took to the streets to force a change in the status quo. As well as being a priceless witness to an activist movement that altered history, she is also making her own history at London’sVeneKlasen gallerythis month, as the first American artist to make their European debut as a centenarian.double quotation markJoan Mitchell appeared off the plane from France. Louise Bourgeois stood in front of MoMA holding a big sheet saying NOMeeting Roser over video link in herNew Yorkhome, everything about her is surprising: she is 101 but could pass for 30 years younger. She was born in the US to Chinese parents, but insists that she never experienced racial discrimination. She doesn’t buy the idea that female artists, herself included, are constantly reforgotten today, as they were in the past. Her memory is as sharp and bright as the art she continues to make in the studio where she has worked for more than 70 years.View image in fullscreenSharp and bright … Voyage into Discovery, 1990.Photograph: © Ce Roser. Courtesy VeneKlasen, New York and London.Of that formative moment in 1971 she recalls: “There was a school of thought that we’re middle-class women, and we are afraid to assert ourselves.” At first only a handful of people were involved, but by the third meeting, the artistElaine de Kooninghad offered her studio. “And by word of mouth, because they wanted to see Elaine’s studio, many more turned up, and we decided we would demonstrate.”The father of one artist was a police officer, who said he could close down 53rd Street in front of the Museum of ModernArt. “So we took advantage. We decided we were going to have a joyous demonstration. We were not going to be like the men and be fierce and aggressive. Of course, we were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce.”The protesters were an A to Z of art history as we know it today.Joan Mitchellappeared off the plane from France.Louise Bourgeoisstood in front of MoMA holding a big sheet with NO written on it.Pat Passlofbrandished a sign that declared: “MoMa loves Papa.” “We made a lot of noise. We danced in the street. We closed it off,” says Roser.The payoff came in 1973, with an offer from the New York Cultural Center to host a show curated by, and featuring, female artists. Roser was one of seven selectors who, in a radical break with tradition, devised a democratic system in which artists nominated each other. Featuring 111 artists, Women Choose Women washailed as a successthat promised women “a large and permanent share of the art world action”, while also proving the value and efficiency of new, democratic forms of curation.View image in fullscreen‘When I went into my studio, I felt like a hand going into a glove’ … Ce Roser in New York in the 1970s.Photograph: Carin Drechsler-Marx/Courtesy VeneKlasenBy the time of the protests, Roser was in her 40s, the widely travelled wife of a US diplomat, who had returned home because their son needed to go to school. “He was speaking Urdu, Tagalog, German, and no English for him to become an American,” she says.Roser herself was a third generation American – the granddaughter of immigrant farmers from China to California, where one grandfather had a hop farm. Her parents had met at university, where her father was studying law and her mother maths and history, and she was the second of six children born to the couple after they settled in Philadelphia. “I didn’t feel Chinese because I grew up in a culture where there were very few Chinese,” she says. “My parents ate American food for breakfast, and you can tell a lot by what people eat for breakfast.”She was introduced to the arts at an early age by a mother who would pay her children five cents for every poem they memorised, while keeping them quiet by sitting them down at the dining table with “lots of crayons and watercolours and paper”. But Roser had no inkling that art might be her vocation and, by 19, was working in the information department at the US embassy, where she met her husband. By 21 she was married and, on postings abroad, found herself hampered by “the many things foreign service wives were not allowed to do …”View image in fullscreenBrushwork of calligraphy… Garden of Delight, 1961.Photograph: © Ce Roser. Courtesy VeneKlasen, New York and London.Fortunately, on their third posting, to the Philippines capital Manila, a sympathetic friend lent her a paint set. “I did a painting from a photograph, and when my husband went to frame it, somebody wanted to buy it, so I decided it must be good,” she says.In the late 1940s the couple were sent to Berlin, where Roser joined the Berlin Art Academy and studied under the German sculptor and Holocaust survivorHans Uhlmann. She dismisses the suggestion that postwar Germany must have been a culture shock, saying that nothing could compare with what she had experienced as a teenager on a visit to an uncle in wartime China, when the family got trapped in Shanghai. “We rode on a boxcar for 40 days. My mother and my grandmother – no men – and my brothers and sisters, and four cousins she insisted upon bringing with us. So I was used to war-torn and bombed-out places.”Uhlmann, she says, “would make us draw a thing from reality and turn it into an abstraction, and take an abstraction and turn it into reality on paper.” He said one thing that she particularly cherishes: “When you paint, be very definite. Do not hesitate. Just do it.”Back in New York, she found the studio overlooking the Hudson River where she has worked ever since. “When I went into my studio, I felt like a hand going into a glove,” she recalls. “It wiped out the domestic. I didn’t cook, I didn’t clean. I was there to paint and do nothing else, though I would always also read. I restricted myself to art criticism, art history, or poetry. Nothing else.”In the bright abstract paintings on display in her retrospective, the rhythms of poetry combine with the brushwork of calligraphy, which she studied under the Japanese masterNankoku Hidai. Whereas Hidai taught her to paint in broad strokes, “and to use my arms instead of my wrists”, poetry remains a key source of inspiration. “You mention a line and I see a painting,” she says.Although her name isn’t as well known as it once was, she still paints away in her eyrie above the Hudson River, sometimes turning out two or three pictures a day, confident in the knowledge that she has works stowed away for posterity in all the New York institutions she once protested against.Ce Roser: Running with the Sun is at VeneKlasen, London, until 5 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtExhibitionsFeminismGenderProtestWomeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Can a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debut | Stage | The Guardian
description: Osipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’
Author: David Jays
Headline: Osipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’
Content: ‘Russian women are very open. We don’t try to be cool’ … Natalia OsipovaPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Russian women are very open. We don’t try to be cool’ … Natalia OsipovaPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianStageInterviewCan a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debutDavid JaysOsipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Natalia Osipova started rehearsals for her first ever play, it didn’t go well. “I cry. I’m shaking. I’m stressed and completely lost on the first day,” she reports. “I think, ‘I’m a piece of shit!’ I want to take a taxi and run away.”It’s the second week of rehearsals when we meet, and Osipova is still here. The Royal Ballet principal plays a Russian ballerina from a previous age:Lydia Lopokova, who danced with Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, then in 1925 unexpectedly married British economist John Maynard Keynes, who is the protagonist of James Graham’s The Standard of Living – a play about, among other things, taking risks and imagining a brave new future.Acting is central to ballet’s appeal for Osipova. “Maybe I’ll never be super perfect for classical ballet because I love stories so much,” she says. Even so, she demurred when former colleague Edward Watson suggested she audition. “You’re stupid!” was his retort. “You need to try because it’s amazing opportunity.”View image in fullscreen‘She for him and he for her’ … Osipova with Pip Carter and Rory Kinnear in rehearsals for The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanA delicate silver necklace shines beneath frank brown eyes. Osipova requested a translator in our previous interviews, but today speaks in an idiosyncratic gallop not unlike Lopokova’s own. Entering Nicholas Hytner’s rehearsal room, joining a classy cast led byRory Kinnear, she felt like Lydia among Keynes’s sneery Bloomsbury friends. “I left rehearsal and cried,” she says, “because I feel, ‘Oh my god, I’m so bad.’ But you learn and listen and every day, step by step, I do better.”double quotation markRussia is my home, my family, my theatre, my friends. It’s my everythingWorking with text for the first time, especially in her second language, is, she confirms, “a whole new world”. She drafted in her husband, dancer Jason Kittelberger, to run through lines at midnight. “Dance is my world,” she says. “I’ve danced since 17, I’m 40 now. It’s my life.” But gradually, she found that the fundamental goal in theatre was the same. “You’re learning your material, you try to understand what’s important. With your partner, you start to play. You listen, you reply, and this is like life.”Graham is also in rehearsal, continually adjusting the script. His play is attentive to Lydia’s physicality: dance solos mark the scene changes, while a frequent stage direction for Lydia is “she stomps”. Osipova delights in making him laugh – they have just rehearsed Lydia’s first entrance, swearing fearsomely in Russian – and she feels kinship with her character.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianLopokova, says Osipova, “is not famous and popular in Russia” – her choreographer brother,Fedor Lopukhov, is better remembered. “She was two years in the Mariinsky, and after migrating with Diaghilev for his Russian season, she didn’t really come back.”She was reportedly strong in drama, irresistible in comedy. “She had a beautiful, huge jump,” Osipova says. “That I have too!” Keynes was her second husband and, to everyone’s surprise, the real thing. Each altered key parts of their identities: Maynard as a man who slept with men (keeping meticulous records of his encounters), Lydia as a feted dancer. “She changed her life to be with him,” Osipova says.She describes Keynes as “a man like a mountain, to hug her and give her everything. She for him and he for her.” Keynes’s Bloomsbury chums were less appreciative. “She was a clever woman with ambition,” Osipova argues, bridling at their jeers. In the play, she is called “that flat-footed, frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl!” Osipova grimaces. “I’m always upset when I hear somebody say that about dancers. It gives me pain because I feel dancers have such a special soul. It’s a different brain.”She’d already researched Bloomsbury for her searing Virginia Woolf in Wayne McGregor’sWoolf Worksearlier this year. When she was listening in the wings to Gillian Anderson’s voiceover, reading Woolf’s suicide note, “I started to have a huge panic attack”, Osipova says. “It’s emotional, the way she finally melts and dies. It’s more than dance, so much more.”View image in fullscreenOsipova with Steven McRae in the 2015 world premiere of Woolf Works at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian“Russian women are very open,” Osipova muses. “We’re not liars. We don’t try to be, ‘I’m cool, I’m nice.’” Lopokova’s Russian identity was crucial to her, yet she never saw her homeland after 1936. In our tumultuous times, can Osipova imagine a homecoming for herself? “I really want, but I don’t think so,” she says. “My husband is American and we have life there – but I want to visit [Russia] because it’s my home, my family, my theatre, my friends. It’s my everything.”From Bloomsbury to Whitehall: new play reimagines life of John Maynard KeynesRead moreOsipova was originally due to duck out of the play to dance Kenneth MacMillan’s tragic heroine Manon, but now won’t do the ballet. She has already retreated from other signature roles, looking beyond Don Quixote and other bravura ballets which made her name – which she delightfully calls her “bravo repertoire”.“I’m a person who is bored doing things again and again,” she says. “That was part of my life – I do it well and amazing, and I never want to come back to it.” Instead, her repertoire includes contemporary pieces and bespoke commissions – and now theatre. “If I don’t do something new, I feel like I’m dying,” she declares. “I can’t breathe. Why do you live if you’re not learning something new?”The Standard of Living is atTheatre Royal Haymarket,London, until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreBalletDanceNatalia OsipovaActingRory KinnearinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Heart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheese | Movies | The Guardian
description: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me
Content: At your service dog … Heart of the Beast.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyView image in fullscreenAt your service dog … Heart of the Beast.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyMoviesReviewHeart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheesePitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & MePeter BradshawTue 22 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of likeOwen Wilson in Marley & Me, only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on thesecond world war action thriller Fury, plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played byJK Simmons(channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. (Belmont has the same setup with Odin.) Booth and Brandy are Mr Hyde to Belmont and Odin’s Dr Jekyll.As for Pitt himself, his acting chops are tested when he has to sob and then laugh with joy when it looks wrongly as if Odin has been fatally wounded – but extravagant emoting is not why we love him. Heart of the Beast is a bit cheesy and the final moments will test your credulity, but Pitt is the right guy in the right film.Heart of the Beast is out on 24 September in Australia, and 25 September in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAction and adventure filmsBrad PittDogsJK SimmonsAnimalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Youth review – Sharon Horgan is back … and she’s better than ever | Television | The Guardian
description: This brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfect
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfect
Content: Is he, isn’t he? … Rupert Friend as Patrick with Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOView image in fullscreenIs he, isn’t he? … Rupert Friend as Patrick with Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewYouth review – Sharon Horgan is back … and she’s better than everThis brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfectLucy ManganTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a moment in Sharon Horgan’s new show, Youth, when – as protagonist Alex (Horgan) is seeing her son off to university – she inadvertently begins to run after the car that’s taking him away. And then she catches herself, and slows. And then she starts up again. It was such a tender, vicious glimpse into the future that I found myself sobbing into the sofa and cursing her name.All of which is to say: Sharon Horgan is back and she’s better than ever. Youth is the representation every woman who has ever slapped on an oestrogen patch after a divorce, looked around and thought “What the hell now?” has been waiting for. Horgan herself has described it in interviews as forming the third part of a loose trilogy that began with Pulling. Co-written with Dennis Kelly, Pulling was about three thirtysomething antitheses to Bridget Jones, whose dark chaos apparently scared the BBC so much they unexpectedly cancelled it just as it was truly getting into its stride. That was followed by Catastrophe, written by and starring Horgan, with Rob Delaney, as a couple who have a fling, find that she’s pregnant and end up making a brutal, hilarious go of things.Youth is Horgan’s even more brutal, even more hilarious take on life’s third act. Alex is a fiftysomething literary agent and divorcee. She has ageing parents (losing toes to diabetes and faculties to early dementia) to the left of her, and a troubled child and useless ex-husband to the right. But hope springs eternal even in the most wearied breast and she is hoping to start dating again, and maybe even improve her standing at work, too, now that son Ruari (Aran Murphy) at least is off her hands for 10-week terms at a time.At her workplace, she explains her timetable to Sam (Sharlene Whyte), her friend and boss – or boss and friend (the fluctuating proportions and concomitant stresses and strains in their relationship is one of the many thickening agents Horgan has stirred into her rich stew). “I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person, tops. I need someone to fall in love with me now so there’s a bit of time left with this me before the old me is like ‘I’m here now’.” All she has to do is muster some “new dick energy” from somewhere, recover from a dislocating jaw (“Just an age thing!” her young doctor tells her), and stop crying as she clears up the smelly mess in Ruari’s room. Can she resist giving in to booty calls to and from her never-quite-boyfriend Patrick (Rupert Friend, perfectly written as a charming borderline cad), and stop finding older men’s wattle and sagging balls a turn-off?The wattle belongs to Michael (Tim McInnerny). The balls too, in fact, though it turns out they are still defying gravity at least as much as you can ever hope for testicles. This is discovered during a sex scene that should be entered into the pantheon of greats. Move over Basic Instinct, Wild Things, 9½ Weeks and whatever else counts as your formative memory, and make way for tears. “I just don’t know if there’s anything left to my life that I like any more!” wails Alex, as she negotiates cunnilingus instead. “I can’t return the favour. But I don’t know you well enough yet to be selfish in bed,” she notes, before deciding that a hand job will do.It is the mark of Horgan’s genius that Michael does not contribute to this decision. It’s absolutely not about him. And it’s a mark of how beautifully she writes all her characters and how well they are always cast that we know that Michael is not the kind to mind. He just waits cheerfully for his next instruction. And we know we want to see more of Michael (not literally – I’ll take his word for it about the balls) and that she should, too. But we do see the attraction of Rupert Friend – I mean, Patrick.At work, there is the deeply disgruntled former client Malcolm (Douglas Hodge), who has written a dreadful romantasy book (The Goblin Seed) that duly takes TikTok by storm and makes him an asset they need to reacquire. Then there’s a bestselling elderly author (Anne Reid) whose books have taken a porno-racist turn that may prove beyond her editors’ powers to save. Lastly, we meet a talented foreign writer, whom Alex is trying to bring on to her list without Sam finding out.And then Ruari comes home, under a cloud and soon permanently under a duvet, while Alex tries frantically to find out what is wrong.All of human life is here – all its heart, all its humour. That is Horgan’s beat. Not just the female bit, not just the perimenopausal bit (though there is no one more acute or funny on either). Her men, her children, her colleagues – they are as real, as rounded, as ridiculous (and at times heartbreaking) as we all are in reality. Not that Horgan’s talent for grotesques has deserted her – the publishing types satirised here are mesmerisingly perfect and awful – but she dwells in the truth always, and there is nothing more bitterly funny or compelling than that.Youth is on HBO MaxThis article was amended on 22 September 2026 to correct the spelling of Tim McInnerny’s surname.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewSharon HorganTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Addiction is not only caused by weak will’: how a talking pigeon got Czechia to face up to its alcohol problem | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudice
Author: Miloš Hroch
Headline: Director Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudice
Content: ‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Claw FilmsView image in fullscreen‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Claw FilmsMovies‘Addiction is not only caused by weak will’: how a talking pigeon got Czechia to face up to its alcohol problemDirector Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudiceMiloš HrochTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCzech film-maker Pepa Lubojacki originally set out to make a film about pigeons. What fascinated the 39-year-old director was that the grey birds are clearly beautiful and highly intelligent creatures, yet human cruelty towards them is socially acceptable in the way it isn’t towards, say, crows or magpies. “You can spot kids kicking and chasing pigeons while their parents cheerfully look on,” she says.The moral blind spot reminded her of the way that people looked at homeless people like her older brother and her cousins. “The public has learned to avert their eyes,” she says. “My cousin was declined care seven times with open wounds in the hospital, and finally, they had to amputate both of his legs.”The birds stayed in the title of her first documentary, one of the most widely discussed and critically lauded films to be released inCzechiain recent years. To make If Pigeons Turned to Gold, Lubojacki spent five years chronicling the lives of four family members on the streets of Prague. In search of answers for why her relatives ended up with addictions and without roofs over their heads, the film wades deep into intergenerational trauma: domestic abuse and the deaths of her biological father and stepfather.Shot mostly on iPhone, the film is narrated by a meme-like talking pigeon and animated family photos with AI voiceovers, including manipulated child portraits of Pepa and her brother. They provide flashbacks to their 90s childhood in prefab estates where “you could get all the drugs your heart desired”, as one of the opening scenes tells us.View image in fullscreenInnovative … the film uses AI to voiceover Pepa and her brother as children.Photograph: Wanda Kaprálová/Claw FilmsThe central focus is Lubojacki’s ever-evasive brother David, and the documentary includes peaceful moments of nostalgic bonding over a rap song, but also documents vicious cycles of alcohol withdrawal and relapse, as Lubojacki struggles to nurture adult David to functionality. It’s an especially pressing issue in Czechia, the home of the world’s most popular beer style in the pilsner, where taxation of alcoholic drinks is traditionally low and the rate of alcohol consumption one of thehighest in the world. (To make things worse, Prague has some of thelowest rates of affordable housing in the European Union.)“I was angry because of the systemic injustice,” Lubojacki says. “Police beat up my brother several times, but caring professions can cause violence too, when medical personnel refuse to treat unhoused persons like him because of their history of addiction.” She used to look up to David – a local skater hero who listened to hip-hop, and knew all the cool stuff – and the mission of her film is audiences can “see my brother how I see him and how beautiful he is, that addiction is not only caused by a weak will”.View image in fullscreenYoung skater hero … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother David.Photograph: Claw FilmsIf Pigeons Turned to Gold unfolds through diary entries, interspersed with footage of herself on the psychiatric ward where she was hospitalised during the making of the film and video-art sequences of her sinking deep in water. Some of the entries read like poetry: “I’m just a little strawberry seed in the sea, a drowned strawberry seed, in an attempt to change something that is not up to me to change.”“Written text is my primary language and is closer to my heart,” reveals Lubojacki, who also has ambitions as a writer. She was inspired by Ottessa Moshfegh, who writes “simply, almost mechanically, as if without emotions, and observes brutal things without pathos”, and Melissa Broder’s “loose narrative of free writing” on addiction.The central question the 110-minute film circles around is whether you can grieve someone who hasn’t died yet. According toone recent study, people sleeping rough on the streets die 16 years earlier than the rest of the population. “I believe we live in an epidemic of addiction,” Lubojacki says. But speaking about this epidemic without shame is difficult: “When I grew up, I felt isolated, as if I was the only one who had this problem – I couldn’t speak about it with anyone, as I was so ashamed.”View image in fullscreenPepa Lubojacki with the Berlinale documentary award for If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Imago/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Relatives of people with addictions often suffer from a secondary trauma, as Barbora Bírová of Czech advocacy organisation Platform for SocialHousingpoints out. “If we understand homelessness as a situation, not as inner personal characteristics, it opens the way to solutions.”Lubojacki had feared rejection, but instead she received acclaim. What began as a student film has already won international recognition on the European film festival circuit. In February, it received the Berlin film festival’s documentary award for “remarkable achievement in recruiting documentary into sustained practice of radical empathy”; at the Karlovy Vary film festival in July, it received a five-minute standing ovation; last month, it was selected as the Czech Republic’s official submission for the 99th Oscars in the International Feature Film category.Hundreds of people have got in touch with Lubojacki to share similar family stories. In her film, pigeons won’t turn to gold or even silver because they are what they are: Lubojacki herself undergoes transformation over the course of the film, from moralising her brother “why don’t you do it for me or mom?” to understanding and acceptance. “Since I understood what was going in his brain, and how I should respond, we have the best relationship we ever had.” The empathy Lubojacki has received gives her hope that people like her brother matter. “We learned to avert our eyes but if one breaks the silence, others will follow.”Explore more on these topicsFilmHomelessnessCzechiaHousingPovertySocial exclusionEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Good music is good music, and most music is not!’ As he hits 90, master minimalist Steve Reich looks back | Steve Reich | The Guardian
description: At 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern living
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: At 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern living
Content: ‘I haven’t quite got there yet’ … Steve Reich at 89.Photograph: Jennifer TaylorView image in fullscreen‘I haven’t quite got there yet’ … Steve Reich at 89.Photograph: Jennifer TaylorSteve ReichInterview‘Good music is good music, and most music is not!’ As he hits 90, master minimalist Steve Reich looks backFlora WillsonAt 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern livingTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Reich is not yet 90 but the celebrations have already begun, with the world premiere of his new piece for large ensemble,In All Your Ways, at the Edinburgh festival last month and alate-night concert at the BBC Proms. But when I ask this most supremely influential of living composers how he feels about becoming a nonagenarian on 3 October, Reich is coy. “I haven’t quite got there yet,” he says. “I don’t want to dot the i before I even get there. I’ll let you know in due course …”Born in New York in 1936, Reich has spent the last six decades producing music that has changed the soundtrack of modern life in Europe and North America, and inspired superlatives from a wide array of music critics. The New Yorker has called him “the most original musical thinker of our time”.Hyperbole? Absolutely not. Alongside his US contemporariesPhilip Glass,Terry RileyandLa Monte Young, Reich was one of the pioneers of musical minimalism. Its repetitive licks, driving rhythms and tonal-ish harmonies have since become the lingua franca of new waves of contemporary classical music, electronic dance music, film soundtracks and more. Reich dislikes the label but explains minimalism to me as “an intuitive movement towards whatwewanted to hear. We loved Stravinsky and Bartók and jazz – and were appreciating Bob Dylan and listening to African and Indian music.”double quotation markWe loved Stravinsky and Bartók and jazzNo wonder Reich’s influence has reached so far. His music has been sampled on records byDavid Bowieand chill-out merchantsthe Orb. Radiohead guitaristJonny Greenwoodhas recorded Electric Counterpoint, a work originally written for American jazz musicianPat Metheny. Twenty years ago, UK pop station BBC Radio 1 celebrated Reich’s 70thbirthday with a remix competition. His is a musical language familiar to millions, whether or not they know his name.Today, Reich may be more conscious than usual of his mortality. He is at home outside New York City when we talk, recovering from a recent fall. He broke a rib and has damaged his wrist. The former “seems to mend itself”, he marvels, but the latter is causing problems because he uses the piano as he composes. “You don’t have to be a great pianist, but you do have to be able to move around. I can do it for a minute or two and then it’sreallypainful.” He has “a few little sketches” for something and is frustrated to be slowed down. But he’s also grateful “that all these wonderful things are happening” for his birthday. “I’m not just laying on my back doing nothing,” he cackles. As if anyone who has met him could imagine that.Reich appears far younger than his 89 years. He joins our video call wearing his trademark black baseball cap and spends the next 90 minutes speaking rapid-fire New York-ese, abandoning long words partway in the scramble to communicate. The composer who once said ofPicasso’s Guernicathat,“as a work of art, it’s a towering masterpiece. As an effective political tool, it’s an absolute waste of time”seems as reluctant as ever to be drawn on his own work’s relationship to politics. But on myriad other aspects of music, sound and listening he is expansive, delivering answers in long paragraphs full of enthusiastic diversions.View image in fullscreen‘Look Ma, no electronics!’ … Reich in his studio in Manhattan studio, New York, in 1989.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesHe also cracks self-deprecating jokes, calls me “kid” when I ask him about his younger colleagues, and gleefully mocks me when I don’t catch the name of a major 20th-century composer he references: “Béla Bartók. He’s considered rather important. You might have heard of him …” He recommends an early piano piece by John Cage, In a Landscape – “you hear it and you say, ‘Is this a minimalist and we don’t know his name?’” – and at the end of our call, he wishes me a happy birthday in return, although “I don’t know when your birthday is”. If his reputation for being a“slightly stern”interviewee was ever fair, it’s obsolete in 2026.Yet the pleasure Reich takes in music is rooted in total seriousness. He doesn’t often listen to his own older works but “felt like I’d better brush up”, so he went back to his seminal 1971 percussion piece Drumming a couple of days before we talk. He recorded it in 1974 with his ensemble,Steve Reichand Musicians. “And I thought to myself, this is incredible! I mean, we were young, we were intense …” He recalls the fabulous acoustic – “it was a pop studio in Hanover” – and dives briefly into the minutiae of the recording process.double quotation markI don’t deny for a moment that opera is great music. But it’s not for meMoments later, Reich is talking me through the “two basic kinds of time” in Music for 18 Musicians, the 1976 work widely credited as one of his finest. Bowie hailed it as “a tonetrack into the future”. Fifty years since its premiere, Reich still is excited to demonstrate how it works: the constant rapid chugging of mallet instruments versus the “human breath” of the clarinets functioning “like waves washing over the grid”.This, unmistakably, is the same composer who turned away from the self-conscious “difficulty” of musical modernism – the serialist works that had “no rhythm that you could tap your foot to and no clear key centre that you could hear”. Instead, Reich announced in 1968: “I want to be able to hear the process happening throughout the sounding music.” Most radically of all, he wanted it to be audible to others, too, insisting that even when “everyone hears what is gradually happening, there are still enough musical mysteries to satisfy all”.View image in fullscreen‘I would move and the tape recorder would stay put’ … Reich, the pioneer of the musical phasing technique, in 1982.Photograph: Nancy R Schiff/Getty ImagesReich remains an energetic, acute thinker. He delivers impromptu lectures ranging across 900 years of music history and sings me some pastiche 12th-century polyphony. He speaks admiringly of fellow musicians from arch-modernist composer-conductorPierre Boulez– “he actually helped me indirectly” – to composersNico MuhlyandCaroline Shaw. He softly declaims lines by William Carlos Williams, his favourite poet, who gave a reading at Cornell University that the composer attended as an undergraduate. “He’d had a stroke and had to work at it,” Reich recalls. “It was a very moving experience.”Only names now prove occasionally elusive. “Approaching 90 means your memory is almost vanished,” he mutters at one point. But many anecdotes trip straight off his tongue. I bring up the much-repeated story of his first encounter withStravinsky’s The Rite of Springas a teenager, which he immediately reiterates was “completely life-changing – literally, I mean, my decision to be a composer really starts at the age of 14.” Alongside Stravinsky, the other musical forces at work on him then wereJS Bachand jazz megalithsCharlie ParkerandMiles Davis(“and then later John Coltrane,” he prompts).Has he experienced other equivalent watershed moments since? There is a rare pause in the torrent of ideas. Reich doesn’t think so. “If it was something on that scale, I wouldn’t have to fish around to try to remember it,” he laughs.Music critics and historians may beg to differ. His postgraduate studies with Italian experimental music giantLuciano Berioin the early 1970s clearly had their own significance. Reich arrived at their initial meeting with his own first (and last) 12-tone work, which Berio looked over before suggesting – Reich mimics this gleefully in a thick accent – “If you want to write tonal music, why don’t you write tonal music?”By then, Reich had already played in the world premiere of Terry Riley’s In C, one of the foundational contributions to what would soon be branded minimalism. He’d also bought two Wollensak tape recorders and created his first compositions from looped samples of recorded speech, It’s Gonna Rain (1965) and Come Out (1966). Those led to his development of what he called “phasing” technique.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jennifer Taylor“When I did Piano Phase” – Reich’s landmark 1967 piece for two pianos – “I made a tape loop on the tape recorder, sat down at the piano, and played against the tape recorder. I could count on the tape recorder to stay put,” he laughs. “And I would move – and that’s how the phasing process was discovered, with the interface of a human being versus a machine. When you ask a human pianist to be the machine, it turns out anything but mechanical, because the person who’s moving is like an organic force and you want to join them …”Phasing underpinned all of Reich’s music until he wrote Drumming. So surely its discovery was another big moment for him? “That playing of Piano Phase by myself and the tape recorder? Huge. Playing it with [pianist] Arthur Murphy and myself? Enormous. I just felt like, ‘Oh right,thisis music. Look ma, no electronics!’”A percussionist as well as a composer, Reich was once the driving force behind most performances of his music. As he put it in 1970, “There’s only one person in the world taking care of my music. If I don’t, who will?” These days there are many answers to that question. But no one is more active in promoting Reich’s music than Scottish percussionistColin Currie, who is headlining many ofthis year’s Reich at 90 events.View image in fullscreen‘I hate you – you’re better than my ensemble!’ … the Colin Currie Group performing Reich’s Drumming in 2011.Photograph: Robin Little/RedfernsThey met 20 years ago when the composer attended a performance of Drumming by the newly formedColin Currie Group. “I was completely knocked out,” Reich says. “Afterwards I just embraced him. I said, ‘You know, this is fantastic on the one hand. On the other hand, I hate you because you’re better than my ensemble and I don’t want to be upstaged!’” He grins before looking suddenly serious again. “But that’s exactly how it should be. I sure wish other people would get involved because I’m not going to be around for ever. Not a lot of things are clear in life, but that is.”Reich has a robust sense of his music’s importance and legacy. But he is also quick to own up to his “closet full of failures”. He has mixed feelings about most of his orchestral works (“Three Movementsis not a bad piece. It’s not a great piece”) and about opera as a whole: “I don’t deny for a moment that it’s great music, but it’s not for me.” His two video-operas,The CaveandThree Tales, created in collaboration with his wife, artistBeryl Korot, contain “great material”, he reckons, but “whether they sustain that for the full length of the piece … maybe they do, maybe they don’t”.Ultimately, Reich is clear about his measure for success. “Good music is good music, and most music is not,” he says emphatically. And what makes good music good? “Can you play it next to Charlie Parker? Can you play it next to Johann Sebastian Bach? Does it still sound worthwhile? If it does – hey, you got something!”Steve Reich at 90 festival is at theGlasshouse, Gateshead, from 2-4 October; Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians is performed by theParaorchestra at the Southbank Centre, London, on 27 September; the Barbican Centre’sSteve Reich at 90celebrations begin with the Colin Currie Group on28 OctoberThis article was amended on 22 September 2026. The Colin Currie Group were not performing Steve Reich’s Drumming in a picture as a caption said. title: Doom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ Revolt | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich prose
Author: Sandra Newman
Headline: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich prose
Content: Quirkiness and intensity … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonView image in fullscreenQuirkiness and intensity … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonBook of the dayFictionReviewDoom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ RevoltThis recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich proseSandra NewmanTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and rampaged through southern England, burning records of debts, killing their oppressors and laying waste to their homes. The book closely follows the events of the rebellion’s 16 days, employing a vast array of points of view, including the young king Richard II, several of his courtiers, dozens of elements of the rebellious Commons, a porpoise and a runaway horse. The title suggests the novel’s portrayal of these events as an inevitable reckoning; a “doom painting” was a picture of the Last Judgment on the wall of a medieval church.As a book of this scope must be, it’s a doorstopper. As any novel by Blakemore will be, it’s dazzlingly rich in lexical glamour, and this is likely to be any reader’s lasting impression of the book. Sometimes it feels as if the author is out to use every word in the English language in a startling, aestheticised, puckish way that expands both the word and the world. The result can be joyously silly. Who else would give us slugs that “blurb their elementary forms from out of the undergrowth to begin a dank and toothlessfesta”, or “lunar-brilliantined mud”? But there is also gravity and passion here, especially when she intimately imagines the lives of the commoners: “they rise, to fry eggs in butter and pork fat; they rise, to whet knives on scarred stone; they rise, to braid the manes of their draught horses; they rise, to count arrows; they rise, setting aside their glitchy dreams of hairy stars and blue-skinned devils; they rise, fearful and powerful, into the bright day.” The cheekily anachronistic appearance of “glitchy” in this medieval scene is typical of Blakemore’s method. All forms of language, high and low, archaic and modern, are here. Her use of detail to convey a historical scene is also extraordinary: the barber’s chair where “a crowd has gathered beneath the ribboned pole to watch the draining of a cyst”; the brewer with “a grotty beard, chlorotic with hops, [that] hangs down almost to his belt”; or “the horseflies waltzing over the liquefying flesh of severed heads”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIf you have any political sensibility, the sweep of the revolt will draw you inBlakemore is less successful in the traditional novelistic areas of plot and character. The primary figure throughout is legendary rebel leader Wat Tyler. Historical accounts of Wat are few and unreliable, so a novelist has a lot of latitude. Blakemore makes him a mercenary traumatised and brutalised by the wars in France, and the details of this history fit well and feel appropriate. However, his actual personality fluctuates from scene to scene. Mostly he’s a coarse, unlettered bruiser, lovable for his simplicity. However, when he’s alone, he’s given to sensitive introspection, spending a lot of time assigning psychological explanations to his choices. In this mode, he’s completely apolitical, and his leadership feels like a tragicomic fluke. In other scenes, though, he expresses strong and coherent political convictions, and occasionally it seems his simplicity is only a mask he assumes to achieve his objectives. Other characters are similarly inconsistent or undefined, and while this doesn’t ruin the story, it does blunt its emotional force. We can’t feel that deeply about how Richard II was transformed by these events if he never came into focus for us in the first place.Another problem is that much of the dialogue feels like action-movie banter in medieval clothing. People say things like: “Is that a scruple? And here, I thought you thoroughly divested of those,” or reply to, “I’d sooner die,” with a jaunty “You very well might”. The tone is occasionally anachronistic enough that it feels like a wink to the reader, as when Wat says, “We’ll sleep when we’re dead”, or turns to a confederate to say: “Your auld mum certainly seems to think so … Because I swived her, see.” Blakemore imagines a romance between Wat and another storied leader of the rebellion, Jack Straw; this could have gone to interesting places if it were made more real. But the execution is cursory enough that it carries a whiff of “shipping” – the demand of 21st-century fandoms to see the heroes kiss. Since the book is generally meticulously realistic and historically appropriate, I was left unsure how these elements were meant to land. In some places, the gorgeous language masks any clash of tones or realities; in others, the narrative fails to meld.Despite these cavils, I very strongly recommend Doom Painting. If you have any sensitivity to language, you can romp around in its prose; if you have any political sensibility, the sweep of the revolt will draw you in. It recreates historical events extravagantly well and must have taken a colossal amount of research, yet it wears its scholarship lightly.It’s a beast and a challenge; in its quirkiness and intensity, it couldn’t be more interesting. In an era of safe bets and timid choices, here is a work of reckless ambition.Doom Painting by AK Blakemore is published by Granta (£20). title: Autumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and place | Kate Mosse | The Guardian
description: The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved Sussex
Author: Ruth Padel
Headline: The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved Sussex
Content: A tunnel through trees near Chichester, West Sussex.Photograph: Patricia Hamilton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA tunnel through trees near Chichester, West Sussex.Photograph: Patricia Hamilton/Getty ImagesKate MosseReviewAutumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and placeThe author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved SussexRuth PadelTue 22 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and then Val McDermid celebrating winter in Scotland, where she grew up and still lives.Bernardine Evaristo will explore summer soon – but, meanwhile, we have Mosse, also deeply and endearingly rooted in her chosen patch.Mosse grew up in the village of Fishbourne. She now lives in Chichester, where she got to know her husband when they revised for A-levels in the shadow of the Bishop’s Palace, and held hands when she turned 17 on the day of the city’s annual Sloe Fair. Twenty-three years later, they celebrated her 40th there, with their children. Today, they live with his 90-something mother Granny Rosie – also “Sussex to her bones” – who remembers watching cattle herded in fields where a supermarket now stands.In Granny Rosie’s youth, “the link between tradition and the natural world was present in every part of everyday life”, and that connection is the real focus of Mosse’s book. She has spent nearly all of her 65 years in Sussex. HerLanguedoc trilogywas inspired by her time in the Aude city of Carcassonne, but it was Sussex that gave her a taste for the combination of landscape, history and storytelling that drives her books. The county’s folklore and countryside informed her gothic thrillerThe Taxidermist’s Daughter, and it was the backdrop for her memoir about family care-giving,An Extra Pair of Hands.Autumn gives us more of it. Walking under oak trees, Mosse pictures far off days when oaks were the only road signs. In her garden, she tells us that the Romans called wild cyclamen “earth truffle”, “believing that ill spells were ineffective where they were found”. If there is, at times, a touch of the guide-book in her telling, she wins your heart by the sheer joy she takes in the details.Mosse sets out what Sussex gave other writers, too. William Blake drafted Jerusalem in Felpham, then threw a drunk soldier out of his garden and was tried in Chichester for sedition (all because the soldier claimed he insulted the king). He was acquitted, but “never set foot in Sussex again”. John Keats was inspired by Chichester’s architecture to write The Eve of St Agnes; Hilaire Belloc became Sussex’s unofficial poet laureate; and James Joyce lived in Bognor Regis while writing Finnegans Wake.Above all, there is “the great Sussex writer”, Rudyard Kipling. I love imagining how that phrase will be read in India; but, in fact, Kipling wrote Kimwhile living in Sussex (where he moved to in the late 1800s). Just So Storiescameimmediately after, and in 1906 he made the village of Burwash the setting for Puck of Pook’s Hill.In the manner of Kipling, Mosse takes infectious delight in weaving her memories through bronze age camps, iron age forts, wetlands, the downs and the Devil’s Dyke, composing a hymn to Sussex’s countryside and braiding rambly byways of fact and legend with personal memories.She loves the place so much that you feel she would have written as joyfully about it at any time of year. But she takes autumn seriously as a season of transition, beginning with her first day at school. There she is, 60 years ago, on 1 September: “Four, rising five.” Her mother is waving goodbye and her world is about to expand. Then, she takes us through the ghosts of Halloween, Bonfire Night in Lewes and Harvest festival.By the time she gets to the last day of November, Autumn itself feels like a kind of harvest. Mosse sees it as a thank you for “the gift of home”. For the luxury of enjoying, intensely, the land where grandparents, children and grandchildren still gather; and for sun-dappled village Englishness. “I take a deep breath to try and capture my pleasure at simply being here.”Autumn by Kate Mosse is published by Hodder & Stoughton (£16.99).
