title: Control Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomena | Games | The Guardian
description: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Content: New York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentView image in fullscreenNew York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentGamesReviewControl Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomenaPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; RemedyA surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safePhil IwaniukTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House. You’d navigate architecturally impossible spaces bridging the subconscious and the bricks-and-mortar world, in order to defeat a malevolent fridge. That’s broadly true again in Resonant, albeit with diminishing returns. This time you’re playing as Jesse’s brother Dylan, waking up after years of containment in the Oldest House to find its contents have escaped into downtown Manhattan. So you head out of the interesting place, and into a setting you’ve explored before inMarvel’s Spider-Man,The Division,Max Payne, and others ad infinitum.It’s disappointing because being bewitchingly strange has historically been Remedy’s great strength. It’s not unusual for games to give a reverent nod to Twin Peaks now and then, but this studio is the alpha and omega of interactive Lynchian nightmares. It’s been refining that skill since 2001’s Max Payne, and at this point there’s really nobody better at nonlinear storytelling or unnerving dream sequences.View image in fullscreenInception-like gravitational spins … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentRemedy’s take on New York has an exhilaratingly free-form structure that lets you take on enemies, missions and places in roughly the order you want. The main missions are fairly rigid, but you can engage with the rest however and whenever you want. You fight a malevolent paranormal force with an imaginative collection of supernatural kung fu moves, whose power and combo potential level up satisfyingly. Your shapeshifting weapon can take many forms, from a dagger-like blade to a scythe or a hammer. Secondary attacks, ranged weapons and passive abilities lend more interest to fights against paranormal entity the Hiss as time goes on, but compared to something like the surgically precise swordplay of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, battles feel a bit blunt here.Your ultimate tests come in the form of the Resonants themselves, a series of bosses lying in wait throughout Manhattan. Remedy’s knack for otherworldly horror comes to the fore in their visual design, which I won’t spoil, and like so much of the game they can be hunted down in any order. Beware, though – beating them changes other enemies’ presence, strength and behaviour afterwards.Dylan’s movement is more imaginative and enjoyable than his arsenal. Here, trading off a fascinating indoor setting for more outdoor space starts to make sense, as you triple-jump your way across rooftops and shift your gravitational grounding to walk on streets that have been bent upwards vertically à laInception. It’s playful about it, too – soon after gaining that latter ability, your bureau handler pumps some EDM down the radio to soundtrack your run through a multistorey car park whose levels fold and distort at impossible angles.It is the little moments like this, not the grand story beats, that prove the most memorable and gratifying. Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.Control Resonant is out now; £49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamesAction gamesGame playPlayStation 5XboxreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Magritte: This Is Still Not a Pipe review – brilliance and trash from the surrealist who sent up Freud | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!
Content: Freud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence … La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), by René Magritte, 1936.Photograph: © 2026 C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkView image in fullscreenFreud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence … La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), by René Magritte, 1936.Photograph: © 2026 C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkArt and designReviewMagritte: This Is Still Not a Pipe review – brilliance and trash from the surrealist who sent up FreudGagosian Gallery, LondonWith his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!Jonathan JonesTue 22 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRené Magritte is the most inexplicable of artists. It’s much harder to get a handle on him than such supposedly difficult modern greats as Cézanne or Picasso. After all, cubism is a perfectly rational attempt to capture the complexity of reality. But Magritte? He confronts you with wilful mysteries. This show sets choice examples of his magic against modern art and is full of quirky, unexpected treasures that give your wonder at Magritte little twists in new and perverse directions.A painting of puffy white clouds held me across the gallery and still floats ineffably in my mind. It’s a shock because it is so painterly and subtle. If you think Magritte fashioned his surrealist images in a deliberately flat, even banal style, think again. This simple painting of clouds in the blue is full of supple shadow and ethereal light, a brilliantly observed view of nature in the vein of Gainsborough, Constable or Hockney.View image in fullscreenThis is not the sky … La Malédiction (The Curse) by René Magritte, 1931.Photograph: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonExcept it’s not. Innocent as these clouds look, real as they look, they are no such thing. These are not clouds. This is not the sky. And the painting’s sunniness is totally undermined by its title: The Curse. Magritte made it in 1931 at the height of surrealism, the revolutionary art movement that took from the psychoanalytic writings of Sigmund Freud the insight that nothing is innocent and no image is simply what it seems.Everything can be a symbol and probably a dirty one. A pipe. Or a nose. Magritte’s 1936 self-portrait The Philosopher’s Lamp combines both in an absurd meta-Freudian image as his nose becomes a fleshy tube curving down into the bowl of his pipe while a candle twists in a waxy, snaking motion around the stiff single leg of the table. Freud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence but the painting makes that so obvious, it’s a joke. Magritte is satirising psychoanalysis and surrealism itself for being too logical in their reading of symbols.The surrealist movement was started in Paris after the first world war by poets and artists traumatised by its mass slaughter and seeking imaginative renewal by escaping into dreams and erotic reveries. Magritte became the movement’s greatest Belgian representative, but he pushed at its limits, taking it to a far less easily decoded level.View image in fullscreenLe Lieu commun (The Commonplace) by René Magritte, 1964.Photograph: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonThat philosophical shift is here in The Interpretation of Dreams, a modern masterpiece lent by its owner the great (and philosophical) American artist Jasper Johns. The English title used here connects it directly with Freud’s most famous book although its actual title in French, La Clef des Songes, translates as The Key of Dreams. Either way, this 1935 painting suggests that dreams and reality are equally bizarre and neither can be explained by the oedipal complex. Four objects are displayed against a neutral background in separate sections. A horse’s head is captioned “the door”; a clock face is labelled “the wind”; under a white jug it says “the bird”. Yet in the bottom right corner, a suitcase is accurately identified as “the valise”.It’s the last that makes this an unsettling demolition of reality rather than a piece of whimsy. If all the images we saw in dreams were fantastically misrecognised, that would be amusing, but one time out of four, says Magritte, the dream is true. You can neither ignore dreams nor understand them. You’re screwed.But if Magritte rejected the psychoanalytic overconfidence that dreams can be decoded, he had no problem recalling the most vivid and appalling nightmares. The Pleasure depicts a girl eating a bird and in The Listening Room a giant apple completely fills a chamber, its bright green skin pushing monstrously against the walls and ceiling.There are so many connections here with modern art – how many installations have echoed that space-swallowing apple? But the patchiest part of this show is its attempt to link with today’s artists. A Jeff Koons train and Aqualung, a floppy Sarah Lucas nude, an obscene wooden statue of a woman interacting with teddy bears by Isabelle Albuquerque – these are one-dimensional compared with Magritte’s conundrums. Gagosian has done a brilliant job of borrowing his work but descends into commercial glibness in its choice of his supposed 21st-century peers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho did this piece of trash, I wondered, in front of a ludicrous cartoony daub of three legs strutting about independently, one with a red nose, moustache and feathered headdress, another puffing a pipe, all rendered in slobbery horrid hues. Then I saw the signature: Magritte. This and a couple of equally lurid daubs come from Magritte’s “Vache” (cow) period when he deliberately did bad, stupid paintings to annoy his family, friends and fans.What a dude. He could paint like Jan van Eyck when he wanted but sometimes preferred to paint like a clumsy moron. Magritte was too intelligent to respect anything, least of all art.This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte, is atGagosian Gallery, London, 24 September to 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designRené MagritteExhibitionsPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists review – It caused fury across Europe. In the UK? Laughter and coughing | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Tiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Tiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing
Content: Provocations … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesView image in fullscreenProvocations … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesTheatreReviewCatarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists review – It caused fury across Europe. In the UK? Laughter and coughingNational Theatre, LondonTiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusingArifa AkbarTue 22 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat does it say about an audience who, while watching a character make a speech that has sparked screeching protests and angry walkouts in its run across Europe, sit politely listening until the end?The booing does come, but only after the actor playing a far-right politician and kidnap victim (Romeu Costa) has finished a half-hour invective that takes in everything from the scourge of minorities to that of elites, homosexuals, and the far-left. It is a masterclass in rightwing rabble-rousing, with its appropriation of the word “freedom”. Yet on press night at its British premiere, all that is summoned in response is nervous laughter, a chorus of coughs and a few loud whistles.Is this because audiences have heard about the furore around Tiago Rodrigues’s play and know what to expect, or is it something more insidiously British in its politeness? There could be a host of excuses: we know it is only theatre; we feel disconnected from fascism in a way thataudiences in Germany– or in Portugal, where the production is from – may not. Or is it simply that we want to hear the character out?Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?Read moreThe politician takes the floor at the end. The central drama features a family that kidnaps and kills a single “fascist” on an annual basis as a ritual protest against the far right. Characters wear old-fashioned dresses and shawls (including the men) and speak in peculiarly comic tones, so they look and sound like Lorcan parodies. They are all called Catarina too, to honour the original Catarina, a protester murdered at the hands of President António de Oliveira Salazar’s authoritarian government in 1954, after which the family’s grandmothercommanded her family to take on these annual killings.If the point of the play is to compel an audience into action, we are Hamlet, immobilised. But it seems more complicated than that. Set in a near-future in which a far-right government is on the verge of changing the constitution in Portugal, its central ethical debate revolves around armed protest and the question of whether to suffer under fascism or to take arms against it. Every family member has abided by Catarina’s rule until one (Beatriz Maia) says she can’t justify it, and refuses to shoot.View image in fullscreenKidnap your enemy … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesThe justifications for political violence here are presented in pithy summaries, via English surtitles: “It is not enough to be against, you must act against,” says one character. “You cannot fight intolerance with tolerance,” says another.But there are so many other gnomic and mannered tics to the dialogue. Characters babble on about nothing, it seems. There are unfunny jokes about veganism (a pop at the “woke” left?) and a riff on the flight of swallows (the birds are later likened to immigrants by the politician). They flog the same arguments on violent protest. You wonder if it is a critique of the political left: that it can only talk on interminably or in-fight in the face of real fascist threat.And as post-dramatic theatre, aware of itself and refusing to cast fourth-wall illusions, it is a play of maddening inaction – the family member who won’t shoot, the drama that won’t give us any drama, or not until its final stretch.So it is arduous to watch, in spite of Fernando Ribeiro’s origami-like set of a slatted house, foregrounded by a dining table reminiscent of The Last Supper, that rearranges itself beautifully. Then, suddenly, the crushing boredom is punctured by the shock of gunfire and the politician’s speech. Have we been deliberately lulled into an almost soporific state?This paradox of boredom and shock might encapsulate the political juncture at which Europe stands, with AfD on the rise in Germany andPresident Le Penpotentially six months away in France. If so, is the play a starting-gun for those of us walking zombie-eyed, or wilfully blind, into a fascist future? The politician rattles on and on. He is not named but we know him. Do we wish him dead?AtDorfman theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatrePolitical theatreThe far rightLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Amar Kanwar review: unflinching Indian artist dares you to step into the darkness (literally) | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Making lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missed
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Making lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missed
Content: ‘An atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility’ ... Amar Kanwar’s Such a Morning, 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.View image in fullscreen‘An atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility’ ... Amar Kanwar’s Such a Morning, 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.Art and designReviewAmar Kanwar review: unflinching Indian artist dares you to step into the darkness (literally)Serpentine North, LondonMaking lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missedBen EasthamTue 22 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe exhibition begins in darkness. A darkness so complete, in fact, that I’m forced to wait at the threshold while my eyes adjust to it. To my left, images flash up on screens that seem to float in the gloom: a peacock preens its wet feathers; dried flowers in a wooden bowl; sunlight scatters on water. When the room has resolved to the point that I can identify a chair to sit on, I realise that these pictures are combined with snippets of text telling stories like parables: about a landlord punished for breaking a promise to a beggar; about two friends who survive a massacre because they are down by the river, arguing over the moon.Welcome to the world of Amar Kanwar: if you want to find beauty and truth, you must be prepared to step into the darkness. Over 40 years making increasingly lyrical films about stories ranging from the collapse of empire to endemic sexual brutality, the Indian artist has developed a method that neither reproduces the violence of these histories as spectacle nor glosses it over. Instead he trains his focus on those parts of the story that normally escape attention: the shadows, the neglected, the blind spots. He does not find revelation there, at least not of the kind that suddenly lights up the world and makes sense of it. But there are enough flashes of light to guide us through the darkness.This idea finds its most literal expression in Such a Morning, a feature-length film installed within one of the enclosed spaces that make this old gunpowder store so well suited to Kanwar’s play with darkness and light, secrets and disclosure (the whole exhibition is superbly staged). It tells the story of a mathematics professor who retreats into an artificial darkness in the hope of finding another way to understand the world around him. Through a characteristic combination of exquisite images – a woman sits in a rattan chair clutching an antiquated rifle as her house is dismantled around her – with overlaid text and a trancelike piano soundtrack, the film conjures an atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility.View image in fullscreenAmar Kanwar’s 2023 film The Peacock’s Graveyard.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.Like much of Kanwar’s work, Such a Morning makes demands on your patience. Anyone attempting to make simple sense of the film is likely to sympathise with the professor groping blindly around in the dark. But it is worth putting in the time, because Kanwar’s commitment to doubt as a precursor of knowledge carries a political charge in the present. If you are inclined to feel, on reading the news, that we have recently entered a new dark age, then Such a Morning proposes that we have been blinded by the lights. Overwhelmed by images masquerading as reality and opinions posing as fact, we might follow the professor’s example and commit to a period of reflection on what we choose to see and how we interpret it. He comes to a simple conclusion: we must all learn to attend to the darkness if we are to change the course of “self-destruction” on which humanity is presently set. It’s a lesson worth heeding.The degrees of darkness the professor identifies are represented by illuminated paper screens that protrude from the wall like torches. It’s a brilliant piece of theatre design that leads you through the prevailing gloom to the final work in the show, another film to combine archive footage with fragments of text. The subject of the evocatively titled The Charcoal Man is the 1947 partition of India. Events from the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi to the mass migrations are told from the perspectives of people who might seem incidental to the action: an absent-minded window maker, a boy who dreams of becoming a drummer.The tension here is between forgetting and remembering, both of which are figured as essential to reconciliation, and The Charcoal Man suggests they might be fused through various kinds of alchemy or transference. In one story, for example, a father instructs his son to remove the circuit boards from the computers in his shop and, through a complex chemical process, to aggregate the gold they contain into a bracelet that could be pawned in the event that he needs at short notice to flee. Memories of a violent past are by these means transformed into insurance against the future. Is this what art might do?The same narrator inherits from his grandfather, a professional photographer, an archive of images documenting the violence of Partition. The seemingly paradoxical condition of the bequest is that these photographs should be conserved for ever but never shown. Instead they might continue to exist in the shadows, alluded to (but never revealed) by the kind of stories that preserve the horrors of the past without restarting the cycles of violence. These, after all, are the kind of stories that Amar Kanwar tells.Amar Kanwar is at Serpentine North Gallery from 23 September 2026 until 31 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtSerpentine GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The truth about Sean Combs: ‘No is not a stopping point for him’ | Sean ‘Diddy‘ Combs | The Guardian
description: Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-ins
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-ins
Content: ‘He lives in different versions for different people, but who is he?’ Combs in at the  Cannes film festival in 2008.Photograph: Eric Gaillard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘He lives in different versions for different people, but who is he?’ Combs in at the  Cannes film festival in 2008.Photograph: Eric Gaillard/ReutersSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsThe truth about Sean Combs: ‘No is not a stopping point for him’Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-insAnna MooreTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, the civil lawsuit that dropped on Sean “Diddy” Combs in November 2023 seemed to come from nowhere. Filed by his ex-partner, the singer Cassie Ventura, it alleged that Combs had beaten and raped her, plied her with drugs and forced her into sexual encounters with male sex workers throughout their decade-long relationship.Roundtree, along with much of the world’s media, was shocked. “I’d grown up in the era of Diddy and Cassie and viewed them as this power couple,” she says. “Her hit Me & U was my song. Diddy was this mogul – I knew him for the music – and she was this style inspiration, this beautiful, talented woman living an amazing life.”At first, Combs and his legal teamissuedblanket denials. The lawsuit, they said, had followed an attempt by Ventura to blackmail Combs, and was “riddled with baseless and outrageous lies”. Despite this, they settled it immediately with a $20m sum, but within days more women came forward. A second lawsuit was filed one week after Ventura’s, by Joi Dickerson-Neal, which alleged that, as a student in 1991, she had been drugged and raped by Combs, who had filmed the alleged assault and shared it with other men. Days later came another. In this, Anna Kane alleged that Combs and two others had gang-raped her in 2003 when she was 17. As the cases piled up, Combs’s team continued the denials – describing the lawsuits as “money grabs”. Then a leaked video forced them to change tack. Security footage from a Los Angeles hotel taken in March 2016 showed Cassie Ventura creeping from a room, pursued by Combs, who is wrapped in just a towel. He beats her, kicks her and drags her back.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment’ … Cheyenne Roundtree.Photograph: Maria Spann/The Guardian“His attorneys took it head on,” says Roundtree. “They were saying: ‘We’re going to own the domestic violence, but that happened in the past – all that is locked in the 2010s and he has changed.He has become Lovesince then. [Combs had declared in November 2017 that he was renaming himself Love, or Brother Love.] He’s a new person, a father figure.’ But all these other lawsuits were telling a completely different story.”Roundtree started digging through the archives, finding stories, interviews and police reports lost to time, often because they weren’t online. Over the next three years, she spoke to people who had known Combs at every stage of his life – as a boy, a teenage intern, a genius producer and the founder of Bad Boy Records, a Grammy-winning artist, a business mogul – and finally as an inmate in a New Jersey prison. The lawsuits led to a federal investigation and, eventually, Combs’s indictment. Now 56, he is serving a 50-month sentence for transporting people across state lines for prostitution.View image in fullscreenCassie Ventura with Combs at her 21st birthday party in September 2007, at the Jet nightclub at the Mirage on Las Vegas Boulevard.Photograph: Denise Truscello/WireImage“To me, he was always ‘Diddy’,” says Roundtree. “When I talk to anyone from New York, he’s Puff or Puffy. Later, he wanted the world to call him Love and now, in this legal sense, he has become Sean Combs. He lives in these different versions for different people, but who is he?” Her book, Bad Boy for Life, attempts to answer this by picking out the patterns and repeat behaviours, the rumours and run-ins that have threaded through every reinvention. It reads like a “making of a monster”, a damning indictment of celebrity culture, where every impulse, however dark, is enabled by yes men. “I never planned to write a book but I was finding so much material, it felt important to preserve all the history in one place,” she says. “I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment.”It begins in Harlem where Combs spent his first years, and where his father, a gangster, was shot dead when Combs was a toddler. His mother, Janice, moved them to Mount Vernon, a suburb of Westchester County, just north of New York City. The Janice remembered by Combs’s childhood friend Tim Patterson cuts a formidable figure – glamorous, determined and ambitious. Patterson describes discipline that goes beyond “tough love”, and wild parties where it was normal to walk in on couples “butt naked”.View image in fullscreenA mugshot of Combs after his arrest by New York Police Department; he was charged in 2001 with possession of a firearm following a shooting at a Manhattan nightclub.Photograph: Donaldson Collection/Getty Images“His childhood leaves questions that only Combs and Janice can answer,” says Roundtree, “but the sources from that time said that being exposed to sexual things quite young, parenting style and growing up in Harlem meant that, by the time he was a teenager at Howard University, you’re seeing that something had manifested.”Janice Combs has complained of “lies” and “inaccuracies” in how she and her son’s upbringing have been portrayed.At Howard, studying business, Combs was well known – for his drive, his style and his legendary parties. Years later, he also described falling in love at Howard, in an ill-fated Romeo and Juliet-style affair. In a magazine interview, Combs said his girlfriend’s parents disapproved because her grades had dropped from As to Bs. They pulled her from Howard, allowing her back only if she ended the relationship. “That hurt so bad. It’s one of those things in life that everybody goes through, but the pain was so intense it was hard for me to handle,” he said.Former classmates remember it differently. In their accounts to Roundtree, Combs was jealous and abusive. His girlfriend’s parents intervened, they said, only after Combs had shown up at her dorm, called her outside, whipped her with his belt and dragged her by her hair, while students watched horrified from their windows.“The way he romanticised all that, and talked about her as if they were destined by the stars but forces kept them apart, was exactly how his attorney talked about Cassie decades later,” says Roundtree. “In the trial last year, the attorney called Combs’s relationship with Cassie ‘a great modern love story’.”The pages of Bad Boy for Life are packed with allegations, many involving women who have since launched civil suits. (Up to 70 lawsuits are believed to be moving through the system.) There are common features: one-night encounters where drinks are spiked, a woman is raped, and the alleged abuse is filmed, and others that tell how Combs would single out a woman and pursue her relentlessly using any means necessary. (“No is not a stopping point for Combs,” says Roundtree.) He was known for his untamed rage. Many former friends and colleagues describe witnessing his assaults on girlfriends – and on any men deemed rivals.View image in fullscreenCombs in a recording studio in 1997.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesRoundtree also shines a light on other criminal activities in his orbit, from long-forgotten police reports to the notorious murders of his protege Biggie Smalls and Biggie’s rival, Tupac Shakur. Again, she picks out parallels. In 2001, after a shooting inside a Manhattan nightclub, Combs was charged with thepossession of illegal weapons and attempted bribery(it was alleged that he had offered his driver $50,000 to take the blame). By then, at 31, Combs was already a multimillionaire with a record label, a fashion brand and a celebrity girlfriend, Jennifer Lopez. “His team conducted – and won – that early case in just the same way they fought the trial in 2025,” says Roundtree. “The smooth PR, the publicists who would talk to journalists and the crowds outside rooting for him.”In that 2001 case, the jury acquitted Combs but his co-defendant, rapper Jamal “Shyne” Barrow, who had been with him on the night, was convicted, sentenced to 10 years, then deported to Belize, his birth country. Combs didn’t attend Barrow’s sentencing, quietly dropped Barrow from his record label and changed his name from Puff Daddy to P Diddy to mark his fresh start. (Barrow later described Combs as “someone who destroyed my life”.)In every chapter of the book – and Combs’s life – people around him are shot, assaulted, imprisoned and broken, and careers are destroyed, yet he remains A-list, ascending to icon status. How? “That’s the biggest question,” says Roundtree. “How is someone with so many incidents around him, so much ruin in his wake, able to just keep doing better and better?“I think part of it was his personality. The media loved him because he played into the spectacle – he wasn’t afraid to be larger than life. He was also building something people really believed in. His record company was everywhere in New York, and he was giving opportunities to young people, straight out of school. He’d created a living legend in Biggie, who died so early. His clothing line was cool. His fragrance was great. His parties were epic. All these things played into a figure so big and so tangible, people think they can see it all right in front of them. So why look any further?”View image in fullscreenBiggie Smalls, Nate Dogg, Snoop Dogg and Combs, circa 1995.Photograph: Nitro/Getty ImagesVentura’s lawsuit was a pulling back of the curtain. “She was the first to let people into that world,” says Roundtree. “It’s really rare to see the inner workings of a public couple, but she laid it all out there, through her lawsuit, her trial testimony with all those photos on screen and text messages that she was asked to read, in front of the jury, in front of the world. She bared it all.”Ventura had signed to Combs’s record label when she was 19, a model turned singer. She had a hit, Me & U, a 10-album deal, and so much promise ahead. The book describes Combs’s focused pursuit of her, despite the 17-year age gap. (One of his personal assistants recalls Combs describing her as “very mouldable” and saying: “I got her right where I want her. She’s young.”)Combs’s inner circle and Ventura’s testimony describe the control he had over every part of her life – her diary, clothes, hair, nails. Even her medical records went directly to Combs’s email and he tracked her menstrual cycle. Her career stalled. Though Ventura recorded hundreds of tracks, her boss – Combs – didn’t release them. “She was his ‘wife partner’ for 10 years publicly,” says Roundtree. “One of the most surprising things to see was that, behind the scenes, she never lived with him, she never spent Christmas with him.”The relationship described by Ventura was dominated by “freak-offs” – coerced, multi-day-long, drug-fuelled sexual encounters with male sex workers, held in hotel rooms. Every aspect was micromanaged, choreographed, directed, watched and filmed by Combs. According to Ventura, she was 22 when Combs first raised the idea, and she “had no concept of how it would be a turn-on”. But she wanted to please him. After the first, she felt “dirty” but glad Combs was “happy” with her, that she “did something right”.Hundreds more took place around the world with unvetted men she didn’t know. Ventura says she felt “disgusting”, “humiliated”. When she attempted to leave Combs, he threatened to share the videos. (In one exchange between them, she talks of showing the world photos of her beaten face and body. “Release the videos also,” Combs shoots back.) Her life became preparing for “freak-offs”, enduring them and recovering afterwards. (“That’s why nothing gets done,” she wrote in one message to Combs, in 2017, their final year together. “Always healing.”)Ventura officially separated from Combs in 2018 and filed her lawsuit five years later. When federal investigators subsequently approached her to build a criminal case, she handed over phones, iPads, video material, the names of sex workers and other witnesses to help corroborate her claims.The US has no federal laws around coercive control and offences such as rape and assault carry statutes of limitations – legal time limits after which prosecution is not possible. But Combs was charged with racketeering conspiracy,sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution.“Those laws were developed to bring down the mafia, to dismantle criminal networks,” says Roundtree.View image in fullscreenCombs performing at Howard University’s Yardfest in 2023.Photograph: Thaddaeus McAdams/WireImageCombs’s 2025 trial lasted seven weeks, with the prosecution arguing that Combs used his business empire as a front for a criminal operation, relying on close associates to force and intimidate women into freak-offs and transport and supply drugs to keep them compliant. The defence argued successfully that what took place did not constitute a formal criminal enterprise.Ultimately, he was acquitted of most charges. “He was only found guilty of the clear examples where he paid for the male escorts to travel across a state line,” says Roundtree. “If they’d stayed within their states, they couldn’t have charged him with that.”The music industry, says Roundtree, is yet to have its “#MeToo fallout”. “Hollywood had this reckoning; music never really has.” R Kelly is the only other high-profile musician now in prison because of abuse uncovered in the me-too fall out. Others have been untouched by swirling rumours and mounting accusations. “Maybe it’s because an artist is so singular,” says Roundtree. “Actors have this whole machine around them, procedures to go through, people to answer to. And we love our music. Those songs are our fondest memories, they take us right back to a place or a time or a person and it’s hard to give that up, to separate the art from the artist. Sean Combs was a producer. Do we give up every song he touched? So we can’t listen to Biggie any more? It’s not realistic.”Combs’s release date is set for early in 2028, and he has multiple civil cases still to answer, although on Thursday it was reported that his attorneys areno longer acting for himin a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills. What lies beyond this? “He’ll definitely want to try to tell his story and make a comeback,” says Roundtree. “He has had a microphone in his hand since he was in his early 20s and I don’t think that desire to be loved and validated has gone away. There’ll be a next chapter for Sean Combs.”Bad Boy for Life: The Rise and Fall of Sean Combs by Cheyenne Roundtree (Simon & Schuster, £25) is out on 29 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsUS crimeRape and sexual assaultfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nimesh Patel on stand-up, Palestine and politics: ‘The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly’ | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism
Content: Nimesh Patel: ‘I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok.’Photograph: Andrew LevyView image in fullscreenNimesh Patel: ‘I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok.’Photograph: Andrew LevyComedyInterviewNimesh Patel on stand-up, Palestine and politics: ‘The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly’Radheyan SimonpillaiThe comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimismTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a single minute in Buy the Dip, Nimesh Patel’s newNetflixcomedy special, in which the comedian nimbly and hilariously goes from describing his wife in labour with their first child to complaining about a Rolex sporting doctor wearing “insurance payments on his wrist” toLuigi Mangione. “He killed one guy, allegedly,” Patel quips, arguing that the terrorism-related charge Mangione got stuck with (which a judgedismissed) was offensive to real terrorists.The hilarious bit is impressive for how much Patel packs into a single minute and how much it all speaks to the comedian’s own experience, expertise and worldview.John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’Read morePatel, who hails from New Jersey, was once a pre-med finance graduate from New York University. He entertained going into healthcare before joining the ranks of finance bros. He abandoned all of that when he found a path in comedy alongside the likes ofHasan MinhajandRami Malek, a generation of brown guys who came of age in the shadow of 9/11 and have had to grow up being associated with Al-Qaida by the most racist swaths of American society. Patel is maybe the only one of them who could land that punchline about Mangione, which exists in the exact same intersection as him: of healthcare, finance and charges of terrorism that don’t stick.“It wasn’t by design that I was going to condense all that into that bit,” Patel says, humbly, on a Zoom call from his home in Brooklyn, New York. “It just so happened that that’s where my brain goes.”The words “it just so happened” gets at Patel’s magic trick as a comedian. In Buy the Dip, and across a lot of his comedy foundonline, Patel maintains the most laidback, effortless and unbothered vibe. He’s the kind of stand-up who makes it genuinely seem as though he’s floating along and the jokes just so happen to make their way to him.Patel understands that passive air to be both a feature and a bug. Throughout our conversation he looks back at moments in his life and career, at times with regret, where he “didn’t deal well with adversity” (he gave up on pre-med after getting a C in one class) or he let fate decide his life choices for him. On the latter front, for instance, Patel lost his job in finance in 2016, at the same time thatChris Rockdiscovered him at the Comedy Cellar in New York, where he had been performing and honing his craft for years.“It was a very star-aligning kind of a moment,” says Patel, looking back at how the decision to commit full-time to comedy was made for him. Rock tapped the newly unemployed Patel to write for his hosting duties at the2016 Oscars, which led to, among other things, Patel becoming the first Indian American to join the writer’s room at SNL, where he lasted a single season that nabbed him an Emmynomination.“I’ll happily admit that I was not good at those jobs,” he adds. “I was still finding and having to cultivate my own voice. I have my own way of delivering my jokes in my worldview. To then recalibrate that and figure out how someone else would say it is actually a pretty difficult thing. Some of those joke writers are the best joke writers on the planet, but I’m a very good stand-up.”double quotation markI’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the faceNimesh PatelThrough our conversation, Patel’s brain regularly goes to finance, whether he’s crunching the numbers on ticket sales growth at his shows (“I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok”) or casually dropping a reference to Apple and Nvidia’s stock growth while calculating what he sacrificed (a $125,000 payday) when backing out of the Saudi Arabia-sponsoredRiyadh comedy festivallast year. “I’ve said and I stated, if it was more money, I definitely would have gone,” says Patel, being bluntly honest about the accounting that would trump hismoral discomfortwith a festival sponsored by the Saudi Arabian government.Even the title to his special, Buy the Dip, is a finance phrase for buying stock while it’s low, which Patel wields playfully. On the one hand, it’s a reference to Donald Trump’s corruption, a big talking point in the special. Over the past year, the president’stariffswreaked havoc on the stock market. In April 2025, Trumppostedadvice to followers on his social media platform Truth Social to buy stock, hours before he announced a pause on tariffs that saw stocks bounce back. “You can’t say ‘buy the dip’ after causing the dip,” says Patel, sounding exasperated. “It seems illegal.”But for Patel, “buy the dip” holds an alternative meaning.“I have a kid,” says Patel. “I’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the face. ‘Buy the dip’ is such an optimistic phrase. It says things will get better. You just gotta believe. Sometimes things get bad but if you, if your thesis remains the same, if you have conviction, you will be rewarded.”Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates parenting while prodding at the broken healthcare system, Maga and anti-immigrant sentiments, all while maintaining that hopeful and yet still unbothered vibe I’ve seen in his social media clips.View image in fullscreenNimesh Patel in Netflix’s Buy the Dip.Photograph: NetflixPatel first landed on my radar because TikTok’s algorithms served me aviral crowd-work clip, recorded at New York’s Comedy Cellar in 2018, when the comic was interacting with an Israeli musician who said he makes “progressive rock”. In one of those moments where a joke just seemed to materialize on the spot, Patel asked what Israeli progressive rock would sound like, before miming guitar play and singing, “Free Palestine”. The room erupted. Even Patel, in that moment, was visibly astonished at how he came up with that.“That clip has had a long shelf life,” says Patel, sharing regret that the joke has only grown more relevant in the years since and that he wasn’t more prepared to go in-depth at the time. In that 2018 interaction, Patel claims ignorance onIsrael’s war on Gaza, and shrinks from taking a stand on the issue. “I wish, at that time, I had more of a knowledge base about the conflict to really dig in on it.”Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’Read more“It should be obvious,” adds Patel, speaking to his position on the matter over the years since. “It should be obvious what my position is because the instant you see the genocide in Gaza, as a brown person, [you know] that is the position of the oppressed.”Patel, whose wife is Jewish, is much more pointed on the issue in Buy the Dip. He has a bit where he speaks out against making false equivalencies between Judaism and the Israeli regime. But then he can’t resist trolling with a punchline knowingly predicated on that very same false equivalency. “When it hits,” says Patel, “it hits really hard.”I push back on the idea that Patel’s position on Israel and Palestine, as a brown person, should be obvious, because there are so many brown people who do support Israel’s actions. Patel gets that. He points to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, as an example. Modi, who is accused by many of stoking violent Islamophobia with his Hindu nationalist rhetoric, is a staunch ally to Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu. Though Patel himself is wary of prescribing Islamophobia as the reason behind their alliance. “It is very interesting and confusing partnership on the surface of it. If it’s based in Islamophobia, that seems very superficial.”“I find it funny that religious people really forget their religion when they start talking about other people’s religions,” says Patel, whose dives into his upbringing within a devout Hindu family in his material. “It’s like the tenet of the Gita to love everybody and treat everybody equally. The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly.”Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates the ideological rifts between himself and other south Asians. It’s his burden, as an Indian American, as a Patel even, to put some distance between his demographic at large and those whose views or prejudices he doesn’t share.Kash Patel, the FBI director whom the comic refers to as Trump’s brand of DEI (“dick-eating Indian”), is a prime target.Patel – Nimesh, that is – is also compelled to clock and respond to a rise in anti-Indian sentiment, which he tells me he’s witnessed in videos and online commentary coming from Canada and the US. The situation reared its head just over a week ago whenBo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner,posteda viral photo on X of students celebrating the University of Texas’s college football win against Ohio State University. A number of the joyful students in the photo appeared to be of south Asian descent. French, in that post and a subsequent post,decriedthat foreigners were displacing Americans. On Saturday, after my conversation with Patel, the US Department of Education’s X account seemed to piggyback on French’s sentiments,postinga photo of the crowd at a University of Texas game with the slogans “make college football great again” and “make education great again”.“Most of those students are probably Indian American,” says Patel. “Those kids likely represent some of the best students in Texas. And they are Americans. They’re rooting football on. They’re drinking beers. What could be more American than that?”Nish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funnyRead morePatel then plays devil’s advocate, speaking directly to the folks who are mad at the sight of Indians, whose anti-immigrant fury is stoked by partisan politics without self-reflection.“The H-1B program in America was signed into law by [George] Bush, the first one,” says Patel, demanding they address the root cause instead of the symptom. “Corporatists taking over the country wanted cheaper labor that was beholden to the visa. These companies hire people who effectively have a gun to their heads, because if they don’t work, they can just be shipped back.“I don’t agree with not letting people in at all. Every place is richer and better because of immigrants and what they bring to the countries that they go to. But if you have a problem with immigrants –and you shouldn’t have problems with immigrants – you should be addressing the people on both sides that foster that situation in the first place.”Patel than takes a step back, turns the lens back on himself and his wider audience, and situates the relationship between the two in this conversation about what it means to be American.“[Buy the Dip] is probably the most Indian special I’ve put out. It’s Indian in that everything is rooted in an Indian POV. But it’s also deeply American, and I think very universal. I hope people see the optimism in it and take something special away for themselves.”Buy the Dip is out onNetflixnowExplore more on these topicsComedyNetflixUS televisionTelevisionSaturday Night LiveinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Skirts given star billing as Prada swerves trousers and dresses in Milan | Prada | The Guardian
description: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house
Content: A model in Prada on the Milan catwalk. ‘I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think,’ said Miuccia Prada.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model in Prada on the Milan catwalk. ‘I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think,’ said Miuccia Prada.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesPradaSkirts given star billing as Prada swerves trousers and dresses in MilanCombination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion houseJess Cartner-Morleyin MilanTue 22 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiuccia Prada’s style formula is simple: begin with a great skirt. Her personal uniform is a knee-length skirt, A-line or pleated, most often with a plain sweater and kitten heels.The Prada collection that openedMilan fashion weekmade a compelling case for her favourite outfit, with a skirt the star of every one of the 63 looks – no dresses, no trousers. It won the room over, so expect to see the personality skirt on a high street near you soon.For the past six years, Miuccia Prada has shared design duties with Belgian designer Raf Simons, 20 years her junior. The arrangement was considered unusual when announced, but the house of Prada has always had a way of spinning gold from quirky ideas, and it has worked.“She had the idea to focus on skirts this time,” Simons explained before this show. “And I said, why not make it an all-skirt show?”View image in fullscreenFour looks from Prada’s Milan show, all featuring skirts.Composite: ShutterstockShe prefers skirts to dresses because “they give you room for contrast”, Mrs Prada said. “The way I think and feel is complicated, contradictory. If I wear something feminine, I want to wear something masculine too. A dress is all one idea, and we are never just one idea.”The skirts were mostly A-line and to the knee. A grey wool skirt, severe from the front, flashed a polka-dot violet slip from beneath splits at each side. A lemon skirt was slashed with a ribbon of embroidered black tulle.There were pleated leather skirts, and daisy-printed silk under a layer of sheer gauze. Bare legs and minimal, elegant high heels throughout. Sometimes, the skirts were worn with lace bras, sometimes with a sweater, elsewhere with a shirt.“Whether you want to go to work, or be sexy, or be relaxed with your kids, you can wear the skirt with whatever you choose,” Simons said.Fashion usually does its talking from the waist up: a slogan T-shirt, a collar and tie, a plunging neckline. Prada’s personality skirt flips the script. “I like my clothes to have ideas,” Mrs Prada explained backstage, “but I don’t want those ideas near my face, because then they get in the way when I am trying to speak. I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think.”View image in fullscreenThree more skirt looks from Prada’s Milan show.Composite: ShutterstockThe Prada empire now extends to ownership of one-time rival, Versace. Donatella Versace, who stepped down from her family brand last year, announced on the eve of Milan fashion week that she was launching a new brand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt 71, Versace remains one of the most popular personalities in fashion, with a 12.2 million Instagram following that dwarfs that of most younger designers. She is partnering with California-based Revolve Inc, whose businesses include a joint venture with rapper Cardi B, for an as-yet-unnamed brand that will launch beauty products next year, with fashion further down the line.There will be no Versace show this Milan fashion week, with new designer Pieter Mulier, newly arrived from Alaïa, preparing for a debut next season instead.Armani, which last week announced the appointment of young designer Dario Vitale to the Emporio Armani brand, positioning him as an eventual successor to the late Giorgio, is also in transition.This state of flux is unusual for Milan. Power in Italian fashion has long been concentrated in family-run fashion dynasties, creating a quasi-hereditary-peerage system in which the establishment are deeply invested in the status quo.Paris fashion is where audacious moguls place big bets, London is where young talents experiment, but Milan has favoured stability. But with upheaval at several headline houses – the powerful Fendi matriarchy have also stepped back and appointed Maria Grazia Chiuri to lead their brand – that trend is changing.Explore more on these topicsPradaSkirtsMilan fashion weekItalyFashion weeksEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Fancy a pint … at Lidl? The bizarre battle over Northern Ireland’s stifled nightlife | Music | The Guardian
description: The country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancing
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: The country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancing
Content: ‘I was shocked at how things were regressing’ … Holly Lester and Boyd Sleator, who are campaigning for reform to Northern Ireland nightlife.Photograph: Niall MurphyView image in fullscreen‘I was shocked at how things were regressing’ … Holly Lester and Boyd Sleator, who are campaigning for reform to Northern Ireland nightlife.Photograph: Niall MurphyMusicFancy a pint … at Lidl? The bizarre battle over Northern Ireland’s stifled nightlifeThe country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancingDavid RenshawTue 22 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first sight The Middle Ale in Dundonald,Northern Irelandlooks just like any other pub. There is a big TV, an array of seating, and beer pumps behind the bar. Look a little closer, however, and you might ask why there are packets of fajitas and gravy granules on the walls.That’s because the pub belongs to the supermarket chainLidl, but the Middle Ale (like “middle aisle”, get it?) isn’t just a wacky marketing stunt. Northern Ireland has ultra-strict laws around licences to sell alcohol, whether as a shop, pub or nightclub. Lidl tried to get a licence to sell alcohol in its Dundonald store, and was refused, but after a court battle it did manage to get a licence for a pub – which it duly opened next door, selling alcohol to take away as well as serving drinks in the pub itself.It’s an absurd chapter of a much bigger story: local activists have long demanded licensing reform that could invigorate Northern Irish nightlife.The Lidl pub situation exposed “the hypocrisy of everything we’re up against,” says Boyd Sleator. In 2021, Sleator and Belfast-based DJ Holly Lester co-founded Free the Night, a charitable organisation formed in 2021 with the aim of creating a safe and progressive nightlife in Northern Ireland.Research conducted by Free the Night claims that obtaining an alcohol licence in Northern Ireland costs, on average, £75,250, but they say they have heard of sums up to £1m changing hands. This is because the current “surrender principle” means that any new pub or club must buy an existing licence from another establishment, a unique “one-in, one out” law. It must also prove an inadequacy of licensed premises to serve the local community.According to the BBC, The Middle Ale cost Lidl more than £500,000 and took six years of planning, numbers that Sleator and Lester say expose the barriers facing those keen to open new venues in the country. “[That’s] something no local can do,” claims Sleator. “In a way I’m glad they did it because it helps us expose how shit the current system is.”There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Lidl. The company did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Gordon Cruikshanks, managing director for Lidl Northern Ireland, previously told the BBC that the pub “was the best option to be able to provide the community in Dundonald with our full range of products”, but any changes to licensing laws were “for others to continue to discuss”.View image in fullscreenLidl pub The Middle Ale in Dundonald, Belfast.Photograph: Lidl/PAFree the Night is mounting a legal challenge over the minister for communities’ decision to reject a 2025 independent review of liquor licensing conducted by the University of Stirling. Key among Free the Night’s aims is a comprehensive review of alcohol licensing legislation, including the removal of the surrender principle. Northern Irish musicians including Bicep, David Holmes and Max Cooper signed an open letter outlining their demands.In a statement, the Department for Communities told the Guardian: “As legal proceedings are ongoing; it would be inappropriate for the Department to comment.”Lester began work on Free the Night during the pandemic when she lost her DJ gigs and returned home to Belfast. “I was shocked at how things were regressing,” she says. “The nightlife ecosystem seemed to be in a worse position than when I’d left eight years previously.”Lester says she finds the night-time economy in Northern Ireland to be “incredibly restrictive” because there are “basically no venues here”. Strict closing times are also problematic, meaning promoters are “trying to cram everything into this very small time frame”. The knock-on effects mean that promoters are less able to attract international talent while also struggling to give opportunities to local talent.Both point to Ulster Sports Club, a historic venue that closed in 2018 before reopening under new management a year later, as an example of one thriving Belfast venue. Bands including English Teacher and Mary in the Junkyard have played there while its 3am weekend closing time offers an opportunity for late-night partying.Sleator has a background in human-rights advocacy, including work around abortion rights and same-sex marriage. He is used to butting heads with the local authorities and speaks of a culture that cares more about the past than the future. “We’ve got an incredibly divided government who still only care about green and orange [traditional Nationalist and Unionist] issues,” he says. The pair also can’t help feeling that their dream of 24-hour clubbing is a little too utopian for those in government. “There’s an attitude of ‘You shouldn’t be shaking your hips, that’s the devil’s work’,” Sleator says with a grim chuckle.One key aim of Free the Night is to give musicians the spaces they need to thrive. The current lack of these has created a “creative drain”, they say. Their research shows that 70% of creatives had thought about leaving Northern Ireland, with 60% actually making the move.View image in fullscreenAn event at Belfast’s AVA festival.Photograph: The Hype Factory/PRDJ Or:la, who signed Free the Night’s open letter, says she has “harboured a real frustration with the licensing laws and lack of venues across the country” since she was a teenager. She has felt “pushed out” in her bid to pursue a career in music and now lives in Liverpool.“It’s clear that Belfast and Northern Ireland more broadly are not yet seen as nightlife destinations in the way that cities such as Berlin, Amsterdam and others across the UK are,” she says. She adds that while Northern Ireland is “flourishing in many areas” its nightlife “seems to be moving backwards”.‘You can let your inner freak out!’: welcome to Pixelate and the growing craze for internet-culture ravesRead moreA court date originally scheduled for mid-September has been delayed as Free the Night requires extra funds to continue its legal action. Free the Night believes that the authorities are overlooking the opportunities that a thriving nightlife economy could bring.“We see clubs and live music venues as spaces that can break down prejudices,” Sleator says. He cites his time raving in the 90s as proof of how music can bring people together. “There’s a lot of stuff in Northern Ireland which is like, ‘Let’s get Catholics and Protestants into a room together …’ We were just going there organically. I think that that’s where a lot of peace-building happened.”Explore more on these topicsMusicBelfastNorthern IrelandPubsClub cultureDance musicLidlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipe  | Food | The Guardian
description: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken and onion on flatbread, with tahini yoghurt and a simple, textured salad
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken and onion on flatbread, with tahini yoghurt and a simple, textured salad
Content: Sami Tamimi’sfattet musakhanwith cucumber and avocado salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’sfattet musakhanwith cucumber and avocado salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFoodSumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipeA rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken, onion and flatbread with tahini yoghurt, and a simple, textured saladSami TamimiTue 22 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 01.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFattet musakhan, a celebration of two beloved Palestinian dishes, takes centre stage here, bringing together crisp bread, creamy yoghurt, sumac-spiced onions, tender chicken and fragrant olive oil in one rich and comforting dish. Alongside, the salad brings a welcome freshness, with crisp cucumber, creamy avocado and bright acidity cutting through the richness of the chicken. Together, they make a beautifully balanced meal, bringing the generous, communal spirit of Palestinian cooking to the table.Fattet musakhanFattet musakhan is a fusion of two dishes – sumac chicken, and crisp flatbread with tahini and yoghurt – brought together into one generous meal.Prep10 minCook1 hr 10 minServes44 pitta(160g), cut into 5cm chunks75ml olive oil,plus extra for servingSalt and black pepper1½ tsp ground cumin1½ tbsp sumac, plus extra for sprinkling¼ tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground allspice800g boneless skinless chicken thighs2 tbsp lemon juice30g pine nuts1 large red onion, peeled and thinly sliced (250g net)5g flat-leaf parsley, roughly choppedFor the yoghurt sauce400ggreek-style yoghurt, to serve40g tahini1garlic clovepeeled and crushed2 tsp lemon zest2 tbsp lemon juice¾ tsp saltHeat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Put the pitta on a tray lined with greaseproof paper, add a tablespoon of olive oil and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt, and mix well. Spread the bread out in one even layer and roast for 10 minutes, turning once halfway, then remove and leave to cool. Turn up the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Put all the spices in a small bowl and mix well. Put the chicken in a large bowl with two tablespoons of oil, half the spice mix, the lemon juice, a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Mix well, then spread out on a second paper-lined baking tray. Roast for about 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Remove from the oven and set aside – keep any juices that have collected in the tray (pour these over the finished dish). When the chicken has cooled slightly, shred the meat into long strips and return to the tray.Meanwhile, put the remaining two tablespoons of oil in a large saute pan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for two to three minutes, until golden. Transfer to a bowl lined with kitchen paper, leaving the oil in the pan.Put the onion and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt in the hot oil left in the pan and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 15 minutes on a medium heat, until the onions are completely soft and pale golden (but not caramelised). Mix in the remaining spice mix and some black pepper, until the onions are completely coated.To make the yoghurt sauce, mix all the ingredients in a medium bowl.To assemble the dish, arrange the pitta in one layer on a large platter or in a deep bowl. Spoon half the yoghurt sauce on top, scatter over half the chicken pieces, followed by half the onions. Repeat with the remaining yoghurt, chicken and onion, then pour all the tray juices around the bread. Garnish with the pine nuts, parsley, a good sprinkle of sumac and drizzle of olive oil.Cucumber and avocado saladView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s cucumber and avocado salad.Fresh, simple and wonderfully refreshing, this brings together avocado and cucumber for a lovely contrast of textures. The bright dressing adds freshness and acidity, making it the perfect accompaniment to rich dishes. I love salads like this, because they’re uncomplicated yet full of character.Prep10 minCook15 minServes43 ripe avocados(350g),peeled and stoned3 tbsp lemon juice300g cucumber(about 4-6 mini cucumbers or 1 large cucumber)1 little gem lettuce, cut into large chunks3-4 spring onions(70g), trimmed and thinly sliced3 tbsp olive oilRed chilli flakes, or your favourite hot sauce, to serve (optional)Cut the avocado flesh into 1cm cubes and put in a large bowl. Add the lemon juice and stir gently.Peel the cucumber in alternating strips, then cut into bite-size pieces and put in the avocado bowl. Add the lettuce, spring onion, olive oil and a teaspoon of salt, then fold everything together until the avocado turns creamy and coats the salad, while most of the avocado remains in chunks.Transfer the salad to a platter and finish with a sprinkle of chilli, if using.Explore more on these topicsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkMain courseBreadChickenMeatHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content
