title: The rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market? | Health | The Guardian
description: People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis
Content: All hail the Big Toothbrush! Animation: Pig Meat/The GuardianHealthThe rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market?People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisisEmine SanerTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleADecember 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”. Progress indeed.Nearly six decades on, electric toothbrushes can do a lot more than merely jiggle, offering multiple speeds and movement sensors forreal-time trackingof where you’ve brushed – some even promise gum-massage or tongue-cleaning modes. Prices range from about £25 for a basic Oral B model to £599.99 for aPhilips Sonicare modelthat gives “smart coverage feedback”.The latest super-toothbrush – a mere £419.99 – features a camera and a built-in water jet to clean between teeth, using AI to identify gaps. Created by Dyson, it’s still, essentially, a stick with a brush on the end (although there is anothertoothbrushon the market that’s shaped like a mouthguard, with individual brushes, that claims to clean your teeth in 20 seconds).View image in fullscreenThe Dyson CameraJet toothbrush.Photograph: DysonIn the UK,59% of adultsuse an electric toothbrush and sales, including replacement heads, reached £361m in the last year, according to market intelligence company Mintel. Any product launch by Dyson – still associated with reinventing the vacuum cleaner – feels like something of an event, so its incursion into oral health does feel significant, says Rachel Bairsto, the head of museum services at the British Dental Association. “We’re seeing more and more expensive toothbrushes,” she says. “Expensive toothpaste as well.”These highly designed everyday objects have become symbols of affluence. “If you see a picture of a swanky bathroom, it will definitely have plug sockets for some kind of rechargeable electric toothbrush,” says Bairsto. “Whereas I’ve tried to look through the archives to find pictures of bathrooms with toothbrushes in them, and I can’t. Was everybody appalled at the sight of a toothbrush in the bathroom? I don’t know.” With many toothbrushes now, she says, “I think there’s definitely a status symbol [aspect] to it.”‘The mouth is a gateway into your body’: the fascinating, frightening links between our gums and our healthRead moreWe’re more interested in oral health than ever, says Dr Zaeem Jafri, a dentist and the founder of Nova Smiles, an online advice website. “From what I’ve seen from my patients, people are more conscious about it, wanting to avoid dental treatment, wanting their teeth to look nice and feel nice, and I think a lot of people are turning to gadgets to help.” Another dentist, Dr Reena Wadia, known as Dr Reena, a periodontist or gum specialist at the RW Perio clinic in London, says: “Gum health has become super topical. One reason why is because there’s really good evidence now that gum health islinked to your general health, so gum health is now part of the wellness conversation. People are taking it more seriously.” There is growing evidence that gum disease, she says, comes with an “increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Those are the two key ones, [but] there’s lots of other conditions related to it.” A poor oral microbiomehas been associatedwith a range of diseases, including Alzheimer’s and several types of cancer, as well as depression.Both Dr Reena and Jafri recommend rechargeable electric toothbrushes over manual ones, but neither are urging their patients to go out and buy a Dyson brush, or spend similar sums on other brands. “There’s no robust research that says a certain kind of electric brush removes plaque at a better rate than others,” says Jafri.Jafri has tested Dyson’s CameraJet, along with many other electric toothbrushes. He found it messy – the water jet was hard to angle, and he says it didn’t seem to find all the gaps between his teeth. He points out that a non-foaming toothpaste is needed for an adequate camera view – sold by Dyson, with the cheapest at £8.49. The live stream to a phone app was a novelty, but in reality he says it was hard to see much with water, teeth and the inside of his cheeks in the way. Cameras in toothbrushes, says Jafri, “have the potential to be good. If patients had cameras that were detecting chipped and broken fillings and can send those images to a dentist to review [and] spot things early, that would be a phenomenal advancement. For Dyson right now, it’s using the camera to detect when the brush is in the right position to shoot the water jet – it didn’t really work that well for me. It’s a bit of an overkill.”View image in fullscreenGood brushing habits start early.Photograph: Oleg Breslavtsev/Getty ImagesAnother concern is that the water jet rinses away the toothpaste when most dentists now recommend spitting, not rinsing, so the fluoride in it stays on and around the teeth for longer. Dr Reena adds: “[The water jet may] make people think, oh, I don’t need to floss, or I don’t need to use interdental brushes. But actually, that jet is an adjunct, not a replacement.” Niamh Turney, a Dyson engineer who worked on the CameraJet, says, however, “The goal is to make interdental cleaning easier and more convenient for those who aren’t already managing to fit flossing into their routine.”There have beenreportsof some brushes overheating, and charging problems; at the time of writing, the brush was unavailable to buy. Dyson says it is aware that “a small number of early batches may have experienced a component issue. We are isolating those batches and are taking all the necessary steps to support our customers,” and that there are “some shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production. We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”Meanwhile, we are in the midst of anoral health crisis. It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children aremore than three timesmore likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.View image in fullscreen‘Wonderful things happen!’ A 1962 advert for GE’s electric toothbrush.Photograph: Patti McConville/AlamyThe first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch andBoots, alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”View image in fullscreen‘Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush.’Photograph: GoodLifeStudio/Getty ImagesOne of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Flixbus left us stranded on the M23 after a police swoop | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: A 90-minute wait on a motorway hard shoulder was terrifying with lorries thundering past
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: A 90-minute wait on a motorway hard shoulder was terrifying with lorries thundering past
Content: A journey on a Flixbus turned into a terrifying experience.Photograph: Andrii Shevchuk/AlamyView image in fullscreenA journey on a Flixbus turned into a terrifying experience.Photograph: Andrii Shevchuk/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer affairsFlixbus left us stranded on the M23 after a police swoopA 90-minute wait on a motorway hard shoulder was terrifying with lorries thundering pastAnna TimsTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy partner and I were among a group of passengers left stranded for 90 minutes on a motorway hard shoulder after our coach driver was arrested for suspected drug driving.We had boarded the Cambridge to Brighton Flixbus service at Gatwick. The coach was an hour late, was visibly damaged on the outside and the driver set off without closing the luggage hatch.Other passengers observed him driving with his eyes closed, and police pulled him over on the M23 because of erratic driving. He was tested at the roadside and detained on suspicion of driving while under the influence.The police asked Flixbus to source an alternative driver, but to no avail. The 90-minute wait was terrifying with lorries swerving past. Eventually, the police drove us to a service station on the outskirts of Brighton and we had to make our own way into the city.We had been due to move into our new rental flat that day, but because of the delay we arrived after the self-storage depot, where our belongings were, had closed and had to spend £100 on sleeping bags and essentials for the night.Flixbus agents told us that compensation was not possible as we had “checked in” for the journey.After a series of complaints, it refunded the ticket price and our expenses minus £30, which it claimed were bank fees. I had to complain again to get this missing sum and this time £5 was deducted.Flixbus has ignored our repeated requests for compensation to reflect the severity of the incident.TBS,BrightonOur FlixBus to Paris will not be stopping in ParisRead moreThis was a terrifying ordeal. You have autism and ADHD and told me that the fear, unpredictability and the sensory overload as traffic shaved past the stationary coach, caused you extreme distress.You reported the incident as it unfolded via Flixbus’s live chat, which is evidently not programmed to address alleged driving offences, as it kept reassuring you that the company aims to offer a safe and reliable experience. Its reasoning was that since you had boarded the bus there was no case for compensation.When you complained by email, Flixbus referred to the incident as “disruption”, as though the issue was heavy traffic.I asked Flixbus how it monitors drivers’ fitness to take the wheel; why another driver was not dispatched to relay you onwards; and why it had ignored your requests for compensation.It did not answer the first questions and claimed that it could not offer compensation for the “distress and inconvenience”. However, it was suddenly prepared to stump up £100 in what it termed “goodwill”. It has also paid you the missing fiver.It says: “The safety of our passengers is our highest priority, and we have a strict zero-tolerance policy regarding alcohol, substance abuse and dangerous driving. We launched an urgent investigation into the incident with the coach operator and we are grateful to police who escorted passengers on their way.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsConsumer championsConsumer rightsTravel & leisurefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea’: a hike along Andy Goldsworthy’s epic art trail in Haute-Provence | France holidays | The Guardian
description: A long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and art
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and art
Content: Sentinel by Andy Goldsworthy, one of three cairns the artist built without using mortar or cement.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyView image in fullscreenSentinel by Andy Goldsworthy, one of three cairns the artist built without using mortar or cement.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyFrance holidays‘To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea’: a hike along Andy Goldsworthy’s epic art trail in Haute-ProvenceA long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and artClaudia CasperTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 69, I had never hiked with a backpack and I had no idea what land art was. Nonetheless, when my friend Jackie, a nature documentary film-maker, invited me to join her and her friends Wendy and Sasha on a hiking trip toRefuges d’Artin the mountainous countryside of Haute-Provence, I said a resounding “yes”. We would be sleeping alongside sculptures by the renowned land artistAndy Goldsworthy.First, I watchRivers and Tides, a documentary on Goldsworthy’s work, and discover he has built exquisite ice sculptures and stone cairns in my own country, Canada. His work seems to speak to an older part of the soul. Then, I start walking up hills, gradually adding weights to my backpack until I can comfortably carry 9kg (20lb).We meet in Digne-les-Bains, a bustling mountain town in the centre of theUnesco geopark of Haute-Provence, and the starting point for a 10-day, 150km (93-mile) hiking route that includes the possibility of staying overnight at seven reservable but free off-grid sleeping cabins. Goldsworthy worked alongside local teams to restore the abandoned shepherd huts, farmhouses, chapel and stone shelters, and created a site-specific artwork for each one. Over four days, we will visit three of these refuges and hike about 45km (28 miles).double quotation markOn the first day, we encounter one of three sentinels that sit like giant mysterious eggs watching over the routeOur first stop in Digne-les-Bains isMaison Alexandra David-Neél, a museum dedicated to the adventurous, peripatetic life of a woman who, in 1924, disguised herself as a beggar to become the first western woman to enter the Forbidden City of Lhasa in Tibet. The keys to the refuges are kept here, no doubt, to inspire hikers for the adventures that lie ahead.On the first day, we encounter one of three sentinels that sit like giant mysterious eggs watching over the route. These 2 to 3-metre tall cairns were made by Goldsworthy without mortar or cement and rely on fitting the right shapes and weights of the stones.View image in fullscreenLa Forest by Andy Goldsworthy, illuminated by natural light.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyJackie has told us the trail is mostly flat and indeed, we start on even gravel, chatting and laughing, getting used to the weight of our packs. After 5km, she says we should look for a path leading up the hill on our right. She checks her satnav and points to a goat path going straight up the rocks. I panic. My backpack suddenly feels extremely heavy. In desperation, I check further down the road and, to everyone’s relief, find a path marked with white and red horizontal lines signifying agranderandonnée, a trail certified by the French government.We begin our ascent, pausing to photograph curlicued and wispy plants right out of Dr Seuss, yellow, scarlet and blue wildflowers, an orange moth sitting on purple brush. Spanish broom perfumes the air. We lift our gaze and see multiple valleys and unique geological formations. It’s easy to imagine our ice-age ancestors walking these trails 15,000 years ago and it’s gratifying to be travelling under our own steam, as they did.We arrive at the first refuge,La Forest, as the sun is setting. The key unlocks the door. Inside, the air is cold. Our eyes adjust to the dark. A table and benches stand in front of us. To the left, a stairway leads to sleeping platforms. To the right, a doorway into a dark, empty room. From its depths glows a cylindrical obelisk, light falling on one large stone where someone could sit. It’s concave, constructed of light grey stone ending in a porthole to the sky. It’s illuminated by natural light and changes with the time, the weather, the season. This art is living and feels sacred.double quotation markIn the flickering orange light, the sculpture comes to life, looking like one of Plato’s eternal formsThat evening, we eat freeze-dried mushroom risotto in the flickering candlelight, play cards, eat chocolate, laugh and share stories. Sasha, who works in film in Germany, teaches us two words:der salzlose– someone who is bland and without flavour; andextrawurst– someone who always demands more. Neither apply to our group. The camaraderie and conviviality bring pure pleasure.We climb the stairs to the sleeping platforms. Wendy and Sasha have brought sturdy sleeping mats on Jackie’s recommendation. We lay them out and say goodnight. The quiet is complete. Then, a tidal wave of sound erupts. Wendy and Sasha have rolled over. The friction on the technical fabric of their sleeping mats is deafening. The price of comfort has been revealed; they must lie like mummies.View image in fullscreenClaudia and friends Jackie and Sasha (left to right) in Le Vieil Esclangon art refuge.Photograph: Wendy ReevesThe next day, we descend, picnic by a river on crackers, avocados and cheese, then start climbing again. Sasha and I subversively agree that it’s psychologically better to be told something is going to be hard and then it turns out easier. I console myself that climbing with a backpack is good for bone density and way less boring than lifting weights.The next refuge,Le Vieil Esclangon, is in a mountain-top meadow. A majestic fan of lifted rock shines across the wide valley. Everywhere we turn there are more mountains and valleys. The first floor of the refuge is a large dark room split in two by a massive fireplace. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms look out on to a sunlit verge. Across from the fireplace, a tall serpentine shape made of dried mud loops back and forth like a meandering river, ending at the top in the source.The wind picks up and the temperature drops. We gather wood and light a fire. In the flickering orange light, the sculpture comes to life, looking like one of Plato’s eternal forms. We eat our freeze-dried pad thai, the art and the hikers transient and temporary but together in this warm and cosy moment.Later, we sleep to the sound of wind and rain, woken only by a mouse rave in the middle of the night.View image in fullscreenLa Ferme Belon, where ‘huge interlinked semicircular stone arches look like a dragon’s body swimming through earth’.Photograph: B WarluzelWe arrive at the third refuge,La Ferme Belon, in time for a late lunch. In the basement, huge interlinked semicircular stone arches look like a dragon’s body swimming through earth. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms are lovely except for one small detail. A colony of bats hang above. I can feign nonchalance because I know Wendy, who is quietly uber-capable, will find us a delightful B&B for the night. Over pizza and cold rosé, Sasha and I confess to Jackie that we would have rather known how challenging the hikes were going to be. “But you wouldn’t have come if I’d told you,” she answers with a twinkle in her eye.Andy Goldsworthy said: “To me there is a tremendous difference between works of art that we observe in a museum just for a few minutes and works of art in which we live for a short while, in which we sleep. To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea.”In Digne-les-Bains we return the keys and soak our stronger bodies in the town’s hot springs. We’ve already said yes to Jackie’s next adventure, sight unseen.Claudia Casper’snovelThe Mercy Journalswon the Philip K Dick award for distinguished science fiction in 2017(Arsenal Pulp Press)Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysWalking holidaysSculptureEurope holidaysWalkingAdventure travelProvence holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant Hacks: can mirrors and foil boost low sunlight? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: The theory is your plants will perk up if you reflect some extra light their way over the long winter months
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: The theory is your plants will perk up if you reflect some extra light their way over the long winter months
Content: A mirror is the more attractive and effective option.Photograph: Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA mirror is the more attractive and effective option.Photograph: Olga Yastremska/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Houseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant Hacks: can mirrors and foil boost low sunlight?The theory is your plants will perk up if you reflect some extra light their way over the long winter monthsGynelle LeonTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe problemMost houseplants are hungry for sunlight, which is in short supply during a UK winter. Plants on a shelf or coffee table often get insufficient light, so they stretch, lean and thin out. Not everyone can move their plant to a south-facing sill, so the hunt is always on to make the most of what little light there is.The hackPlace tinfoil, a mirror or a sheet of white card behind your plants to bounce natural light. The theory is that light is redirected on to the plant, giving it a more even, generous dose.Houseplant hacks: can a lint roller banish pests?Read moreThe methodPosition a reflective surface behind or beside your plant. A mirror gives the most powerful reflection; kitchen foil works if you keep it as flat and smooth as possible. Rotate the plant pot occasionally for even growth.The testI set a mirror behind a leggyEuphorbia trigonathat had been leaning hard towards the window. The reflected light noticeably softened the lean. Foil worked too, though it didn’t look great.The verdictA mirror is the most effective and by far the most attractive option, but make sure it doesn’t get direct sunlight or it could be a fire risk. I wouldn’t use foil, as it looks like a messy science project scattered through the house.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A little love at Larkrise has worked wonders for wildlife | Rewilding | The Guardian
description: St Dominic, Tamar valley: After just a few years, this rewilded plot of soggy land is home to voles and shrews and vigorously growing indigenous plants
Author: Virginia Spiers
Headline: St Dominic, Tamar valley: After just a few years, this rewilded plot of soggy land is home to voles and shrews and vigorously growing indigenous plants
Content: One of the deeper ponds at Larkrise, home to moorhens.Photograph: Jack SpiersView image in fullscreenOne of the deeper ponds at Larkrise, home to moorhens.Photograph: Jack SpiersCountry diaryRewildingCountry diary: A little love at Larkrise has worked wonders for wildlifeSt Dominic, Tamar valley:After just a few years, this rewilded plot of soggy land is home to voles and shrews and vigorously growing indigenous plantsVirginia SpiersTue 22 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt last, proper rain has greened the scorched pastures and washed shrivelled leaves and nut husks along the narrow lanes. Springs dribble and streams remain low; inspection of our well, dug more than a century ago by the legendary “Diver/Diviner” Cullas of Metherell, reveals a water level better than feared, but we remain cautious in our use.On the exposed northern edge of the parish, overlooked by Kit Hill and the distant blue haze of Dartmoor, Larkrise’s rewilded 10 acres ofpoorly drained landshows ever more growth. The thorny boundary hedge, with purple sloes, blackberries, scarlet hips and masses of haws, encroaches on planted trees – extra protection from predatory deer. The mix of guarded trees are tall and vigorous, interspersed with open patches of seeding knapweed, grasses, plantains and rattle. The guelder rose, spindle, holly and buckthorn already produce berries, less than seven years after this project began.Particularly sturdy are the seedling oaks, growing in-situ near their parent, a 200-year-old spreading oak tree. Formerly grazed off by livestock, rabbits and deer, these strongly rooted saplings have been meticulously marked, staked and guarded and their leaves host spangle andsilk-button galls.View image in fullscreenBullocks on an adjoining sparse pasture.Photograph: Jack SpiersDespite the drought, none of the recently excavated ponds have dried up completely. Clayey sides and bottoms, and heaps of stony spoil are colonised with vegetation, helped by the owners James and Marywhotransplant and spread indigenous plants, seeds and cuttings.Towards the lowest boggy ground, the widest and newest expanse of water is a regular feeding station for skimming swallows. Today, blue sky reflects among water weeds in one of the deeper ponds; two young buzzards cruise overhead, sounding distinctively melancholic; goldfinches swoop among thistledown, and this year’s ubiquitousclouded yellowsflit about purple loosestrife and buddleia. Trip cameras record the regular presence of fox, roe deer and barn owl. Moorhens live here and the local small mammal society documents assorted vole and shrew species plus weasels.Homewards, via Down Lane, where hedgerows are thick with incipient hazel catkins, we pass the adjoining farmed enclosure. Inside a gateway of hard trampled earth, bullocks range across the sparse pasture, where grazing is supplemented with winter’s fodder.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsRewildingCountry diaryRural affairsPlantsTrees and forestsBirdsMammalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it? | Cancer research | The Guardian
description: Alongside warnings about its ability to destroy humanity, artificial intelligence is also hailed for its potential to revolutionise health treatment. Just how far can it take us?
Author: Jackson Ryan
Headline: Alongside warnings about its ability to destroy humanity, artificial intelligence is also hailed for its potential to revolutionise health treatment. Just how far can it take us?
Content: There has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer.Illustration: Jason Solo/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThere has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer.Illustration: Jason Solo/The GuardianCancer researchBig tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?Alongside warnings about its ability to destroy humanity, artificial intelligence is also hailed for its potential to revolutionise health treatment. Just how far can it take us?Jackson RyanTue 22 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 21.02 EDTShareHer name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window. With her liver failing, her skin was a ghostly apricot. June – I called her Nan – had been stalked by the king of terrors, the emperor of all maladies: cancer.That son of a bitch.The cancer was in her pancreas. Odds of survival? “Not good” – putting it lightly. The maths, putting it darkly: it’s the 12th most common cancer worldwide, the sixth most common cause of cancer death. The WorldHealthOrganization says it is “one of the cancer types with the least favourable prognosis”. It was not favourable for my grandmother.AI may help us cure countless diseases – and usher in a new golden age of medicine | Samuel HumeRead moreJune died nine years ago. Lately I’ve been thinking about alternate futures – the ones in which my grandmother, and the many millions diagnosed with cancer each year, are still here. The thoughts creep in as we are bombarded by artificial intelligence chief executives making bold proclamations such as “AI will cure cancer in five to 10 years” or“AI will cure cancer in our lifetimes”. Those claims stand in contrast to apocalyptic scenarios, including AI beingresponsible for human extinctionbefore 2030. AI, we hear, is both saviour and annihilator.Park theworld-ending scenariosand you’ll find there has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer. If there is a future where a supposed AI apocalypse is averted, then it may be one in which cancer therapy has been completely redefined. But just how far can AI take us towards a cure?Today AI is being turned towards drug development, treatment plans and, in some places, it’s being used clinically,studying imagery of lungsfor early signs of malignancy andhelping to remove brain tumours. Words like “efficiency” and “personalised care” are everywhere; the notion AI can free up time for doctors and medical professionals to get away from the busywork abound.Cancer is not a single diseaseEven with such positive advances, speak to clinicians, oncologists and researchers working at the coalface and you quickly find there is tension between the more grandiose claims of big tech and its race to “solve” disease, and the deliberate, considered progress of science.“Until AI can actually think and do experiments itself at scale, I’m not sure that we’re going to find a cure for all cancer or medical illness in the next 10 years,” says Sherene Loi, a medical oncologist who specialises in breast cancer treatment at the Peter MacCallumCancerCentre in Melbourne.But Loi and other cancer experts the Guardian has spoken to believe there will be efficiencies for treatment, diagnostics and pathology services that will bear fruit, heralding more personalised and more equitable cancer care.Cancer is not a single disease. It’s a catch-all term that describes the uncontrollable growth of abnormal cells. Typically, we describe cancers based on the location within the body that they are found: breast, prostate, lung, brain, blood, pancreas. These are complex, highly variable diseases, affecting a variety of different cells and underpinned by a host of genetic changes. In addition, cancer outcomes depend on many factors, including the biology of the disease and the treatments available. Asinglecure for cancer is not only unlikely but nigh on impossible.View image in fullscreenPancreatic cancer cells under a microscope.Photograph: Min Yu/USC/NIH/APJust take the brain. Though not all are cancerous, “there are more than 100 types of tumours in the brain, much more than in any other single organ”, says Felix Sahm, a neuropathologist at the University Hospital Heidelberg. “There are so many unresolved questions in brain tumour research and brain tumour care.”We’ve made great leaps in cancer survival rates over the past century; chemotherapy and radiation have enabled solid tumours to be cured, monoclonal antibodies ushered in more direct targeting of abnormal cells, andemerging treatments are rewriting how we combat the disease. But, as Loi notes, “Human disease is very complex.” So where does AI fit in?A shadow on a scan“AI can improve several parts of that process by helping us identify risk, detect disease, characterise tumours, select treatments and monitor,” says Ajit Goenka, a radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.Medical imaging, in particular, stands to benefit from advances in AI and machine-learning models. Training models on huge amounts of patient data, such as CT scans, X-rays or tissue samples, enables those models to detect changes or patterns that may be imperceptible to the human eye.Goenka has been exploring the early detection of pancreatic cancer with machine-learning tools since 2021, before the release of ChatGPT fully turned the public’s head towards generative AI. Since then, OpenAI and its rival Anthropic have pushed into new realms beyond chatbots: partnering with companies to accelerate access to treatment; striking deals with research centres; and working with pharmaceutical companies to incorporate large language models and AI into drug discovery.Cancer is now a story of the good, the bad and the ugly – but also hope | Devi SridharRead moreGoenka noticed that some patients who developed pancreatic cancer had undergone CT scans months or years before diagnosis. Those scans were interpreted as normal but Goenka reasoned there could be microscopic, measurable changes invisible to a radiologist. “We began studying whether quantitative imaging and machine-learning methods could detect that signal,” he says.In a proof-of-concept paper published in 2022,he confirmed that hunch. Machine-learning tools can detect pancreatic tumours, including in pancreases that appeared normal, before clinical diagnosis. Further studies by Goenka’s group have explored how robust and reproducible the method is and whether it is useful across institutions. The opportunity, he says, is to identify evidence of cancer earlier. My grandmother’s pancreatic cancer appeared as if out of nowhere, a shadow on a scan. Goenka’s models may have been able to see it sooner, which could have improved her outcome.Reducing the duration of uncertaintySahm leads a European multidisciplinary collaboration calledEUcanAI, which is using agentic AI to improve the way brain tumours and central nervous system cancers are treated. The idea is that “every single chunk of this journey gets informed by the previous one and informs the next one in the sequence, so that it gets more efficient, quicker and less cumbersome for a patient”, he says.He provides one example of a teenager who presented with a tumour in his brain stem. The expectation was that it was fatal, based on imaging and the patient’s age. The patient went in for surgery, his tumour was biopsied and rapidly sequenced to determine the mutations driving his disease.double quotation markWe cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure itEmilia Javorsky, Future of Life InstituteTraditionally, these results go to a board of specialists to discuss the next steps in surgery and treatment. But today, these results can be delivered during a surgery, saving patients time and money. Sahm imagines a world where agentic AI accelerates this process even further – a surgeon could biopsy and image a tumour, then have an AI provide answers about the kind of mutation and potential drugs that may treat it. Sahm says this work is already happening in trials but stresses it is not yet routine.The key for Sahm is a more tailored journey for each patient that “reduces the duration of uncertainty”. It’s about providing a wholly optimised approach to managing a patient’s cancer journey. He also notes it could provide more patients with better care.This was a common thread in discussing AI tools for cancer diagnostics. “I think it will help with regards to equity of care, and access to care,” Loi says.For instance, she says, in rural communities or locations that do not have cancer facilities or access to specialists or specialist diagnostic tools, access to machine-learning models could help medical professionals provide faster, more complete answers.Can AI ‘solve’ disease?The dream of curingcancer is one that big AI firms constantly seed. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, has suggested that within a decade, cancer – and many other diseases – could be cured. The Google DeepMind spin-off, IsoLabs, has a bold mission statement to “solve” all disease.Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, has similar lofty goals, suggesting the ability to solve disease might just be a problem of how much computing power backs our AI systems. “Maybe with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer,”he wrote. As AI firms experience growing backlash to theenvironmental cost of datacentres, the argument that just a little more compute could offer life-saving opportunities could be hard to sell.But Emilia Javorsky, a physician and scientist at the Future of Life Institute,argues the opposite: “We cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure it.”View image in fullscreenEven if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape.Photograph: Phanie/AlamyIn her March essay on AI and cancer, she outlines the complicated process of developing and testing any new medication. “Thirteen years into the AI drug discovery movement, we still lack a single [Federal Drug Authority]-approved drug that cleared the full bar of regulatory approval, reimbursement, and clinical adoption,” she says.Javorsky argues that curing cancer is a noble goal but the research community must be smart about where investment goes. It’s not intelligence that limits progress but the data, regulation and incentives that surround cancer research.Even if all the data from research across the world was placed into these models, would that be enough tosolvethese diseases today? What about in five or 10 years? For Sahm, there are biological truths we are yet to uncover. In his work, he still encounters rare, unknown pathology that doesn’t “fit into a box”. While AI may be able to devise technology or tools to understand rare subtypes, it’s only as good as its training data.‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcastRead moreThe complexity of human physiology and biological processes comes up a lot in discussions with those working in cancer. Although AI may speed up the process of, for instance, hypothesising and creating new drugs that can treat specific forms of cancer, it is fundamentally limited in applying those learnings to the real world. “Someone actually has to go back and do the experiment, right?” Loi says.An articlepublished in The Australiannewspaper in March revealed that a Sydney data scientist had been able to synthesise a bespoke cancer vaccine for his dog, Rosie, by uploading her genetic information to ChatGPT. And whilesome were astoundedby the development,others notedthat the hard work had still been done by humans in a lab.Even if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape. Sahm notes that the majority of AI-assisted or AI-led research being performed is experimental and remains in clinical trials. Even if AI tools were deemed safe for test patients, he says, the EU lacks a clear regulatory path to allow them to reach the market. “That ends up in a lot of AI research going on, a lot of surprising and promising things happening … but also surprisingly few of those really being applied,” he says.The most vocal proponents of AI – those building the models – may make grand claims about cures but on the ground the reality is different. There’s a lack of understanding of cancer complexity, many researchers working in the space argue.But it’s clear that AIdoesprovide a sense of hope for clinicians and researchers. Alone it cannot dethrone the king of terrors; it cannot bring down the emperor of all maladies. Curing cancer will require more than extra-efficient computation.“AI can come up with a million hypotheses,” Loi says – but we will still need humans to help understand which of them are true.“Technology,” says Goenka, “is only one part of the answer.”
