title: Hurricane Polo, rapidly intensifying from strong El Niño patterns, rages off coast of Mexico | Hurricanes | The Guardian
description: Polo, with sustained winds of 165mph, is churning 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo but is unlikely to directly hit Mexico
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Polo, with sustained winds of 165mph, is churning 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo but is unlikely to directly hit Mexico
Content: Hurricane Polo over the Pacific Ocean near Mexico on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Noaa/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHurricane Polo over the Pacific Ocean near Mexico on 21 September 2026.Photograph: Noaa/AFP/Getty ImagesHurricanesHurricane Polo, rapidly intensifying from strong El Niño patterns, rages off coast of MexicoPolo, with sustained winds of 165mph, is churning 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo but is unlikely to directly hit MexicoRichard LuscombeTue 22 Sep 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA tropical storm off the south-west coast ofMexicohas intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usualEl Niñoweather patterns in the Pacific Ocean.Hurricane Polowas sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state.On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as themost extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally.California braces for record El Niño storms as governor declares emergencyRead moreForecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, butwarnedthat further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions.El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average.Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season.Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record.“The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’sfall hurricane outlooklast month.“We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.”Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlanticblogthat El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”.Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November.By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far.It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.Explore more on these topicsHurricanesEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weatherMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
Content: Donald Trump at the 81st United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the 81st United Nations general assembly at UN headquarters in New York City on Tuesday.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for himRobert Taitin WashingtonUS president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member stateTue 22 Sep 2026 14.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTShareDonald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to theUnited Nationsgeneral assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state.Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” overIran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February.Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speechRead more“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader.But this seemed more shocking.The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting.Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience.Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise.The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979.Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons.No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower.The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran.Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes.“It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.”US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened.“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared.He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil.“It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said.There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said.Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration.This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”.He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex.With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI.Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”.Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents.“Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUnited NationsUS foreign policyIranCubaTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IrananalysisShareReuse this content

title: British Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shooting | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use
Content: A memorial for Tumbler Ridge victims in February. Canada’s British Columbia is suing OpenAI over the school killings and alleges CEO Sam Altman promised reforms after the attack but never followed through.Photograph: Christinne Muschi/APView image in fullscreenA memorial for Tumbler Ridge victims in February. Canada’s British Columbia is suing OpenAI over the school killings and alleges CEO Sam Altman promised reforms after the attack but never followed through.Photograph: Christinne Muschi/APOpenAIBritish Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shootingCanadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if  company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT useNick Robins-Earlyand agenciesTue 22 Sep 2026 00.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish Columbia has suedOpenAI, saying a mass shooting at a school in the Canadian province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to ​plan the attack.The lawsuit, filed inSan Franciscofederal court on Monday, names OpenAI and its CEO,Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence.Nine people, primarily children, were killed in theschool shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police.“The people of Tumbler Ridge have endured an unimaginable loss, and they deserve answers and accountability,” said Niki Sharma, British Columbia’s attorney general, in a statement this week on the suit.AI companies are facing increasing scrutiny over how their products may lead to a range of harms from cyberattacks and disinformation to facilitating violence and worsening mental health. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits from family members of victims in the British Columbia mass shooting, as well as the family of a victim in aFlorida State University shootingfrom earlier this year.Canadian high school where deadly mass shooting occurred to be torn downRead moreAltman published a letter in April ​to the community in Tumbler Ridgesaying he was “deeply sorry”OpenAI had not contacted ‌law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never ‌followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says.The school where the shooting took place is in the process ofbeing ‌demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit.One survivor, Maya Gebala,recovered from being shot three times, including in the skull. She suffered catastrophic brain injuries and permanent disabilities from the attack, according to court documents. Gebala’s family has documented her life since the shooting in online posts, including sharing images of her celebrating her 13th birthday this week.A spokesperson forOpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.”British Columbia alleges that OpenAI has failed to take proper accountability and action for the killing, however, with Sharma stating that the company must strengthen its safeguards and increase transparency on its products.“To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community,” the attorney general said.The province’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attackfiled lawsuitsin California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent ‌the shooting.Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by ​suicide.The incident, one of theworst mass shootingsin Canada’s history, devastated the small northern mining town and shocked the country. It also prompted Canadian officials tocall in OpenAI executives for questioning, as well as resulted in a call between Canada’s AI minister, Evan Solomon, and Altman.Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were firstflagged by the companyin June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting.The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack.After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the ⁠account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did ​not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law ​enforcement.The lawsuit comes after a series of ​cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claimsChatGPTfacilitated violence, ​including lawsuits related to a mass ‌shooting at Florida State ​University last year.In June, Florida became the ​first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users.OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.Explore more on these topicsOpenAITumbler Ridge school shootingCanadaAI (artificial intelligence)ChatGPTCaliforniaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’ | Puzzle games | The Guardian
description: Lian Yunzhi solves 3x3 puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state media
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lian Yunzhi solves 3x3 puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state media
Content: 0:56Six-year-old breaks women's world Rubik's Cube record – videoPuzzle gamesSix-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’Lian Yunzhi solves 3x3 puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state mediaAgence France-Presse in BeijingTue 22 Sep 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA six-year-oldChinesegirl has set a new women’s world record for solving a Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds, state media reported.“Speedcuber” Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice this month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving theRubik’s Cubefive times.The girl, who is from Chengdu, is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV said.A video posted by the broadcaster showed her wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube.After solving the puzzle she was seen placing the cube on the table, clapping her hands and pumping a fist in the air.Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the six-year-old was introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class – alongside various other extracurricular activities such as dance and music lessons, her mother, Lin Yangxi, told local media outlets.Lin “gradually realised” that cubing was an “excellent activity for fostering a child’s comprehensive abilities” and shifted her focus towards it, she told Chengdu’s Red Star News.Her daughter has now mastered more than 1,300 Rubik’s Cube solving algorithms, practising daily for two to three hours, Lin said.Photos from Red Star News showed the girl’s trophies displayed on a shelf in her home.“Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing,” Lin said.“It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions,” she added.Explore more on these topicsPuzzle gamesChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong | Arms trade | The Guardian
description: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed
Content: Containers at the terminals at the port in Kwai Chung in Hong Kong, China. F-35 parts bound for the US remain unaccounted for months later after their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersView image in fullscreenContainers at the terminals at the port in Kwai Chung in Hong Kong, China. F-35 parts bound for the US remain unaccounted for months later after their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.Photograph: Tyrone Siu/ReutersArms tradeAustralia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong KongDisappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSarah Basford CanalesTue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister,Richard Marles, has said.Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, asfirst reported by Politico over the weekend.The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion toHong Kong.The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region ofChina– has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.View image in fullscreenA Royal Australian Air Force F-35 flying over New South Wales.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia,despite reported concernsfrom the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.More than70 Australian companieshave production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” aremanufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”Explore more on these topicsArms tradeAustralian foreign policyUS militaryAustralian politicsHong KongAsia PacificRichard MarlesnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least four people killed in Japan as typhoon Dujuan triggers heavy rain, landslides  | Japan | The Guardian
description: Rescuers search for missing in collapsed homes after storm causes landslides, travel chaos and power outages
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rescuers search for missing in collapsed homes after storm causes landslides, travel chaos and power outages
Content: Residential area in Sakura, Japan, flooded due to heavy rain caused by Typhoon Dujuan.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersView image in fullscreenResidential area in Sakura, Japan, flooded due to heavy rain caused by Typhoon Dujuan.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersJapanAt least four people killed in Japan as typhoon Dujuan triggers heavy rain, landslidesRescuers search for missing in collapsed homes after storm causes landslides, travel chaos and power outagesAgence France-PresseTue 22 Sep 2026 00.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTyphoon Dujuan has killed at least four people and injured 22 inJapan, while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday.Dujuan – whichbrought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph)– was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings.But the typhoon had already caused deaths, destruction and widespread chaos, including disruption of some events at the Asian Games and forcing the early closure in Tokyo of the one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs.‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El NiñoRead moreThe city of Yokosuka in Kanagawa prefecture, near Tokyo, reported multiple landslides because of the torrential rain. Mud flowing into a home killed a woman in her 60s in Yokosuka, the public ​broadcaster NHK said. Police and firefighters said they were trying to find a couple in their 70s.View image in fullscreenRescue workers search a house hit by a landslide triggered by typhoon Dujuan in Miura, Japan.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersLocal authorities in Chiba, near Tokyo, said three people were killed in a series of landslides that hit the prefecture, according to NHK. Two people, believed to have been inside homes that collapsed, were missing.Officials said 45,000 households ​were still ​without electricity in Chiba on Tuesday morning.The storm forced Japan Airlines to cancel 135 flights and All Nippon Airways to scrap 140, and more than 1.6 million residents in and around Tokyo were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations were not mandatory.View image in fullscreenA boy cycles through a flooded street as typhoon Dujuan brings heavy rain, in Ichikawa, in Chiba prefecture.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersAlthough Dujuan weakened as it moved north-east, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area.Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, was drenched with 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, NHK reported. And rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours.Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn. But scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water.Typhoon Dujuan is the latest extreme weather event in a ⁠year of unusually intense rain, floods and tropical ​cyclones that have hit ‌regions across ‌the globe, from east Asia to North America ‌and Europe.Explore more on these topicsJapanExtreme weatherAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Taylor distances himself from Bragg’s proposal to let homebuyers use super as collateral for mortgages  | Liberal party | The Guardian
description: Opposition leader said the idea for Australians to use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan ‘is not our policy’
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Opposition leader said the idea for Australians to use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan ‘is not our policy’
Content: Opposition leader Angus Taylor speaks to media at Parliament House in Canberra.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenOpposition leader Angus Taylor speaks to media at Parliament House in Canberra.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPLiberal partyTaylor distances himself from Bragg’s proposal to let homebuyers use super as collateral for mortgagesOpposition leader said the idea for Australians to use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan ‘is not our policy’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsTue 22 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 03.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAngus Taylor has immediately distanced himself from the latest policy proposal from Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg that would let first home buyers use their superannuation savings as collateral for a loan.Bragg, the shadow housing minister, floated “a range of ways” on Tuesday that Australians’ retirement savings could be used to help more people into home ownership.One Nation says renters and mortgage holders should have early access to their super. Is it a good idea?Read more“You could keep the money in the system and it could operate as collateral or an offset,” he said on ABC radio. “You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first home loan.”Bragg was asked on ABC’s Radio National on Wednesday morning about Taylor distancing the party from the idea, responding that it wasn’t “controversial” to have “big debates” about housing.“We’re a great country, and we should be able to have big debates, as we had in the 80s and 90s about national savings and housing and the like, which led, in fact, to the super guarantee.”As Richard Marles, the acting prime minister, accused the Coalition of a “wholesale attack” on the compulsory super system, Taylor emphasised that no policy had been finalised.When asked about the idea of using super to increase a would-be homeowner’s borrowing capacity, Taylor said “the proposal you’re talking about there is not our policy”.“We’ll say more about housing policy more generally over the next little while,” he said.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereBragg has become an outspoken advocate across a range of issues, including in a recent National Press Club address where he suggested cutting net overseas migration to below 180,000 a year.That intervention on 15 Augusttriggered a rebukefrom the opposition leader, and split the party, which has yet to finalise its policy.Marles hailed the $4.8tn compulsory super system as “profoundly important” for Australians’ security in retirement, a day afterthe latest intergenerational reporthighlighted the long-term challenges of paying for the needs of a rapidly ageing population.“What you’ve seen from Coalition governments, and indeed One Nation, is a wholesale attack on superannuation,” he said.Peter Tulip, the chief economist at the Centre for Independent Studies, said using super as collateral for a home loan was a better approach than the existing first home guarantee scheme, which allows first home buyers to borrow to buy a home with a deposit worth as little as 5% of the value of the home.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTulip said it was preferable that people risked their own super savings, rather than taxpayer money, when buying a home, as it would help reduce more reckless borrowing.That said, neither approach – the super for housing idea or the existing first home guarantee scheme – would help in the current situation where demand for homes outstripped supply, he said.“Both these policies have the huge problem that they boost housing demand. And while I think super for housing is a good idea, my support is qualified because in the current situation it will make prices go up and worsen affordability.”Health, wealth and housing: here’s what forecasters think Australia will look like in 2066Read moreMatthew Bowes, a senior associate at the Grattan Institute, said it was not clear that the super for housing policy would help those most struggling to buy homes.“The fundamental issue with using super to help stop the decline in home ownership is that it [the decline] has been strongest among young Australians on low incomes – and they are the group least likely to have substantial amounts of superannuation,” Bowes said.“Clearly there are some people with super who would be better off. But they already have a lot of subsidies thrown their way and that doesn’t solve the underlying issue, which is a lack of supply of affordable first homes in places where people want to live.”In a speech to the Financial Service Council, Bragg further qualified his earlier comments by saying “to be clear, none of these ideas are our policy but we are keeping an open mind and they are options worthy of a debate in a country like Australia”.Explore more on these topicsLiberal partyAngus TaylorSuperannuationHousingAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cost of raising two children in Australia has risen 134% in two decades, study says | Childcare Australia | The Guardian
description: Parenting advocate Georgie Dent says rising childcare cost has pushed the overall burden to $36,500 a year and calls for more paid parental leave
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Parenting advocate Georgie Dent says rising childcare cost has pushed the overall burden to $36,500 a year and calls for more paid parental leave
Content: The cost of raising two children in Australia has risen to at least $36,500 a year, an increase of 134% in two decades.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenThe cost of raising two children in Australia has risen to at least $36,500 a year, an increase of 134% in two decades.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPChildcare AustraliaCost of raising two children in Australia has risen 134% in two decades, study saysParenting advocate Georgie Dent says rising childcare cost has pushed the overall burden to $36,500 a year and calls for more paid parental leaveFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorTue 22 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 21.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year, according to new research, with the money needed to run a family home increasing by 134% in two decades.Data released by advocacy group The Parenthood on Wednesday shows household income has only grown by 102% in the same period,with childcare costsmaking up 33% of the total cost of having children today. In 2003, the figure was 27%, according to the analysis by firm Connell Griffin.The $36,500 a year figure covers two or more children in total, and has grown by about 96% since 2003. Costs for larger families accelerated sharply in the early 2020s, suggesting recent economic conditions have hit multi-child households especially hard.Parenthood chief executive, Georgie Dent, will address the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, arguing that having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years of parenthood.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailShe will say families need two incomes to stay afloat in the current economy and even with both parents working, they have less breathing room in their household budget.“For many families it feels like a cruel game of whack-a-mole,” Dent will say.“For parents of young children seeking to raise and provide for their family one obstacle towers over the others: early childhood education and care.“Too many face an impossible bind. They cannot access it, they cannot afford it, or they cannot trust what is available. This isn’t perceived: the options families have are largely determined by what the market has delivered.”Dent will call for a policy pathway from government for the provision of 52 weeks of paid parental leave, up from 26 weeks currently paid for by taxpayers, and meaningful parental leave for fathers and partners.Health, wealth and housing: here’s what forecasters think Australia will look like in 2066Read moreShe will push Labor to deliver on its policy aspiration of a universal childcare system, with well paid workers and fee controls and a new national commission established.The speech comes afterMonday’s intergenerational reportshowed that, for the first time, more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time.Australia’s fertility rate is projected to decline to 1.34 by 2065–66, down from 1.5 children per woman in 2030–31.Fertility rates have been below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman for 50 years, contributing to a projected drop in population of 1.7 million people and an increase in the projected median age by 1.7 years in 2065–66.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe report found a complex mix of economic, social and cultural factors was to blame, including greater access to contraception, more time spent in education, career development, longer periods living with parents, and delays in forming partnerships and having children.The treasurer,Jim Chalmers, told Guardian Australia’s weekly Australian Politics podcast on Tuesday that the government remained committed to moving to a universal childcare system in Australia.Pauline Hanson’s stance on paid parental leave and childcare could turn clock back by decades, economists warnRead moreAnthony Albanese wants the reform to be part of his political legacy, and the government has commissioned consulting firm Deloitte to help design a universal system.Its report on the policy “pathway” is due in time for the next election.“It is still our ambition,” Chalmers said. “You don’t go from zero to 100. We’ve always seen it as a series of steps.”He pointed to the government’sthree-day childcare funding guaranteeand the $1bn program to build childcare centres in areas with poor access as significant steps.“It remains the government’s aspiration to get as close to universal as we can,” Chalmers said.Explore more on these topicsChildcare AustraliaAustralian politicsCost-of-living crisisParents and parentingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceed | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted
Author: Timothy Pratt
Headline: Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted
Content: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers at home in Tunis in February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames ‘Fergie’ Chambers at home in Tunis in February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesUS foreign policySpain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceedLawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecutedTimothy PrattTue 22 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts.Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including theSameer Project,in Gaza.His legal defense team, an array of Spanish parliamentarians, and some celebrity supporters havepublicly opposedthe request, calling it political persecution, which would render it illegitimate under Spanish law.The 22-member council of ministers could have rejected the US petition outright on Tuesday but instead opted to remand the request to the Spanish justice system, beginning a legal process which could now take months.Meanwhile, Chambers has begun the process from prison of applying for asylum inSpain– which by law makes it impossible for the country to extradite him until the process is concluded, according to attorney Aitor Martínez, part of Chambers’ legal team.The attorney also told the Guardian that a third request to allow his client to be released on bond while his situation is resolved awaits a judge’s decision, after previous requests have been denied since Spanish police detained him in Ibiza on 10 July.Elma Saiz, minister of inclusion, social security and migration, devoted less than a minute to announcing Tuesday’s council decision to the Spanish press, calling it “purely procedural”.View image in fullscreenElma Saiz called the government’s decision ‘purely procedural’.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPADetails from the weekly meetings are not public, but sources close to the council told the Guardian: “There was debate, and five ministers from Sumar – including the vice-president – pushed back in the meeting.” Sumar, a leftwing coalition, governs jointly with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party.Sánchez’s government has repeatedly expressed support for the Palestinian people, putting him at odds with the Trump administration.Baltasar Garzón,the international human rights lawyer leading Chambers’ legal team, said that Tuesday’s decision “sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause”.“Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and the protection of those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution by the US government, as it is directed against an individual because of his political activity and solidarity withPalestine.”Ione Belarra, secretary-general of Podemos – a progressive party also vital to Sánchez’s interests – said the government “has chosen to keep [Chambers] imprisoned by giving the green light for Trump’s political persecution to proceed to the courts”. Belarra appeared in Parliament on Tuesday afternoon wearing a T-shirt that said “Free Fergie”.She also noted that Spain must hold a general election by August, and said many of her colleagues in Spain’s Congress “are deeply concerned that by the time Fergie Chambers’ case has gone through the judicial process … Spain could have a more conservative, pro-Israel government”The possibility of Chambers being extradited “risks opening the floodgates to Trump’s repression reaching into Spain and the rest ofEuropeand targeting other progressives”, Belarra said.The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to supportHamas.His partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel, told the Guardianlast monththat the $7.5m went to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, paying off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields.View image in fullscreenIone Belarra of Podemos.Photograph: David Canales/Sopa/ShutterstockThe self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s charges of “international money laundering” do not hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means.His money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold them stock worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time and his donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries.Chambers’ views and donations have been extensivelyprofiledin US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.Sealed charges against Chambers were originally filed in New Hampshire.Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have previously brought controversy. A weekafter the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he postedon X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”He has also been a staunch critic of the US, tellinga reporterin 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”“I am heartbroken,” Schnabel told the Guardian. The two have a young son and Schnabel is just over three months pregnant. “Fergie could spend the first year of our baby’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass – even though he has not been convicted of any crime,” she said.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policySpainEuropeHamasPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms | European Union | The Guardian
description: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc
Content: Alisher Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek businessman, shakes hands with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in 2018.Photograph: SPUTNIK/ReutersView image in fullscreenAlisher Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek businessman, shakes hands with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in 2018.Photograph: SPUTNIK/ReutersEuropean UnionEU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline loomsAlisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the blocJennifer Rankinin BrusselsTue 22 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war onUkrainefor the next three years.With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve theRussiablacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.Ukraine war briefing: Sanctions must continue, EU’s top diplomat stresses, as Russian attacks kill fiveRead moreFrance stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.View image in fullscreenMikhail Fridman was removed from the sanctions list.Photograph: Pavel Golovkin/APUkraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense ‌of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionRussiaUkraineEuropeFranceLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: US to build new military bases in Greenland as deal seeks to end tensions between Nato allies - as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: Agreement signed at the UN general assembly in New York
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Agreement signed at the UN general assembly in New York
Content: 12.00 EDTNew US military bases, Greenland's Nato membership - what's in the deal?Jakub KrupaWe are getting a bit more detail on the dealas signed by the three leaders just now.US president Donald Trump, prime minister of Denmark Mette Frederiksen, US secretary of state Marco Rubio and prime minister of Greenland Jens-Frederik Nielsen shake hands during the signing of a security pact between the US, Denmark, and Greenland during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesIn a big win for Denmark andGreenland,it includesa specific explicit provision on “reaffirming the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark,and recognising that the People of Greenland constitute a people pursuant to international law with the right to self-determination.”The US will “modernise and expand its activities in Pituffik Space Base,”– that’s the base visited by JD Vance last year –and establish military bases inNarsarsuaq(it alreadyhada military base there in the 50s)and inMestersvig,“in accordance with modalities and technical details to be mutually agreed by the parties.”“The United States may establish additional defence areas in Greenlandand strengthen its military operations or facilities,” the text says.US aircraft may also “fly over and land in any territory in Greenland,”the agreement stipulates, including the territorial waters.Denmark and Greenland also agreed to “review requests to establish unmanned military installations in Greenlandoutside of the defence areas under accelerated governmental approval procedures.”In what Trump touted as his win, the agreement is explicit in what was anyway believed to be true already when it says that “no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenlandnor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland, unless otherwise agreed by the Parties.”There is also a further provision thatany investment from a non-Nato member of partner country should not be allowed to “have control, significant influence or access to non-public informationthat may constitute a threat to national security or public order.”This paragraph will be seen by the US as an attempt to fend off any interest fromChinaorRussia. A different part of the deal also talks about working together to counter the threat of espionage.The agreement has no end date, andcuriously considers potentially relevant future scenarios, such as Greenland’s independence in the future.It says the independentGreenland would need to “agree to remain in Nato”and continue all arrangements as agreed in the treaty.The full text ishere.ShareUpdated at12.03 EDT

title: US fighter jet crashes at air base in western Germany | US military | The Guardian
description: Officials say one pilot safely ejected as F-16 believed to have crashed on approach to Spangdahlem after training drill
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials say one pilot safely ejected as F-16 believed to have crashed on approach to Spangdahlem after training drill
Content: Officials said the cause of the incident was under investigation.Photograph: US Air Force/PAView image in fullscreenOfficials said the cause of the incident was under investigation.Photograph: US Air Force/PAUS militaryUS fighter jet crashes at air base in western GermanyOfficials say one pilot safely ejected as F-16 believed to have crashed on approach to Spangdahlem after training drillReutersTue 22 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google⁠An F-16 fighter jet assigned to the US air ⁠base Spangdahlem ⁠in ​western Germany crashed on Tuesday, theUS militarysaid, ⁠adding that one pilot had ejected safely and was receiving ⁠medical treatment.The cause of the incident ​is under ‌investigation, the military ‌said in a statement, with ‌emergency response personnel at the scene of the crash.Germany’s air traffic control authority, in a separate statement, said a total of four F-16s ‌had been taking part in a training exercise.“Two were still ​in the training area, while two were returning to Spangdahlem air base. title: Skirts given star billing as Prada swerves trousers and dresses in Milan | Prada | The Guardian
description: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house
Content: A model in Prada on the Milan catwalk. ‘I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think,’ said Miuccia Prada.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model in Prada on the Milan catwalk. ‘I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think,’ said Miuccia Prada.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesPradaSkirts given star billing as Prada swerves trousers and dresses in MilanCombination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion houseJess Cartner-Morleyin MilanTue 22 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiuccia Prada’s style formula is simple: begin with a great skirt. Her personal uniform is a knee-length skirt, A-line or pleated, most often with a plain sweater and kitten heels.The Prada collection that openedMilan fashion weekmade a compelling case for her favourite outfit, with a skirt the star of every one of the 63 looks – no dresses, no trousers. It won the room over, so expect to see the personality skirt on a high street near you soon.For the past six years, Miuccia Prada has shared design duties with Belgian designer Raf Simons, 20 years her junior. The arrangement was considered unusual when announced, but the house of Prada has always had a way of spinning gold from quirky ideas, and it has worked.“She had the idea to focus on skirts this time,” Simons explained before this show. “And I said, why not make it an all-skirt show?”View image in fullscreenFour looks from Prada’s Milan show, all featuring skirts.Composite: ShutterstockShe prefers skirts to dresses because “they give you room for contrast”, Mrs Prada said. “The way I think and feel is complicated, contradictory. If I wear something feminine, I want to wear something masculine too. A dress is all one idea, and we are never just one idea.”The skirts were mostly A-line and to the knee. A grey wool skirt, severe from the front, flashed a polka-dot violet slip from beneath splits at each side. A lemon skirt was slashed with a ribbon of embroidered black tulle.There were pleated leather skirts, and daisy-printed silk under a layer of sheer gauze. Bare legs and minimal, elegant high heels throughout. Sometimes, the skirts were worn with lace bras, sometimes with a sweater, elsewhere with a shirt.“Whether you want to go to work, or be sexy, or be relaxed with your kids, you can wear the skirt with whatever you choose,” Simons said.Fashion usually does its talking from the waist up: a slogan T-shirt, a collar and tie, a plunging neckline. Prada’s personality skirt flips the script. “I like my clothes to have ideas,” Mrs Prada explained backstage, “but I don’t want those ideas near my face, because then they get in the way when I am trying to speak. I think of a skirt the way some people think of a T-shirt – a place to express what I think.”View image in fullscreenThree more skirt looks from Prada’s Milan show.Composite: ShutterstockThe Prada empire now extends to ownership of one-time rival, Versace. Donatella Versace, who stepped down from her family brand last year, announced on the eve of Milan fashion week that she was launching a new brand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt 71, Versace remains one of the most popular personalities in fashion, with a 12.2 million Instagram following that dwarfs that of most younger designers. She is partnering with California-based Revolve Inc, whose businesses include a joint venture with rapper Cardi B, for an as-yet-unnamed brand that will launch beauty products next year, with fashion further down the line.There will be no Versace show this Milan fashion week, with new designer Pieter Mulier, newly arrived from Alaïa, preparing for a debut next season instead.Armani, which last week announced the appointment of young designer Dario Vitale to the Emporio Armani brand, positioning him as an eventual successor to the late Giorgio, is also in transition.This state of flux is unusual for Milan. Power in Italian fashion has long been concentrated in family-run fashion dynasties, creating a quasi-hereditary-peerage system in which the establishment are deeply invested in the status quo.Paris fashion is where audacious moguls place big bets, London is where young talents experiment, but Milan has favoured stability. But with upheaval at several headline houses – the powerful Fendi matriarchy have also stepped back and appointed Maria Grazia Chiuri to lead their brand – that trend is changing.Explore more on these topicsPradaSkirtsMilan fashion weekItalyFashion weeksEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran and US have held talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Donald Trump | Iran | The Guardian
description: Senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran
Content: Speaking at the UN in New York, Trump urged other nations to join the US in attempting to isolate Iran’s economy.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenSpeaking at the UN in New York, Trump urged other nations to join the US in attempting to isolate Iran’s economy.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APIranIran and US have held talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Donald TrumpSenior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on TehranPatrick Wintourin New YorkTue 22 Sep 2026 17.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly,Donald Trumpdisclosed on Tuesday.He said there would a further meeting in the very near future.Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understandingin Switzerland in June.Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar.A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, as long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran.Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions.View image in fullscreenScott Bessent, the US treasury secretary,Steve Witkoff and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, watch as Donald Trump meets his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the UN on Tuesday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APThe new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions.The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader,Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran.Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however.Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall duringTrump’s speech on Tuesdayafter he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth.But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time,a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament.The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official.Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours.View image in fullscreenMasoud Pezeshkian, seen departing Iran, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday.Photograph: Iranian Presidency Office/APExperience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a barely disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks.Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the supreme leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions.Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country.“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections. “There are two options; one could be a very bad thing, and the other could lead to greatness and progress for this country. Therefore, I think they want to do this.”Trump praises relations with Burnham despite tensions over AI and IranRead moreOverall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal.Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman.Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with itscurrency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions.Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the six-month-old peace plan to withdraw from Gaza.The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walkout by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience, can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.”View image in fullscreenThe Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, was among several speakers at the UN to criticise the Israeli military’s conduct in Gaza.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAJordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.”A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under thefirst phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.Explore more on these topicsIranDonald TrumpUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East crisis: Trump says Iran will make a deal after US midterms – as it happened | Iran | The Guardian
description: This live blog is now closed.
Author: Yohannes Lowe
Headline: This live blog is now closed.
Content: 15.09 EDTClosing summaryDonaldTrump has called on nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices, as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran.“I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation ofIran,” the US president said in a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror … and oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict.” It comes as numerous US allies have complained about soaring energy prices and growing international instability during his US administration.During the speech, Trump repeated a threat to “annihilate” Iran, which he has made dozens of times since the US and Israellaunched joint strikes in February.“I have a big decision to make: will a deal be made with Iran that let them rebuild and create a far greater country than ever was before,” he said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill or destroy people and continents?” Trump denied that he was under political pressure to end the war and said the upcoming US midterm elections would have absolutely no influence on his decision-making around the conflict. He also denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (“we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using”).Trump also expressed support for a diesel ban amid price soars due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.When asked about the issue at a meeting with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said: “I’ve called for that too. I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline.”Meanwhile, Jordan’sKing Abdullah IItold the assembly thatglobal political inaction on Israel is a wilful “choice”, and the result is a “state without restraint”. He said that preventing the creation of a Palestinian state has become firm Israeli policy, and that Israel’s forced displacement of Palestinian people in the occupied West Bank is “a war crime”.Turkish⁠presidentRecep TayyipErdoğanalso condemned Israel’s actions in Gaza, which he saidhas become “the most inhuman and shameful concentration camp of our time”.He called on member nations to exert “greater pressure on Israel” to end its war and expressed his hope for a future Palestinian state.Away from the UN general assembly,Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said that Tehran would “undoubtedly intensify” its response if the US launched new attacks on the Islamic republic.“If they act recklessly and history repeats itself, our resistance will undoubtedly intensify, bolstered by the experience we have gained. This time, we will not merely retaliate; we will adopt an offensive posture, and America will come to regret its actions, suffering greater humiliation than ever before,” said Mohebi in an interview with AFP.Mohebi said that the United States had tried to establish contact with the Guards, but they had rebuffed the effort.“The Americans have tried to contact us but we refuse any such contact. Our dealings with the enemy – as long as they remain hostile – are conducted solely through arms,” said Mohebi, adding that diplomacy was handled by Iran’s foreign ministry.Russian president Vladimir Putin held ⁠a phone call with Saudi crown prince ⁠Mohammed bin Salman ⁠today, Reuters reported.They discussed the security ⁠situation in the Gulf and the need to keep ⁠vital waterways open, according to the Kremlin.Gaza’s health ministry said in its latest update that at least 1,399 people have been killed by Israeli attacks since a supposed ‘ceasefire’ was signed between Israel and Hamas last October.Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan ​by the US to end the war on Gaza, which includes the Israeli withdrawal from the strip and the disarmament ⁠of Hamas. Israel ​says Hamas has been violating the deal.The UK agreed to provide defensive air support toSaudi Arabiato help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.The renewed US-Iran efforts to resolve the dispute about control of the strait of Hormuz comes amid reports of Saudi Arabia attacking areas under Houthi control in Yemen.Among the latest reports is of an attack by Saudi Arabia on a prison in northwestern Yemen that killed nine detainees, according to a Houthi official, who spoke to the Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Iran-backed militia.According to a report in the New York Times, Donald Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on appeals from Saudi Arabia for military help in fighting the Houthis.On Wednesday, the president had reportedly met with advisers and said he did not favour strikes.Iran’s national airline said it had not received any ban on serving neighbouring countries, a day before US sanctions are due to be tightened against the Iranian aviation sector.“Iran Air has not received any notification or official instruction from the civil aviation authorities of Turkey, the Republic of Azerbaijan, or Iraq regarding a halt or suspension of the airline’s flights to Istanbul, Baku and Najaf,” the company said in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA.Share

title: Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Thousands flee renewed fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces
Author: William Christou
Headline: Thousands flee renewed fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces
Content: Houthi fighters pose amid the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that the group claimed to have downed in the province of Marib.Photograph: Houthi Group press Service/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters pose amid the wreckage of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet that the group claimed to have downed in the province of Marib.Photograph: Houthi Group press Service/UPI/ShutterstockYemenUp to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heightsThousands flee fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forcesMiddle East live – latest updatesWilliam Christouin BeirutTue 22 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-alignedHouthisbattle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence.Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict.The Houthis accusedSaudi Arabiaof striking the port city of Mocha on Tuesday, killing six civilians, including two children. The group also said a Saudi strike on a prison in al-Jawf province, north-western Yemen, killed nine detainees.The Saudi government, which backs Yemen’s UN-recognised government against Houthi forces, on Tuesday issued an alert in the south of the country before potential strikes, after the Houthis launched strikes at the Saudi capital, Riyadh, at the weekend for the first time in years.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from AFPTV footage of Saudi-backed government fighters engaging Houthi forces in al-Jawf province, in the north-west of Yemen.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country.The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month.Last week theHouthis took control of Mochaand other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz.The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced.View image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemeni people receive medical care at a camp in Ras Imran, a coastal area on the western outskirts of Aden.Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/APYemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government.
