A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias.A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive.In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range.Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks.The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions.View image in fullscreenHouthi-aligned detainees arrive in Sana’a after being freed from prisons run by Saudi-backed forces in Mocha after Houthis made gains in the region.Photograph: Mohammed Hamoud/Getty ImagesSince the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies.Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success.Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend butcalled them off at the last minute, while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention.Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens.“We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read.The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating.View image in fullscreenPeople fleeing the fighting queue to receive supplies after crossing the Red Sea and arriving in Djibouti.Photograph: Abdourahim Arteh/ReutersBabar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued.Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused.Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins | Trade policy | The Guardian
description: MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank
Content: The Israeli government wants to build 3,400 houses in the E1 zone near the Ma’ale Adumim settlement in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenThe Israeli government wants to build 3,400 houses in the E1 zone near the Ma’ale Adumim settlement in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APTrade policyBritish banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban beginsMPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West BankPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorTue 22 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months.A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks agoplans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlementsand new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament.The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of asmany as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections.Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, holding a map showing the proposed E1 settlement.Photograph: Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty ImagesFinance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in theWest Bankbut to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections.UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade banRead moreThe all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”. The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.”The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.”It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel.Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?”The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.Explore more on these topicsTrade policyBankingEthical foreign policyForeign policyWest BankIsraelPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘What we have is unique’: the Indian craftsmanship behind global luxury fashion | World news | The Guardian
description: Generations of artisans from Mumbai to Lucknow have shaped the world’s most coveted designs. Plus, the gen Z memes giving classic Bollywood a new life
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: Generations of artisans from Mumbai to Lucknow have shaped the world’s most coveted designs. Plus, the gen Z memes giving classic Bollywood a new life
Content: Mumbai-based embroidery atelier Chanakya International has a network of 2,500 artisans, with some coming from 13 generations of craftspeople.Photograph: Hashim Badani/Photo by Hashim Badani Courtesy Chanakya International and FoundationView image in fullscreenMumbai-based embroidery atelier Chanakya International has a network of 2,500 artisans, with some coming from 13 generations of craftspeople.Photograph: Hashim Badani/Photo by Hashim Badani Courtesy Chanakya International and FoundationThis Is IndiaWorld news‘What we have is unique’: the Indian craftsmanship behind global luxury fashionGenerations of artisans from Mumbai to Lucknow have shaped the world’s most coveted designs. Plus, the gen Z memes giving classic Bollywood a new lifeNiha MasihTue 22 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThezardozi embroideryon a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelierChanakya Internationalis at the forefront.Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says,France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have inIndiatoday is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, orchaandjaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing itspartnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. TheKalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-basedthe Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.View image in fullscreenJaipur-based Gem Palace has worked with the French fashion house Dior on a jewellery collection.Photograph: Courtesy of Gem Palace and DiorWith increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collectionattracted criticismafter many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)Then, Fendicame under firewhen people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in asocial media videoshowcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.A recentFinancial Timesreport noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, acontroversythat showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection,Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.View image in fullscreenKarishma Swali with Chanakya School of Craft students.Photograph: Hashim Badani/ Chanakya InternationalMight these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author ofInspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buyajrakhandmashrusilks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just apartof luxury, but a luxury itself.What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenTime Out has named Mumbai’s Bandra West one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world.Photograph: Danto ProductionTravel| Time Out just confirmed what everyone in Mumbai’sBandra Westknows: that it’s one of the coolest neighbourhoods in the world. The other Indian spot to make the cut is Delhi’s food and fashion centre, Humayunpur. The top spot went to Jongno 3-ga in Seoul – my second home!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBusiness| India will levy a0.4% charge on merchantsfor UPI payments above Rs 2,000, starting on 15 October. The charges will not be applicable when the payment is made from one person to another.Ashneer Grover, co-founder and former CEO of fintech firm BharatPe slammed the move, describing it as “tax collection”.Immigration| An investigation byScroll’s Rokibuz Zamanhas revealed a troubling pattern in West Bengal: since June, at least nine Muslim men and two children have been picked up by the police from their homes over allegations that they are Bangladeshi nationals – without being given a chance to prove their citizenship. Most were picked up and detained in midnight raids, the report said, and family members accused the police of not producing warrants.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenA Jamdani saree by Payal Khandwala.Fashion designerPayal Khandwala, whosespring-summer ’26 collectionfeatured handwoven silks, cottons and brocades, recommends the perfect saree weave: “The delicate poetry of a Jamdani saree is definitely my favourite. A 2,000-year-old craft, typically woven in fine muslin and of Bengali origin, it’s somewhat an unsung hero. The weaving process itself is exceptionally intricate. Using a supplementary weft technique, thousands of markings are meticulously mapped on to the warp to recreate the pattern, interlaced by hand with a wooden shuttle and metallic needle to guide the motifs in silver and gold yarn, on fine mulberry silk and organza.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenForeign portfolio investors have pulled out £1.2bn from Indian equities.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters13,138Foreign investorshave pulled outRs 13,138 crore (£1.02bn)from Indian equities in the first half of September, wiping out about half of the net inflows recorded in August.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenOld Bollywood, new jokes … the memes giving classic film stills a gen Z makeover.Photograph: Bahaish KapoorThe true measure of my love for my friends is in the number of memes I send them. One of the accounts I rely on isBahaish Kapoor’s. The screenwriter-turned-meme evangelist pairsblack-and-white Bollywood stills with contemporary gen Z sass, and lets incongruity do the rest. What makes an image meme-worthy? “I always look for people who are in a deep philosophical, romantic, dramatic action moment which I can repurpose to bring in a whole new meaning,” he tells me. “I try to mix and match and see what’s working.” His 340,000-plus followers include Sharon Stone and Hrithik Roshan.“I just want to make people feel a little better,” says Kapoor, adding that he receives a lot of DMs from people about how his page helped them through a bad day. “People confessing that they are lighter because of this experience is all that I can hope for. I mean, that’s the endgame.”Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaLuxury goods sectornewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap grows | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London
Author: Will Parman
Headline: Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London
Content: Food banks say many more people will be forced to rely on charity unless local housing allowance is more closely linked to rents.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverView image in fullscreenFood banks say many more people will be forced to rely on charity unless local housing allowance is more closely linked to rents.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverUK cost of living crisisPay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap growsWirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in LondonPatrick ButlerandWill ParmanTue 22 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you prioritise paying the rent, putting food on the table or keeping the house warm in winter? In practice, says Laura Braddock, a single mum from Wirral, Merseyside, you always pay the rent first and improvise the rest. “If I’ve got a roof over our head, then everything else I can muddle through.”The pressing problem for Braddock, 39, is that muddling through is getting harder. The monthly rent for her two-bedroom flat far outstrips the local housing allowance (LHA) she receives – and the gap may widen.She pays her landlord £550 a month, but receives £425 in housing allowance, leaving her to make up a £125 “rent gap” out of her grocery and heating budgets.The former shop worker has a range of tried and tested strategies to cope, and to shield her son as far as possible from cost of living pressures. She may pay half the gas bill. She’ll eat cheap pasta and beans – or skip her own meals altogether.In January, however, these strategies, and the constant juggling with ever tighter budgets, failed. She was forced to go to a food bank for the first time in years to make end meet.It’s hard, she reflects, and the stress can affect her mental health. “When I’m tired or hungry or whatever, that then has an impact on me, the way I parent. I’ve got no energy sometimes … It’s difficult.”View image in fullscreenLetting sign in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month.Photograph: William Barton/AlamyView image in fullscreenLetting signs in London, where rent costs can outstrip housing support by as much as £324 a month.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyHundreds of thousands of low-income households are feeling the same pressures, said Trussell, the food bank network. Unless the government links LHA more closely to actual rents, it added, many more will be forced to turn to charity food.The growing gap between LHA rates and local rents means more than half (62%) of private renters receiving housing support have gone without food and heating in the past six months because they could not afford them, Trussell estimated.The gap is expected to reach record levels this autumn. According to the Resolution Foundation thinktank, theaverage difference between rent and LHAfaced by a low-income household renting a two-bedroom home in the private sector is £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 a month in parts of London.Trussell wants the government to relink LHA to the cheapest 30% of local rents. It estimates this would lift 105,000 peopleout of severe hardship by 2028-29, including 40,000 children. TheResolution Foundationestimates this would cost £2bn a year.Campaigners will focus on the LHA gap– the consequence of years of austerity and rising private rents – in the run-up to next month’s budget, arguing it is an effective way to give low-income families “breathing space” from cost of living pressures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBeatrice Orchard, the head of policy at Trussell, said: “Nobody should be forced to choose between paying the rent and putting food on the table. But for increasing numbers of UK renters, this is already a bleak reality. Keeping LHA frozen while rents rise is driving people to food banks.”Governments have often been reluctant to match rents and housing support, fearing landlords will simply put up rents, or that tenants will move to plusher rented homes.Braddock, who fears that her landlord is preparing to put up her rent, tightening her budget even further, disagrees: “If the local housing allowance matched the going rate for a two-bedroom or a one-bedroom [place] then people don’t need to move. It’ll just mean they don’t struggle to get through the month, because the rent’s being paid.“I don’t think the government understands … From a parent’s point of view, you’ve got to think about keeping your kids safe and your kids warm. And they wonder why there’s an epidemic of mental health [concerns]”.A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “We’re tackling the impact of rising rents and the housing shortage with our commitment to build 1.5m homes – including the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation.“Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisHousingHousing benefitBenefitsRenting propertyCommunitiesFood banksnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank says | Devolution | The Guardian
description: IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding
Content: Andy Burnham plans to give England’s mayors significantly greater control over funding and public services.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham plans to give England’s mayors significantly greater control over funding and public services.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Pool AFP/APDevolutionEngland’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank saysIPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in fundingJosh HallidayNorth of England editorTue 22 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda being “derailed by one bad decision”, a thinktank has said.Ministers will set out plans next month to give regional leaders control over potentially billions of pounds of additional funding under a “transformational” shift of power outside Whitehall.From 2028, mayors will be able tokeep a share of income taxgenerated in their areas – giving them greater scope to borrow for major infrastructure projects – as well as retain business rates from 2027 and raise further funds through a “tourist tax”.IPPR North, whose researchers have worked closely with Burnham’s government, welcomed the “bold and ambitious” plans as a step towards “reversing decades of damaging over-centralisation that has held the country back”.It called for mayors to be allowed to keep a 5% share of income tax, which would move an extra £3.8bn a year out of Whitehall and roughly double the funding under their control.However, the thinktank said increasingly powerful mayors should be subject to much tougher oversight.In its 30-page report, IPPR North warned: “A bad decision or mismanaged funding from any one authority risks turning public opinion against devolution and undoing progress.”Its proposals include establishing new regional audit offices to scrutinise how money is spent and what it delivers. It is also proposed that each region should be overseen by a senior accounting officer, similar to the model of permanent secretaries running government departments.Larger mayoral authorities, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, should be overseen by beefed-up accountability committees to guard against any “misuse of funds, corruption and elite capture by lobbying interests”, the thinktank said.Burnham, a former Greater Manchester mayor, has placed the transfer of power outside Whitehall at the heart of his government, establishing No 10 North in Manchester to act as the engine room of rapid devolution.Proposals outlined in aCabinet Office paperin July, weeks after Burnham became prime minister, would represent the most dramatic shift of authority to the English regions in modern times.There are concerns, however, about the capacity of newer and smaller combined authorities to take on these expanded powers, which include employment support, local transport, housing, innovation, local energy and cultural investment.View image in fullscreenRegional mayors at Downing Street for a devolution meeting in July 2024.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyWhile some mayoral authorities are well established, others, such as the Reform UK-led bodies in Hull and East Yorkshire and Greater Lincolnshire, were only founded last year. Several other planned mayoral authorities, spanning millions of people along the south coast and in north-westEngland, have not yet been established.Ministers are due to set out a timeline for fiscal devolution to the English regions in a white paper to be published alongside the autumn budget on 28 October.Aditi Sriram, the lead author of the IPPR North report, said Britain was at a “defining moment” in how it is governed and that accountability was essential to the success of devolution.“For too long, mayors have been expected to drive growth with one hand tied behind their backs, reliant on Whitehall for the money and permission to get things done,” she said. “Critics are loud, political trust is faltering, and the public wants to see action, so the devolution agenda cannot afford to fail.”Jim O’Neill, the former Treasury minister who advised Burnham before he became prime minister, said in a foreword to the report that critics would dismiss devolution as an “irrelevance and a probable source of wasted taxpayers’ money”.But he said the best answer to those “cynics” would be to hand mayors of the most populated areas the greatest powers. “This is assuming they have the capacity to cope, the desire to be accountable and, of course, just like Greater Manchester has had, the aspiration to be bold,” he said.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionMayoral electionsTax and spendingAndy BurnhamLabourLocal politicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Children as young as 13 being referred to UK hospital suffering from ‘ketamine bladder’ | Drugs | The Guardian
description: County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysis
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysis
Content: Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnalysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Photograph: gorodenkoff/Getty ImagesDrugsChildren as young as 13 being referred to UK hospital suffering from ‘ketamine bladder’County’s first such clinic, at Alder Hey in Liverpool, treating children suffering from chronic bladder problems with severe cases needing dialysisAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 22 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren as young as 13 in the UK have been referred to a specialist clinic for a “devastating” bladder condition linked to sustained use of ketamine.Medics at Alder Hey children’s hospital in Liverpool opened the first ketamine clinic in the UK for young people amid a surge in urology problems linked to addiction of the drug.Now analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.Excessive use of ketamine can cause serious health problems as the drug and its breakdown products sit in the bladder for a long time, where they can damage the lining and muscle tissue.Ketamine-induced uropathy – also known as ketamine bladder – is a severe and painful condition caused by the drug damaging the bladder, urinary tubes and kidneys. Symptoms include frequent urination, loss of bladder control and blood in the urine.View image in fullscreenKetamine use can damage the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, say experts.Photograph: Joe Bird/AlamySome of the children affected are using incontinence pads and urinating in buckets next to their bed at night due to bladder problems caused by addiction to ketamine.“The damage caused by ketamine can be devastating,” said Harriet Corbett, a consultant paediatric urologist at Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust.“It can affect the bladder wall, causing ulceration and fibrosis, and the effects can be irreversible.Young peoplecan experience chronic bladder pain and incontinence and, in the most severe cases, may go on to require major surgery or dialysis.”Doctors were being referred to a rising number of children with bladder symptoms caused by non-prescribed ketamine use, Corbett added.“What this first year of analysis has highlighted is the importance of understanding the young person behind the diagnosis.”Analysis of the first patients to use the service shows some are as young as 13, with most being girls and most living in deprived areas.“By looking at factors such as age, where they live, their background and their life experiences, we can start to build a much clearer picture of who is being affected and how we can best support them.“This problem is preventable. Understanding more about the young people who are presenting to us is an important step towards preventing further harm,” Corbett said.View image in fullscreenAlder Hey children’s hospital has opened the UK’s first ketamine clinic for young people.Photograph: Mark Waugh/AlamyAnalysis of the clinic’s first 60 patients by researchers at Alder Hey and Lancaster University showed their average age was 14, ranging from 13 to 15.About two-thirds were girls, and roughly the same proportion lived in the most deprived areas, according to the analysis published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood medical journal.Of the 60, 16 had autism or ADHD, or both. One in five had experience of the care system. Almost three-quarters (72%) had experienced emotional trauma during childhood.The agony of ketamine addiction: ‘I felt like I was peeing glass’Read moreProf Rachel Isba, a consultant in paediatric public health medicine at Alder Hey and professor emerita of children and young people’s health at Lancaster University, said: “One of the most important things about this work is that we are trying to understand the wider picture.“Ketamine use does not happen in isolation, and our analysis is helping us explore the different factors that may be associated with young people developing serious health problems.”The clinic at Alder Hey takes a “non-judgmental” approach, Isba said. “We want to give young people a safe space to talk about what is happening in their lives and work with them to develop a plan to stop using ketamine and prevent further damage.”Explore more on these topicsDrugsChildrenHealthYoung peoplePovertyHospitalsAutismnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause | Women's health | The Guardian
description: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies
Content: The new test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer for rapid diagnosis.Photograph: andrei_r/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe new test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer for rapid diagnosis.Photograph: andrei_r/Getty Images/iStockphotoWomen's healthUK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopauseTest using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopiesAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 22 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause.The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems.Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer.Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly.The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester UniversityNHSfoundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive.Thousands of women could be spared painful cancer exam by new NHS AI blood testRead moreIn a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests.Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer.The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’sHealth.Researchers said the test was not accurate enough to rule cancer out on its own but could fast-track women at the highest risk for urgent investigation while sparing lower-risk women immediate invasive testing, with repeat sampling or full assessment if symptoms continued.They cautioned that the samples in the study were assessed by highly trained specialist cytologists, so it was not known whether the same accuracy could be reproduced in other settings, and that the test had not been studied in women without symptoms.Researchers said the test could be used to triage women suspected of having womb cancer, to “support rapid diagnosis, provide quick reassurance and reduce the burden of invasive testing for women with postmenopausal bleeding”.‘It was barbaric. I was crying my eyes out’: why are so many women left in agony by routine womb examinations?Read moreProf Emma Davidson, of the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, said: “Bleeding after the menopause is understandably alarming for women because it can be a sign of cancer, but the vast majority of those investigated will not have the disease.“At the moment, many women face invasive, uncomfortable tests that can be stressful as well as costly for health services before cancer can be ruled out. Our study shows that a simple test using urine and vaginal samples could help identify the women most likely to have cancer while safely reassuring many others much earlier in the diagnostic pathway.“If further studies confirm these findings in routine practice, this approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women every year.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthCancerMenopauseNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: US supreme court declines to intervene in custody fight over baby born via surrogate | Texas | The Guardian
description: Surrogate who rejected abortion request had asked justices to halt court order recognizing LA couple as legal parents
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Surrogate who rejected abortion request had asked justices to halt court order recognizing LA couple as legal parents
Content: McKenna West, the surrogate who gave birth in Texas, had asked the supreme court to block a lower court order.Photograph: LM Otero/APView image in fullscreenMcKenna West, the surrogate who gave birth in Texas, had asked the supreme court to block a lower court order.Photograph: LM Otero/APTexasUS supreme court declines to intervene in custody fight over baby born via surrogateSurrogate who rejected abortion request had asked justices to halt court order recognizing LA couple as legal parentsMaya YangTue 22 Sep 2026 18.38 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute between an Alaska surrogate and aCaliforniacouple whose child was born with a rare and serious heart defect.On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan denied an emergency request from McKenna West, an Alaska nurse and surrogate who hadaskedthe US’s highest court to halt a California court order recognizing the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, as the boy’s legal parents.In recent weeks, the case has garnered nationwide attention, sparking broader discussions about surrogacy and abortion.In a 9 Septemberfiling, West’s attorneys urged the supreme court to intervene in what they described as “extraordinary circumstances”, arguing that “a life hangs in the balance”.Following a scan that discovered the baby having hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery, Ahmed and Gilkar asked West to abort the pregnancy.According toNBC, the couple signed a contract last August with West that included a clause stating that the pregnancy could be terminated in the case of a “fetal abnormality”.However, West refused to terminate the pregnancy and instead traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to give birth. Republican attorney general Ken Paxtonintervened, shining a national spotlight on the case. A Dallas judge subsequently issued an order requiring the baby to receive medical care.Kagan’s refusal to intervene comes just days after the Texas supreme court ruled that the month-old child can leave Texas and relocate to aLos Angeleshospital for treatment.View image in fullscreenNausheen Gilkar, center, and Omar Ahmed, in court in Dallas last month.Photograph: LM Otero/AP“Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the courtsaid.West has since argued for custody of the child, claiming that his legal parents will not provide the necessary medical care because they had previously sought an abortion.West’s attorneys say that because their client “is now completely excluded from the life of the medically fragile infant she brought into the world, much less from the ability to make critical health decisions that protect him, time is of the essence”.In West’s filing to the supreme court, her lawyers argued that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save”.During acourt hearingin Dallas last month, the child’s parents said West was “unstable”. Gilkar added: “He’s our child … He’s the most beautiful person I’ve never seen … He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot.”Explore more on these topicsTexasUS supreme courtCaliforniaLos AngelesWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for Senate  | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party
Content: Abdul El-Sayed and former vice-president Kamala Harris in a roundtable discussion on reproductive health in Detroit, Michigan, on 22 September 2026.Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersView image in fullscreenAbdul El-Sayed and former vice-president Kamala Harris in a roundtable discussion on reproductive health in Detroit, Michigan, on 22 September 2026.Photograph: David Guralnick/ReutersMichiganKamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for SenateFormer VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured partyJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonTue 22 Sep 2026 18.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending her popularity among Black voters to a progressive Senate nominee still working to unite a party fractured by a bruising primary – and the former vice-president’s loss to Donald Trump in the state.Appearing with El-Sayed at aDetroitbirth center, Harris used a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame that November’s contest against the Republican Mike Rogers as a fight over women’s access to care.“Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America. Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars,” she said, hammering Rogers for his support of the president’s agenda.Harris also criticized the Trumpadministration for halting federal research funding it classified as diversity-related, including studies of fibroids and said the Senate should act as a check on the White House.Arab Americans in Michigan warn centrist Democrats attacking Hasan Piker: ‘They haven’t learned from 2024’Read more“The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, nodding to El-Sayed. The crowd murmured in agreement.El-Sayed, a physician, thanked Harris for “uplifting the issues that we are here to talk about today”, adding his gratitude for her work on them.The senate seat is open following the retirement of the Democratic senator Gary Peters and holding it is a must for the party’s path to a Senate majority. But even with a win in Michigan,Democratswould need to flip at least four Republican-held seats to control the chamber for Trump’s final two years in office.El-Sayed, who backs universal healthcare and sits to the left of his party’s leadership, narrowly defeated the congresswoman Haley Stevens in August, following a bitter primary thatdividedkey constituencies. Black voters in Detroit, the backbone of the Democratic coalition in the state, tended to favor Stevens, and Rogers has also been courting them in the city.The joint appearance also papers over a rift between the Democrats. El-Sayed has called Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide, a sharp break from the Biden-Harris administration’s military support for Israel, but a position that puts him in step with a growing share of the electorate.A Quinnipiac University pollreleased this monthfound 38% of voters more sympathetic to Palestinians and 35% to Israelis, the highest share siding with the Palestinians since the university began asking the question in December 2001.InMichigan, home to a large Arab American community, that shift has already shown up at the ballot box, and El-Sayed was part of it. In 2024, he backed the “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest at US military aid to Israel. He endorsed Harris when she replaced Biden as the nominee later that year. Many of the movement’s supporters did not follow him and the state narrowly went to Trump.The trip also comes amid speculation about Harris’s own political ambitions, as she mulls whether to run again for the White House. Michigan is set to hold the fifth contest on the Democrats’ revised 2028 primary calendar and Harris has further campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia.Closing her remarks, Harris urged the room to remind voters “that they have power and voice in the outcome of this election, which will directly impact their lives in many ways”.Explore more on these topicsMichiganKamala HarrisDetroitDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: California and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projects | US politics | The Guardian
description: US officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuels
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuels
Content: Breckenridge, Michigan, Construction of a wind farm. The 133-turbine, 212.8-megawatt project is being constructed by Invenergy Wind LLC and DTE Energy.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBreckenridge, Michigan, Construction of a wind farm. The 133-turbine, 212.8-megawatt project is being constructed by Invenergy Wind LLC and DTE Energy.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesUS politicsCalifornia and New York sue over Trump push to halt wind energy projectsUS officials have begun to buy back wind leases as president seek to block renewables in favor of fossil fuelsAssociated PressTue 22 Sep 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued theTrump administrationover its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.California attorney general Rob Bonta said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts.New York attorney general Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off theNew Yorkand New Jersey coast.The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country.View image in fullscreenThe Breckenridge wind warm in Michigan.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesThe Interior Department started buying back offshore wind leases in March after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action.In exchange for reimbursements of lease fees, companies are investing in fossil fuel projects and geothermal energy. Interior secretary Doug Burgum has said that companies “are shifting investment back toward dependable, secure energy infrastructure that can power our economy and lower utility costs”.James called the deals illegal and said they would ultimately increase Americans’ electricity bills by sabotaging states’ ability to meet growing energy demands.“Americans are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need,” James said in a statement. “These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers’ bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states.”Bonta said that as a national and global leader in the fight against climate change, California finds itself enmeshed in “avoidable and unnecessary battles with our own federal government” to advance climate action and move toward clean energy.Bonta, speaking at a Climate Week event in New York, said climate action needs to match the scope, speed and scale of the problem.“Because we have to go to court and block an unlawful action by the Trump administration each time, it takes time. It slows the process down and we know we are running out of time and we need to be urgent and aggressive,” Bonta said Tuesday in remarks just before Trump addressed the UN general assembly.“We’re still all in, in California,” Bonta said. “No matter what the Trump administration does, we’re going to push to participate in the climate action that is needed to meet this moment and to rise to the occasion.”Later in the day, Bonta was among the California and New York officials participating in a Climate Week panel about state leadership on wind energy. California energy commission chair David Hochschild said at the New York City bar that the power to drive a transition away from fossil fuels still rests primarily with the states.While Trump, who often talks about his hatred of wind power, can slow it down and make it more expensive, Hochschild said, “he can’t put the genie back in the bottle”.Trump has said his goal is to not let any “windmills” be built.New York state energy research and development authority president Doreen Harris said they are all confident they will ultimately succeed in court, however they need energy infrastructure in their states for a reliable grid.“The reality is, even if successful, the question becomes who is going to invest,” Harris said. She added: '“We just want to get back to building.”Attorneys general in Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont joined New York’s suit.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsWest CoastCaliforniaNew YorkTrump administrationDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hats, pencils and baby pacifiers: Yellowstone staffers retrieve record amount of trash from hot springs | US news | The Guardian
description: The park is the most highly visited and high winds make trash problem worse, with gusts blowing away items
Author: Cecilia Nowell
Headline: The park is the most highly visited and high winds make trash problem worse, with gusts blowing away items
Content: Frequent finds collected by the Yellowstone national park geology team during the summer season in 2026.Photograph: Margery Price/National Park ServiceView image in fullscreenFrequent finds collected by the Yellowstone national park geology team during the summer season in 2026.Photograph: Margery Price/National Park ServiceUS newsHats, pencils and baby pacifiers: Yellowstone staffers retrieve record amount of trash from hot springsThe park is the most highly visited and strong winds make trash problem worse, with gusts blowing away itemsCecilia NowellTue 22 Sep 2026 16.46 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHold on to your hats – Yellowstone national park staffershave removeda record-setting 20,100 pieces of trash from hydrothermal areas around the geyser-filled park so far this yearThe most commonly found items include 280 hats, 54 camera lens caps, 47 hair ties, 42 pencils, 36 pairs of sunglasses, 20 hotel key cards and 17 baby pacifiers.“The issue is made worse by the park’s high winds: unexpected gusts easily blow away tissues, maps, food wrappers, and even heavier items like sunglasses and hats!” Margery Price, a physical science technician with the Yellowstone National Park Geology Program, said ina blog postfor the US Geological Survey.View image in fullscreenHats collected by the Yellowstone national park geology team and other park staff from hydrothermal areas during the summer 2026 season.Photograph: Margery Price/National Park ServiceThat – and park visitors treating the hot springs like wishing wells. The Yellowstone Geology team collected more than $18 in coins during summer 2026, in currencies ranging from the dollar and pesos to yen and euros.With more than 4.5 million visitors annually, Yellowstone is one of the most highly visited national parks in the United States.“No matter the type of debris, it needs to be removed. Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature, whether from clogging its water supply, blocking or diverting its runoff channel, or polluting it with chemicals and sediment,” Price said.In the 1900s, the park’s Morning Glory Poolfamously changed colorfrom all of the trash visitors were leaving in the pool, which was nicknamed “trash can” by the 1950s.This year, the park’s geological staff retrieved six Invisalign retainers, eight mini race cars, three golf tees, and fifteen fake nails.While the park’s staff understands that much of that trash gets swept away by accident, they encourage visitors to “stash your trash” when visiting Yellowstone. That is, packing wrappers, tissues and even hats carefully away in windy areas. At the end of the season though, they’ll be sure to wash and donate all of the hats left behind.Explore more on these topicsUS newsNational parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump made over 1,000 July stock trades worth up to $270m, filings reveal | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: President made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks
Content: Trump speaks to reporters as he arrives for the UN general assembly session in New York on Tuesday.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump speaks to reporters as he arrives for the UN general assembly session in New York on Tuesday.Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump made over 1,000 July stock trades worth up to $270m, filings revealPresident made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocksGaya GuptaTue 22 Sep 2026 16.13 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 16.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump made over a thousand stock sales and purchases worth between $79m and $270m in July, according to a Guardian analysis of his latest financial disclosure released Tuesday.His two largest sales were of Amazon and Microsoft stock, selling between $5m and $25m each on 20 July. That same day, he also sold up to $5m worth of Oracle and Costco stock, $500,000 to $1m in Nvidia, and bought up to $5m worth of shares in Intuit and Salesforce, among dozens of other transactions.Overall, he made more than 700 sales that totaled between $35m and $137m, and made more than 440 purchases that totaled between $43.5m and $134m. Financial disclosures, which presidents and vice-presidents are required to file by law, only include a date and a range of the transaction amount.The White House said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio was “independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and that there were no conflicts of interests in the latest disclosure.“All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson.“Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.”TheJuly disclosurecomes as Trump and the Republican party continues tochampiona ban on stock trading among members of Congress, which would exclude him from any restrictions. The president made more trades than all of Congress combinedbetween the start of his second term and June,a Bloomberg analysis found.Trump’s last annual financial disclosures revealed thathe made more than $2.2bnlast year from his network of businesses and investments, including $1bn in crypto revenue. Disclosures from his staffhave also revealedlarge $45,000 cash gifts to three White House officials, including his close personal aide, Natalie Harp, which sparked calls from watchdog groups for further investigation.Trump also made up to $15.5m from his investments into oil and gas companies, the Senate’s joint economic committee found, because of gas prices driven up by the US war with Iran.The president, vice-president and members of Congress are legally allowed to trade stocks and are required to disclose their trades within 45 days of the transaction.But the practice is widely unpopular with voters. A recent survey from the Economist and YouGov found that about 75% of respondents, which included majorities of Democrats andRepublicans, believed that elected officials should not be allowed to buy and sell individual stocks in public office.The Trump-endorsed Stop Insider Trading Act passed by the House of Representatives in July, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The ban, however, would not affect Trump or JD Vance.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpStock marketsUS politicsRepublicansDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patrick Clancy interview on 60 Minutes fails to provide big ratings boost for CBS | US news | The Guardian
description: Amid show’s major overhaul by Bari Weiss, Sunday’s episode draws third-smallest audience for a second episode in the past 25 years
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Amid show’s major overhaul by Bari Weiss, Sunday’s episode draws third-smallest audience for a second episode in the past 25 years
Content: Patrick Clancy during his 60 Minutes interview.Photograph: CBS NewsView image in fullscreenPatrick Clancy during his 60 Minutes interview.Photograph: CBS NewsUS newsPatrick Clancy interview on 60 Minutes fails to provide big ratings boost for CBSAmid show’s major overhaul by Bari Weiss, Sunday’s episode draws third-smallest audience for a second episode in the past 25 yearsJeremy Barrin WashingtonTue 22 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released Tuesday.Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77m total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firingseveralhigh-profilecorrespondentsin the run-up to the new season.The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode.That episode was the show’s lowest-rated season debut in the 21st century, thoughCBSNews touted it as the most-watched non-sports program of the week and released a statement expressing satisfaction with the content of the program. “We are so proud of the exceptional journalism on display in our season premiere and we can’t wait to bring our audience another amazing show this coming Sunday,” the network said last week.The 20 September episode of the show barely edged last season’s second episode (6.45 million viewers), and it was likely hurt by not having NFL football as a lead-in program in all markets. But it featured what should have been an audience-boostinginterview, with new correspondent Ross Douthat sitting down with Patrick Clancy, who described the killings of his children and the aftermath. Clancy’s new wife, fertility doctor Rachel Danis, also gave a brief interview.In a nod to the interview’s cultural significance and importance for the show, Weiss was in attendance for the conversation, sources said. The show also featured a timely segment on pushback against datacenters reported by correspondent Norah O’Donnell, along with a whodunnit piece from longtime sports-focused correspondent Jon Wertheim about Shergar, an Irish racehorse kidnapped in the 1980s.While Douthat’s interview with Clancyreceived generally favorable reviews, it evidently was not the ratings draw that CBS News executives had hoped. The show’s debut episode had also featured a blockbuster interview, with one of the American fighter pilots shot down over Iran in April.The Guardian has reached out to CBS News about Sunday’s ratings.On a positive note for the network, the episode attracted 179.2m social views, surpassing last week’s record of 116.7m views.Explore more on these topicsUS newsCBSTV ratingsUS television industryBari WeissShareReuse this content

title: Trump says he backs diesel export ban to curb soaring energy costs | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: But industry trade group says plan would backfire and lead to even higher prices for gasoline
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: But industry trade group says plan would backfire and lead to even higher prices for gasoline
Content: A Shell gas station in Shoreline, Washington, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA Shell gas station in Shoreline, Washington, on 20 September 2026.Photograph: M Scott Brauer/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockTrump administrationTrump says he backs diesel export ban to curb soaring energy costsBut industry trade group says plan would backfire and lead to even higher prices for gasolineUS politics live – latest updatesGuardian staff and agenciesTue 22 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpon Tuesday said he backed ⁠the idea of a ban on diesel exports, which some US politicians are calling for ⁠as a way ⁠to curb ​the soaring cost of energy.Diesel prices have rallied inEuropeand the US to ⁠record highs as wars inIranandUkrainesharplycut exportsfrom some of the biggest producers ⁠such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. A gallon of diesel fuel in the US was $6.53 on Tuesday, the highest average on record and over 75% higher than a year ago.“I’ve ​said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Key ally urges Trump to back US farmers amid anger over rising pricesRead moreThe US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, speaking at the same meeting, said: “We’re examining whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.”On Sunday, Trump urged Zelenskyy to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices, the Financial Timesreported. On social media, Trump wrote that Russia “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry”.Some Republican Senate candidates in the most ​competitive midterm races called for the administration to implement the export ban to try to alleviate high costs for Americans.“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” wrote the US representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican who is in a competitive Senate race in Iowa,on X. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”In a statement, the American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers trade groupsaidthat an export ban would “backfire”, noting that domestic refiners would have to reduce production and “producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline”.Trump said he and Zelenskiy would ⁠discuss Ukrainian attacks on refining sites inRussia.“It is ​a serious ​hit on the Russians. ​It’s also a serious hit on the price ​of diesel,” said ‌Trump, who ​also told ​reporters the two leaders would discuss working out a solution to end Russia’s war inUkraine.“I think it’s going to happen,” Trump said, of a potential solution to the war.Reuters contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationEnergyInflationUS-Israel war on IranUkraineRussiaUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: EU spends three times more on imports from China than bloc exports there | European Union | The Guardian
description: Days before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump, new study shows trade deficit ran at more than €1bn daily in July
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Days before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump, new study shows trade deficit ran at more than €1bn daily in July
Content: China and the EU are locked in talks to avert a trade war.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina and the EU are locked in talks to avert a trade war.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionEU spends three times more on imports from China than bloc exports thereDays before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump, new study shows trade deficit ran at more than €1bn daily in JulyLisa O’CarrollTue 22 Sep 2026 07.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConsumers and businesses in the EU are spending three times more on Chinese imports than their counterparts inChinaare buying from the bloc, a study has shown.Customs data showed the gap between the EU’s imports fromChinaand exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1bn (£860m) a day in July.The new data comes just days after the European commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the trade imbalance must be arrested, and before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump on Thursday in Washington.China’s stranglehold on rare earths must be ended, says hopeful supplier to EURead moreThe Mercator Institute for China Studies (Meric) said: “The problem is no longer simply that the EU is buying more Chinese goods. China is selling more to Europe while buying less from it.”China and the EU are locked in talks about averting a trade war, and the EU’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, will travel to Beijing to meet his Chinese counterpart on 8 October.“With the bilateral deficit now exceeding €1bn a day, the widening imbalance will almost certainly be high on the agenda at the planned EU-China meeting in October,” Meric said.Analysis of Chinese customs data by Meric showed the EU’s trade deficit hit €36.5bn in July alone, up from €32.2bn in July 2025. From January to July, the total deficit now stands at €234bn, about €21bn more than the first seven months of 2025.“The imbalance has now moved beyond three to one. For every €1 of goods the EU exported to China in July, it imported €3.10. The deficit was equivalent to €1.18bn a day,” Meric said.Sources in Brussels said one of the measures being considered is introducing quotas on hybrid vehicles and certain types of chemicals imported from China.Sales of hybrid vehicles rocketed after the imposition of extra tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024 omitted to include hybrid electric cars, causing concern in the EU car industry.The latest figures show imports of hybrid cars that do not have to be plugged in have grown tenfold, from just under 4,000 vehicles sold in October 2024, to 50,000 in July 2026.The Financial Times reported last week that the EU has askedChina to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrids.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina has repeatedly warned it is ready for a trade war but its commerce ministry last week maintained a diplomatic stance before the October summit.“Any solution ​between China and the EU must ensure a ​balance of interests, comply ‌with World Trade Organization ​rules and ​the respective domestic laws of every side, and fully take into account the interests of industries on both sides,” it said.Chinese exports will be high on the agenda at Thursday’s summit in Washington, with expectations that a 12-month suspension of Beijing’s rare earth export restrictions will be extended.Kurt Tong, the former US consul general to Hong Kong and managing director of the Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said if a reprieve was not announced this week it could be announced at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit next month.China introduced the rare earth export restrictions in April 2025, almost bringing the car industry in the EU, Mexico, US and the UK to a halt amid shortages of permanent magnets.Itsuspended the ban last October when Trump met Xi in South Koreabut did not offer any further concessions when the two presidents last met in May in Beijing.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionInternational tradeGlobal economyEconomicsChinaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Giants’ Jaxson Dart could reportedly miss rest of season with knee injury | New York Giants | The Guardian
description: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Content: Jaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APView image in fullscreenJaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APNew York GiantsGiants’ Jaxson Dart could reportedly miss rest of season with knee injuryTesting said to reveal injury is worse than anticipatedQuarterback was hurt against Rams on MondayGuardian sportTue 22 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart will be out for an extended period of time and could miss the rest of the NFL season aftersuffering a knee injuryin Monday night’s loss to the Los Angeles Rams, according to reports Tuesday.ESPNreportedthat the injury to Dart’s left knee was more severe than initially anticipated. Adam Scheftersaidfurther testing has left the Giants and Dart facing the possibility of season-ending surgery.Rams crush Giants but Jaxson Dart escapes ‘devastating outcome’ after knee injuryRead moreThe second-year quarterback was hurt on the opening possession of the Giants’ 28-6 defeat to the Rams. Initial reports said that Dart sprained his MCL and avoided broken bones, with an MRI set for Tuesday. Head coach John Harbaugh said Monday that he believed a “devastating outcome” had been avoided and that he did not expect Dart to be out long-term without giving a further recovery timeline.The 23-year-old started the season strong in New York’s Week 1 win over Dallas but left the field after taking a huge hit from Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart on the Giants’ seventh play Monday night. Dart watched the second half in a track suit on the sidelines. Jameis Winston could not get much going after Dart’s exit, throwing an end-zone interception as New York got all of their points from field goals.Dart was one of several quarterbacks injured around the league in Week 2.Caleb Williamsof the Chicago Bears is week-to-week and will miss some time with a hamstring injury suffered against the Vikings, while the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow in a defeat to the Cowboys and has no timeline for return.Explore more on these topicsNew York GiantsUS sportsNFLnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacle  | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge him
Content: Gianni Infantino has reasserted his intention to stand for re-election as Fifa president.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Getty Images for Fanatics; BSR Agency/Getty Images; Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino has reasserted his intention to stand for re-election as Fifa president.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Getty Images for Fanatics; BSR Agency/Getty Images; Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesSoccerWill anyone topple Infantino? How Fifa president is trying to cling on after World Cup sell-off debacleFifa president continues to lobby for re-election despite no other candidates coming forward to challenge himMatt HughesTue 22 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForGianni Infantinothere is no international break. The Fifa president is widely expected to make an appearance at the United Nations general assembly this week in New York, where he will lobby heads of state for their federations’ support as he continues his campaign to be re-elected next year.Infantino has not been idle during the lull since Fifaabandoned its World Cup sell-off planlast month, instead crisscrossing the globe on a private jet provided by Qatar Airways as part of its sponsorship deal with world football’s governing body.Infantino proposes an ‘independent external review’ of Fifa governanceRead moreFrom his strongholds in Doha, Rabat and Miami, Infantino has also visited Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Kyrgyzstan and various other countries, his trips often coinciding with the approval of funding for development projects worth millions of dollars. His would-be opponents have been conspicuous by their silence.Whether Qatar Airways facilitating Infantino’s re-election campaign should be considered legitimateFifapresidential business is a moot point, which neatly encapsulates the huge incumbency bias that will benefit Infantino if a vote takes place at the Fifa congress in March.
