That ballot appears to be in doubt, with multiple sources involved in the push to remove Infantino telling the Guardian they are running out of hope of finding a candidate to beat him.Although dozens of the 200 member associations that had submitted letters of endorsement for Infantino withdrew them after the emergence of his Fifa Forward Enterprise sale plan in July, the prevailing view is that the silent majority remain steadfastly behind him.A meeting with the Caribbean Football Union, where funding projects were approved, may have splintered the vote at Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – and there are increasing concerns that the European alliance may not be watertight.“As long as Gianni is running, I don’t think anyone else will raise their hand,” one source said. “They would effectively be running against Fifa the institution. Fifa declared his candidacy, provides staff, aeroplanes and cars, even a personal video team.“If he doesn’t step down before March, the election will not be contested. Uefa and others could stage a boycott so the victory would be tainted, but Gianni will win a clear majority of whoever shows up.”Infantino first declared at the April congress in Vancouver his intention to seek a fourth and final term of office. Fifa statutes limit presidents to three full terms but under a recent change he will be permitted a fourth because his first term lasted three years, rather than the usual four, after his 2016 election to replace the disgraced Sepp Blatter.The 56-year-old reasserted his intention to stand after attending the first match of the Under-20 Women’sWorld Cupin Poland a fortnight ago. That came via a statement issued by Fifa’s media team.As it stands Infantino does not have an opponent, despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to go. Beyond the obvious difficulties of taking on an incumbent who controls the machinery of office and funding budgets – the last Fifa president beaten at the ballot box was Sir Stanley Rous in 1974 – there are specific reasons why none of the would-be candidates have declared.The most credible challenger is regarded as Concacaf’s president, Victor Montagliani, but the Canadian is committed to standing for re-election at his confederation, and the vote is due to take place in February. Standing in both elections is not regarded as feasible, and Montagliani is understandably reluctant to walk away from Concacaf in favour of fighting a potentially losing battle against Infantino.View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani (right), president of Concacaf, is reluctant to walk away from his current role but would be the most credible challenger to Infantino.Photograph: Elizabeth Ruiz Ruiz/Getty ImagesThe AFC president, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, was beaten by Infantino in the 2016 election, the only time Infantino has faced an electoral opponent, and is further hamstrung by the fact that his confederation’s main powers, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, are backing Infantino. Qatar’s position would also appear to rule out a challenge from Nasser al-Khelaifi, the chair of European Football Clubs, and an openly European move led by Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin, would have no chance of success. Ceferin, in any case, has his own presidential contest in March to focus on.To compound the difficulties for Infantino’s would-be challengers, any election would be a secret ballot, making any promises from member associations during the campaign period all but worthless. As a result, Uefa is focusing most of its efforts on legal avenues to remove Infantino, accusing him of “criminal mismanagement” in a 56-page document lodged with US state courts in New York, Miami and Colorado last month seeking the disclosure of all documents relating to FFE.Fifa responded strongly the week after Uefa made its legal complaint, filing a response in New York in which it sought to block the discovery process. Its submission accused Uefa of mounting a smear campaign against Infantino in the absence of any evidence of wrongdoing.Fifa’s submission said: “Uefa’s application suffers from a fundamental defect: Uefa seeks discovery in aid of a foreign criminal proceeding that does not exist and that Uefa admittedly lacks the authority to initiate.“While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of Uefa’s smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership.”Although there is widespread confidence that at least one of the three jurisdictions will grant discovery, the process grants Fifa the right of appeal, so there is little prospect of new material being made public before the 18 November deadline for presidential candidates to come forward.An initial decision from the courts is expected next month, but an appeal from the losing party appears inevitable whatever the outcome.“The issue with discovery is that it takes a long time,” a source said. “It’s likely to run beyond the date of the election in March. If the process is under way by then, Fifa congress could decide to wait until we find out what the courts discover and postpone the election. But there would still have to be a vote on that.”Uefa’s not-so-secret hope is that the discovery process finds evidence that FFE was deliberately undervalued at $20bn (£15bn) to provide a guaranteed future windfall for Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital, which had seemingly agreed to pay $4.2bn for 21% of the new commercial venture, giving it a significant share of future Fifa revenues.Thrive subsequentlybought 20% of the LA Lakerslast month as part of a larger transaction with the former Disney chief executive Bob Iger that valued the NBA franchise at $12.5bn, a deal that has further highlighted Infantino’s valuation of the World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa’s revenues for the four years to 2026 were $15bn, a figure projected to grow to $18bn over the next four-year cycle owing to larger broadcast deals, without accounting for any expansion of the World Cup and Club World Cup, which remains on the agenda.A corporate fraud lawyer said that undervaluing FFE could potentially constitute a criminal offence by Fifa, a case Uefa would take to the Swiss courts. “If you’re doing a deal that is way off market then you are deceiving the stakeholders, in this case the member associations,” the legal source said. “That is criminal. If Uefa has a criminal case that’s where it will be. It’s about how the valuation was done, by whom, and what conflicts were there.“All of that should come out during disclosure. If beyond that there were personal deals being struck on the side, that could also be criminal. All those details should be disclosed.”Beyond the $20bn valuation, the identity of the would-be investors and Fifa’s claim that it would retain control over governance, very little has been made public about the development of FFE, with a sales deck produced by the US bank JP Morgan containing no details of a tender process, voting rights or future exit terms. A senior investment banker who has been involved in similar deals said it is inconceivable such details were not agreed before Thrive agreed to commit $4bn, albeit much of the funding was due from other investors.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino before the World Cup final.Photograph: Pablo Morano/BSR Agency/Getty Images“I don’t think Thrive was going to be involved with Fifa for the next 25 years,” they said. “This looks like a quick in-and-out play. The plan would have been to buy it low and sell it high. I think the investors saw an amazing deal.”There is no evidence of any wrongdoing or criminality on the part of the any of the parties involved in the proposed FFE deal.Thrive has revealed little about its intentions beyond a statement issued last month in which it presented FFE as a proposal to be voted on by Fifa’s members, rather than a done deal.Significantly, however, it also expressed an element of regret at getting involved given the political backlash, which many within football have interpreted as an attempt to distance the firm from Infantino.“It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination,” Thrive said. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to. Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents. Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved.”Uefa and Concacaf, in particular, appear prepared to dig in for the long haul, despite concerns that Infantino will be re-elected. The two confederations are continuing to work together to develop a unified Nations League competition,revealed by the Guardian last month, and last week wrote a joint letter to Fifa demanding that it release funds from its $6bn reserves to fund an additionalpayment of at least $10m to each of its 211 member associationsduring the next four-year cycle.Some sort of payment appears inevitable given Infantino promised to provide $20m more to the member associations via FFE, but Uefa and Concacaf are hoping Infantino does not accrue political and electoral credit for it.Ceferin and Montagliani are expected to meet at next week’s general assembly of the European Football Clubs in Copenhagen, where Infantino may also make an appearance. Infantino addressed the EFC’s 900 members at last year’s EFC meeting in Rome, where his suggestion that more international tournaments should take place during European winters to accommodate the global south caused controversy, although that pales compared with his pronouncements and plans since.Uefa has made one accommodation with Fifa by withdrawing its threat to boycott the Under-20 Women’s World Cup that finishes on Sunday, and Infantino has agreed to its demand to commission an external governance review, which he communicated in a letter to the member associations this week. Suggestions that this move could lead to a truce with Uefa are given short shrift by those close to the leadership.Despite the electoral gloom, those agitating for change are also clinging to memories of the fate of Infantino’s predecessor, Blatter, who was forced to resign in 2015 amid an FBI corruption investigation days after winning a fifth term against Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan. Blatter himself has never been charged in relation to the investigation.For those looking to remove Infantino, the presidential election is not necessarily the end of the process. “This is a fight to the death now and we have to keep going,” one source said.“The fact that Gianni is the only guy running at the moment does not mean it’s over. Look what happened to Blatter. He was re-elected in May 2015, but was gone in June. Eventually the truth will come out.”Explore more on these topicsFootballGianni InfantinoFifaWorld CupFootball politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hardships never last’: Jenn Lichter’s path from Colombian orphanage to ultrarunning records  | Sport | The Guardian
description: Jenn Lichter’s childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summer
Author: Andy Cochrane
Headline: Jenn Lichter’s childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summer
Content: Jenn Lichter says she has found balance in her running as her career has progressed.Photograph: Andy CochraneView image in fullscreenJenn Lichter says she has found balance in her running as her career has progressed.Photograph: Andy CochraneSport‘Hardships never last’: Jenn Lichter’s path from Colombian orphanage to ultrarunning recordsJenn Lichter’s childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summerAndy CochraneTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 27 June, Jenn Lichter lined up for her first 100-mile race, the Western States 100. The oldest and most prestigious 100-miler in the world, Western States attracts a highly competitive field from around the globe – the athletes run across the Sierra Nevada from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California. Despite 18,000ft of climbing and daytime temperatures often flirting with triple digits, Lichter went in confident. “I wanted to win, there was no secret to that,” she says. “That’s just who I am.”The race remained close for the first half, until the 30-year-old made a move on the climb to Devil’s Thumb. The gap grew and at the final aid station, Lichter had a sizable lead over the athlete in second place. A mile from the finish, Nick Cornell, Lichter’s fiance, told her she was just ahead of the course record. “That was the first I had heard about it,” Lichter says. “He knew my competitive side would jump at the challenge.”Lichter sprinted the final mile down the streets of Auburn and on to the Placer High track, breaking the tape in 15 hours 28 minutes 5 seconds, 88 seconds faster than Courtney Dauwalter’s previous course record. Before 2026, only one woman had come within 50 minutes of Dauwalter’s time, making the record seem nearly unbreakable to most fans. Two months later, Lichter is only just putting that moment into perspective.“It took a while to process,” Lichter says. “It’s only hitting as I’m wrapping up the season and have the time to look back and realize what I did. It’s like summiting one of the most beautiful peaks in the world and at first you can’t fully understand what you’re seeing.”Lichter’s road to that record-shattering win was far from traditional. She was born in Bogotá, Colombia, and at two years old she was picked up by childcare services and placed in an orphanage, along with her older brother and younger sister. Her father had been shot and killed while involved with drug cartels and her mother struggled with addiction, leaving the children to fend for themselves on the streets.“Life in the orphanage was very regimented,” Lichter says. “Breakfast, lunch, dinner, and recess were always at the same time, but ignorance is bliss. When you’re a kid, you don’t know better.” Lichter’s mom would visit on the weekends, while trying to get back on her feet. When Lichter was seven, she and her siblings, Harold and Kim, were moved to an orphanage that worked to get them adopted together.“Despite the circumstances, we were happy and a big reason for that is we had each other,” she says. “That kept our mental state intact and made the whole experience less frightening. From birth, we’ve felt attached at the hip. Like twins, we can feel each other’s emotions. Our souls are intertwined.”Through those years, Lichter also learned how to rely on herself to get through challenges. “If shit ever hits the fan, I just pick myself up and dust myself off and continue on,” she says. “Life can be hard but it doesn’t mean you have to succumb to it. Hardships never last for ever.”Ultrarunner Megan Eckert shatters US men’s and women’s records with 636 miles in six daysRead moreWhen she was nine, Lichter and her siblings were adopted by a family in La Crosse, Wisconsin, on the banks of the Mississippi. She only knew a handful of English words – hello and goodbye, water, a few colors – so her adopted parents hired a bilingual nanny to help translate, carried a dictionary everywhere they went and covered the house in sticky notes with Spanish words and their English equivalent together, to help the kids learn the new language.The biggest culture shock for Lichter was the freedom she suddenly had. “I remember thinking, what do you mean we can have a snack whenever we want? Go outside whenever we want? Have a toy that’s not communal? Have seconds at dinner? The little, simple things that most people take for granted were everything to us.”Her new life was much more freeing than her time in the orphanage – going out to restaurants, road trips, and meeting new friends – but it came with challenges. “The language was hard at first, but I trusted that the longer I was in it, the better I would get,” Lichter says. “After a year I was fluent, happy and felt secure.”View image in fullscreenJenn Lichter stands at the finish line of the Western States.Photograph: Ryan ThrowerIn elementary school Lichter played basketball and enjoyed it, but in middle school she stopped growing and felt out of place. Her mom suggested cross-country running, which Lichter had never heard of. “I tried it out and thought it was the most uncomfortable thing in the world,” she says, “but I also had a sense that I could keep going.”Lichter stuck it out for a season, mostly out of curiosity. She found success and was recruited by the high school team, but the sport soon turned dark for her. “I liked the competition,” Lichter says, “but truly I like it because it was just something I could control. It’s just you, your body and your thoughts. That’s where the obsession started.”Running brought up the trauma around leaving Colombia that Lichter had repressed for years. She wrestled with the feeling of abandonment and used running as an outlet, driven by a search for control. At 12, Lichter was diagnosed with anorexia and for the next three years was in and out of treatment centers, working through the emotions of leaving her birth mother and loving her adopted mother.As a senior in high school, Lichter started winning races, sometimes by minutes. She received offers from a number of Division III and Division II schools, but instead opted for a walk-on scholarship from University of Toledo, her only Division I offer. “I felt like working for my spot would bring out the best in me,” Lichter says. “I had a fantastic freshman year, then dealt with RED-S [relative energy deficiency in sport] the rest of college. After that, I didn’t think running was meant to be in my life.”After graduating, Lichter packed up her car and roadtripped west with her mother, with plans to land in Portland, Oregon. Along the way they visited Montana’s Glacier national park and Lichter immediately fell in love. After the trip, Lichter stayed in Portland just 10 days before packing up again and driving back to Montana. “I had this moment when I realized I was a grown adult and I could do what I want,” she says, “so I drove back to Kalispell and the rest is history.”She started working as a hiking guide, living out of her tent for much of the summer. “I was 23 and felt so alive,” Lichter says. “I thought I’d hit the apex of my life, found my dream job.”That’s where Lichter met Cornell, who also worked as a guide. On their days off, they would go on trail runs together, and the joy of running slowly came back to Lichter. In the fall of 2021, Cornell suggested they race The Rut 50k in Big Sky, Montana.“I didn’t realize I still had the competitive spirit in me until we were driving to the race and I told Nick I wanted to win,” says Lichter, who went on to run the third fastest time in course history. After the race, The North Face offered Lichter her first professional trail running contract, and she jumped at the opportunity.Lichter recommitted to running, but planned to do it differently this time around. “In middle school and high school and college I had snippets of potential, but kept getting in my own way,” she says Licht. “Now I’m focused on taking care of myself first … actually taking easy runs easy, and not running myself into the ground. My sense of control is a lot different than it used to be.”That refreshed mentality has paid dividends. Lichter has won some of the most competitive 50k races around the United States – The Rut twice more, Broken Arrow Skyrace twice, Speedgoat and Gorge Waterfalls. Last year she decided to bump up in distance and told her team manager that her goal was to win Western States. To do that, she first had to qualify.Lichter lined up for the Black Canyon 100k in February, surrounded by a stacked field all wanting to earn a golden ticket to Western States. She won by mere seconds. After four more months of training, Lichter did the unthinkable, breaking Dauwalter’s record at the country’s most competitive 100-mile race.With months to reflect, Lichter says very little has changed after stunning the trail running world. “I feel more confident, but truthfully, my life is still the same,” she says. “I just keep putting in the work and being willing to take shots at new things. With my two feet on the ground, I have a sense of safety and control I used to not have, which gives me the confidence to try just about anything.”Explore more on these topicsSportUltrarunningRunningUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to evade Taliban wins Asian Games silver | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph ‘something special’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph ‘something special’
Content: Afghanistan’s Fariba Hashimi celebrates with her medal alongside her sister Yuldoz Hashimi and teammate Zahra Rezayee.Photograph: Bryan Foo/ReutersView image in fullscreenAfghanistan’s Fariba Hashimi celebrates with her medal alongside her sister Yuldoz Hashimi and teammate Zahra Rezayee.Photograph: Bryan Foo/ReutersCyclingAfghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to evade Taliban wins Asian Games silverFariba Hashimi fled after Taliban returned to power‘This medal can show resilience from Afghan women’Agence France PresseTue 22 Sep 2026 04.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday, hoping it inspires other women in a country whereTalibanauthorities have sharply curtailed their freedoms.Fariba Hashimi, who is based in Italy, powered home second behind China’s Guo Li in the women’s road race near Nagoya in Japan, calling the triumph “something special”.Thirteen-year-old swim sensation sets women’s 200m butterfly record at Asian GamesRead more“I can’t explain my feelings now,” the 23-year-old said, before reflecting on how she was attacked with stones and trained disguised as a man when she started out in the sport as a teenager along with her sister Yulduz, who is also now a pro cyclist.“I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I’m really happy that I have fought against that,” she said. “I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.”The Taliban authoritiesreturned to power in 2021andhave since imposed a series of ruleslimiting women’s access to education and public life, including sport. “They took away our freedom, they took away everything from us,” said Hashimi, who hails from the Faryab province in northern Afghanistan and left the country after the Taliban authorities took over.“This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I’m really happy. I’m not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me.”After fleeingAfghanistanwith the help of the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto, Hashimi relocated to Italy where she now lives and trains. She and her sister competed at the Paris Olympics two years ago, and the 2028 Los Angeles Games are now looming into view. “I never want to give up and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles.”Hashimi reserved a special thanks for the Japanese team for playing a part in her silver medal. “I’m here without a mechanic, without any preparation. We brought one guy with us from the national federation, and he just drove the car. We were fixing the bike ourselves. I was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself. Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingTalibanAfghanistannewsShareReuse this content

title: Mikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030 | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Mikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season
Content: Mikel Arteta celebrates with the Premier League trophy in May, ending Arsenal’s 22-year wait to be champions.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta celebrates with the Premier League trophy in May, ending Arsenal’s 22-year wait to be champions.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianArsenalMikel Arteta agrees contract extension expected to keep him at Arsenal until 2030Manager’s current deal to expire at end of the seasonSpaniard can expect big increase on £10m-a-year salaryEd AaronsTue 22 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has agreed a long-term contract extension with Arsenal that includes a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season and could take his reign as the manager beyond a decade.The three-year deal he signed in September 2024 expires at the end of this season and talks have been ongoing since May whenArsenal ended their long wait to be champions. Negotiations were put on hold during the summer transfer window but the Spaniard has reached a ­verbal agreement to extend his stay for a second time.Football Daily | Brighton’s organised chaos viciously pecks Arsenal into submissionRead moreThe length of the contract is unknown but it is understood Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, will commit his future for at least another three years. The 44-year-old is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City at the end of last season.Arsenal have been keen to reward Arteta for transforming the club. His current contract is believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal will cement his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world.As well as leading Arsenal to a first Premier League title since 2004, Arteta last season guided them to the Champions League final, which theylost to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootoutin Budapest. The club started this season with seven straight wins in all competitions before Saturday’s surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton.Arteta reiterated before that game that he was relaxed about his contract situation. “I think we are all very much aligned,” he said. “Whenever the time is right, we’ll get that done. There is nothing to be concerned about. I think we both have the same ambition and the same will.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsenal are also keen to extend Declan Rice’s contract, the England midfielder having entered the final two years of his deal. It is understood the club have an option to extend it by 12 months but would like to agree new terms in line with their policy of securing Arteta’s most important players on long-term contracts.Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Klopp, Xavi, Zidane, Mancini: big nations ready to unleash bigger dogs | Soccer | The Guardian
description: In today’s Football Daily: At least there are some big names to entertain us in the international wilderness
Author: Barry Glendenning
Headline: In today’s Football Daily: At least there are some big names to entertain us in the international wilderness
Content: International big dogs, earlier.Composite: Getty Images; AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInternational big dogs, earlier.Composite: Getty Images; AFP/Getty ImagesFootball Daily newsletterSoccerKlopp, Xavi, Zidane, Mancini: big nations ready to unleash bigger dogsSign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!Barry GlendenningTue 22 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleINTERNATIONAL SUPERSTARSWhile Thomas Tuchel continues togaslight his employers at the FA into believing he was in no way responsible for England’s comically shambolic semi-final exit at the hands of Argentina, not every head coach who underperformed at the Geopolitics World Cup is still in their job. A total of 17 different managers who took teams to North America have since left their roles, with safety-first’s Steve Clarke, failing-up’s Roberto Martínez and tyranny’s Marcelo Bielsa among them. In Europe, teams such as Portugal (Jorge Jesus), Croatia (Slaven Bilic), Scotland (Sébastien Pocognoli), Czechia (Santi Denia) and Belgium (Mark van Bommel) will go into the Nations League under new management, but it is towards the bigger dogs of the football pack where Football Daily wishes to turn today’s beady gaze.Germany:Having been accused of using his role as a TV pundit to undermine Julian Nagelsmann during the GWC, it was no great shock to see Jürgen Klopp take over from the 39-year-old when he stepped down. Klopp immediatelyfired a volleyacross the bows of the German press pack and will begin his first role in international management with a trip to the Netherlands. Unlike his predecessor, the former Liverpool boss is unlikely to rock up to training on a skateboard and it will be intriguing to see how successfully he instils his ethos of heavy-metal football in a group of players he only gets into the rehearsal room three or four times a season. “This is the pinnacle, the absolute high point of my footballing career as coach,” he parped, raising sceptical eyebrows on Merseyside. “I will give everything I have got.”Netherlands:Upon replacing Ronald Koeman, Xavi Hernández was eager to emphasise his deep connection with the Dutch. While it remains to be seen if the former Spanish midfield maestro is a bike-riding windmill enthusiast with a capacity for extreme bluntness, he was handed his Barcelona debut by Louis van Gaal and name-dropped club legends Johan Cruyff and Rinus Michels during his unveiling. Third choiceon a shortlist of fourbehind Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot, Xavi can at least sleep safe in the knowledge the Dutch FA considered him a slightly more glamorous candidate than Michael Reiziger, and will begin his international reign with a match against a fellow newbie. “I feel motivated because we are playing against Germany,” he cheered, before his opening game in Amsterdam. “So yeah, it’s a big challenge from the beginning, but I think we will be ready.”Italy:Having suffered the indignity of failing to qualify for their third successive World Cup, Italian football suits didn’t so much go back to the drawing board, as back in time when it came to replacing Gennaro Gattuso.Roberto Mancini is backfor his second spell in charge, having previously masterminded victory in the European Championship in 2021 and subsequent failure to get to the HRWC in 2022. “I believed that the best person to become head coach was ‌Roberto Mancini,” tooted FIGC top brass Giovanni Malagò, shortly after his organisation’s plot to install Andrea Pirlo in the rolewas foiledby the former midfielder’s commercial ties to a Russian betting firm. A famously patient people when it comes to their national football team, fans of theAzzurriare surely unlikely to get upset if early results against Belgium and Turkey don’t go their team’s way …France:It was a matter of when, not if Zinedine Zidanetook over the national teamand despite his pedigree as a three-time Bigger Cup-winning coach of Real Madrid, he has extremely big boots to fill. After taking over from his former French water carrier, Didier Deschamps, Zizou played all the right notes. “I’ve been looking forward to this moment,” he cheered. “It’s a dream come true. The France national team has been the most beautiful thing that has ever happened to me. It’s a great adventure that I hope is just beginning.” Kylian Mbappé has already described the prospect of working under Zizou as being “like a film”. Its box-office success will almost certainly stand or fall on the chemistry – or lack of it – between two of French football’s most iconic leading men.LIVE ON BIG WEBSITEJoin Will Unwin at 5.45pm (BST) for Women’s Bigger Cup updates on Bayern Munich 2-2 Manchester City.QUOTE OF THE DAY“Every time I see it, I’m cringing, I’m in disbelief. It’s horrible to watch back and to see what could have been. Thankfully I was fortunate I did manage to fall on to the floor at the right time, so nothing snapped as the roller went over me … I was able to get my left arm up and relieve some of the pressure, and then I was able to get my teammates around me who were able to lift it, and I was able to squeeze out but at that moment where it was crushing my left leg, it was quite terrifying, I must say” – Andros Townsend explains what it was like to be run over bythatpitch roller in Thailand and just how much he thanks his lucky stars for not coming to more harm than suffering a few cuts and bruises.RECOMMENDED LOOKINGIt’s our man David Squires on … Big Sir Jimlamenting the declineof once-mighty empires.View image in fullscreenZing!Illustration: David Squires/The GuardianFOOTBALL DAILY LETTERSdouble quotation markPrize o’ the day to Barry Glendenning, surely, for mentioning Johnny Crumplin (football genius) inMonday’s Football Daily. As an Ipswich fan marooned in Sussex, I spent much of my teenage years at the Goldstone which, despite being a dump (I stood on the crumbling South Stand), held a certain magic for me. It still does, actually. Haven’t been to the Amex yet – hopeless nostalgia is undoubtedly a factor. The team weren’t much better than the ground for most of that time, but the 1987-88 promotion season was memorable. Garry Nelson was a bit special, Doug Rougvie had played under Fergie at Aberdeen and Gerry Armstrong had legendary status after *that* goal, but the rest of the team probably (and unfairly ) fall into the journeyman category. I loved them all. Keith Dublin dribbling his way into and then out of trouble, sleeves-up Kevin Bremner who grafted and worked the Albion into the promotion places, Deano (one of the Wilkins brothers) classy and, of course, Barry Lloyd, who never brought a sub on until the last four or five minutes, frustrating us beyond belief. And into this pantheon came teenage Johnny C who, to start with, was utterly hapless, hence the nickname football genius. Somehow, despite this, we took to him from the off and it was lovely to see how he grew into becoming an Albion legend in what were fallow years. Blimey, not sure where that all came from – you can probably tell I’m stuck out in the middle of the Fens on a slow-moving train. But thank you for bringing it all back to me!” – Jonathan Foulkes.double quotation markI know the powers that be have listened to Football Daily’s ‘Stop Football’ pleas and given us very little to do for the next three weeks but, as we are just five games in to the Premier League season, can everyone stop going on about therace for the Golden Bootand which team are going to bloody champions” – Nigel Sanders.double quotation markJudging by the photo of him sitting behind their ‘Life’s Good’ logo inyesterday’s Quote of the Day, LG could do a lot worse than appoint José Mourinho as a brand ambassador for their campaign. As football watchers have long known, he exudes the spirit of that exclamation from every single pore” – Andrew Parker.double quotation markSo, Jonathan Wilson has a new book, about football in Eastern Europe,Behind the Curtain, while his take on Zidane as the new France manager will reveal the ‘wizard behind the curtain’. Brilliant effort from the subeditor and marketing team working in harmony” – Paul Vickers.If you have any, please send letters tothe.boss@theguardian.com.Today’s letter o’ the day prize goes to … Jonathan Foulkes, who wins a copy ofBehind the Curtainby Big Website’s Jonathan Wilson. It’s out now and available inThe Guardian Bookshopalongside loads of other great football titles. title: ‘It’s bordering on exploitation’: how pseudoscience is duping football | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Cryotherapy chambers and other practices in the elite game have little evidence behind them, says Dr Claire-Marie Roberts, a top performance director
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: Cryotherapy chambers and other practices in the elite game have little evidence behind them, says Dr Claire-Marie Roberts, a top performance director
Content: Claire-Marie Roberts has spent decades working in elite athlete performance and professional football.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClaire-Marie Roberts has spent decades working in elite athlete performance and professional football.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianSoccerInterview‘It’s bordering on exploitation’: how pseudoscience is duping footballSam CunninghamCryotherapy chambers and other practices have little evidence behind them, says top performance directorTue 22 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDr Claire-Marie Roberts was working atCoventry Citywhen she received a call from someone asking whether she knew how much oxygen was in the atmosphere. As the performance director, responsible for optimising players’ potential, she was accustomed to being pitched the latest gimmick promising miraculous gains. At times, she could receive up to 50 LinkedIn messages a week offering a device, supplement or technology that claimed to produce magical results.“It is only 21%,” the caller told her. That’s GCSE chemistry, she thought. Then came the sales pitch: “So what we’ve done is put oxygen in a can and we think you might want to use it.”Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionRead more“Right … oxygen in a can,” Roberts says, laughing at the memory. Suffice to say, she did not take the caller up on his offer to buy oxygen in a can for Coventry’s players.Roberts has spent decades working in elite athlete performance and professional football, including nine years at the Premier League and two at Coventry, where she played a key role in theirpromotion as Championship championsbefore joining the Formula One team McLaren as director of human performance in the summer. She is shocked by how professional football is being duped by pseudoscience: from coaches and performance staff misled by snake-oil sellers, to players desperate for a shortcut and with money to burn.“It’s the science-practice gap, which is widening in my experience,” Roberts says. “I think it’s getting much worse. There’s so much sparkly marketing behind all these things. It’s bordering on exploitation.“They’re taking a population that is very susceptible to: ‘How can I hack my performance advantage? How can I shortcut my preparation and recovery?’ Which I don’t think is a great starting point.”Roberts says some of the practices commonplace in elite football have little evidence behind them. She includes cryotherapy chambers – a common feature at elite training grounds. If unavailable, ice baths are a fallback. Players enjoy them so much that Harry Kane was photographed standing in a wheelie bin full of ice after a Bayern Munich match at last year’s Club World Cup.View image in fullscreenClaire-Marie Roberts was part of Frank Lampard’s staff during Coventry’s Championship-winning season.Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters“Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them, because there’s no evidence for them apart from a very slim piece of work that says it might help prevent dementia,” Roberts says. “There’s very sketchy evidence on cryotherapy.”They could even be detrimental to recovery, Roberts says. “There’s a recent suggestion that cryotherapy might blunt muscular adaptation. When are you using it and why are you using it? If you’re using it for recovery, sleep and nutrition are your best recovery modalities. No amount of putting anybody in a whole-body cryotherapy chamber is going to help them recover more if those two things aren’t taken care of.”But players are constantly attempting to shortcut nutrition, too. Supplements are a multibillion-pound industry that has its claws in the game. But beyond vitamin D, in which it is “evidence-based” that people in the northern hemisphere are commonly deficient owing to a lack of sunlight, and vitamin C, which is usually short in our diets, supplementation should, Roberts says, be targeted to deficiencies.“You’ve got people popping pills not really asking what they’re for. It should always be needs-based. If you don’t eat fish and fish oil is important to you, you might supplement it. It should all be based on need.“Your athletic performance and recovery is based on sleep quality and nutritional quality and amounts. No amount of supplementation will improve a bad diet, but people think it will. We don’t do enough of the basics and think we can shortcut and hack everything.”View image in fullscreenClaire-Marie Roberts: ‘Most clubs have got cryotherapy chambers – most people cannot articulate to you why they use them.’Photograph: Eddie Keogh for The FA/Rex/ShutterstockRoberts says she used an evidence-based, scientific approach to support Frank Lampard’s squad and that many clubs follow practices from the top of the game when often they are flawed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“People passively suck these things up,” she says. “Because England or Manchester City or Chelsea who have all the resources under the sun have got this, there’s a misappropriation of confidence and understanding of the scientific basis or evidence. It’s powerful in driving behaviour, but it’s driving the wrong behaviour.”Roberts, a former swimmer who missed the 1996 Atlanta Olympics owing to injury, says: “Football is more susceptible to it than any other sport I’ve experienced first-hand. I think because the stakes are higher.”Kinesiology tape – or k-tape, as it is commonly known – is another trend that baffles Roberts. Players from Cristiano Ronaldo to Gareth Bale and David Beckham have been spotted wearing it over the years, often resembling strips of gaffer tape stuck to limbs.“There’s no evidence kinesiology tape has any impact on injury prevention or performance-related outcomes. It gives you a bit of proprioception – maybe you feel like someone has done something – but in any environment I’ve worked in you’d never see anyone wearing k-tape. It’s a big white elephant.“If an athlete has dislocated their shoulder, you should strap it – strapping is different. It provides an element of external support that can provide minimal protection to the joint and reminds the person they’ve got a problem. It’s a risk-mitigation strategy. It’s not hugely successful, but you’d do it rather than not do it. K-tape is a placebo.”Often, managers who have been in the game for decades insist on practices they have adopted for years, or because another coach, with no scientific background, has heard about a revolutionary new product. Roberts believes that until football puts science at the centre of decision-making and employs qualified staff to scrutinise claims, the problem will worsen.“We think we can accelerate to an outcome without putting the hard yards in – the basic things: diet and sleep and the quality of your training,” she says.“Football in general is very anti-intellectual and it has been for a long time. There are a few clubs that do it well, but the majority don’t. The game is definitely anti-science. There’s a reason for that. There isn’t a critical mass of people that are applying critical thought to situations.”Explore more on these topicsFootballCoventry CityinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against Køge | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Mariona Caldentey scored a penalty in injury time in Arsenal’s 1-0 win against HB Køge, after a Chloe Kelly goal in the 13th minute was disallowed by VAR
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Mariona Caldentey scored a penalty in injury time in Arsenal’s 1-0 win against HB Køge, after a Chloe Kelly goal in the 13th minute was disallowed by VAR
Content: Mariona Caldentey celebrates scoring from the spot after after Selina Cerci was brought down in injury time.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMariona Caldentey celebrates scoring from the spot after after Selina Cerci was brought down in injury time.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Champions LeagueMariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against KøgeSuzanne Wrackat Mangata Developments StadiumTue 22 Sep 2026 17.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMariona Caldentey’s 93rd-minute penalty delivered a win and a hefty dose of relief to fans bouncing behind the goal in the North Bank after the ball hit the back of the net, but ­Arsenal’s narrow defeat of HB Køge in their Champions League opener left more questions unanswered than answered for the struggling Gunners.The puffed cheeks of the manager, Renée Slegers, said it all when the full-time whistle went. If it had been revealed after the final whistle that a force field surrounded the opposition goal at Meadow Park, many would have believed it, such was the extent of Arsenal’s ridiculous profligacy in front of goal in their league-phase opener.“It was a mentality and resilience win today,” said Slegers. “The football didn’t give us the win … but we get the goal as a squad.”Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern MunichRead moreExactly what is stopping Arsenal from getting the ball in the back of the net with a swagger reflective of their talent-laden squad is hard to pinpoint.Yes, teams are defending excellently against them, as a battling Køge and their goalkeeper Alberte Vingum did on Tuesday night, but this feels like an Arsenal problem: a mentality one, a training ground one, a ruthlessness one.Practically solving the issue is a multifaceted undertaking, but “making things simple and easy to understand and easy to execute are probably the main two” focuses for Slegers.“Then it’s also about involving the players as much as possible. Getting their input: ‘What do you see? What do you feel on the pitch? What’s your perception in the moment and your analysis afterwards?’”The shadow of Sunday’s trip to Stamford Bridge loomed large at Meadow Park with eight changes made to the team thatsalvaged a point against Manchester Uniteddeep into added time on Saturday.The hope, without being ­disrespectful to their Danish opposition, was that this game would alleviate the frustration the Gunners are experiencing in front of goal, breaking the mental block several players seem to be suffering from. ­Unfortunately, the A-Liga leaders had other ideas.The Gunners’ pressure in the opening 20 minutes, which the Køge manager, Kristian Mørch, described as “like plunging into ice-cold water” that they just had to “try to survive, calm the panic, calm the fear, and then act our way out of it”, seemed to have yielded the breakthrough in the 13th minute, when Caitlin Foord kept an attack alive before sending the ball to Taylor Hinds. The full-back fed Kyra Cooney-Cross and the Australian midfielder’s neat flick was turned in by Chloe Kelly on the volley with the outside of her leg. It was a fine finish but the video assistant referee intervened to penalise an offside Stina Blackstenius for straying into the line of sight of Vingum. Had the hosts got an early goal, the game may have opened up for them a little.View image in fullscreenChloe Kelly scores in the 13th minute before the goal was disallowed with Stina Blackstenius ruled offside.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesThat the match reached half-time still goalless was somewhat inexplicable, but also symbolic of Arsenal’s stuttering start to the season, with just five points from their three Women’s Super League games after consecutive draws, against Crystal Palace and Manchester United.The scale of the achievement for the visiting team was demonstrated by the buoyant celebrations of their coaching staff as soon as the half-time whistle was blown. Mørch bellowed “good job in here”, before tripping on a railing and receiving a chorus of boos from the home fans behind the opposition dugout. He walked across the pitch towards the dressing room with a smile on his face and a finger to his lips shushing the crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTheir decision to celebrate every positive action was a conscious one. “We agreed before the game that we’re going to celebrate every possible win, even just the goalkeeper sometimes catching the ball, that’s a win,” said Mørch. “I could see that some of the Arsenal players got a bit annoyed by it, but we had to try and do whatever we could.”“We noticed it,” said Slegers with a smile. “And I understand it from their perspective. It’s a good tactic, I guess, to keep morale in the team high and maybe intimidate the opposition.”Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG peg back Real MadridShowParis Saint-Germaincame from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw atReal Madridin their Women's Champions League opener.Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – asBenficadispatchedJuventus2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game forInterwith a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish sideBK Häckento a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack.Press AssociationPhotograph: Alberto Gardin/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.As the clock edged towards full time, every effort placed high, wide or cut out was wildly celebrated by the Køge substitutes. They were silenced eventually, when Yukina Sakabe upended Selina Cerci in a rare blip from the visiting team and Caldentey converted from the spot.It was crushing for the visiting team, but Mørch was delighted with his team. “Around minute 80, I came to terms with the idea that if something happens, something happens,” he said. “We were so pressed at that point that these things will sometimes happen. So, for me, I’m not going to say the game ended there, but my judgment of the overall ­performance kind of ended there. I’ve seen what I could dream of from the team.”Relief filled the stands packed with red and white after the goal, but with Chelsea up next, nerves of another wasteful season will not settle.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueArsenal WomenHB Køge WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Wamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern Munich | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Carlotta Wamser scored a late equaliser as Manchester City battled back from a two-goal deficit to draw 2-2 with Bayern Munich in the Women’s Champions League
Author: Sophie Downey
Headline: Carlotta Wamser scored a late equaliser as Manchester City battled back from a two-goal deficit to draw 2-2 with Bayern Munich in the Women’s Champions League
Content: Manchester City's Carlotta Wamser (left) is embraced by Laura Blindkilde Brown after her late equaliser for Manchester City.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenManchester City's Carlotta Wamser (left) is embraced by Laura Blindkilde Brown after her late equaliser for Manchester City.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APWomen's Champions LeagueWamser rescues point for Manchester City in WCL fightback at Bayern MunichSophie Downeyat Uhlsport ParkTue 22 Sep 2026 14.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City produced a gutsy performance to fight back and earn a valuable 2-2 draw away at Bayern Munich on their return to the Champions League. José Barcala’s side took the lead through Giulia Gwinn and an unfortunate Kerstin Casparij own goal but Beth Mead and Carlotta Wamser earned the visitors a hard-earned point.City’s head coach, Andrée Jeglertz, was pleased with the resolve of his side after a difficult first half. “It [a comeback] has happened before because we know the quality is there,” he said. “The mentality of ­winning and the belief is there. It shows ­something about this group again.Mariona Caldentey penalty provides late WCL relief for Arsenal against KøgeRead more“There were definitely two phases of this game. In the first half, Bayern were very good. I think we were a bit slow on the ball … It was almost like we were surprised by the tempo. I know we weren’t but it looked like that. At the end of the first half, we got a little bit back. The trust and the belief at half-time was good so I felt that this is still possible.”It was always going to be a challenging start for the English champions against a Bayern team who have historically thrived in the league phase of this competition. They came into this unbeaten in their last 15 home group-stage matches and on the back of a semi-final run last ­season that, according to Gwinn, had left them “even hungrier and eager for more”. Not only that but the German team have kicked off the defence of their Frauen-Bundesliga title in stunning fashion with five wins from five.City also arrived in Germany full of confidence after an equally impressive start to the season. Their4-2 win over Liverpoolon Friday had been a further sign of their mettle, finding a way to win despite not being at their best.Quick GuideWCL roundup: PSG peg back Real MadridShowParis Saint-Germaincame from behind to clinch a 1-1 draw atReal Madridin their Women's Champions League opener.Felicia Schröder gave the Spanish club the lead after just 96 seconds to make it six goals in five appearances since her June transfer from BK Häcken. But Sakina Karchaoui (pictured) was on target from the penalty spot with 16 minutes left to secure a point for PSG.Marit Bratberg Lund scored twice – once from the spot – asBenficadispatchedJuventus2-1 at Allianz Stadium. Alba Redondo grabbed a late consolation for the hosts.The Malta striker Haley Bugeja settled a hard-fought opening game forInterwith a fifth-minute winner that condemned Swedish sideBK Häckento a 1-0 defeat at U-Power Stadium. Häcken's keeper Jennifer Falk was sent off in the 90th minute for a trip as Inter staged a late attack.Press AssociationPhotograph: Alberto Gardin/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.European football, however, presents a different test altogether and they came into this game with plenty of unknowns. How would they measure up after a year out of the competition? Could their injury-hit squad juggle the load of European football and domestic challenges?Reality hit in a first half during which a refreshed Bayern took control of proceedings. Barcala had been able to make five changes to his starting XI, having completely rested Klara Bühl and Gwinn against Köln on Saturday, and they looked full of energy.Bühl immediately stretched every sinew of City’s fragile-looking defence with her pace and guile. The 25-year-old was at the heart of everything Bayern created early on, firing a volley wide before setting up the equally prolific Pernille Harder for a half chance.It did not come as a surprise, therefore, that the hosts broke the deadlock with 11 minutes on the clock. It was a move that cut through the heart of Manchester City as Linda Dallmann broke clear to send Gwinn on her way. The full-back saw the pitch open up in front of her, dispatching a cool finish past Ayaka Yamashita in the City goal.View image in fullscreenGiulia Gwinn reacts after opening the scoring.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APIt was moment when the 4,291-strong crowd raised the decibel level, buoyed by their team’s domination and, perhaps also, the Oktoberfest celebrations. This was Bayern’s first outing at Sportpark Unterhaching and the raucous crowd seemed to settle in straight away at their new home.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe pressure on City continued. Struggling to find space in possession, they were guilty of playing into Bayern’s hands, channelling their attack centrally rather than trying to exploit the wide areas. Things got worse when an unwitting Casparij diverted a dangerous Harder cross into her own net to double the score.This City side are made of stern stuff, however, and Jeglertz’s ­players were handed a lifeline just before the break, albeit in controversial fashion. As a blue smoke flare blazed on the pitch, the referee allowed play to continue while Casparij burst forward. Her cross was met by Khadija Shaw, whose shot was deflected into the path of Mead, who tapped home.View image in fullscreenBayern Munich and Manchester City try to stay focused despite a flare on the pitch.Photograph: Michaela Stache/AFP/Getty ImagesThe second half was a much more even affair as the pendulum of momentum swung between the teams. City should have had an equaliser when Aoba Fujino was brought down by Ena Mahmutovic only for the goalkeeper to step up and save Shaw’s penalty.Despite the hosts still looking potent going forward, City could sense that the tide was shifting and found an equaliser with four minutes to play. Wamser, signed from Bayer Leverkusen this summer, arrived unmarked on the edge of the box to rifle home a finish on her return to Germany.The substitute Edna Imade had two big chances to win it for Bayern late on but the visitors held strong. With one of their most difficult games out of the way, they face Real Madrid next week in Manchester with a chance of making another statement on the European stage.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueBayern Munich WomenManchester City WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid call for La Liga president’s removal over his response to derby complaints | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid want a new La Liga president in light of what they called ‘intolerable’ comments from Javier Tebas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Real Madrid want a new La Liga president in light of what they called ‘intolerable’ comments from Javier Tebas
Content: José Mourinho confronts the referee Miguel Ángel Ortiz Arias during Real’s defeat to Atlético.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APView image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho confronts the referee Miguel Ángel Ortiz Arias during Real’s defeat to Atlético.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APLa LigaReal Madrid call for La Liga president’s removal over his response to derby complaintsJavier Tebas accused club of ‘permanent conspiracy’ talkReal Madrid hit back at president’s ‘intolerable’ behaviourAgenciesTue 22 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid want a new La Liga president in light of what they called “intolerable” comments from the incumbent, Javier Tebas, ⁠who said on Tuesday that claims of officiating bias against the club belonged to “another galaxy”.Afterlosing 2-1 to Atlético Madridon ⁠Sunday, Real headlined the ⁠match report ​on their website: “Terrible refereeing decides the derby.”Paper trail of protests: José Mourinho plays the hits in Madrid derby defeat | Sid LoweRead moreReal were furious that Atlético’s Cristian Romero was not sent off for a stamp on ⁠Jude Bellingham and also complained about a challenge by Lee Kang-in on Federico Valverde.Real’s manager, José Mourinho, aimed sharp criticism at the referee, Miguel Ángel Ortiz ⁠Arias, and those who appointed him. Mourinho said his side could win the title “if they ​let us compete on a level playing ‌field”.He brought two printed screenshots of what he thought were red-card tackles committed by players to his post-match press conference.Tebas responded to a pro-Real article on social media with a lengthy riposte to allegations of a “conspiracy” against the 15-time European champions.“Here they go again, the mouthpieces and the regime’s television, building the same old narrative – the permanent conspiracy,” said Tebas, who has often been at odds with Real Madrid and the club’s outspoken president, Florentino Pérez.“This article goes further – it claims that referees harm ‘the business that feeds them’. What exactly is it asking for? Refereeing based on revenue, viewership, or the badge? What a way to understand equality in the competition.“Real Madrid are crucial toLa Liga. But claiming that ‘La Liga is worth nothing’ without them reveals the disdain for the other clubs, their fans, and their history. The competition belongs to no one.”Real responded with a statement on their website, saying: “Our club considers it intolerable that the president of La Liga uses his institutional position to continue discrediting and attacking ​Real Madrid.“Given this inappropriate and persistent behaviour, we believe that the professional football competition in Spain urgently needs a leader capable of managing it and realising its full potential with the fundamental duty of neutrality.“Real sit six points behind the reigning champions and early leaders, Barcelona.Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Branthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England call | England | The Guardian
description: Jarrad Branthwaite has credited a ‘complex’ rehabilitation programme in Germany as the turning point in his battle with injuries
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Jarrad Branthwaite has credited a ‘complex’ rehabilitation programme in Germany as the turning point in his battle with injuries
Content: The Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite says of his return this month to the England squad: ‘It is a proud moment.’Photograph: Lee Durkin/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite says of his return this month to the England squad: ‘It is a proud moment.’Photograph: Lee Durkin/Action Plus/ShutterstockEnglandBranthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England callDefender has battled hamstring and groin problemsEverton player credits Munich clinic for turning pointAndy HunterTue 22 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJarrad Branthwaite has credited a “complex” rehabilitation programme in Germany, which analysed links between his injuries and his brain and movement, with his return to theEnglandsquad.The Everton defender’s fine start to the season has been rewarded with a place inThomas Tuchel’s squadfor the Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia. If selected, it will be Branthwaite’s second appearance for the England senior side having been blighted by hamstring and groin problems in recent years.‘Embrace the chaos’: Tuchel aims to harness England’s football cultureRead moreThe centre-half has been ever-present in the Premier League after being restricted to 10 appearances last season by repeated hamstring issues. In the search for a solution to his injury problems,Evertonsent the 24-year-old to the MYOS sports and health clinic in Munich at the start of the summer. Branthwaite believes that was a turning point.“I sat down with the club after the three or four times where I was picking up the injuries,” he said. “It was to look at the wider picture, look at the holistic approach of the body essentially. I went over there for three or four weeks working with a team alongside the club, just to assess different things, and hopefully that has helped. There were a lot of different things looked at like movement patterns, the brain; it was quite complex, but fingers crossed it has worked.”Branthwaite was carried off in tears after sustaining another hamstring injury in the Merseyside derbydefeat by Liverpool in April. The setback ended his season and his prospects of making a late play for the World Cup squad, and Everton’s form also plummeted in his absence.“It is probably the worst thing as a footballer not to be on the pitch and I think when it keeps happening it is mentally tough because you are sort of doubting your body and going on the pitch wary of what is going to happen. I think now I am in a position where I got managed throughout the pre-season, managed my load well and hopefully I can stay on the pitch this season.”Branthwaite made his England debut as a substitute in a win againstBosnia and Herzegovina in June 2024, and a recall was a target this season alongside a return to full fitness.“I found out when I was having breakfast – it was a good start to the day,” the Everton defender said of his call-up last week. “It is a proud moment. Over the last season or so it has been a target of mine. When I have been out and not on the pitch, I wanted to get back playing and give myself the best possible chance to be in and around the England squad after missing such a lot of time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The season has started well individually and as a team. England’s got unbelievable talent and players all over the pitch. I believe I am good enough to be in the England squad so hopefully I can show that.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandNations LeagueEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups
Content: Gary Bennett, pictured in 2024, said he was was ‘surprised, shocked and disappointed’ by the council’s decision.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGary Bennett, pictured in 2024, said he was was ‘surprised, shocked and disappointed’ by the council’s decision.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianReform UKReform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red CardCharity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groupsJosh HallidayandRobyn VinterTue 22 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led byReform UKended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card.Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader ofSunderlandcity council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”.Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding.The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”.Bennett, who became only thesecond black player in Sunderland’s historywhen he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996.View image in fullscreenGary Bennett in Sunderland’s stripes in 1994.Photograph: PA/AlamyThe former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years.Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces.He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.”Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”.While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants.“You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight. There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.”Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”.He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”.Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum.Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities.The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”.The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest.In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.”He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.Explore more on these topicsReform UKSunderlandCharitiesLocal politicsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: England beat Sri Lanka by 89 runs: first men’s one-day cricket international – as it happened | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Will Jacks starred with bat and ball as England proved too strong for Sri Lanka on a tricky Durham pitch
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Will Jacks starred with bat and ball as England proved too strong for Sri Lanka on a tricky Durham pitch
