We’re creating news first and foremost for immigrant communities, and that looks very different than news created for non-immigrant communities.”Adapting to the momentEmmy-winning journalist Maritza Félix startedConecta Arizona’s WhatsApp group, La Hora del Cafecito (Coffee Time), during the pandemic to provide timely, accurate news for immigrant communities in Spanish. The online gathering space, which has thousands of members across platforms, has a weekly Q&A with expert guests, including immigration attorneys, education policy experts and labor rights specialists.But as ICE raids continue, members are engaging less in the public group chat and more in one-on-one direct messages with the staff.“They’re afraid of being a screenshot, or having their message forwarded to someone,” Félix said. “Listening to our community taught us that what works today might not work next week. We are listening to what they say and their silences at the same time.”Having a dialogue with the local Bay Area immigrant community has been crucial for El Tímpano, which is Spanish for “eardrum”. In addition to SMS messaging that reaches more than 7,000 Spanish-speaking immigrants, the outlet’s disinformation defense initiative,Comunidades Informadas, has trained more than 400 Latino immigrants in the Bay Area to recognize and address disinformation and misinformation.“By equipping immigrants with an understanding of how disinformation works, it can empower them, so that when they see a rumor of an ICE raid, their immediate response isn’t to panic,” Bair said. “Instead, they can check with a source they trust or call their local rapid response hotline. We’ve received really positive responses to these workshops and to the information that we provide to combat that fear.”In May, the Alameda county library partnered with El Tímpano for a disinformation defense initiative workshop in Spanish via Zoom for its staff members. Attenders found the content easy to understand, and it helped them articulate how to identify disinformation not just to community members, but also to their own family members.“After going through the workshop, I was like, ‘I can talk to this with mytiaand mytios, and explain it to them in the way that I didn’t really have the language before,’” said Jaqueline Martinez, the Alameda county library’s equity services coordinator.Building trust within immigrant communitiesFor many of these outlets, the work and impact started before the recent ICE surge. In 2019, Documented co-founders Mazin Sidahmed and Max Siegelbaum spoke with community organizations across New York that were concerned about workers’ wages being stolen. Joined later by reporter Lam Thuy Vo, they launched an investigation, seeking out New York state and federal wage data for four years. The result wasDocumented’s Wage Theft Monitor, which inspired NY state legislators tointroduce three bills to prevent and punish wage theft.“The dual impact of protecting immigrant workers, but also helping the general public understand how pervasive this issue is, has been one of the most rewarding parts of seeing this project come to light,” Sidahmed said.Similarly,LA Taco, which isn’t part of the INC, originally built trust among Los Angeles immigrant communities through its coverage of food, culture and cannabis. Then last June, as ICE raids swept through Los Angeles, LA Taco journalist Memo Torres began posting daily recaps of ICE activity on the publication’s Instagram account. By reporting verified information about raids during a time when misinformation ran rampant, Torres became one of LA’s most trusted journalists for immigrant communities, increasing LA Taco’s membership from 1,500 to 77,000 and earning attention from state and federal government officials.View image in fullscreenIzzy Ramirez and Aisha Wallace-Palomares at LA Taco’s offices on 28 May 2026.Photograph: Mallory Carra“I was getting information from people, I started reaching out to rapid responders and building trust with them, and then got included in the network with them,” he said, recalling how he started the Daily Memo.Over the summer, the Daily Memo wound down, while LA Taco’s political cartoons byPulitzer prize finalist Ivan Ehlers, called Sunday Taquitos, took off. In July,his humorous yet poignant illustration about Flock camera surveillancereceived more than 7m Instagram views and inspired fan-created versions in five different languages. The Ecuadorian American artist said the political cartoons are his short-form way of fighting misinformation and disinformation.“If I can get someone’s attention for five seconds, I can get people to look at important issues and say, ‘Hey, I didn’t know that was happening. Oh man, this is terrible,’” he said. “People will go in and do more research, read more about it, talk to their friends or share it, and that’ll start conversations.”Ehlers has also served as creative director for one of LA Taco’s zines, showcasing the outlet’s reporting on local protests and immigrant communities. Its release in early September was just one of many in-person events LA Taco has held this year to engage with its readers.“The bigger issue is building a community and building support systems and showing people that they’re not alone,” Ehlers said. “We have a lot of people who are willing to fight together, work together and build something together.”Explore more on these topicsNewspapers & magazinesBuilding powerUS immigrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)WhatsAppSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market? | Health | The Guardian
description: People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisis
Content: All hail the Big Toothbrush! Animation: Pig Meat/The GuardianHealthThe rise of Big Toothbrush: how did our mouths become such a lucrative market?People in the UK are more interested in oral health than ever - and you can now buy prebiotic toothpastes and brushes that cost up to £600. Yet we remain in the midst of a serious dental crisisEmine SanerTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleADecember 1969 report from the consumer magazine Which? explored a relatively new gadget that, it predicted, many people would be giving as Christmas presents: the electric toothbrush. For those who hadn’t yet seen one, the magazine described it as “not that much different in principle from an ordinary brush – you have a stick with a brush on the end. The difference is that an electric one moves the brush head for you”. Progress indeed.Nearly six decades on, electric toothbrushes can do a lot more than merely jiggle, offering multiple speeds and movement sensors forreal-time trackingof where you’ve brushed – some even promise gum-massage or tongue-cleaning modes. Prices range from about £25 for a basic Oral B model to £599.99 for aPhilips Sonicare modelthat gives “smart coverage feedback”.The latest super-toothbrush – a mere £419.99 – features a camera and a built-in water jet to clean between teeth, using AI to identify gaps. Created by Dyson, it’s still, essentially, a stick with a brush on the end (although there is anothertoothbrushon the market that’s shaped like a mouthguard, with individual brushes, that claims to clean your teeth in 20 seconds).View image in fullscreenThe Dyson CameraJet toothbrush.Photograph: DysonIn the UK,59% of adultsuse an electric toothbrush and sales, including replacement heads, reached £361m in the last year, according to market intelligence company Mintel. Any product launch by Dyson – still associated with reinventing the vacuum cleaner – feels like something of an event, so its incursion into oral health does feel significant, says Rachel Bairsto, the head of museum services at the British Dental Association. “We’re seeing more and more expensive toothbrushes,” she says. “Expensive toothpaste as well.”These highly designed everyday objects have become symbols of affluence. “If you see a picture of a swanky bathroom, it will definitely have plug sockets for some kind of rechargeable electric toothbrush,” says Bairsto. “Whereas I’ve tried to look through the archives to find pictures of bathrooms with toothbrushes in them, and I can’t. Was everybody appalled at the sight of a toothbrush in the bathroom? I don’t know.” With many toothbrushes now, she says, “I think there’s definitely a status symbol [aspect] to it.”‘The mouth is a gateway into your body’: the fascinating, frightening links between our gums and our healthRead moreWe’re more interested in oral health than ever, says Dr Zaeem Jafri, a dentist and the founder of Nova Smiles, an online advice website. “From what I’ve seen from my patients, people are more conscious about it, wanting to avoid dental treatment, wanting their teeth to look nice and feel nice, and I think a lot of people are turning to gadgets to help.” Another dentist, Dr Reena Wadia, known as Dr Reena, a periodontist or gum specialist at the RW Perio clinic in London, says: “Gum health has become super topical. One reason why is because there’s really good evidence now that gum health islinked to your general health, so gum health is now part of the wellness conversation. People are taking it more seriously.” There is growing evidence that gum disease, she says, comes with an “increased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Those are the two key ones, [but] there’s lots of other conditions related to it.” A poor oral microbiomehas been associatedwith a range of diseases, including Alzheimer’s and several types of cancer, as well as depression.Both Dr Reena and Jafri recommend rechargeable electric toothbrushes over manual ones, but neither are urging their patients to go out and buy a Dyson brush, or spend similar sums on other brands. “There’s no robust research that says a certain kind of electric brush removes plaque at a better rate than others,” says Jafri.Jafri has tested Dyson’s CameraJet, along with many other electric toothbrushes. He found it messy – the water jet was hard to angle, and he says it didn’t seem to find all the gaps between his teeth. He points out that a non-foaming toothpaste is needed for an adequate camera view – sold by Dyson, with the cheapest at £8.49. The live stream to a phone app was a novelty, but in reality he says it was hard to see much with water, teeth and the inside of his cheeks in the way. Cameras in toothbrushes, says Jafri, “have the potential to be good. If patients had cameras that were detecting chipped and broken fillings and can send those images to a dentist to review [and] spot things early, that would be a phenomenal advancement. For Dyson right now, it’s using the camera to detect when the brush is in the right position to shoot the water jet – it didn’t really work that well for me. It’s a bit of an overkill.”View image in fullscreenGood brushing habits start early.Photograph: Oleg Breslavtsev/Getty ImagesAnother concern is that the water jet rinses away the toothpaste when most dentists now recommend spitting, not rinsing, so the fluoride in it stays on and around the teeth for longer. Dr Reena adds: “[The water jet may] make people think, oh, I don’t need to floss, or I don’t need to use interdental brushes. But actually, that jet is an adjunct, not a replacement.” Niamh Turney, a Dyson engineer who worked on the CameraJet, says, however, “The goal is to make interdental cleaning easier and more convenient for those who aren’t already managing to fit flossing into their routine.”There have beenreportsof some brushes overheating, and charging problems; at the time of writing, the brush was unavailable to buy. Dyson says it is aware that “a small number of early batches may have experienced a component issue. We are isolating those batches and are taking all the necessary steps to support our customers,” and that there are “some shortages of supply as we are in the process of scaling up production. We expect the next wave to be available in the coming weeks.”Meanwhile, we are in the midst of anoral health crisis. It is slowly improving on previous years, but access to NHS dentists remains low – 60% of the adult population in England have not seen an NHS dentist in the two years to March 2026. Inequality has a huge effect on oral health – in the most deprived areas, adults are less likely to brush their teeth twice a day, and children aremore than three timesmore likely to have tooth extractions related to decay. The proportion of adults who use an electric toothbrush is 47% in the lowest income groups, compared with 76% in the highest income. Jafri says that the people who are considering spending hundreds of pounds on an electric toothbrush, or those who track their brushing on apps, are likely to be “health-conscious individuals who are brushing their teeth well to begin with, and [this is] probably not solving the bigger problem we have”.View image in fullscreen‘Wonderful things happen!’ A 1962 advert for GE’s electric toothbrush.Photograph: Patti McConville/AlamyThe first electric toothbrushes, says Bairsto, had a “clunky side-to-side action, and that’s about all they could do.” There was an increased interest in dental and oral health in the 1960s – programmes to add fluoride to drinking water were rolled out – and electric toothbrushes were part of this, even if they were slow to take off. That 1969 Which? report tested “all 11 we could find on the market”, including those made by Bosch andBoots, alongside several by US manufacturer Ronson, more famous at the time for its cigarette lighters. Women, it claimed, preferred brushes with a softer touch; men liked something more vigorous “as you might expect”. Children liked them, the report said, “perhaps because they are a good way of doing action paintings with toothpaste on the bathroom mirror”.Now the market is dominated by Oral B, owned by Procter & Gamble. Jafri says dentists don’t earn commission from selling products but, he adds, “in dental school, they come in with free pizzas and give everyone an Oral B brush. All the dental students kind of associate with Oral B quite quickly. There will be the ‘Oral B lecture’ that everybody talks about because it’s free pizza.”It has a market share of approximately 60% according to Ziyu Tian, a personal care research analyst at Mintel. “Other brands like Philips, [own labels such as] Superdrug and Boots, and Colgate are also the big players,” she says. The Dyson launch, says Tian, while a premium product that won’t appeal to everyone, will raise the bar for consumer expectations and may force existing players in the sector to innovate. Alongside the increased awareness around oral health’s links to general health, she says, “teeth whitening and the beauty element of oral care is something that the younger generation is really embracing. So oral care is not only about cleaning the teeth or freshening the breath, it’s more about the beauty and wellness routines in general.”As more evidence emerges, particularly links to the gut microbiome, companies will lean on this in their marketing, says Tian. You can already see it in products such as toothpaste that contains “prebiotics and probiotics for our microbiome, magnesium for evening wind-down, and exosomes [“messengers” between cells, already used in skincare] for tissue regeneration, anti-ageing and longevity”. Toothpaste flavours are branching out, too, from the traditional mint, with berries, chocolate and even fried chicken. “I think it is tied to the rise of the GLP-1 [weight loss injections],” says Tian. “Consumers might not get these indulgent flavours from food and drink, and oral care like toothpaste and other things can be a substitute.”View image in fullscreen‘Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush.’Photograph: GoodLifeStudio/Getty ImagesOne of the more recent incomers to the toothbrush market is Suri (from £65), launched in 2022, which makes nicely designed, recyclable, largely plastic-free electric toothbrushes. Its founders, Mark Rushmore and Gyve Safavi, both previously worked in marketing for Procter & Gamble. They were driven, says Rushmore, by the environmental impact of toothbrushes. “Billions of brushes are thrown away – manual, electric – and end up in landfills and oceans. Every brush you’ve probably ever used since you were a child still exists somewhere.”Damien Walmsley, an emeritus professor of dentistry at the University of Birmingham, has worked with all the big powered toothbrush companies, and most recently with Suri. He says he is probably still under non-disclosure agreements so won’t go into detail; “but I’ve seen some wacky ideas out there, some strange ones”. Companies are constantly trying to add new features, “so that people feel they’re getting a newer product, and people will then be attracted to it. If it’s something new, it will catch the imagination, and that’s what this new Dyson has done.” If it encourages people to brush their teeth more effectively, and more often, “that’s really good”. But Walmsley questions how long the novelty lasts. “We’d like to see more long-term studies evaluating the cost. Was it worth paying the extra money, and did it bring about extra value from that? Those studies aren’t out there.”Walmsley was one of a number of scientists involved in the 2003 review of literature by the Cochrane library, with the latest update in 2014, concluding that powered toothbrushes were more effective in removing plaque than manual brushes – by 11% in the short term, and 21% after three months – and at reducing gingivitis (early-stage gum disease). Many of the studies were small, short-lived – and run by Oral B. Should consumers be concerned about that? Research studies are expensive, says Walmsley, and over the years Oral B was among the few companies doing them. “We have certain criteria, and we checked that [studies] followed that, and we followed up the evidence,” says Walmsley. “It was as open as it can be.” He also points out that toothbrushing technique and usage in a controlled trial may be different compared to use by a wider population in everyday life.“Dental professionals should be showing their patients how to brush,” says Dr Reena. “It sounds basic, but actually, [many people have] never been shown. Essentially brushing along the gum line [at around a 45-degree angle] to remove bacteria that are trapped. The bristles should be going under your gum line a little bit.” But not too hard, which can lead to gum recession. A pressure sensor is a valuable feature. “Different modes [in speed for instance] are quite helpful as well, if someone’s got sensitivity or gum issues.” She is interested in the idea of a camera in a toothbrush, especially if it can provide “real-time feedback on what a patient is doing. But the key thing it always comes back to is that technique and consistency are more important.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsHealthDentistsHealth & wellbeingDyson LtdBootsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Six-year-old breaks women's world Rubik's Cube record – video | Games competitions | The Guardian
description: Six-year-old Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice at two World Cube Association-certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday. She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving the Rubik’s Cube five times. She is the first female speedcuber to average less than 4.5 seconds.

title: Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’ | Puzzle games | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Lian Yunzhi solves 3x3 puzzle on several occasions in average time of under 4.5 seconds, according to state media

GoogleA six-year-oldChinesegirl has set a new women’s world record for solving a Rubik’s Cube in just over four seconds, state media reported.“Speedcuber” Lian Yunzhi broke the women’s 3x3 average world record twice this month at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds, after solving theRubik’s Cubefive times.The girl, who is from Chengdu, is “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”, CCTV said.A video posted by the broadcaster showed her wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik’s Cube.After solving the puzzle she was seen placing the cube on the table, clapping her hands and pumping a fist in the air.Nicknamed “Zhizhi”, the six-year-old was introduced to the Rubik’s Cube after being enrolled in a class – alongside various other extracurricular activities such as dance and music lessons, her Chengdu’s Red Star News.Her daughter has now mastered more than 1,300 Rubik’s Cube solving algorithms, practising daily for two to three hours, Lin said.Photos from Red Star News showed the girl’s trophies displayed on a shelf in her home.“Solving a Rubik’s Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing,” Lin said.“It’s not just about blindly memorising formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions,” she added.Explore more on these topicsPuzzle gamesChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this title: Control Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomena | Games | The Guardian
description: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Content: New York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentView image in fullscreenNew York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentGamesReviewControl Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomenaPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; RemedyA surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safePhil IwaniukTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House. You’d navigate architecturally impossible spaces bridging the subconscious and the bricks-and-mortar world, in order to defeat a malevolent fridge. That’s broadly true again in Resonant, albeit with diminishing returns. This time you’re playing as Jesse’s brother Dylan, waking up after years of containment in the Oldest House to find its contents have escaped into downtown Manhattan. So you head out of the interesting place, and into a setting you’ve explored before inMarvel’s Spider-Man,The Division,Max Payne, and others ad infinitum.It’s disappointing because being bewitchingly strange has historically been Remedy’s great strength. It’s not unusual for games to give a reverent nod to Twin Peaks now and then, but this studio is the alpha and omega of interactive Lynchian nightmares. It’s been refining that skill since 2001’s Max Payne, and at this point there’s really nobody better at nonlinear storytelling or unnerving dream sequences.View image in fullscreenInception-like gravitational spins … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentRemedy’s take on New York has an exhilaratingly free-form structure that lets you take on enemies, missions and places in roughly the order you want. The main missions are fairly rigid, but you can engage with the rest however and whenever you want. You fight a malevolent paranormal force with an imaginative collection of supernatural kung fu moves, whose power and combo potential level up satisfyingly. Your shapeshifting weapon can take many forms, from a dagger-like blade to a scythe or a hammer. Secondary attacks, ranged weapons and passive abilities lend more interest to fights against paranormal entity the Hiss as time goes on, but compared to something like the surgically precise swordplay of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, battles feel a bit blunt here.Your ultimate tests come in the form of the Resonants themselves, a series of bosses lying in wait throughout Manhattan. Remedy’s knack for otherworldly horror comes to the fore in their visual design, which I won’t spoil, and like so much of the game they can be hunted down in any order. Beware, though – beating them changes other enemies’ presence, strength and behaviour afterwards.Dylan’s movement is more imaginative and enjoyable than his arsenal. Here, trading off a fascinating indoor setting for more outdoor space starts to make sense, as you triple-jump your way across rooftops and shift your gravitational grounding to walk on streets that have been bent upwards vertically à laInception. It’s playful about it, too – soon after gaining that latter ability, your bureau handler pumps some EDM down the radio to soundtrack your run through a multistorey car park whose levels fold and distort at impossible angles.It is the little moments like this, not the grand story beats, that prove the most memorable and gratifying. Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.Control Resonant is out now; £49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamesAction gamesGame playPlayStation 5XboxreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech | Ted Widmer | The Guardian
description: Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead
Author: Ted Widmer
Headline: Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead
Content: ‘The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations.’Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations.’Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionUS newsTrump invades the UN with a brutish speechTed WidmerGone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years aheadTue 22 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 21.45 EDTShareExpectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has madeno secretof his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the USdecided to withdrawfrom in July 2025).His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peacein January(just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the presidentwonderedif his new creation might simply replace.Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon.Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for himRead moreBut even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s.In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader.A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect.In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it.Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree to work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks).Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly beingdepleted.There was a lengthy assault on climate crisis, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied arecordfor the hottest month ever recorded, and several importantsciencereports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, thetemperatureon the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when hebraggedthat the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his2025 speechto the UN.Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick.On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US andChinamight cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized.Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speechRead moreOther topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship withCanada, once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now. It will take years to repair the damage to a vital strategic relationship to the North.Instead, more attention was paid toGreenland. The president claimed the US would now be enjoying basing rights – which we already enjoy – and he also suggested that foreign adversaries would not be allowed on their bases. That is hardly news – they have never been allowed bases on Greenland.While discussing his own vision of sovereignty, including his claims to Venezuelan oil, Trump drew from a sordid page of US history, and quoted a corrupt New York politician, William M “Boss” Tweed, to say “to the victor belong the spoils”. Tweed, the leader of Tammany Hall, was later convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars from the public, and died in jail.Perhaps the saddest aspect of this speech was its utter lack of American idealism – the very force that led to the UN’s creation. In the 250th year of the United States, there were plenty of themes that might have won over a skeptical audience, but there were no inspiring words about fighting poverty, or reducing nuclear tests or keeping weapons out of space (asJohn F Kennedypromised in 1963).Or human rights (introduced as a major theme by JimmyCarterin 1977), or about reducing tensions with Russia (which RonaldReaganspoke about in 1988), or the end of the cold war (which George HWBushcelebrated in 1990), or the need to fight terrorism while avoiding Islamophobia (as BillClintonexplained carefully in 1998).It was just raw power; and a power that is likely to diminish in the years ahead. The power of persuasion has always been critical to presidents coming into the United Nations. But the United States is now at historically low levels of approval around the world, as measured by the Pew GlobalAttitudesproject, with only 23% of people (across 36 nations) expressing confidence in Trump’s leadership. The number is unlikely to go up after today’s performance.Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, is the editor of American Speeches, and the recently published The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text, both published by the Library of AmericaExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicsUnited NationsDonald TrumpUS foreign policyClimate crisisChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
Author: John Crace
Headline: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
Content: Andy Burnham joked about Donald Trump calling Manchester ‘some town’ in their first meeting, while Trump called Burnham a ‘great businessperson’.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham joked about Donald Trump calling Manchester ‘some town’ in their first meeting, while Trump called Burnham a ‘great businessperson’.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamCall it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King BabyJohn CraceMeeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President TrumpUS politics live – latest updatesTue 22 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 18.25 EDTShareHow do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby.Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guessDonald Trumpis a fool’s errand.So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover.The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at theUnited Nationsgeneral assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident.All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed?And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”?View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham met Donald Trump while in the US to attend the United Nations general assembly.Photograph: Toby Melville/PATaking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water.It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that.Burnham then bigged up thedeal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual.Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old.Then a question on thesanctions imposed on illegal settlementsin the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal.There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting?Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchDonald TrumpUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Logan and Jake Paul.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicView image in fullscreenLogan and Jake Paul.Photograph: Taylor Hill/FilmMagicOpinionUS politicsThe Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencersArwa MahdawiJake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policyTue 22 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTShareWe’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in amatter of weeks. Prices are rising, troopmorale is plummeting, and there is little evidence things will improve.The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recentlythreatenedto “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doingidiotic stuntson YouTube and gettinghit in the faceduring boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department ofWar Crimes?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech.In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzingerwrote, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.” That about sums it up.The Paul brothers, to be fair, rose to the occasion as best they could. In a speech which channelled Churchill, if Churchill had suffered several major blows to the head, Logansaidthat touring the Pentagon had been “a cool experience”. Albeit not quite as cool as being deployed to fight and possiblydiein an illegal bombing campaign started by president Trump, a convicted felon, on the advice of Benjamin Netanyahu, an accused war criminal. “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country,” Logan said. Which is why you won’t see him doing it; easier to pocket millionsfighting on TV.As well as giving a pep talk to the military, Jake met up withtreasury secretaryScott Bessent and the US treasurer todiscusshow “to get more young Americans financially empowered.” That must have been an interesting chat considering how, back in 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the YouTuber with unlawfully promoting crypto assets without disclosing that he was being paid to do so; he eventuallysettledwithout admitting or denying the charges. (Logan has also faced a lawsuit linked to a dodgycrypto venture, although the case was eventually dismissed). Exactly the sort of person you want the treasury secretary expending energy talking to when US debt recentlytopped $40tnfor the first time ever and a financial crisis seems to bearound the corner.Just how Jake Paul and Bessent hope to financially empower young Americans is unclear. But it is unlikely to be via the traditional method of working hard at school and then going to university. Jake very much shares the Trump administration’s contempt for education. In 2020 hetweetedthat he’s “sick of our education system and how it’s teaching kids 0 real life skills for them to secure there [sic.] own future.” He also oncedescribedhigh school as “kids sitting in Geography to learn where Timbuktu is for no reason.” The reason you learn where Timbuktu is, Jake, is so the US can overthrow it after they’re done with Iran and Greenland.There has always been a strong vein of anti-intellectualism in US politics. “[T]he subordination of men of ideas to men of emotional power or manipulative skill are hardly innovations of the twentieth century,” Richard Hofstadter wrote in his 1963 book Anti-intellectualism in American Life. “[T]hey are inheritances from American Protestantism.” But while this may not be a new impulse, the Trump administration’s embrace of ignorance is doing damage that can’t be easily undone. The US is stuck in a vicious vacuousness cycle: the Trump administration has slashed research funding and disruptedthousandsof grants, leading many promising young academics toflee the US. As expertise is eliminated and critical thinkingpurgedfrom government institutes, chancers like the Paul brothers are elevated.Still, I suppose we should count our blessings, before even they are affected byIran-induced inflation. At least the boneheaded Paul brothers are simply having meetings with high-level Trump administration officials. At least they’re not directly involved with military or economic policy. Although, the way things are going it’s only a matter of time. “I’m going to make a prediction that you will be, in the not-too-distant future, running for political office,” Trump told Jake, who has been a vocal Maga supporter, on stage at arally earlier this year. “You have my complete and total endorsement.” Could another blond buffoon with zero qualifications become president of the US? Tune in to find out in the next season of America: the Empire ImplodesArwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Never mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American people | Leslie Vinjamuri | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear, says Leslie Vinjamuri, CEO of Chicago Council on Global Affairs
Author: Leslie Vinjamuri
Headline: Mark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing ear, says Leslie Vinjamuri, CEO of Chicago Council on Global Affairs
Content: Nato leaders including Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni and French president Emmanuel Macron meet Donald Trump at The Hague, June 2025.Photograph: Haiyun Jiang/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNato leaders including Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni and French president Emmanuel Macron meet Donald Trump at The Hague, June 2025.Photograph: Haiyun Jiang/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionNatoNever mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American peopleLeslie VinjamuriMark Rutte has the right idea – go beyond Washington and make the case for the transatlantic alliance to the public. They may well have a willing earTue 22 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareAt a moment when Europe is focused on persuading Donald Trump to remain committed to Nato, it needs to convince Americans, too. So the presence this evening of the Nato secretary general,Mark Rutte, in front of a public audience in Des Moines, Iowa, is significant. This is the home town of Trump’s ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker, and the visit brings the debate over Nato’s future directly to a midwestern audience in a red state that operates far from elite foreign-policy circles in Washington. Rutte’s appearance is long overdue.Russia’s war in Ukraine and uncertainty over the US commitment to European security have forced European leaders toconfront their dependence on Washington. While some are pressing for building European capabilities as a means to separate from the US, others see greater European defence spending as essential to keeping the US engaged. Either way, European governments can’t rely solely on meetings with Trump to secure the alliance’s future.Instead, Europe’s leaders need to look beyond Washington and take a tip from Rutte. Making the public case for Nato, the transatlantic partnership, and shared security across the middle of the country, is essential, not optional. This case should begin with the American people.For decades, Americans have supported the transatlantic relationship because they understood that Europe’s security is closely connected to their own.Natoand the transatlantic partnership were part of a wider ambition, designed to make the world safe for democracy, not least for the growth and prosperity this created. Public support has been essential to this undertaking.For many Americans, democracy is now failing to deliver on the promise of prosperity, and in some key areas the contrast with Europe is stark. In the Commonwealth Fund’s2023 survey, 46% of US adults with lower or average incomes reported skipping or delaying needed healthcare because of cost, compared with 16% in each of the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. Populists have been quick to highlight the shortcomings of America’s democracy, and this message has resonated across swaths of the population, particularly rural voters and Americans without a university degree – both central to Trump’s electoral coalition.When it comes to the American public, there is plenty of room for optimism, but in a political context that is ripe for populists to cultivate antagonism toward spending on foreign causes, there is little room for complacency. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ polling consistently shows that Americans support Nato and the transatlantic partnership.Its recent survey with Ipsosfound that 68% of Americans supported maintaining or increasing the US commitment to Nato. Yet only 47% were confident that European allies would come to America’s defence if it were attacked, down from 62% in 2025. Public support for Ukraine has also remained substantial, even as Americans debate the scale and duration of US assistance; a2024 surveyfound that 58% supported sending additional arms and military supplies to Ukraine, and the same number supported economic assistance.European leaders would be wise to invest in a public diplomacy strategy in order to cultivate understanding among Americans outside Washington’s foreign-policy establishment. The secretary general’s decision to travel to Iowa should be seen as a crucial part of Europe’s midwest strategy. Other leading foreign policy organisations have sought to do the same. Over the summer, the Ditchley Foundation used the occasion ofAmerica’s 250thto deepen its partnerships across the US, convening roundtables in South Carolina and Illinois.This outreach is essential to counter the persistent myth that Europeans are free-riding on America’s coattails. Europe’s renewed commitment to defence is significant, with a 20% increase in 2025 compared with 2024 among the EU’s 27 member states. This remains poorly understood in the US. Nato’sAnnual 2025 reportnotes that all of Nato’s 32 members met or exceeded the 2% of GDP expenditure target for that year. Allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP annuallyby 2035in defence and related security. The precise figures matter, but so does the broader message: that Europe is investing in the capacity to defend itself and contribute to shared security.It would also be smart to highlight the opportunities created by this investment for American companies. Defence cooperation supports jobs and growth opportunities. It also boosts transatlantic supply chains and research partnerships. But the ties that bind Europe and America reach deeper than military procurement. The case for the alliance should ultimately be made in terms that people recognise in their own lives: the security of their jobs, the price and availability of energy, the resilience of the technology they rely on and, above all, the prospect of their families living without the threat of a wider war.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe transatlantic partnership cannot be secured through presidential diplomacy alone. European leaders should continue engaging the White House, but they must also make their case to the American public. The long-term future of Nato will depend not only on what presidents decide, but on whether citizens on both sides of the Atlantic continue to see the alliance as essential to their security, democracy and prosperity.Leslie Vinjamuri is president and CEO of Chicago Council on Global AffairsExplore more on these topicsNatoOpinionUS politicsEuropeMark RuttecommentShareReuse this content

title: AI is generating a new wave of economic populism. It could be a tipping point | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: It’s becoming obvious to many Americans that corporations have been raking it in while workers take it on the chin
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: It’s becoming obvious to many Americans that corporations have been raking it in while workers take it on the chin
Content: ‘AI is on the way to causing far more inequality – generating billions for its backers while reducing the number of jobs and real wages.’Photograph: David A Lieb/APView image in fullscreen‘AI is on the way to causing far more inequality – generating billions for its backers while reducing the number of jobs and real wages.’Photograph: David A Lieb/APOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI is generating a new wave of economic populism. It could be a tipping pointRobert ReichIt’s becoming obvious to many Americans that corporations have been raking it in while workers take it on the chinTue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTShareLast week, the unlikely duo of Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon spoke before a Washington group demanding a stop to AI and its datacenters.Notably, both lambasted the corporate oligarchs behind AI.The most potent force inUS politicsis anti-establishment fury at a system seen as rigged against average working people. AI has become exhibit A.Until recently, both parties largely avoided criticizing the wealthy corporate elites that funded their campaigns. In politics as in nature, one does not bite the hands that feed.Trump Republicans have instead aimed populist fury at immigrants, LGBTQ+ people, Black and Latino people, “communists”, Muslims, so-called “woke” leaders, “coastal elites”, “childless cat ladies” and other scapegoats.Can Trump and Xi cooperate to guide humanity through the AI revolution? Humanity might depend on it | Alan FinkelRead moreDemocrats – with the exceptions of Sanders, AOC and a few others – have also avoided criticizing wealthy corporate elites, aiming their populist fury at Trump.This may be changing.It’s becoming obvious to much of the US that giant corporations have been raking it in while workers have been taking it on the chin.As of mid-2026, according to theBureau of Labor Statistics, the percentage of the total economy going to workers as wages had fallen to a record low of 52.9% (down from above 65% when tracking began in 1947) – leaving the rest to investors, business owners, and corporate profits.AI is on the way to causing far more inequality – generating billions for its backers while reducing the number of jobs and real wages.Trump and his regime, meanwhile, have exposed the greed, venality, cupidity and corruption of the US’s wealthy corporate elites by allowing them to do anything they wish – including create energy-guzzling, water-depleting AI datacenters – as long as they kiss his assets by funding his Pac, paying for his ballroom and singing his praises.Trump has thereby revealed the truth about corporate America that for years had been hidden behind corporate PR about “corporate social responsibility”, corporate charity and “trickle-down” economics: the captains of corporate America are willing to throw average working Americans under the bus to make billions more.Corporate avarice under Trump has become so blatant and corporate America’s contempt for the needs of average Americans so flagrant that most Americans are now catching on. In a recent NBCpoll, 54% of Americans agreed that “when it comes to politics and society, nothing really matters because powerful people will always do whatever they want.”AI may well be the final tipping point.Labor unions must unite against AI datacenters | Tyler TurnerRead moreData centers are unpopular – about70%of the public opposes them. And Americans harbor deep suspicions of AI. More than60%believe AI could destroy humanity (this includes60%of Trump supporters).Fears about AI are provoking larger concerns about wealthy corporate elites bribing politicians – not just to get generous subsidies for AI but also to reduce the corporate elite’s tax bills, kill off unions, slash social safety nets, deregulate Wall Street, attain no-bid government contracts, receive exclusive licenses, open tax loopholes, get tariff exemptions, use public lands, and become even bigger monopolies.Because of Trump, Americans are coming to view those wealthy corporate elites as more aligned with Republicans than with Democrats. According to last week’sTimes-Sienna poll, when likely voters were asked which party the word “elitist” describes, a remarkable 43%said Republicans while 33% said Democrats.This is something of a return to how the US’s two major political parties used to be seen. Ninety years ago, Democrats were assumed to be on the side of working people against wealthy corporate elites.On the eve of his 1936 re-election, Franklin D Roosevelt told the American people they were fighting “business and financial monopoly, speculation, reckless banking, class antagonism, war profiteering … We now know that government by organized money is just as dangerous as government organized by the mob.”Will Democrats seize the moment and embrace the new AI-fueled economic populism? Or will they continue to succumb to the siren songs of big money?According toPolitico, some Democratic political consultants are quietly urging candidates in the toughest battleground races to stay mum on AI “over fears that powerful and well-resourced pro-AI interest groups could spend money pummeling them in the final weeks of the midterms”.It’s not just the future of the Democratic party that’s at stake; it’s the future of America.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different story  | Hossein Hamdieh | The Guardian
description: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point, says Hossein Hamdieh, a social researcher based in Tehran
Author: Hossein Hamdieh
Headline: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point, says Hossein Hamdieh, a social researcher based in Tehran
Content: ‘If the intention is to encourage Iranians to turn against their own state, the war may be doing the opposite.’Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreen‘If the intention is to encourage Iranians to turn against their own state, the war may be doing the opposite.’Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAOpinionIranTrump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different storyHossein HamdiehIf anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this pointTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 17.39 EDTShareThe US president, Donald Trump, asked recently on one ofhis Truth Social rants: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” So frenetic and all-over-the-place are Trump’s statements that one does not know which are actual policies and which are simply noise. But if counting on the “Iranian people” to rise up and fight is indeed US policy then, as far as I can tell from within Iran, it is a failed one. And miserably so. At least for now.There is no reliable nationwide polling that can tell us what Iranians think about the war in real time. So this is an observation, not a poll. It comes from conversations I have had with many people.Though a social researcher, I work closely with Iranian startups and the digital ecosystem. Before the war began, my understanding was that this environment was hardly a hotbed of support for the Iranian state. Quite the opposite: being an advocate of the state was generally frowned upon, not least because ofthe internet blackoutsthat had repeatedly disrupted the very infrastructure upon which the digital economy depends.And yet, even in this milieu, one can feel a growing detestation of the US and its war in Iran.I am talking about some of the loudest voices. Businesspeople with money to spend, large profiles on social media and enough influence to shape conversations. These are the people many young Iranians look up to, and they are becoming increasingly outspoken against the war.Majid Hosseini Nejad, an entrepreneur and the founder of Alibaba, an Iranian online travel agency,wrote on X on 2 September: “God willing, the day isn’t far off when attacking Iran becomes a terrifying nightmare for them, and they won’t even have the guts for such wishful thinking.” His social media feed is littered with similar anti-US and anti-Israel sentiments.Many people within these circles share this sentiment. This does not necessarily translate into support for the state, of course. But one can witness the birth of a strong dislike for the US, alongside a growing desire to build Iran back better. There is a wider sense that this war is clarifying something.That feeling is being nurtured by the images and stories coming out of the war: the shattering tragedy of theschool in Minab, thesports complex in Lamerd, demolished homes in Tehran and, most recently,a weddingin a small southern village where people were killed and maimed.View image in fullscreenA man taking a photograph of memorials at the shattered Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, hit by a US airstrike in February.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APFor the most part, these incidents do not inspire people to pour on to the streets in support of the invaders. If anything, they demonstrate how those waging a war from afar can come to see their prey as a faceless, nameless, storyless pile of human bodies. Their deaths are counted as the necessary and negligible cost of one man’s war against Iran.Tales and images of fellow ordinary citizens slaughtered have a tendency to unify a divided country against foreign invasion. Such incidents rightly bring back memories of Iraq, Libya and Afghanistan. If they are intended to encourage people to “rise up and fight”, they appear to be producing quite the reverse effect.In meetings, talks and public events, an image that was once assumed widespread – that Iran is a nation kidnapped by our political establishment – is beginning to erode. In its place is another idea: that we are a nation at war with a hostile regional foe and its imperial backer.More and more people appear to be drawn towards this conclusion. Even if they do not support the state, they cheer it on if it is standing up to the bully.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis is the important distinction that Washington seems to be so naively missing. A person can dislike the Islamic Republic and still dislike an American war against Iran. One can oppose the state and yet not want to see one’s country bombed into submission. One can demand political change and still believe that such change should come from within.Nationalist and anti-imperialist sentiments are on the rise. If I had been asked in February, I would have said that the chasm between the state and the nation was perhaps unbridgeable. Now I would say it has a chance.A homegrown uprising is what the US appears to be counting on. But if the intention is to encourage Iranians to turn against their own state, the war may be doing the opposite.The more Iranian civilians are killed, the harder it becomes to maintain the distinction between the Iranian people and the Iranian state. And the more that distinction disappears, the less likely people are to rise up on behalf of the foreign power attacking them.From where I stand, people do not look likely to rise up. They may instead be closing ranks.Hossein Hamdieh holds a joint PhD in Geography and Anthropology from Humboldt University of Berlin and King’s College London. He is currently based in Tehran, where he works as a social researcherExplore more on these topicsIranOpinionUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaUS foreign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must change | Kathryn Sikkink | The Guardian
description: The rights of overseas voters are protected by US federal law. It’s not hard – but Americans should start planning now
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The rights of overseas voters are protected by US federal law. It’s not hard – but Americans should start planning now
Content: ‘The UK hosts the second largest population of voting-age US citizens outside the United States.’Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/APView image in fullscreen‘The UK hosts the second largest population of voting-age US citizens outside the United States.’Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/APOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Many Americans live in the UK – but few vote back home. This year, that must changeKathryn SikkinkThe rights of overseas voters are protected by US federal law. It’s not hard – but Americans should start planning nowTue 22 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTShareThe UK hosts the second largest population of voting-age US citizens outside the United States, but Americans living in the UK vote at very low levels in US elections.The US government’s Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP)estimatedthat there were 298,268 voting-age US citizens in the UK in 2022, second only to Canada. But FVAP also estimated that only 3.8% of these US citizens in Britain voted in that year’s midterm elections. Why do hundreds of thousands of eligible US voters in the UK not exercise their right to vote, even though US rules for voting abroad are relatively welcoming compared to many other countries?The UK has recently conducted its own experiment in overseas enfranchisement. In January 2024, Britainabolishedthe 15-year limit on overseas voting, potentially enfranchising about 2.3 million additional British and eligible Irish citizens living abroad. The UK expanded overseas voting rights deliberately embracing “votes for life”, a policy long practiced in the US to allow all overseas voter-age Americans to vote, regardless of how long they have lived out of the country.The US supreme court issued a fragile win for voting rights – the real test comes later | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreThe UK government expanded overseas voting rights, while the Trump administration has sought to restrict mail-in voting, including for overseas Americans. But last week, the US supreme courtrejectedthe Trump administration’s efforts to limit mail-in voting before the midterm elections.US citizens in the UK can take this opportunity to vote when they can still make their voices heard.For Americans living abroad, voting in federal elections is easier than many think. The rights of overseas voters are protected by US federal law under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act. This law requires states to allow eligible overseas citizens to register and vote absentee and to transmit ballots in a timely manner. Voters abroad can use the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), which combines voter registration and a request for an absentee ballot. The process is manageable, but it can take time, so overseas voters should start now.TheUS Vote Foundationand theOverseas Votewebsites provide clear, non-partisan guidance on how to register and vote from abroad. Try the US Vote Foundation’s user-friendly interactive tools, such as the “Journey Map for How to Vote in America”, to help plan and track your process.Some myths and misunderstandings about the connection between voting abroad and paying taxes may be fueling the low turnout by US overseas voters in the UK. But voting from abroad for federal candidatesdoes not exposeUS overseas voters to federal tax obligations. That is, voting for president, vice-president, and US Congress has no influence on your tax profile or status.Votingbelowthe federal level, in state or local/municipal elections,could incur state tax liabilityin some states. The most important elections in the upcoming midterms are the federal elections for the House of Representatives and the Senate, so voters abroad can still have an important impact without any danger of affecting their taxes by voting only at the federal level, and leaving the rest of the ballot blank.US citizenship itself – not voting – is what creates the tax relationship. A US citizen living permanently in the UK is generally subject to US tax rules on worldwide income and may have to file a US federal tax return, regardless of whether that person has voted in a US election in decades – or has never voted at all.So, basically, to go back to an old trope in US-British relations, if they don’t vote, US citizens living in the UK can have “taxation without representation”. Voting from abroad for federal offices does not lead to more taxation, but it does permit some representation. Americans abroad remain subject to US fiscal obligations while extraordinarily few exercise the political right that gives them some say over the government imposing those obligations.Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven GreenhouseRead moreSome eligible voters may be discouraged by recent efforts in Washington to restrict access to voting. But Donald Trump’s Save America Act, which includes proof-of-citizenship and voter-identification requirements, did not pass the Senate before it recessed in August. An attempt to pass narrower voter-ID legislationalso failed.Given the size of the eligible population and persistently low participation, Americans abroad represent a largely untapped electorate. The UK is particularly important: it has hundreds of thousands of US citizens, close cultural and economic ties to the United States, and extensive access to British and American political news.Research on voter participation has found that personal contact can increase turnout. In practice, that suggests informal networks – friends, colleagues and community groups – can play a meaningful role in encouraging Americans abroad to vote. People in the UK can remind their US friends and neighbors that US elections have far-reaching consequences for the world.Kathryn Sikkink is the Ryan Family professor of human rights policy at the Harvard Kennedy SchoolExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS voting rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Coalition wants ‘discrete’ First Nations content in schools. But children must be taught to critically assess concepts such as national pride | Tony Birch | The Guardian
description: A law passed in Victoria in 1886 left aftershocks felt across Australia today. Yet few white people have ever heard of it
Author: Tony Birch
Headline: A law passed in Victoria in 1886 left aftershocks felt across Australia today. Yet few white people have ever heard of it
Content: ‘The Aborigines Protection Act 1886 was legislated to quash the renewed vitality and political organisation among Aboriginal people incarcerated on reserves and missions,’ Tony Birch writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreen‘The Aborigines Protection Act 1886 was legislated to quash the renewed vitality and political organisation among Aboriginal people incarcerated on reserves and missions,’ Tony Birch writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionAustralian educationThe Coalition wants ‘discrete’ First Nations content in schools. But children must be taught to critically assess concepts such as national prideTony BirchA law passed in Victoria in 1886 left aftershocks felt across Australia today. Yet few white people have ever heard of itTue 22 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTShareOn Saturday in a speech to a major education conference, the shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, said he had asked for a copy of Australia’s constitution for his 10th birthday (I wanted a yo-yo).I have no doubt that Leeser is a man of serious intellect. He states that one of his goals is to improve the standards of Indigenous education and the delivery of Indigenous history and culture in schools. He wants to remove the current practice of embedding Indigenous curriculum as a cross-curricular priority across disciplines. He wants to shift the delivery of Indigenous curriculum to “discrete, carefully planned topics that fit properly within geography or history or science classes”.‘National pride’ and ‘Western values’ the focus of Coalition education plan that would reduce First Nations contentRead moreConsidering that most students begin tertiary study with little serious knowledge of Indigenous history and culture, a shift to “discreteness” would not seem to be the answer to a serious problem.In my role as chair of Australian literature at the University of Melbourne I visit many high schools each year. The most common discussion I have with teaching staff indicates that they want more resources and expertise from Indigenous educators to ensure that the curriculum is delivered in a more vibrant and energetic manner.In 1886 the Victorian colonial government formalised a piece of legislation that would violently affect the Aboriginal community, with ramifications that are still felt today. The Aborigines Protection Act 1886 was legislated to quash the renewed vitality and political organisation among Aboriginal people incarcerated on reserves and missions. “The half-caste act”, as it is more commonly known by Aboriginal people, introduced forms of blood quantum that would subsequently include the demeaning and racist categories of “half-caste, quarter-caste [and] octoroon”.The act’s intention was clear. A Victorian government official commented at the time that, “Regarding the full bloods, within a generation the whole of them will have passed away.” The remaining Aboriginal community of Victoria would have their identity destroyed with the stroke of a pen. They would be denied contact with family members, including parents, they would have no access to financial support and their legitimate connection to land and country would be denied to them.double quotation markEducation policy and practice is not a slogan on a T-shirt. All societies hold values, not only the westNext year will be the 30th anniversary of the release of the Bringing Them Home report. It was based on formal hearings across Australia that investigated the removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from families and communities during the 20th century, producing theStolen Generationsof children who suffered serious trauma as a result of this terrible history.How much does Australia really care about democracy and the constitution? Maybe we need our own Hamilton | Julianne SchultzRead moreThe report makes it clear that the Victorian 1886 act (and subsequent legislation introduced by state and commonwealth governments last century) remains the foundation stone of complex and hypocritical identity legislation, as do aspects of the crude science of eugenics that underpinned the child removal policies.And yet the 1886 act is known by few white Australians. In more than 30 years of teaching at a tertiary level, of both Australian and Aboriginal history, I have often asked incoming undergraduates if they are aware of it. Not one student has ever raised their hand. Few academics, unless working in a relative discipline, are aware of it.
