This is an indictment on the nation’s education system, considering that the 1886 act also informed aspects of framing of the commonwealth constitution of 1901, including the infamous White Australia policy.In Leeser’s speechhe also championedwestern values and national pride. Education policy and practice is not a slogan on a T-shirt. All societies hold values, not only the west. All societies are deeply flawed, historically speaking. And most countries claim national pride as a sacred mantra. We need to trust our children. We must educate them to critically assess concepts such as “values” and “pride”, rather than teach them to hoist a flag.The 1886 act resulted in the forced separation of families. The banishments affected Aboriginal people for generations. Some parents never saw their children again.The 1886 act should be taught in schools across Australia, not to trigger a state of “white guilt” but as a means of asking critical questions about what truly constitutes a national identity – and who is included and excluded.Prof Tony Birch is the chair of Australian literature at the University of MelbourneExplore more on these topicsAustralian educationOpinionIndigenous AustraliansStolen GenerationsCoalitionAustralian politicsAustralian lawRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham  | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: I want him to start the fightback next week against extremists who peddle hate and those who despise this country. That would be true patriotism, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: I want him to start the fightback next week against extremists who peddle hate and those who despise this country. That would be true patriotism, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Anti-migrant protesters in Dover, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreenAnti-migrant protesters in Dover, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeOpinionRaceThere is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy BurnhamPolly ToynbeeI want him to start the fightback next week against extremists who peddle hate and those who despise this country. That would be true patriotismTue 22 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.46 EDTShare“The speech” may have been in the making a long while, maybe for a lifetime, but Andy Burnham has only a week left for revision before his first conference as Labour leader. Expect hope, of course, that the future will be better, though the way is hard. Already his optimism means that fewer people think they will beworse off next year. But his most urgent task is the cultural wildfire that needs extinguishing before it takes hold.The rise of anti-migration neofascism is more threatening than anything I’ve seen in my lifetime. Shock tactics by a few hundred people in black shirts and balaclavas are designed to invade the national consciousness, their noxious hate bleeding into the mainstream – and they do.Keir Starmer began well,hosing downthe summer 2024 rioters with rapid arrests. But since then, the truth is that Labour has looked ambivalent in challenging aggressive St George’s flag-raisers, and the asylum hotel protesters who claim to be “protecting” the country whose values they are trashing. At the same time, the self-proclaimed patriots of GB News, the Mail, the Telegraph and Elon Musk’s X pump out daily hate of the country. Burnham’s task is to face them down with top-level leadership, and the sheer force of his positivity.It won’t be easy. Nick Lowles, the founder of the advocacy group Hope Not Hate,says the cordon sanitairethat once defended democratic politics from the far right and ethno-nationalist thuggery is gone. He has patrolled that line all his working life, and now he’s alarmed about the feeble responses from mainstream politicians to the swelling ranks of racist demagogues intent on wrecking what is, still, a remarkably cohesive multicultural society.View image in fullscreenAn anti-migrant march through Portsmouth, 12 September 2026.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesBut Lowles is encouraged by his latest talks with Downing Street. “They are ready to push back,” he says. “Good people need to stand up.” Keep immigration policy separate, is his advice. “It’s not binary, people want the small boats stopped – but they value the cohesive communities they live in.”Burnham of the north, immune to the rightwing branding of southerners as “woke”, is the right man to speak plainly against racism to the “red wall” tendency. There is a decency argument to be made. Look how the best-of-British RNLI had toclose a stationas volunteers were threatened for risking their lives for anyone in peril on the sea. Consider the truth thatonly 1.2% of RNLI’s emergency launchesinvolve refugees.Consider that when Sagal Abdi-Wali, once a Somali child refugee and now a local council leader, theLabourcandidate for Holborn and St Pancras, a respected public servant, faces ferocious abuse for seeking to serve the public, it’s a direct threat to democracy.When a poll indicates that37% of menbetween 25 and 34 like Tommy Robinson, there can be no doubt that the sewer of hate and misogyny, operating via dark algorithms, needs to be checked, not protected as “free speech”. When tax-exile billionaire Jim Ratcliffe opines from Monaco that immigration and taxes are destroying the country, it’s for Labour to be the patriots who rebut him.Things are bad when the former prime minister Rishi Sunak, born and bred in the UK, feels obliged, as he did in the Sunday Timesat the weekend, to defend his right to be brown and British. Calling himself a beneficiary of “the world’s most successful multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy”, he was shocked by footage of “someone referring to me as a ‘Paki’ and others questioning the Englishness of a ‘brown Hindu’”. He insisted: “We cannot allow race to be reintroduced into our politics … they are trying to turn Britishness into a DNA test.”Ed Davey of the Liberal Democratssees it ashis “moral responsibility to stop Reform”, as it is for Labour, and should be for traditional Tories. But Westminster has been muted. When Nigel Farage first announced he would deport 600,000 people, including children, Labour – like the Tories –only opposedhis scheme’s cost and impracticality.Deporting whichever migrants Farage targets next may appeal to some, but it’s for Labour to spell out what that midnight knock would come to mean – not just for millions as British as Sunak, but for us all, with our liberties diluted, and division and hate concentrated.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators from the anti-fascist Stand Up to Racism group stage a counter-protest in Portsmouth on 12 September 2026.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesThe tempting counterattack is more hate: knuckle-dusters against knuckle-draggers. But that’s not the right way, says Lowles, who has himself been the target of violence and death threats. His organisation seems to be carrying a lot of the burden here. It’s scrutiny of that dark world – infiltrating and exposing the extremism, gathering names and evidence when violence has been planned – that has prevented outrages and saved lives. The police appear to know far less.Hope Not Hate, which relies on donations, runs community groups in places at risk of tensions. In mainly white areas of Bradford, Gateshead, Sunderland and elsewhere, it offers free meals in school holidays and provides food banks to bring people together to talk community politics. When racist trouble breaks out anywhere, “we try to get there within 24 hours, to bring together local faith groups and local mothers who don’t want violence,” Lowles says. “Calming down, not countering hate with hate.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a world where Trumpites and our own extremists own the loudhailers, his remedy lies with community groups, knowing your neighbours, joining up, being active. He offersreassuring polling: 53% of British adults like “living in a community with people who come from different backgrounds”.A reflection of that better Britain is what he expects from Labour next week, and so do I. Go on chasing down small boats (arrivals are41% downthis year), but also celebrate the country we live in, protect its social success against opportunistic pedlars of hate.In my lifetime, I’ve seen what I thought was overt racism made untenable: just watch the toe-curling TV sitcoms of yesteryear. In 2005 Michael Howard, the then Tory party leader, bombed with his shameless dog-whistle campaign slogan, “Are you thinking what we’re thinking?”. No, good people were not.Those people are still there; the challenge is having the credibility and the will to speak for and to them. Burnham can do that. Next week he should.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistThis article was amended on 22 September 2026. In an earlier version, an image showing counter-protesters from Stand Up to Racism was incorrectly captioned as showing the “South Coast Patriots” group.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsRaceOpinionLabourAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage? | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solution, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solution, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘[The issue is] making fools of MPs, who will say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable, but have to keep pretending otherwise in public.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘[The issue is] making fools of MPs, who will say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable, but have to keep pretending otherwise in public.’Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionPensionsBritain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?Gaby HinsliffThe issue cannot be avoided any longer. Andy Burnham and his chancellor must face the fear of a pensioner backlash, and find a fair solutionTue 22 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.21 EDTShareThere is always something oddly unreal about party conference season. In theory, everyone is getting away from Westminster to better reflect on the state of the nation. In practice, the whole circus just briefly relocates to the coast, to live off warm white wine and gossip for three days, before coming back with a streaming cold. But this year, reality seems more elusive than usual.Everyone knows hard choices loom, but everyone is frightened to make them. Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock, whose future will be vigorously debated on the fringes and in private conversation this autumn, but less so on the stage.George Osborne’sshameless 2011 bid for pensioner votes– under which the state pension rises, come rain or shine, by whichever is the highest of inflation, average earnings growth for working people, or 2.5% – has alreadycost around three times as muchas the Treasury originally expected.TheOffice for Budget Responsibility reckons that by 2030 it will be swallowing more than £15bn a year – almost enough to fund the cause over which chancellor John Healey was recently willingto resign, namely raising defence spending to 3% of GDP in time to prevent a Russian attack on Nato.But even if you’re willing to roll the dice on another war, there’s no shortage of alternative proposals for spending the money.The British Chambers of Commerce wants it diverted intotackling youth unemploymentvia cuts to national insurance, while the rightwing thinktank Centre for Social Justice argues for spending it on boostingthe life chancesof working-class boys. But perhaps more fittingly, it could pay forAndy Burnham’s dreamof free social care for the very age group that is liable to lose out from breaking the lock. Would pensioners rather have a3.9% rise next year– though it could be higher, if inflation really rockets this autumn – or relief from the fear of having to sell family homes to fund nursing care? Because right now, it’s difficult to see how they can have both. Yet the failure to be honest about these tradeoffs is bending British politics out of shape.It’s making fools of MPs, who will readily say in private that the triple lock is unaffordable but have to keep pretending otherwise in public, even as they’re being asked to nod throughpainful cuts to disability benefits. It’s sending young and painfully squeezed people a message that nobody cares about them, fuelling intergenerational resentment. And it’s encouraging a phoney debate about tax and spend, in which parties of the left pretend they can find serious money from unicorn taxes – the magical kind that raise billions but somehow without hitting anyone likely to vote for them, or driving the highly mobile rich to Monaco – while parties of the right pretend they can make huge welfare savings they somehow missed during 14 years in power.Breaking the triple lock is becoming enough of a no-brainer to attract genuine cross-party consensus, stumped only by the cross-party conviction that the public will hate them for it.That fear is not unfounded. According to YouGov, two-thirds of Britons – and 70% of over-65s –want to keep the lock. Labour remains terrified of repeatingRachel Reeves’ 2024 gambit,when she tried to take winter fuel allowance away from better-off pensioners in a hurry, but couldn’t bring herself to make the political case for doing so, and was eventually forced into retreat.For the Tories, going after pensioners would be suicidal, and the same goes for the Liberal Democrats, so long as they’re trying to hold on to the formerly true-blue shire seats they captured two years ago.Only the Greensseem to be keeping their options open, and they’re not going to win the next election. Fear of a pensioner backlash is distorting everything, like a dam in a river that forces the water to find other ways around it, eroding the banks until they eventually collapse.Nobody is arguing that pensioner poverty has ceased to be a problem. (If anything, retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers did, which means this conversation may get harder the longer it’s deferred.) And even for those who aren’t on the breadline, the prospect of losing money at an age when you can no longer try to earn your way out of trouble is genuinely frightening.But there are better ways of helping older people who genuinely need it than a triple lock that benefits both rich and poor, and working-age poverty is real too. Choosing to shield pensioners from the harsh economic realities of the last few years has hit some of their children and grandchildren unfairly hard: while pensioner benefits rose in real terms by£900 between 2010-11 and 2024-25, benefits for children and working-age people fell by £1,400, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank.Yet anyone daring to make that case at the next election for breaking the lock can expect to be mercilessly shelled by rivals, including those who deep down agree with them.What is focusing minds now is the realisation that for the first time, next spring, the state pensionmay rise high enough to attract tax(though ministers say anyone poor enough to rely solely on it would be exempt). The stealth option would be to keep the triple lock nominally in place, but tax away the increase for wealthier pensioners – essentially giving with one hand and taking with the other, a bit like the Tories did overchild benefit for higher-rate taxpayers. It avoids an outright confrontation, but plenty of pensioners will notice the money being clawed back and resent it nonetheless.Better, surely, to break the lock as part of a new and much broader deal on generational fairness, which protects vulnerable elderly people but recognises that the young are also struggling – while lifting the burden of social care andsettling arguments around pension tax reliefinto the bargain.Smart spending in an era of shrinking resources ought to mean working out how to use the same money differently to meet new challenges, not just clinging to the past because you can’t face talking about the future. But for now, it seems, that’s just a little too much reality to bear.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPensionsOpinionFamily financesAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyLabourState pensionsWelfarecommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s decision to ban journalists from the White House – and One Nation’s actions – shows why Australia urgently needs a media freedom bill | Peter Greste | The Guardian
description: Australians can’t afford to be complacent – Pauline Hanson also thinks it’s OK to shut out reporters she doesn’t like
Author: Peter Greste
Headline: Australians can’t afford to be complacent – Pauline Hanson also thinks it’s OK to shut out reporters she doesn’t like
Content: ‘We shouldn’t wait until journalists deemed unfriendly are being kicked out of Parliament House or worse before we think about writing their role into legislation,’ Peter Greste writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreen‘We shouldn’t wait until journalists deemed unfriendly are being kicked out of Parliament House or worse before we think about writing their role into legislation,’ Peter Greste writes.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionAustralian mediaTrump’s decision to ban journalists from the White House – and One Nation’s actions – shows why Australia urgently needs a media freedom billPeter GresteAustralians can’t afford to be complacent – Pauline Hanson also thinks it’s OK to shut out reporters she doesn’t likeMon 21 Sep 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.53 EDTShareNo politician loves journalists. The relationship between media and governments has always been fractious, combative, resentful and at times downright hostile. But that is how it is meant to be. Governments wield power; media monitor and report on it.That dynamic is critical to any functioning democracy. Formal checks and balances will only go so far in exposing abuses of power, so the system requires vigorous, professional and independent individuals devoted to investigating and reporting how governments behave. It isn’t always pretty but it has been an essential component of every effective modern democracy.That is why the US has its storiedFirst Amendment– arguably the world’s most elegant constitutional guarantee of basic freedoms including freedom of speech and freedom of the press.At the weekend, Donald Trump banned journalistsfrom CNN, MS Now and Politicofrom the White House. He described them as “fake news”, without giving more details.“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he told a news conference. “You just get sick of it.”It is worth pausing for a moment to reflect on how big a deal this is. Barack Obama articulated it well in a response at the weekend.“If you have a certain cohort – let’s call it 30 to 35 per cent of the country right now – which thinks that’s OK, what that means is we have not developed the kind of understanding of what democracy requires,” the former president said.“I’m trying to think what would have happened if I’d said, ‘You know what, Fox News … you’re outta here.’ It’s unimaginable.”The Washington press corps needs to boycott White House events   | Margaret SullivanRead moreIn solidarity, four other big US broadcasters who routinely film and distribute White House events on behalf of the media – ABC, NBC, Fox News and CBS – have suspended what’s known as the press pool.That won’t stop the news from getting out. The White House’s own feed and others will still cover the events but it is a sharp escalation of the administration’s attacks on media coverage it doesn’t like.Australians cannot afford to be complacent. One Nation –now slightly in front of Laboras our most popular political party – also thinks it is OKto ban journalists. It has repeatedly shut out reporters from the ABC and the Guardian from its news conferences and signalled that it will do the same for other news organisations it doesn’t like.In the US, the three news organisations have goneto the district courtto challenge the ban as a violation of their First Amendment rights. In Australia, we have no such protection.In fact, we are the only liberal democracy in the world without any protection for press freedom or freedom of speech enshrined in our constitution or in a bill of rights. The most we have is an “implied freedom of political communication”that the high court has inferred from our constitution.At times, that implied freedom has helped protect the rights that most of us assume are hardwired into our political system. But because that right is merely inferred, and not part of any explicit constitutional clause, it can – and has been – overridden at critical points. The ABC discovered that to its cost whenit tried and failedto use the implied freedom to overturn a search warrant that the Australian federal police used in 2019 when it investigated the broadcaster’s Afghan Files reporting.Trump said he would probably lose the lawsuit brought by the three media organisations and expected to “go for appeal”. But even though there is no guarantee that the US media companies will win their court case, the First Amendment remains a powerful bulwark against the kinds of attacks the Trump administration is now launching.It is unrealistic to think we can get some kind of constitutional reform like the First Amendment but the US experience shows that it would be naive to assume press freedom is a given here, even with our robust and longstanding traditions.That is why the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom is advocating for a media freedom bill. Our bill, that we expect to publish later this year, would enshrine the principle of media freedom in our legal code. Under it, parliament would have to treat press freedom as something to be protected like any other human right, and the courts would have to recognise the public interest in the work that journalists produce, whenever they are interpreting existing laws.Trump’s attack on press freedom is an inflection point – one that shows how far democratic norms have shifted under his presidency. It also shows that relying on convention rather than established law is dangerous.The three news organisations might well lose their district court challenge but at least they have that constitutional backstop. We don’t, and we shouldn’t wait until journalists deemed unfriendly are being kicked out of Parliament House or worse before we think about writing their role into legislation. By then, it will be too late.Peter Greste is the executive director of the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom and a professor of journalism at Macquarie UniversityExplore more on these topicsAustralian mediaOpinionAustralian politicsOne NationPress freedomFreedom of speechcommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s economic challenges are mounting as deaths start to outnumber births. But ‘baby bonus’ policies would be pointless | Nicki Hutley | The Guardian
description: Slower overall economic growth doesn’t have to be a bad thing. It is the quality of that growth that matters
Author: Nicki Hutley
Headline: Slower overall economic growth doesn’t have to be a bad thing. It is the quality of that growth that matters
Content: ‘Population growth is expected to slow to just 0.9% over four decades, compared with 1.4% over the past four,’ writes Nicki Hutley.Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Population growth is expected to slow to just 0.9% over four decades, compared with 1.4% over the past four,’ writes Nicki Hutley.Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty ImagesOpinionAustralian economyAustralia’s economic challenges are mounting as deaths start to outnumber births. But ‘baby bonus’ policies would be pointlessNicki HutleySlower overall economic growth doesn’t have to be a bad thing. It is the quality of that growth that mattersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 21 Sep 2026 20.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.52 EDTSharePoliticians are frequently accused of short-termism, so Australia’s intergenerational report (IGR) is unusual in projecting the big trends affecting the economy, and in particular the federal budget, over a 40-year horizon.The former treasurer Peter Costello introduced the concept of the IGR, now in its seventh edition, shortly after the millennium. The idea was to garner support for budget reforms given the challenges that were coming with an ageing population and a shrinking number of workers needed to support them. Oh, for the good old days when the “boomer bulge” appeared to be the most significant budgetary problem that we faced.With each new IGR, the challenges have been mounting – not just for Australia, but for the whole world. I’m certainly finding it harder and harder to keep my usually optimistic frame of mind in the face of geopolitical fragmentation, rising trade tensions, apocalyptic predictions on AI, fading productivity, the climate crisis and demographic change.More Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years as major report predicts future of lower growthRead moreIn one respect in particular, the 2026 IGR’s projections represent a watershed moment. Women are projected to continue to have fewer babies over the next 40 years such that population growth is expected to slow to just 0.9% over four decades, compared with 1.4% over the past four. And that growth only comes through migration, as deaths start to outnumber births.The IGR points out the significance of this slowdown for economic prospects: our future growth will be held to around 2% rather than the average 3% we have become accustomed to.This has raised alarm bells among many, but slower overall economic growth doesn’t have to be a bad thing. It is thequalityof that growth that matters.As the latest IGR lays out, economic growth is driven by the “three Ps” – population, participation and productivity. Of these three, it is only the latter two that deliver growth with better living standards.Population growth makes the economic pie (as measured by GDP) bigger, but not the size of our individual slices (as measured by GDP per person). To keep the culinary analogy, it is an empty sugar hit. And before you object, I acknowledge that GDP is not a particularly good or complete measure of our wellbeing by any means. It ignores a multitude of social and environmental impacts – but that is a whole other article!And, of course, the shape of the population matters as well as relative size and growth rates. Increasing numbers of older people relative to the number of workforce-aged people puts a large tax burden on the latter. Unless, of course, we want to cut back on health and aged care, not to mention pension payments for those unable to save for their retirement.Participation and productivity, on the other hand, can deliver a bigger serve that is also a high-protein meal – one that has economic, social and environmental benefits, if well managed.The IGR tells us the participation rate – the number of us that are in, or actively looking for, work – will rise a little over the next 15 years, buoyed mainly by more women and older workers. However, after 2040 the participation rate will decline again as the population ages even more.More Australians to live into their 90s as life expectancy forecast to rise over coming decadesRead moreSo that leaves us entirely reliant on productivity growth to drive per capita economic growth. We’ve heard this song before, yet Australia’s productivity performance has beenpretty woefulin recent years, and on a downward trajectory over a number of decades. This is the result of insufficient investment by businesses coupled with the apparent evaporation of willingness among governments at all levels to introduce meaningful reforms (does anyone remember last year’sproductivity roundtables?)Despite this current poor state of affairs, the IGR tells us that productivity growth over the forecast period will average 1.2% a year. And what will drive this much-needed fillip? Why – drumroll, please – AI of course! (AI appears 1,352 time in this IGR, which tells you just how much is hanging on it. This compares, for example, to just 39 references to that other existential crisis, climate change.)We do not yet know either the timing or the extent to which AI technologies will shift productivity in Australia. Nor does it consider its likely impact on the workforce – which the IGR assumes is benign and will have no impact on GDP over the forecast period.Nevertheless, if we put on our rose-coloured glasses and assume that we can achieve the forecast level of long-term productivity growth, that is what will deliver sustainable improvements in living standards for Australia.Better, then, that the government spends its scarce revenues and political capital on supporting technology uplift, rather than pointless policies of the “baby bonus” type. And let’s not equate our economic prospects with women’s fertility, but rather with encouraging their participation in the workforce and the resultingincreased productivityfrom greater access to more brain power.Nicki Hutley is a consulting economistExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Magritte: This Is Still Not a Pipe review – brilliance and trash from the surrealist who sent up Freud | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!
Content: Freud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence … La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), by René Magritte, 1936.Photograph: © 2026 C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkView image in fullscreenFreud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence … La Lampe philosophique (The Philosopher’s Lamp), by René Magritte, 1936.Photograph: © 2026 C. Herscovici/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New YorkArt and designReviewMagritte: This Is Still Not a Pipe review – brilliance and trash from the surrealist who sent up FreudGagosian Gallery, LondonWith his clever conundrums, the Belgian loved satirising both psychoanalysis and surrealism – and occasionally painted rubbish to annoy his family. What a dude!Jonathan JonesTue 22 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRené Magritte is the most inexplicable of artists. It’s much harder to get a handle on him than such supposedly difficult modern greats as Cézanne or Picasso. After all, cubism is a perfectly rational attempt to capture the complexity of reality. But Magritte? He confronts you with wilful mysteries. This show sets choice examples of his magic against modern art and is full of quirky, unexpected treasures that give your wonder at Magritte little twists in new and perverse directions.A painting of puffy white clouds held me across the gallery and still floats ineffably in my mind. It’s a shock because it is so painterly and subtle. If you think Magritte fashioned his surrealist images in a deliberately flat, even banal style, think again. This simple painting of clouds in the blue is full of supple shadow and ethereal light, a brilliantly observed view of nature in the vein of Gainsborough, Constable or Hockney.View image in fullscreenThis is not the sky … La Malédiction (The Curse) by René Magritte, 1931.Photograph: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonExcept it’s not. Innocent as these clouds look, real as they look, they are no such thing. These are not clouds. This is not the sky. And the painting’s sunniness is totally undermined by its title: The Curse. Magritte made it in 1931 at the height of surrealism, the revolutionary art movement that took from the psychoanalytic writings of Sigmund Freud the insight that nothing is innocent and no image is simply what it seems.Everything can be a symbol and probably a dirty one. A pipe. Or a nose. Magritte’s 1936 self-portrait The Philosopher’s Lamp combines both in an absurd meta-Freudian image as his nose becomes a fleshy tube curving down into the bowl of his pipe while a candle twists in a waxy, snaking motion around the stiff single leg of the table. Freud would surely diagnose a fear of impotence but the painting makes that so obvious, it’s a joke. Magritte is satirising psychoanalysis and surrealism itself for being too logical in their reading of symbols.The surrealist movement was started in Paris after the first world war by poets and artists traumatised by its mass slaughter and seeking imaginative renewal by escaping into dreams and erotic reveries. Magritte became the movement’s greatest Belgian representative, but he pushed at its limits, taking it to a far less easily decoded level.View image in fullscreenLe Lieu commun (The Commonplace) by René Magritte, 1964.Photograph: © 2026 ADAGP, Paris and DACS, LondonThat philosophical shift is here in The Interpretation of Dreams, a modern masterpiece lent by its owner the great (and philosophical) American artist Jasper Johns. The English title used here connects it directly with Freud’s most famous book although its actual title in French, La Clef des Songes, translates as The Key of Dreams. Either way, this 1935 painting suggests that dreams and reality are equally bizarre and neither can be explained by the oedipal complex. Four objects are displayed against a neutral background in separate sections. A horse’s head is captioned “the door”; a clock face is labelled “the wind”; under a white jug it says “the bird”. Yet in the bottom right corner, a suitcase is accurately identified as “the valise”.It’s the last that makes this an unsettling demolition of reality rather than a piece of whimsy. If all the images we saw in dreams were fantastically misrecognised, that would be amusing, but one time out of four, says Magritte, the dream is true. You can neither ignore dreams nor understand them. You’re screwed.But if Magritte rejected the psychoanalytic overconfidence that dreams can be decoded, he had no problem recalling the most vivid and appalling nightmares. The Pleasure depicts a girl eating a bird and in The Listening Room a giant apple completely fills a chamber, its bright green skin pushing monstrously against the walls and ceiling.There are so many connections here with modern art – how many installations have echoed that space-swallowing apple? But the patchiest part of this show is its attempt to link with today’s artists. A Jeff Koons train and Aqualung, a floppy Sarah Lucas nude, an obscene wooden statue of a woman interacting with teddy bears by Isabelle Albuquerque – these are one-dimensional compared with Magritte’s conundrums. Gagosian has done a brilliant job of borrowing his work but descends into commercial glibness in its choice of his supposed 21st-century peers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho did this piece of trash, I wondered, in front of a ludicrous cartoony daub of three legs strutting about independently, one with a red nose, moustache and feathered headdress, another puffing a pipe, all rendered in slobbery horrid hues. Then I saw the signature: Magritte. This and a couple of equally lurid daubs come from Magritte’s “Vache” (cow) period when he deliberately did bad, stupid paintings to annoy his family, friends and fans.What a dude. He could paint like Jan van Eyck when he wanted but sometimes preferred to paint like a clumsy moron. Magritte was too intelligent to respect anything, least of all art.This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte, is atGagosian Gallery, London, 24 September to 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designRené MagritteExhibitionsPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Can a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debut | Stage | The Guardian
description: Osipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’
Author: David Jays
Headline: Osipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’
Content: ‘Russian women are very open. We don’t try to be cool’ … Natalia OsipovaPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Russian women are very open. We don’t try to be cool’ … Natalia OsipovaPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianStageInterviewCan a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debutDavid JaysOsipova plays the wife of bisexual economist John Maynard Keynes in a new play. The ballerina talks about the allure of her Russian character, dismissed as a ‘frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl’Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Natalia Osipova started rehearsals for her first ever play, it didn’t go well. “I cry. I’m shaking. I’m stressed and completely lost on the first day,” she reports. “I think, ‘I’m a piece of shit!’ I want to take a taxi and run away.”It’s the second week of rehearsals when we meet, and Osipova is still here. The Royal Ballet principal plays a Russian ballerina from a previous age:Lydia Lopokova, who danced with Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, then in 1925 unexpectedly married British economist John Maynard Keynes, who is the protagonist of James Graham’s The Standard of Living – a play about, among other things, taking risks and imagining a brave new future.Acting is central to ballet’s appeal for Osipova. “Maybe I’ll never be super perfect for classical ballet because I love stories so much,” she says. Even so, she demurred when former colleague Edward Watson suggested she audition. “You’re stupid!” was his retort. “You need to try because it’s amazing opportunity.”View image in fullscreen‘She for him and he for her’ … Osipova with Pip Carter and Rory Kinnear in rehearsals for The Standard of Living.Photograph: Manuel HarlanA delicate silver necklace shines beneath frank brown eyes. Osipova requested a translator in our previous interviews, but today speaks in an idiosyncratic gallop not unlike Lopokova’s own. Entering Nicholas Hytner’s rehearsal room, joining a classy cast led byRory Kinnear, she felt like Lydia among Keynes’s sneery Bloomsbury friends. “I left rehearsal and cried,” she says, “because I feel, ‘Oh my god, I’m so bad.’ But you learn and listen and every day, step by step, I do better.”double quotation markRussia is my home, my family, my theatre, my friends. It’s my everythingWorking with text for the first time, especially in her second language, is, she confirms, “a whole new world”. She drafted in her husband, dancer Jason Kittelberger, to run through lines at midnight. “Dance is my world,” she says. “I’ve danced since 17, I’m 40 now. It’s my life.” But gradually, she found that the fundamental goal in theatre was the same. “You’re learning your material, you try to understand what’s important. With your partner, you start to play. You listen, you reply, and this is like life.”Graham is also in rehearsal, continually adjusting the script. His play is attentive to Lydia’s physicality: dance solos mark the scene changes, while a frequent stage direction for Lydia is “she stomps”. Osipova delights in making him laugh – they have just rehearsed Lydia’s first entrance, swearing fearsomely in Russian – and she feels kinship with her character.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianLopokova, says Osipova, “is not famous and popular in Russia” – her choreographer brother,Fedor Lopukhov, is better remembered. “She was two years in the Mariinsky, and after migrating with Diaghilev for his Russian season, she didn’t really come back.”She was reportedly strong in drama, irresistible in comedy. “She had a beautiful, huge jump,” Osipova says. “That I have too!” Keynes was her second husband and, to everyone’s surprise, the real thing. Each altered key parts of their identities: Maynard as a man who slept with men (keeping meticulous records of his encounters), Lydia as a feted dancer. “She changed her life to be with him,” Osipova says.She describes Keynes as “a man like a mountain, to hug her and give her everything. She for him and he for her.” Keynes’s Bloomsbury chums were less appreciative. “She was a clever woman with ambition,” Osipova argues, bridling at their jeers. In the play, she is called “that flat-footed, frivolous foghorn of a chorus girl!” Osipova grimaces. “I’m always upset when I hear somebody say that about dancers. It gives me pain because I feel dancers have such a special soul. It’s a different brain.”She’d already researched Bloomsbury for her searing Virginia Woolf in Wayne McGregor’sWoolf Worksearlier this year. When she was listening in the wings to Gillian Anderson’s voiceover, reading Woolf’s suicide note, “I started to have a huge panic attack”, Osipova says. “It’s emotional, the way she finally melts and dies. It’s more than dance, so much more.”View image in fullscreenOsipova with Steven McRae in the 2015 world premiere of Woolf Works at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian“Russian women are very open,” Osipova muses. “We’re not liars. We don’t try to be, ‘I’m cool, I’m nice.’” Lopokova’s Russian identity was crucial to her, yet she never saw her homeland after 1936. In our tumultuous times, can Osipova imagine a homecoming for herself? “I really want, but I don’t think so,” she says. “My husband is American and we have life there – but I want to visit [Russia] because it’s my home, my family, my theatre, my friends. It’s my everything.”From Bloomsbury to Whitehall: new play reimagines life of John Maynard KeynesRead moreOsipova was originally due to duck out of the play to dance Kenneth MacMillan’s tragic heroine Manon, but now won’t do the ballet. She has already retreated from other signature roles, looking beyond Don Quixote and other bravura ballets which made her name – which she delightfully calls her “bravo repertoire”.“I’m a person who is bored doing things again and again,” she says. “That was part of my life – I do it well and amazing, and I never want to come back to it.” Instead, her repertoire includes contemporary pieces and bespoke commissions – and now theatre. “If I don’t do something new, I feel like I’m dying,” she declares. “I can’t breathe. Why do you live if you’re not learning something new?”The Standard of Living is atTheatre Royal Haymarket,London, until 12 DecemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreBalletDanceNatalia OsipovaActingRory KinnearinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We didn’t set out to make a show for animals!’ The Netflix seal cartoon that’s a huge hit … with pets | Television | The Guardian
description: Videos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdict
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Videos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdict
Content: Seal of approval? Ozzy gets up close to watch the Netflix show Sealook.Photograph: Courtesy Rich PelleyView image in fullscreenSeal of approval? Ozzy gets up close to watch the Netflix show Sealook.Photograph: Courtesy Rich PelleyTelevision‘We didn’t set out to make a show for animals!’ The Netflix seal cartoon that’s a huge hit … with petsVideos of cats and dogs transfixed by Netflix kids’ show Sealook – or pawing at its characters – are everywhere. We tried to find out why … and asked a goldendoodle for its verdictRich PelleyTue 22 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOzzy the four-month-old goldendoodle isn’t normally allowed on the sofa. But today he has been granted special privileges because I’ve come round specifically to watch TV with him. We’re not watching Paw Patrol, Scooby-Doo, or even Crufts. We’re watching Sealook, the Netflix kids’ cartoon about a colony of seals that dogs and cats online are supposedly obsessed with. But is this really a thing? And will Ozzy care?I hit play. A gang of wide-eyed pastel-coloured seals are in a slapstick scrape. There’s no dialogue: they mostly lie around on the ice, and try to annoy each other by doing silly things like making funny noises, throwing snowballs or keeping each other awake. Ozzy seems more interested in chewing his pizzle stick – which I discover, slightly too late, is the dried penis of a bull. Then again, perhaps this is just canine second-screening: Sealook on the telly, bull penis in the mouth.View image in fullscreen‘They mostly lie around on the ice’ … Sealook, NetflixPhotograph: NetflixOzzy may be playing hard to impress, but he’s in the minority. Search #sealook and there are loads of dogs pawing at the TV and cats batting at the characters. “They do watch television, but not this intently,” says Jessica Blumen from Oregon, who has had nearly 10m views for an Instagram video of her two goldendoodles’ reaction. Benny, nearly one, and five-month-old Myrtle, certainly seem to be converts, judging by their reaction to watching a group of animated seals banging on the ice. “The minute the seals started drumming, Benny sat up and Myrtle had these subtle head tilts.”It’s even become a sort of doggy mindfulness regime. “Last night Benny was getting a little wild – goldendoodles get zoomies at night – so I turned it on and he immediately settled. Even when an episode ends and flashes up a yellow bar saying ‘fin’, that still keeps his attention.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueŠvepsė, a one-and-a-half-year-old rescue cat in Lithuania, is already a TV fan, enjoying animal documentaries and having previously been fascinated by a Lithuanian strongman competition. But Sealookproduced an even stronger reaction. “She became very focused on the screen and tried to catch the characters with her paws. Sometimes, she simply sat there watching very carefully without taking her eyes off the screen,” says owner Erika. “We’re used to her watching animal documentaries, but seeing her try to catch the characters in Sealook was something we hadn’t seen before.”Rio, a six-month-old golden retriever owned by Melly Roman in Houston, Texas, is another fan. “We have the TV on for background noise and he never normally watches,” she says. “But he started barking when one of the seals came really close to the screen. We tried again later and he sat and watched a couple of episodes.” The clip helped take Rio’s Instagram following from about 115 to nearly 4,000.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThis, I tell Ozzy, is exactly the sort of behaviour that could help boost his own Instagram following of 137. Watching television is a far better party trick than barking at his own reflection or stealing hair scrunchies from his human mum. I’d offer to become his social media manager, but I don’t have any interest in freebies from Bonio.Still, before I write off Ozzy as a hopeless influencer, what are cats and dogs seeing when they watch Sealook? One possible reason is the colour palette: it’s all white snow, pale-blue ice and brightly coloured seals. Cats and dogs see blues and yellows particularly well, which perhaps makes Sealook about as easy to ignore as a bowl of Whiskas or Pedigree Chum.Dr David Williams, an associate lecturer in veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Cambridge, thinks movement may be just as important as colour. “Cats and dogs are particularly interested in movement because they’re interested in chasing a mouse or another prey item,” he says. “They’re also crepuscular – most active around dawn and dusk – so movement in low light matters particularly to them.”Sound may matter too. Dr Emily Blackwell, a companion animal behaviour expert at Bristol Veterinary School, says the seals’ “high-pitched squeaking noises may mimic the sounds of prey species – rodents – and also sound very similar to the squeaky toys that many of our pets have”.View image in fullscreenRich Pelley and Ozzy settle down to watch Sealook.Photograph: courtesy Rich PelleyDr Freya Mowat, an associate professor of veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who studies how dogs watch television, says dogs seem particularly drawn to animal-like movement. “My own research has shown that dogs prefer watching dogs to humans,” she says. “Seals? I don’t know, but they are closer to dogs than people! Cartoons are great content for dogs: high contrast, lots of movement, nice fun music – it’s the whole package.”Was any of this deliberate? Apparently not, says Leah Yeon, communications lead at The Pinkfong Company, the South Korean co-producer of Sealook. “Seeing cats and now dogs as well becoming so absorbed in Sealook has been a fun and unexpected surprise.”The show’s simple snowy landscapes, vivid colours and short, repetitive movements were designed for audiences of children, although the team suspects the same ingredients may help explain its appeal to pets. The trend began with cats, then dogs jumped on the bandwagon. “We didn’t set out to make a show for animals,” says Yeon, “but it continues to be fascinating – and very amusing – to see it connect with this new audience.”Which leaves one final experiment. Williams suggested turning the sound off to see whether Ozzy’s interest changes. Right then, Ozzy. Volume down.Nothing. I turn the sound back on and, finally, Ozzy looks up. A seal slides across the ice; his ears prick up. Another squeaks and he edges towards the screen. At last! I grab my phone, visions of 4,000 followers dancing before me. But seconds later, Ozzy wanders off in search of a hair scrunchie or bull penis. Sealook, it seems, has yet to earn his seal of approval. Doggy stardom will have to wait.Sealook is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAnimation on TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheese | Movies | The Guardian
description: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me
Content: At your service dog … Heart of the Beast.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyView image in fullscreenAt your service dog … Heart of the Beast.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyMoviesReviewHeart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheesePitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & MePeter BradshawTue 22 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of likeOwen Wilson in Marley & Me, only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on thesecond world war action thriller Fury, plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played byJK Simmons(channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. (Belmont has the same setup with Odin.) Booth and Brandy are Mr Hyde to Belmont and Odin’s Dr Jekyll.As for Pitt himself, his acting chops are tested when he has to sob and then laugh with joy when it looks wrongly as if Odin has been fatally wounded – but extravagant emoting is not why we love him. Heart of the Beast is a bit cheesy and the final moments will test your credulity, but Pitt is the right guy in the right film.Heart of the Beast is out on 24 September in Australia, and 25 September in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsAction and adventure filmsBrad PittDogsJK SimmonsAnimalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists review – It caused fury across Europe. In the UK? Laughter and coughing | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Tiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Tiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusing
Content: Provocations … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesView image in fullscreenProvocations … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesTheatreReviewCatarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists review – It caused fury across Europe. In the UK? Laughter and coughingNational Theatre, LondonTiago Rodrigues’s play has incensed audiences abroad with one character’s hellfire rightwing invective. But its combination of boredom and shocks ultimately feels confusingArifa AkbarTue 22 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat does it say about an audience who, while watching a character make a speech that has sparked screeching protests and angry walkouts in its run across Europe, sit politely listening until the end?The booing does come, but only after the actor playing a far-right politician and kidnap victim (Romeu Costa) has finished a half-hour invective that takes in everything from the scourge of minorities to that of elites, homosexuals, and the far-left. It is a masterclass in rightwing rabble-rousing, with its appropriation of the word “freedom”. Yet on press night at its British premiere, all that is summoned in response is nervous laughter, a chorus of coughs and a few loud whistles.Is this because audiences have heard about the furore around Tiago Rodrigues’s play and know what to expect, or is it something more insidiously British in its politeness? There could be a host of excuses: we know it is only theatre; we feel disconnected from fascism in a way thataudiences in Germany– or in Portugal, where the production is from – may not. Or is it simply that we want to hear the character out?Jeers, walkouts, stage invasions: will Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists trigger British audiences too?Read moreThe politician takes the floor at the end. The central drama features a family that kidnaps and kills a single “fascist” on an annual basis as a ritual protest against the far right. Characters wear old-fashioned dresses and shawls (including the men) and speak in peculiarly comic tones, so they look and sound like Lorcan parodies. They are all called Catarina too, to honour the original Catarina, a protester murdered at the hands of President António de Oliveira Salazar’s authoritarian government in 1954, after which the family’s grandmothercommanded her family to take on these annual killings.If the point of the play is to compel an audience into action, we are Hamlet, immobilised. But it seems more complicated than that. Set in a near-future in which a far-right government is on the verge of changing the constitution in Portugal, its central ethical debate revolves around armed protest and the question of whether to suffer under fascism or to take arms against it. Every family member has abided by Catarina’s rule until one (Beatriz Maia) says she can’t justify it, and refuses to shoot.View image in fullscreenKidnap your enemy … the cast of Catarina and the Beauty of Killing Fascists, 2025.Photograph: Carlos FernandesThe justifications for political violence here are presented in pithy summaries, via English surtitles: “It is not enough to be against, you must act against,” says one character. “You cannot fight intolerance with tolerance,” says another.But there are so many other gnomic and mannered tics to the dialogue. Characters babble on about nothing, it seems. There are unfunny jokes about veganism (a pop at the “woke” left?) and a riff on the flight of swallows (the birds are later likened to immigrants by the politician). They flog the same arguments on violent protest. You wonder if it is a critique of the political left: that it can only talk on interminably or in-fight in the face of real fascist threat.And as post-dramatic theatre, aware of itself and refusing to cast fourth-wall illusions, it is a play of maddening inaction – the family member who won’t shoot, the drama that won’t give us any drama, or not until its final stretch.So it is arduous to watch, in spite of Fernando Ribeiro’s origami-like set of a slatted house, foregrounded by a dining table reminiscent of The Last Supper, that rearranges itself beautifully. Then, suddenly, the crushing boredom is punctured by the shock of gunfire and the politician’s speech. Have we been deliberately lulled into an almost soporific state?This paradox of boredom and shock might encapsulate the political juncture at which Europe stands, with AfD on the rise in Germany andPresident Le Penpotentially six months away in France. If so, is the play a starting-gun for those of us walking zombie-eyed, or wilfully blind, into a fascist future? The politician rattles on and on. He is not named but we know him. Do we wish him dead?AtDorfman theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreNational TheatrePolitical theatreThe far rightLondonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The amazing life of 101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser: ‘We made noise. We closed the streets’  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Sick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a day
Author: Claire Armitstead
Headline: Sick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a day
Content: ‘We were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce’ … Ce Roser in her studio in New York.Photograph: Dario Lasagni/Courtesy VeneKlasenView image in fullscreen‘We were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce’ … Ce Roser in her studio in New York.Photograph: Dario Lasagni/Courtesy VeneKlasenArt and designInterviewThe amazing life of 101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser: ‘We made noise. We closed the streets’Claire ArmitsteadSick of her friends getting nowhere, she co-founded The Women in the Arts Foundation and they protested across New York. Ahead of a UK show, Roser talks about escaping wartime Shanghai – and still painting three a dayTue 22 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn January of 1971, the American art historian Linda Nochlin published a landmark essay,Why Have There Been No Great Women Artists?It was a provocation and a call to arms that was to send shockwaves through the arts establishment.“It wasn’t just a problem for artists,” says Ce Roser, more than half a century on. “My older friends could not get shows, although they had had brilliant careers before, and that happened also to all of my friends who were poets or writers. Nobody seemed to be able to establish themselves as career artists. So we got together, we complained, and I decided we should have a meeting and really talk seriously about it.”That first meeting at Roser’s home in New York led to the establishment of theWomen in the Arts Foundation, which took to the streets to force a change in the status quo. As well as being a priceless witness to an activist movement that altered history, she is also making her own history at London’sVeneKlasen gallerythis month, as the first American artist to make their European debut as a centenarian.double quotation markJoan Mitchell appeared off the plane from France. Louise Bourgeois stood in front of MoMA holding a big sheet saying NOMeeting Roser over video link in herNew Yorkhome, everything about her is surprising: she is 101 but could pass for 30 years younger. She was born in the US to Chinese parents, but insists that she never experienced racial discrimination. She doesn’t buy the idea that female artists, herself included, are constantly reforgotten today, as they were in the past. Her memory is as sharp and bright as the art she continues to make in the studio where she has worked for more than 70 years.View image in fullscreenSharp and bright … Voyage into Discovery, 1990.Photograph: © Ce Roser. Courtesy VeneKlasen, New York and London.Of that formative moment in 1971 she recalls: “There was a school of thought that we’re middle-class women, and we are afraid to assert ourselves.” At first only a handful of people were involved, but by the third meeting, the artistElaine de Kooninghad offered her studio. “And by word of mouth, because they wanted to see Elaine’s studio, many more turned up, and we decided we would demonstrate.”The father of one artist was a police officer, who said he could close down 53rd Street in front of the Museum of ModernArt. “So we took advantage. We decided we were going to have a joyous demonstration. We were not going to be like the men and be fierce and aggressive. Of course, we were aggressive, but we weren’t fierce.”The protesters were an A to Z of art history as we know it today.Joan Mitchellappeared off the plane from France.Louise Bourgeoisstood in front of MoMA holding a big sheet with NO written on it.Pat Passlofbrandished a sign that declared: “MoMa loves Papa.” “We made a lot of noise. We danced in the street. We closed it off,” says Roser.The payoff came in 1973, with an offer from the New York Cultural Center to host a show curated by, and featuring, female artists. Roser was one of seven selectors who, in a radical break with tradition, devised a democratic system in which artists nominated each other. Featuring 111 artists, Women Choose Women washailed as a successthat promised women “a large and permanent share of the art world action”, while also proving the value and efficiency of new, democratic forms of curation.View image in fullscreen‘When I went into my studio, I felt like a hand going into a glove’ … Ce Roser in New York in the 1970s.Photograph: Carin Drechsler-Marx/Courtesy VeneKlasenBy the time of the protests, Roser was in her 40s, the widely travelled wife of a US diplomat, who had returned home because their son needed to go to school. “He was speaking Urdu, Tagalog, German, and no English for him to become an American,” she says.Roser herself was a third generation American – the granddaughter of immigrant farmers from China to California, where one grandfather had a hop farm. Her parents had met at university, where her father was studying law and her mother maths and history, and she was the second of six children born to the couple after they settled in Philadelphia. “I didn’t feel Chinese because I grew up in a culture where there were very few Chinese,” she says. “My parents ate American food for breakfast, and you can tell a lot by what people eat for breakfast.”She was introduced to the arts at an early age by a mother who would pay her children five cents for every poem they memorised, while keeping them quiet by sitting them down at the dining table with “lots of crayons and watercolours and paper”. But Roser had no inkling that art might be her vocation and, by 19, was working in the information department at the US embassy, where she met her husband. By 21 she was married and, on postings abroad, found herself hampered by “the many things foreign service wives were not allowed to do …”View image in fullscreenBrushwork of calligraphy… Garden of Delight, 1961.Photograph: © Ce Roser. Courtesy VeneKlasen, New York and London.Fortunately, on their third posting, to the Philippines capital Manila, a sympathetic friend lent her a paint set. “I did a painting from a photograph, and when my husband went to frame it, somebody wanted to buy it, so I decided it must be good,” she says.In the late 1940s the couple were sent to Berlin, where Roser joined the Berlin Art Academy and studied under the German sculptor and Holocaust survivorHans Uhlmann. She dismisses the suggestion that postwar Germany must have been a culture shock, saying that nothing could compare with what she had experienced as a teenager on a visit to an uncle in wartime China, when the family got trapped in Shanghai. “We rode on a boxcar for 40 days. My mother and my grandmother – no men – and my brothers and sisters, and four cousins she insisted upon bringing with us. So I was used to war-torn and bombed-out places.”Uhlmann, she says, “would make us draw a thing from reality and turn it into an abstraction, and take an abstraction and turn it into reality on paper.” He said one thing that she particularly cherishes: “When you paint, be very definite. Do not hesitate. Just do it.”Back in New York, she found the studio overlooking the Hudson River where she has worked ever since. “When I went into my studio, I felt like a hand going into a glove,” she recalls. “It wiped out the domestic. I didn’t cook, I didn’t clean. I was there to paint and do nothing else, though I would always also read. I restricted myself to art criticism, art history, or poetry. Nothing else.”In the bright abstract paintings on display in her retrospective, the rhythms of poetry combine with the brushwork of calligraphy, which she studied under the Japanese masterNankoku Hidai. Whereas Hidai taught her to paint in broad strokes, “and to use my arms instead of my wrists”, poetry remains a key source of inspiration. “You mention a line and I see a painting,” she says.Although her name isn’t as well known as it once was, she still paints away in her eyrie above the Hudson River, sometimes turning out two or three pictures a day, confident in the knowledge that she has works stowed away for posterity in all the New York institutions she once protested against.Ce Roser: Running with the Sun is at VeneKlasen, London, until 5 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtExhibitionsFeminismGenderProtestWomeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Swan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brother | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stage
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Amid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stage
Content: Charles Spencer's book in a London bookshop.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenCharles Spencer's book in a London bookshop.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersAutobiography and memoirReviewSwan Song by Charles Spencer review – a furious exercise in score-settling by Diana’s brotherAmid genuinely touching passages about his sister, the earl can’t help but put himself and his grievances centre stageEmma BrockesTue 22 Sep 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharles Spencer’s Swan Song, a memoir of his relationship with his sister, the lateDiana, Princess of Wales, is a fascinating document that tells us a little about Diana and a great deal about Charles Spencer – perhaps more than we needed to know. If that sounds snarky, after 400 pages of score settling, chest thumping, wild indiscretion and some truly touching passages about his late sister, the reader is left with a head-spinning story of the world that created Diana and a certain sourness at the manner in which it is told.Let’s start with the headlines in last week’s Daily Mail, the newspaper to whom Spencer sold serialisation of a book which includes a line describing tabloid journalists as “those who inhabit the murky swamps of malevolence, and who need to suck their victims dry of their souls”. Perhaps he meant a different set of hacks. Anyway the top line in the Mail was that, shortly after Diana’s death, King Charles insulted her in a phone call to Spencer: “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’” Your take on this quote will likely dictate how you receive the book, and here’s mine: I’m willing to believe the king behaved badly, but “hissed” is a red flag, one of those embellishments, like “snarled” or “flounced”, that writers tend to use to make those they’re writing about appear worse. Spencer, always the injured party, has so many axes grinding away in this book that at times it’s impossible to hear what he’s saying.Before we get to that, the question on everyone’s lips is: why write this book now? Spencer maintains it’s because, as the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death drew near, he kept being asked to contribute to other people’s projects. Rather than allow the narrative to be guided by “some TV producer” from a network “I will never watch” he promptly got on with his own. Likely that’s not the sole reason; elsewhere in the book he writes about how, back in the day, his father was always at risk of running out of cash to run Althorp, the family’s Northamptonshire estate, and one wonders if the present earl is having similar difficulties.Never mind. For fans of petty grievances, among whom I count myself, the book is an absolute corker of resentment, and in Spencer we have a hero who, decades after the fact, is still harping on about a great many things involving a large cast of characters who he has absolutely not forgiven for any of it. While telling the story of his and Diana’s relationship, there are drive-bys on Peter Carter-Ruck, Princess Michael of Kent, Princess Margaret, his three ex-wives, whom he describes in an amazing parenthetical take down as “all double divorcees”, and members of a police protection squad who, in 1986, let sniffer dogs jump all over his furniture.double quotation markSpencer writes that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtshipIf too many words are spent on, for example, the perfidiousness of Martin Bashir, I could read an entire book on the subject of Spencer’s horror at what his stepmother, Raine, did to the interiors at Althorp, including installing “exceptionally ugly double glazing”, “shiny velveteen” upholstery, and “unsightly wall-to-wall carpeting”. (This is before we get to the scene in which Raine, standing at the top of the staircase in search of breakfast, bellows to staff below, “where’s my fucking egg?”)Interspersed with these delights is a portrait of Diana that is affectionate, sad, and lovely in places. Spencer suffers the pain of the less famous sibling who doesn’t want to give up his own version of their childhood and there’s a stiffness to some passages as Spencer insists it was all less unhappy than the record implies. His portrait of their mother, Frances, feels like a useful corrective to a figure who has been publicly maligned, and who comes across in the book as the parent most responsible for Diana’s gifts: spirited, mildly eccentric, a more interesting character than the plodding males in the Spencer line. (Charles, winningly, allows that this is the case, pointing out that the men in his family have always been outclassed by the women.)And of course there is the devastating account of the coldness and aggression of the then Prince of Wales. Spencer tells us that Charles’s poor behaviour towards his sister began from the very start of their courtship, during which he commented on her weight, ignored her at parties and told her he didn’t love her, to the extent that, Spencer writes, Diana tried to get out of the engagement. Their father told her it was too late. This all chimes with other accounts of the doomed marriage, albeit in gorier detail, and explains the fury of Spencer’s finest hour, the speech he gave at Diana’s funeral in which he lambasted not only the press but the royals, reclaiming the young princes William and Harry for their mother’s “blood family”.At his best, in these passages, Spencer acts as a proxy for the rest of us by registering the absolute lunacy of those days after Diana’s death – by which I mean not the public outpouring, but the behaviour of the royal family, who remained deaf to the nation’s needs until they were forced to change course.“What was Prince Charles actually doing there?” writes Spencer, incredulously, in relation to his former brother-in-law’s prominent role at the funeral, pointing out to some comic effect that no one wants their “ex” at their funeral? Diana’s former husband was there because the young princes were there, walking for two miles behind their mother’s coffin while mourners wailed and shouted out at them, an outcome Spencer had vigorously argued against. Now, he writes flatly, “It all seemed mad to me – the more so as I began to appreciate the extent of the ordeal we had embarked on.”To be honest, at times in this book, they all seem quite mad. “That’s it ... it’s curtains ... Duch is dead,” Spencer reports his sister Jane as saying to him on the phone when news of Diana’s death was confirmed. Before the funeral, per Spencer’s account, Prince Charles wanted to walk behind the coffin in the middle, centre stage, until brought up short by his father, Prince Philip, who said words to the effect of don’t be so bloody silly, and put Charles Spencer in the centre, with the boys either side and Diana’s ex-husband and ex-father in law on the outside. There was a split second, writes Spencer, when it seemed as if the pall-bearers might buckle under the weight of Diana’s reinforced, lead-lined coffin. All of this is fascinating and Spencer tells it well.Still, the book suffers from problems of self pity and self regard (I won’t get into the passages about Spencer’s ADHD or the weasily justifications he gives for telling Diana, in her hour of need, that she couldn’t move into a property on the Althorp estate; the main house has 90 rooms). Every few chapters we return to the unfolding play-by-play of how he wrote his speech – the decision he made to substitute the word “power” for the word “strength”; how his oratory gathered, his greatness formed, and look, it was a fantastic speech, but at some point in the book you start to think, alright Alexander Hamilton, give it a rest. Before the funeral, Spencer visits Diana lying in her casket and reads out his speech to her, sensing that his dead sister is “applauding my words, with soft insistence”. Even here, Spencer manages to take centre stage.After the book’s litany of bitter grievances I came away wondering whether Spencer has been in the ear of his nephew Prince Harry these last few years. Mostly, however, I felt sadness for the insurmountable difficulties his sister faced marrying into that family. The king is peevish all the way through and Spencer is peevish right back at him. You come away feeling the pair thoroughly deserved each other. And in the middle Diana, 30 years dead, frozen in time and – as she ever was – at the mercy of other people’s interpretations.Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer is published by Michael Joseph (£28). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAutobiography and memoirDiana, Princess of WalesKing Charles IIIreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Miranda Richardson | Movies | The Guardian
