description: She has lit up screens large and small playing Ruth Ellis, Queen Victoria’s mother, Barbara Castle, and the hilarious Queenie in Blackadder. Alternatively, you could ask about birds of prey, orangutans or playing the cello
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: She has lit up screens large and small playing Ruth Ellis, Queen Victoria’s mother, Barbara Castle, and the hilarious Queenie in Blackadder. Alternatively, you could ask about birds of prey, orangutans or playing the cello
Content: Do you still practice falconry? … Miranda Richardson will answer your questions.Photograph: Mike Marsland/WireImageView image in fullscreenDo you still practice falconry? … Miranda Richardson will answer your questions.Photograph: Mike Marsland/WireImageFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Miranda RichardsonShe has lit up screens large and small playing Ruth Ellis, Rita Skeeter, Barbara Castle and the hilarious Queenie in Blackadder. Alternatively, you could ask about birds of prey, orangutans or playing the celloRich PelleyTue 22 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJudging by the size of her awards cupboard,Miranda Richardsonhas had quite the career. She won a Bafta for the 1992 psychological drama Damage, opposite Jeremy Irons, and Golden Globes for the 1991 historical drama Enchanted April and the 1994 Nazi thriller Fatherland, and was Oscar-nominated for both Damage and the 1994 historical drama Tom & Viv. Her other notable performances include IRA member Jude in The Crying Game, Ruth Ellis in Dance With a Stranger and Lady Van Tassel in Sleepy Hollow.View image in fullscreenQueen of puddings … Miranda Richardson as Queenie in Blackadder’s Christmas Carol, 1988.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyShe’s pretty handy at comedy, too – and probably just as familiar for playing acid-tongued Daily Prophet journalist Rita Skeeter inHarry Potterand the Goblet of Fire, the murderous chicken-farm owner Mrs Tweedy in Chicken Run and, of course, the gloriously unhinged Queenie in Blackadder II: “I may have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a concrete elephant.”Richardson initially considered becoming a vet before deciding on acting and training at Bristol Old Vic, graduating in 1979 in the same class as Daniel Day-Lewis. After starting out in repertory theatre and making her West End debut in 1981, she made her major film breakthrough as Ruth Ellis – the last woman to be hanged in Britain – in Mike Newell’s 1985 drama Dance with a Stranger. On set, she would entertain the crew by slipping into the voice of a screechy schoolgirl. A year later, having turned down the role in Fatal Attraction that eventually went to Glenn Close, she was merrily ordering executions, bickering with Nursie, fancying Lord Flashheart and tormenting Blackadder – using that same voice she’d invented on the set of Dance with a Stranger.She’s barely stopped since, with roles ranging from Barbara Castle in Made in Dagenham and Clementine Churchill in Churchill to Madame Tracy and Shax in Good Omens, and Emily in And Then There Were None. In 2003 she was nominated for a Bafta and a Golden Globe for her role as Queen Mary in The Lost Prince, before playing Queen Victoria’s mother in The Young Victoria, alongside Emily Blunt. In 2023, she returned as Mrs Tweedy in Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget. She now appears in The Yellow Tie, the biopic of Romanian conductor Sergiu Celibidache, playing his wife Ioana opposite John Malkovich as the older Celibidache.So what would you like to ask her when she sits for the Guardian reader interview? Did she have a favourite orangutan after earning an Emmy nomination for narrating Operation Orangutan? Does she still practice falconry, after getting hooked on birds of prey when sherescued a dazed kestrel as a child? How far did she get with thecello she began learning in her 50s? And whose head would she most like to see on a spike in Blackadder’s Traitor’s Cloister? Post your questions below by 6pm on Thursday 24 September and we’ll publish her answers as part of our readers interview series.The Yellow Tie is in cinemas from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewMiranda RichardsonHarry PotterAwards and prizesActingScience fiction and fantasy filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Terry Denton, beloved Australian illustrator best known for Treehouse series, dies aged 76 | Australian books | The Guardian
description: The illustrator and author ‘gave joy to millions of children around the world’, his family says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The illustrator and author ‘gave joy to millions of children around the world’, his family says
Content: Terry Denton (left) and children’s author Andy Griffiths. The pair worked together for three decades, with Griffiths saying Denton was a ‘true clown and much beloved’.Photograph: James Penlidis PhotographyView image in fullscreenTerry Denton (left) and children’s author Andy Griffiths. The pair worked together for three decades, with Griffiths saying Denton was a ‘true clown and much beloved’.Photograph: James Penlidis PhotographyAustralian booksTerry Denton, beloved Australian illustrator best known for Treehouse series, dies aged 76The illustrator and author ‘gave joy to millions of children around the world’, his family saysGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastGuardian staffTue 22 Sep 2026 04.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe beloved Australian illustrator and author Terry Denton, most famous for his work on the Treehouse series, has died aged 76.His publisher, Curtis Brown,released a statement on social mediasaying Denton died surrounded by his family on Monday.Denton was the author and illustrator of more than 30 of his own books, including the Gasp! series, which was adapted for screen.He also collaborated with authors including Mem Fox, Paul Jennings and Gillian Rubinstein.This ‘bum-poo-fart author’ is Australia’s biggest writer: Andy Griffiths on ending the Treehouse booksRead moreDenton’s children paid tribute to the illustrator whose work they said “gave joy to millions of children around the world”.“And after all those stories and all those lives he touched, he always came home to us.“We are so grateful that his stories will continue to live on, bringing wonder, laughter and comfort to generations yet to come and most especially to his beloved grandchildren, whoever will grow up knowing him through the magic he left behind.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAndy Griffiths, the author of the Treehouse series and a longtime friend and collaborator with Denton, said: “Working – and playing – with Terry over three decades has been an incredible honour and a pure delight.“I’ve never laughed so hard as I did when working with him, whether in the writing room or on stage. He was a true clown and much beloved – both in real life and as a character in the Treehouse series. Jill and I will miss him greatly.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGriffiths told theGuardian in 2023that he owed much of his success to the talented illustrator. When he first searched for a publisher, he had little luck but one took a punt on a textbook that was published in 1993 and was illustrated by Denton.Griffiths said that when they met for the first time, they recognised a streak of madness in each other that would fuel the next 30 years of work together.Denton is survived by his wife, Kristen, his children Max, Imogen and Eve, and his grandchildren Georgia, Lucy, Charlie, Alfie and Felix.Explore more on these topicsAustralian booksChildren and teenagersIllustrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brigitte Bardot’s personal items sell for nearly €1m at auction in Paris | Brigitte Bardot | The Guardian
description: Dog collars, guitars and self-portraits among 285 objects, with money going to her animal welfare foundation and son
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dog collars, guitars and self-portraits among 285 objects, with money going to her animal welfare foundation and son
Content: Brigitte Bardot in Paris in 1982. Thee auction of her personal belongings fetched almost 20 times its estimate.Photograph: Duclos/APView image in fullscreenBrigitte Bardot in Paris in 1982. Thee auction of her personal belongings fetched almost 20 times its estimate.Photograph: Duclos/APBrigitte BardotBrigitte Bardot’s personal items sell for nearly €1m at auction in ParisDog collars, guitars and self-portraits among 285 objects, with money going to her animal welfare foundation and sonGuardian staff and Agence France-PresseTue 22 Sep 2026 03.14 EDTFirst published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn auction of the French film star turned animal rights activist Brigitte Bardot’s personal items has fetched nearly €1m (£858,000, US$1.15m, A$1.61m) in Paris, almost 20 times the estimate, according to the auction house Millon.A total of 285 objects were auctioned, ranging from straw hats, sunglasses and nightgowns to tableware and furniture from Bardot’s homes in Paris and Saint-Tropez, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported.Bardot, who diedin December aged 91, retired from acting in the 1970s and became an outspoken campaigner for animal rights. She also becameincreasingly active politicallyon the far right, alienating some fans in her later life with her hardline views on immigration. Bardot was convicted five times for hate speech, particularly about Muslims, and up until her death she expressed her pleasure at the rising share of the vote gained by the anti-immigration National Rally party.The proceeds from the auction will go to her animal welfare foundation and to Nicolas-Jacques Charrier, her only child.Founded by the actor in 1986, the Brigitte Bardot Foundation says it has taken in 13,000 animals through four shelters and 150 partner facilities, supports 350 groups in France and operates in 70 countries.About 3,000 French and international bidders registered for the auction.“Brigitte Bardot has once again proved to be a remarkable alchemist: she transformed about €50,000 in estimates into nearly €1m, including fees,” the auctioneer Alexandre Millon said.Two dog collars, with an ID tag bearing Bardot’s name and a telephone number, estimated at €30 for the pair, sold for €9,400 to a Russian buyer.View image in fullscreenBardot’s widower has said her belongings should have been preserved as part of her legacy.Photograph: Urman Lionel/ABACA/ShutterstockA self-portrait fetched nearly €40,000 while the typewriter she used to write an autobiography raised €4,634.Estimated at between €300 and €500, two of her guitars soared to €8,600 and €1,900, while three stuffed toys representing baby seals sold for nearly €2,200.“This sale is the logical continuation of the one she herself organised in 1987 with her most precious belongings to create her foundation,” Ghyslaine Calmels-Bock, the managing director of the Bardot Foundation, told AFP after the sale. “Today, her fight continues through this auction.”Two days before the auction Bardot’s last husband, Bernard d’Ormale, deescribed it as a “joke”.“These are personal items,” he said. “Why hold this sale? For the animals?” He said it amounted to a “disrespect to Brigitte’s memory”.Her belongings should have been preserved as part of her legacy, he told AFP, adding that Bardot “would not have agreed to this sale”.The foundation rejected the criticism, saying the auction had been approved by the board in June when the widower was its president.D’Ormale said he had not understood the auction would involve such personal items.The dispute comes days after he was removed as head of the foundation, a role he had held since Bardot’s death.Explore more on these topicsBrigitte BardotFranceAnimal welfareEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Youth review – Sharon Horgan is back … and she’s better than ever | Television | The Guardian
description: This brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfect
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfect
Content: Is he, isn’t he? … Rupert Friend as Patrick with Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOView image in fullscreenIs he, isn’t he? … Rupert Friend as Patrick with Sharon Horgan as Alex in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewYouth review – Sharon Horgan is back … and she’s better than everThis brutal, hilarious new show about life as a fiftysomething is full of all the heart and humour of human life. At points it’s mesmerisingly perfectLucy ManganTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a moment in Sharon Horgan’s new show, Youth, when – as protagonist Alex (Horgan) is seeing her son off to university – she inadvertently begins to run after the car that’s taking him away. And then she catches herself, and slows. And then she starts up again. It was such a tender, vicious glimpse into the future that I found myself sobbing into the sofa and cursing her name.All of which is to say: Sharon Horgan is back and she’s better than ever. Youth is the representation every woman who has ever slapped on an oestrogen patch after a divorce, looked around and thought “What the hell now?” has been waiting for. Horgan herself has described it in interviews as forming the third part of a loose trilogy that began with Pulling. Co-written with Dennis Kelly, Pulling was about three thirtysomething antitheses to Bridget Jones, whose dark chaos apparently scared the BBC so much they unexpectedly cancelled it just as it was truly getting into its stride. That was followed by Catastrophe, written by and starring Horgan, with Rob Delaney, as a couple who have a fling, find that she’s pregnant and end up making a brutal, hilarious go of things.Youth is Horgan’s even more brutal, even more hilarious take on life’s third act. Alex is a fiftysomething literary agent and divorcee. She has ageing parents (losing toes to diabetes and faculties to early dementia) to the left of her, and a troubled child and useless ex-husband to the right. But hope springs eternal even in the most wearied breast and she is hoping to start dating again, and maybe even improve her standing at work, too, now that son Ruari (Aran Murphy) at least is off her hands for 10-week terms at a time.At her workplace, she explains her timetable to Sam (Sharlene Whyte), her friend and boss – or boss and friend (the fluctuating proportions and concomitant stresses and strains in their relationship is one of the many thickening agents Horgan has stirred into her rich stew). “I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person, tops. I need someone to fall in love with me now so there’s a bit of time left with this me before the old me is like ‘I’m here now’.” All she has to do is muster some “new dick energy” from somewhere, recover from a dislocating jaw (“Just an age thing!” her young doctor tells her), and stop crying as she clears up the smelly mess in Ruari’s room. Can she resist giving in to booty calls to and from her never-quite-boyfriend Patrick (Rupert Friend, perfectly written as a charming borderline cad), and stop finding older men’s wattle and sagging balls a turn-off?The wattle belongs to Michael (Tim McInnerny). The balls too, in fact, though it turns out they are still defying gravity at least as much as you can ever hope for testicles. This is discovered during a sex scene that should be entered into the pantheon of greats. Move over Basic Instinct, Wild Things, 9½ Weeks and whatever else counts as your formative memory, and make way for tears. “I just don’t know if there’s anything left to my life that I like any more!” wails Alex, as she negotiates cunnilingus instead. “I can’t return the favour. But I don’t know you well enough yet to be selfish in bed,” she notes, before deciding that a hand job will do.It is the mark of Horgan’s genius that Michael does not contribute to this decision. It’s absolutely not about him. And it’s a mark of how beautifully she writes all her characters and how well they are always cast that we know that Michael is not the kind to mind. He just waits cheerfully for his next instruction. And we know we want to see more of Michael (not literally – I’ll take his word for it about the balls) and that she should, too. But we do see the attraction of Rupert Friend – I mean, Patrick.At work, there is the deeply disgruntled former client Malcolm (Douglas Hodge), who has written a dreadful romantasy book (The Goblin Seed) that duly takes TikTok by storm and makes him an asset they need to reacquire. Then there’s a bestselling elderly author (Anne Reid) whose books have taken a porno-racist turn that may prove beyond her editors’ powers to save. Lastly, we meet a talented foreign writer, whom Alex is trying to bring on to her list without Sam finding out.And then Ruari comes home, under a cloud and soon permanently under a duvet, while Alex tries frantically to find out what is wrong.All of human life is here – all its heart, all its humour. That is Horgan’s beat. Not just the female bit, not just the perimenopausal bit (though there is no one more acute or funny on either). Her men, her children, her colleagues – they are as real, as rounded, as ridiculous (and at times heartbreaking) as we all are in reality. Not that Horgan’s talent for grotesques has deserted her – the publishing types satirised here are mesmerisingly perfect and awful – but she dwells in the truth always, and there is nothing more bitterly funny or compelling than that.Youth is on HBO MaxThis article was amended on 22 September 2026 to correct the spelling of Tim McInnerny’s surname.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewSharon HorganTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Nigella enters the Bake Off tent – and causes quite a stir | Television | The Guardian
description: Lawson sets the first challenges for the eager new contestants, with mixed results. Plus: the final episode of 70 Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Lawson sets the first challenges for the eager new contestants, with mixed results. Plus: the final episode of 70 Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: ‘Sumptuous!’ The Bake Off judges hear from a baker.Photograph: Patch DolanView image in fullscreen‘Sumptuous!’ The Bake Off judges hear from a baker.Photograph: Patch DolanTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Nigella enters the Bake Off tent – and causes quite a stirLawson sets the first challenges for the eager new contestants, with mixed results. Plus: the final episode of 70 Up. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Jack Seale,Phil HarrisonandPriya ElanTue 22 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Great British Bake Off8pm, Channel 4Nigella Lawson enters the tent as a new judge and all it takes is her saying “sumptuous” to crack Noel Fielding: “I think I might be pregnant.” Chocolate stout cake is the first task for the eager batch of bakers – with one of them daring to put a twist on Nigella’s own recipe. They then need to recreate a coffee and walnut cake from a picture, before doing their self-portrait cake showstoppers. You will gasp in horror at least twice.Hollie RichardsonRace Against the Tide7.30pm, BBC TwoIn its inherent ephemerality, sand-sculpting requires technical mastery, incredible patience and a philosophical acceptance of entropy. While Rachel and Athena race against the tide in this final episode, Yusuf and Johannes’s ambitious “journey through life” concept seems doomed even before the North Sea walks off with it.Ali CatterallEmergency 24/79pm, BBC TwoThe last visit, for now, to the NHS trauma team who always seem to tackle cases designed to show off their excellent organisational skills. This time it’s a man with alcohol withdrawal who might have deeper issues, plus two patients in their 80s whose broken bones cannot, because of their advanced years, easily be mended.Jack Seale70 Up9pm, ITV1View image in fullscreenSue takes a trip down memory lane in 70 Up.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVIt’s the final (ever) part of this epic, revelatory documentary series and, as befits a show that has spanned not only most of our lifetimes but also the lifetime of television as a mass medium, the tone is reflective. This time, we hear from Sue, Bruce, Jackie, Suzy, Peter, John and Andrew as they ponder mortality. Tissues at the ready.Phil HarrisonPaul C Brunson: Red Flag9pm, U&WThe early warning signs for Ellie and Gareth, who tell their stories in back-to-back episodes of this excellent series, were love bombing and subtle indications of possessiveness. While Gareth was financially and emotionally abused by his girlfriend, Ellie suffered sexual violence.Priya ElanTempting Fortune9.30pm, Channel 4“Why take the moral high ground when you could have three grand?” This quote sums up this adventure challenge hosted by Rob Beckett in which 12 strangers slog through the Malaysian rainforest, dreaming of a share of £300k but waylaid by temptations ranging from clean clothes to fast food. A show designed to bring out the worst in its participants.PHLive sportOne-Day International Cricket, England v Sri Lanka,noon, Sky Sports Main EventThe first in a three-match series, from Chester-le-Street.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightThe Great British Bake OfffeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Autumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and place | Kate Mosse | The Guardian
description: The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved Sussex
Author: Ruth Padel
Headline: The author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved Sussex
Content: A tunnel through trees near Chichester, West Sussex.Photograph: Patricia Hamilton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA tunnel through trees near Chichester, West Sussex.Photograph: Patricia Hamilton/Getty ImagesKate MosseReviewAutumn by Kate Mosse review – tender reflections on time and placeThe author of Labyrinth on the turning of the seasons and the lore and landscape of her beloved SussexRuth PadelTue 22 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKate Mosse’s new book is a love-song to West Sussex, part of a series designed to bring out its authors’ personal connections to a home landscape. It began last year, with Michael Morpurgo welcoming spring in Devon, where he has lived – at the farm that inspired War Horse – for over 50 years; and then Val McDermid celebrating winter in Scotland, where she grew up and still lives.Bernardine Evaristo will explore summer soon – but, meanwhile, we have Mosse, also deeply and endearingly rooted in her chosen patch.Mosse grew up in the village of Fishbourne. She now lives in Chichester, where she got to know her husband when they revised for A-levels in the shadow of the Bishop’s Palace, and held hands when she turned 17 on the day of the city’s annual Sloe Fair. Twenty-three years later, they celebrated her 40th there, with their children. Today, they live with his 90-something mother Granny Rosie – also “Sussex to her bones” – who remembers watching cattle herded in fields where a supermarket now stands.In Granny Rosie’s youth, “the link between tradition and the natural world was present in every part of everyday life”, and that connection is the real focus of Mosse’s book. She has spent nearly all of her 65 years in Sussex. HerLanguedoc trilogywas inspired by her time in the Aude city of Carcassonne, but it was Sussex that gave her a taste for the combination of landscape, history and storytelling that drives her books. The county’s folklore and countryside informed her gothic thrillerThe Taxidermist’s Daughter, and it was the backdrop for her memoir about family care-giving,An Extra Pair of Hands.Autumn gives us more of it. Walking under oak trees, Mosse pictures far off days when oaks were the only road signs. In her garden, she tells us that the Romans called wild cyclamen “earth truffle”, “believing that ill spells were ineffective where they were found”. If there is, at times, a touch of the guide-book in her telling, she wins your heart by the sheer joy she takes in the details.Mosse sets out what Sussex gave other writers, too. William Blake drafted Jerusalem in Felpham, then threw a drunk soldier out of his garden and was tried in Chichester for sedition (all because the soldier claimed he insulted the king). He was acquitted, but “never set foot in Sussex again”. John Keats was inspired by Chichester’s architecture to write The Eve of St Agnes; Hilaire Belloc became Sussex’s unofficial poet laureate; and James Joyce lived in Bognor Regis while writing Finnegans Wake.Above all, there is “the great Sussex writer”, Rudyard Kipling. I love imagining how that phrase will be read in India; but, in fact, Kipling wrote Kimwhile living in Sussex (where he moved to in the late 1800s). Just So Storiescameimmediately after, and in 1906 he made the village of Burwash the setting for Puck of Pook’s Hill.In the manner of Kipling, Mosse takes infectious delight in weaving her memories through bronze age camps, iron age forts, wetlands, the downs and the Devil’s Dyke, composing a hymn to Sussex’s countryside and braiding rambly byways of fact and legend with personal memories.She loves the place so much that you feel she would have written as joyfully about it at any time of year. But she takes autumn seriously as a season of transition, beginning with her first day at school. There she is, 60 years ago, on 1 September: “Four, rising five.” Her mother is waving goodbye and her world is about to expand. Then, she takes us through the ghosts of Halloween, Bonfire Night in Lewes and Harvest festival.By the time she gets to the last day of November, Autumn itself feels like a kind of harvest. Mosse sees it as a thank you for “the gift of home”. For the luxury of enjoying, intensely, the land where grandparents, children and grandchildren still gather; and for sun-dappled village Englishness. “I take a deep breath to try and capture my pleasure at simply being here.”Autumn by Kate Mosse is published by Hodder & Stoughton (£16.99). title: Doom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ Revolt | Fiction | The Guardian
description: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich prose
Author: Sandra Newman
Headline: This recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich prose
Content: Quirkiness and intensity … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonView image in fullscreenQuirkiness and intensity … AK Blakemore.Photograph: Sophie DavidsonBook of the dayFictionReviewDoom Painting by AK Blakemore review – a dazzling epic of the Peasants’ RevoltThis recklessly ambitious doorstopper follows the 16 days of England’s medieval uprising from a vast array of viewpoints, and in startlingly rich proseSandra NewmanTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAK Blakemore’s third novel tells the story of the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, when commoners of all classes – not only peasants, but merchants, servants, smugglers, and some local lords and officials – rebelled at the imposition of a poll tax and rampaged through southern England, burning records of debts, killing their oppressors and laying waste to their homes. The book closely follows the events of the rebellion’s 16 days, employing a vast array of points of view, including the young king Richard II, several of his courtiers, dozens of elements of the rebellious Commons, a porpoise and a runaway horse. The title suggests the novel’s portrayal of these events as an inevitable reckoning; a “doom painting” was a picture of the Last Judgment on the wall of a medieval church.As a book of this scope must be, it’s a doorstopper. As any novel by Blakemore will be, it’s dazzlingly rich in lexical glamour, and this is likely to be any reader’s lasting impression of the book. Sometimes it feels as if the author is out to use every word in the English language in a startling, aestheticised, puckish way that expands both the word and the world. The result can be joyously silly. Who else would give us slugs that “blurb their elementary forms from out of the undergrowth to begin a dank and toothlessfesta”, or “lunar-brilliantined mud”? But there is also gravity and passion here, especially when she intimately imagines the lives of the commoners: “they rise, to fry eggs in butter and pork fat; they rise, to whet knives on scarred stone; they rise, to braid the manes of their draught horses; they rise, to count arrows; they rise, setting aside their glitchy dreams of hairy stars and blue-skinned devils; they rise, fearful and powerful, into the bright day.” The cheekily anachronistic appearance of “glitchy” in this medieval scene is typical of Blakemore’s method. All forms of language, high and low, archaic and modern, are here. Her use of detail to convey a historical scene is also extraordinary: the barber’s chair where “a crowd has gathered beneath the ribboned pole to watch the draining of a cyst”; the brewer with “a grotty beard, chlorotic with hops, [that] hangs down almost to his belt”; or “the horseflies waltzing over the liquefying flesh of severed heads”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIf you have any political sensibility, the sweep of the revolt will draw you inBlakemore is less successful in the traditional novelistic areas of plot and character. The primary figure throughout is legendary rebel leader Wat Tyler. Historical accounts of Wat are few and unreliable, so a novelist has a lot of latitude. Blakemore makes him a mercenary traumatised and brutalised by the wars in France, and the details of this history fit well and feel appropriate. However, his actual personality fluctuates from scene to scene. Mostly he’s a coarse, unlettered bruiser, lovable for his simplicity. However, when he’s alone, he’s given to sensitive introspection, spending a lot of time assigning psychological explanations to his choices. In this mode, he’s completely apolitical, and his leadership feels like a tragicomic fluke. In other scenes, though, he expresses strong and coherent political convictions, and occasionally it seems his simplicity is only a mask he assumes to achieve his objectives. Other characters are similarly inconsistent or undefined, and while this doesn’t ruin the story, it does blunt its emotional force. We can’t feel that deeply about how Richard II was transformed by these events if he never came into focus for us in the first place.Another problem is that much of the dialogue feels like action-movie banter in medieval clothing. People say things like: “Is that a scruple? And here, I thought you thoroughly divested of those,” or reply to, “I’d sooner die,” with a jaunty “You very well might”. The tone is occasionally anachronistic enough that it feels like a wink to the reader, as when Wat says, “We’ll sleep when we’re dead”, or turns to a confederate to say: “Your auld mum certainly seems to think so … Because I swived her, see.” Blakemore imagines a romance between Wat and another storied leader of the rebellion, Jack Straw; this could have gone to interesting places if it were made more real. But the execution is cursory enough that it carries a whiff of “shipping” – the demand of 21st-century fandoms to see the heroes kiss. Since the book is generally meticulously realistic and historically appropriate, I was left unsure how these elements were meant to land. In some places, the gorgeous language masks any clash of tones or realities; in others, the narrative fails to meld.Despite these cavils, I very strongly recommend Doom Painting. If you have any sensitivity to language, you can romp around in its prose; if you have any political sensibility, the sweep of the revolt will draw you in. It recreates historical events extravagantly well and must have taken a colossal amount of research, yet it wears its scholarship lightly.It’s a beast and a challenge; in its quirkiness and intensity, it couldn’t be more interesting. In an era of safe bets and timid choices, here is a work of reckless ambition.Doom Painting by AK Blakemore is published by Granta (£20).
