title: ‘Addiction is not only caused by weak will’: how a talking pigeon got Czechia to face up to its alcohol problem | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudice
Author: Miloš Hroch
Headline: Director Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudice
Content: ‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Claw FilmsView image in fullscreen‘I see him and how beautiful he is’ … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother in If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Claw FilmsMovies‘Addiction is not only caused by weak will’: how a talking pigeon got Czechia to face up to its alcohol problemDirector Pepa Lubojacki’s heartbreaking film chronicles the lives of her brother as he struggles with drink and homelessness – and her own shame in the face of societal prejudiceMiloš HrochTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCzech film-maker Pepa Lubojacki originally set out to make a film about pigeons. What fascinated the 39-year-old director was that the grey birds are clearly beautiful and highly intelligent creatures, yet human cruelty towards them is socially acceptable in the way it isn’t towards, say, crows or magpies. “You can spot kids kicking and chasing pigeons while their parents cheerfully look on,” she says.The moral blind spot reminded her of the way that people looked at homeless people like her older brother and her cousins. “The public has learned to avert their eyes,” she says. “My cousin was declined care seven times with open wounds in the hospital, and finally, they had to amputate both of his legs.”The birds stayed in the title of her first documentary, one of the most widely discussed and critically lauded films to be released inCzechiain recent years. To make If Pigeons Turned to Gold, Lubojacki spent five years chronicling the lives of four family members on the streets of Prague. In search of answers for why her relatives ended up with addictions and without roofs over their heads, the film wades deep into intergenerational trauma: domestic abuse and the deaths of her biological father and stepfather.Shot mostly on iPhone, the film is narrated by a meme-like talking pigeon and animated family photos with AI voiceovers, including manipulated child portraits of Pepa and her brother. They provide flashbacks to their 90s childhood in prefab estates where “you could get all the drugs your heart desired”, as one of the opening scenes tells us.View image in fullscreenInnovative … the film uses AI to voiceover Pepa and her brother as children.Photograph: Wanda Kaprálová/Claw FilmsThe central focus is Lubojacki’s ever-evasive brother David, and the documentary includes peaceful moments of nostalgic bonding over a rap song, but also documents vicious cycles of alcohol withdrawal and relapse, as Lubojacki struggles to nurture adult David to functionality. It’s an especially pressing issue in Czechia, the home of the world’s most popular beer style in the pilsner, where taxation of alcoholic drinks is traditionally low and the rate of alcohol consumption one of thehighest in the world. (To make things worse, Prague has some of thelowest rates of affordable housing in the European Union.)“I was angry because of the systemic injustice,” Lubojacki says. “Police beat up my brother several times, but caring professions can cause violence too, when medical personnel refuse to treat unhoused persons like him because of their history of addiction.” She used to look up to David – a local skater hero who listened to hip-hop, and knew all the cool stuff – and the mission of her film is audiences can “see my brother how I see him and how beautiful he is, that addiction is not only caused by a weak will”.View image in fullscreenYoung skater hero … Pepa Lubojacki’s brother David.Photograph: Claw FilmsIf Pigeons Turned to Gold unfolds through diary entries, interspersed with footage of herself on the psychiatric ward where she was hospitalised during the making of the film and video-art sequences of her sinking deep in water. Some of the entries read like poetry: “I’m just a little strawberry seed in the sea, a drowned strawberry seed, in an attempt to change something that is not up to me to change.”“Written text is my primary language and is closer to my heart,” reveals Lubojacki, who also has ambitions as a writer. She was inspired by Ottessa Moshfegh, who writes “simply, almost mechanically, as if without emotions, and observes brutal things without pathos”, and Melissa Broder’s “loose narrative of free writing” on addiction.The central question the 110-minute film circles around is whether you can grieve someone who hasn’t died yet. According toone recent study, people sleeping rough on the streets die 16 years earlier than the rest of the population. “I believe we live in an epidemic of addiction,” Lubojacki says. But speaking about this epidemic without shame is difficult: “When I grew up, I felt isolated, as if I was the only one who had this problem – I couldn’t speak about it with anyone, as I was so ashamed.”View image in fullscreenPepa Lubojacki with the Berlinale documentary award for If Pigeons Turned to Gold.Photograph: Imago/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Relatives of people with addictions often suffer from a secondary trauma, as Barbora Bírová of Czech advocacy organisation Platform for SocialHousingpoints out. “If we understand homelessness as a situation, not as inner personal characteristics, it opens the way to solutions.”Lubojacki had feared rejection, but instead she received acclaim. What began as a student film has already won international recognition on the European film festival circuit. In February, it received the Berlin film festival’s documentary award for “remarkable achievement in recruiting documentary into sustained practice of radical empathy”; at the Karlovy Vary film festival in July, it received a five-minute standing ovation; last month, it was selected as the Czech Republic’s official submission for the 99th Oscars in the International Feature Film category.Hundreds of people have got in touch with Lubojacki to share similar family stories. In her film, pigeons won’t turn to gold or even silver because they are what they are: Lubojacki herself undergoes transformation over the course of the film, from moralising her brother “why don’t you do it for me or mom?” to understanding and acceptance. “Since I understood what was going in his brain, and how I should respond, we have the best relationship we ever had.” The empathy Lubojacki has received gives her hope that people like her brother matter. “We learned to avert our eyes but if one breaks the silence, others will follow.”Explore more on these topicsFilmHomelessnessCzechiaHousingPovertySocial exclusionEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Heresy review – feminist folk horror summons something scary in the woods with supply of fresh blood | Horror films | The Guardian
description: A childless woman flees into the forest and emerges with a swollen belly in director Didier Konings’ short, sharp fable
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: A childless woman flees into the forest and emerges with a swollen belly in director Didier Konings’ short, sharp fable
Content: Dark intensity … Anneke Sluiters in Heresy.Photograph: GrimmVisionView image in fullscreenDark intensity … Anneke Sluiters in Heresy.Photograph: GrimmVisionHorror filmsReviewHeresy review – feminist folk horror summons something scary in the woods with supply of fresh bloodA childless woman flees into the forest and emerges with a swollen belly in director Didier Konings’ short, sharp fablePhil HoadTue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore fertility tourism, the only option for your average medieval serf struggling to conceive was heading to the nearest foreboding woods and summoning weird, antlered dryads. Or so it seems from Didier Konings’ short but memorable folk-horror debut, in which wide-eyed villager Frieda (Anneke Sluiters) flees into the trees after escaping an attempted rape by local butcher Gelo (Léon van Waas). He has already told her, after scoffing a pig foetus, that he likes his meat weak and defenceless.The dryads beat IVF hands down. Previously chided for her lack of childbearing by husband Hikko (Len Leo Vincent), Frieda emerges with a swollen abdomen. But the villagers fear it is the devil’s work, especially after finding Gelo in the woods, dismembered but freakishly still conscious. That’s about the extent of the story here, but Konings pares the focus effectively down to the essentials of this obscurantist hole: the crawling fear of evil among the villagers, and the necessary projection of it on to everything outside their control – female bodies and emotions, the natural world. Though her character verges on symbolic, Frieda – as well as the “wise women” of the forest, as per the original Dutch title – allow this fable’s feminist credentials to howl out unmistakably.The flipside of this suspicion and hate is Frieda’s ecstatic embrace of nature, par for the pagan course for folk-horror films. Conveying this surrender, Konings taps the sap of his background in concept art and VFX in a few miasma-wreathed, almost Dionysian trip sequences. Alternating between a dark intensity and an authentic grimness elsewhere that’s ingrained in the dialogue, this visual sharpness lends an extra edge in what would otherwise be familiar hoary witch-hunt territory. With the folk-horror gods requiring a constant supply of new blood, on this fervent evidence Konings could shape up as a possible successor to the likes of Robert Eggers and Ari Aster.Heresy is on digital platforms from 28 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Babystar review – a new arrival upends camera-ready life in disturbing family influencer satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Every ethical issue surrounding parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods for money is raised in Joscha Bongard’s debut, but it releases the dysfunctional tension too easily
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Every ethical issue surrounding parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods for money is raised in Joscha Bongard’s debut, but it releases the dysfunctional tension too easily
Content: Phones at the table … L to r, Liliom Lewald, Maja Bons and Bea Brocks in Babystar.Photograph: Jakob Fliedner/PRView image in fullscreenPhones at the table … L to r, Liliom Lewald, Maja Bons and Bea Brocks in Babystar.Photograph: Jakob Fliedner/PRMoviesReviewBabystar review – a new arrival upends camera-ready life in disturbing family influencer satireEvery ethical issue surrounding parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods for money is raised in Joscha Bongard’s debut, but it releases the dysfunctional tension too easilyCath ClarkeTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen teenager Luca (Maja Bons) wants to watch the film of her birth, she finds it on YouTube. Same with the sweet, thoughtful chat her mum gave her about periods when she was nine or 10; it was filmed in the family’s podcast studio. None of life’s special moments go unmonetised in this satire fromGermany, a horror story of family dysfunction. It’s a look at the dark side of the family influencer industry, raising just about every possible ethical question about parents vlogging their kids’ childhoods, and it’s impressively disturbing, up to a point.Sixteen-year-old Luca is the only child of Stella (Bea Brocks) and Chris (Liliom Lewald), social media stars who make viral videos of their perfect-looking family life for their 4 million followers. They live in a beautiful, sterile minimalist home in the countryside, and we often watch them through CCTV cameras fitted in every room. Shrewdly, first time film-maker Joscha Bongard doesn’t portray Stella and Chris as monsters; they love their daughter Luca, who they affectionately call Nunki. But fundamentally they do their best parenting in front of the camera, all bright smiles and proud affectionate glances.One day the couple tell Luca that they’re thinking about having another child. It’s hard to know what to make of this. Do they want a baby, or to increase branding opportunities with pregnancy and baby content? Their daughter hates the idea. Bons gives a brilliantly subtle performance as Luca, her face almost blank apart from twitches of tension in her cheek. Her mum wants to do a video about Luca’s feelings about the new baby; after all, personal videos get the most clicks. But Luca rebels and moves out. It’s a shame that all the tension and claustrophobia trapped in the house follows her out the door – and the last section of the film is a bit mannered by comparison.Babystar is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsDrama filmsSocial mediaComedyDigital mediaGermanyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nimesh Patel on stand-up, Palestine and politics: ‘The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly’ | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism
Content: Nimesh Patel: ‘I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok.’Photograph: Andrew LevyView image in fullscreenNimesh Patel: ‘I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok.’Photograph: Andrew LevyComedyInterviewNimesh Patel on stand-up, Palestine and politics: ‘The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly’Radheyan SimonpillaiThe comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimismTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a single minute in Buy the Dip, Nimesh Patel’s newNetflixcomedy special, in which the comedian nimbly and hilariously goes from describing his wife in labour with their first child to complaining about a Rolex sporting doctor wearing “insurance payments on his wrist” toLuigi Mangione. “He killed one guy, allegedly,” Patel quips, arguing that the terrorism-related charge Mangione got stuck with (which a judgedismissed) was offensive to real terrorists.The hilarious bit is impressive for how much Patel packs into a single minute and how much it all speaks to the comedian’s own experience, expertise and worldview.John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’Read morePatel, who hails from New Jersey, was once a pre-med finance graduate from New York University. He entertained going into healthcare before joining the ranks of finance bros. He abandoned all of that when he found a path in comedy alongside the likes ofHasan MinhajandRami Malek, a generation of brown guys who came of age in the shadow of 9/11 and have had to grow up being associated with Al-Qaida by the most racist swaths of American society. Patel is maybe the only one of them who could land that punchline about Mangione, which exists in the exact same intersection as him: of healthcare, finance and charges of terrorism that don’t stick.“It wasn’t by design that I was going to condense all that into that bit,” Patel says, humbly, on a Zoom call from his home in Brooklyn, New York. “It just so happened that that’s where my brain goes.”The words “it just so happened” gets at Patel’s magic trick as a comedian. In Buy the Dip, and across a lot of his comedy foundonline, Patel maintains the most laidback, effortless and unbothered vibe. He’s the kind of stand-up who makes it genuinely seem as though he’s floating along and the jokes just so happen to make their way to him.Patel understands that passive air to be both a feature and a bug. Throughout our conversation he looks back at moments in his life and career, at times with regret, where he “didn’t deal well with adversity” (he gave up on pre-med after getting a C in one class) or he let fate decide his life choices for him. On the latter front, for instance, Patel lost his job in finance in 2016, at the same time thatChris Rockdiscovered him at the Comedy Cellar in New York, where he had been performing and honing his craft for years.“It was a very star-aligning kind of a moment,” says Patel, looking back at how the decision to commit full-time to comedy was made for him. Rock tapped the newly unemployed Patel to write for his hosting duties at the2016 Oscars, which led to, among other things, Patel becoming the first Indian American to join the writer’s room at SNL, where he lasted a single season that nabbed him an Emmynomination.“I’ll happily admit that I was not good at those jobs,” he adds. “I was still finding and having to cultivate my own voice. I have my own way of delivering my jokes in my worldview. To then recalibrate that and figure out how someone else would say it is actually a pretty difficult thing. Some of those joke writers are the best joke writers on the planet, but I’m a very good stand-up.”double quotation markI’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the faceNimesh PatelThrough our conversation, Patel’s brain regularly goes to finance, whether he’s crunching the numbers on ticket sales growth at his shows (“I might have been the first comedian that proved that you could sell tickets via TikTok”) or casually dropping a reference to Apple and Nvidia’s stock growth while calculating what he sacrificed (a $125,000 payday) when backing out of the Saudi Arabia-sponsoredRiyadh comedy festivallast year. “I’ve said and I stated, if it was more money, I definitely would have gone,” says Patel, being bluntly honest about the accounting that would trump hismoral discomfortwith a festival sponsored by the Saudi Arabian government.Even the title to his special, Buy the Dip, is a finance phrase for buying stock while it’s low, which Patel wields playfully. On the one hand, it’s a reference to Donald Trump’s corruption, a big talking point in the special. Over the past year, the president’stariffswreaked havoc on the stock market. In April 2025, Trumppostedadvice to followers on his social media platform Truth Social to buy stock, hours before he announced a pause on tariffs that saw stocks bounce back. “You can’t say ‘buy the dip’ after causing the dip,” says Patel, sounding exasperated. “It seems illegal.”But for Patel, “buy the dip” holds an alternative meaning.“I have a kid,” says Patel. “I’m trying to remain an optimist in this world that tries to shake down optimism and punch it in the face. ‘Buy the dip’ is such an optimistic phrase. It says things will get better. You just gotta believe. Sometimes things get bad but if you, if your thesis remains the same, if you have conviction, you will be rewarded.”Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates parenting while prodding at the broken healthcare system, Maga and anti-immigrant sentiments, all while maintaining that hopeful and yet still unbothered vibe I’ve seen in his social media clips.View image in fullscreenNimesh Patel in Netflix’s Buy the Dip.Photograph: NetflixPatel first landed on my radar because TikTok’s algorithms served me aviral crowd-work clip, recorded at New York’s Comedy Cellar in 2018, when the comic was interacting with an Israeli musician who said he makes “progressive rock”. In one of those moments where a joke just seemed to materialize on the spot, Patel asked what Israeli progressive rock would sound like, before miming guitar play and singing, “Free Palestine”. The room erupted. Even Patel, in that moment, was visibly astonished at how he came up with that.“That clip has had a long shelf life,” says Patel, sharing regret that the joke has only grown more relevant in the years since and that he wasn’t more prepared to go in-depth at the time. In that 2018 interaction, Patel claims ignorance onIsrael’s war on Gaza, and shrinks from taking a stand on the issue. “I wish, at that time, I had more of a knowledge base about the conflict to really dig in on it.”Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’Read more“It should be obvious,” adds Patel, speaking to his position on the matter over the years since. “It should be obvious what my position is because the instant you see the genocide in Gaza, as a brown person, [you know] that is the position of the oppressed.”Patel, whose wife is Jewish, is much more pointed on the issue in Buy the Dip. He has a bit where he speaks out against making false equivalencies between Judaism and the Israeli regime. But then he can’t resist trolling with a punchline knowingly predicated on that very same false equivalency. “When it hits,” says Patel, “it hits really hard.”I push back on the idea that Patel’s position on Israel and Palestine, as a brown person, should be obvious, because there are so many brown people who do support Israel’s actions. Patel gets that. He points to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, as an example. Modi, who is accused by many of stoking violent Islamophobia with his Hindu nationalist rhetoric, is a staunch ally to Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu. Though Patel himself is wary of prescribing Islamophobia as the reason behind their alliance. “It is very interesting and confusing partnership on the surface of it. If it’s based in Islamophobia, that seems very superficial.”“I find it funny that religious people really forget their religion when they start talking about other people’s religions,” says Patel, whose dives into his upbringing within a devout Hindu family in his material. “It’s like the tenet of the Gita to love everybody and treat everybody equally. The way that religion’s been weaponized is ugly.”Throughout Buy the Dip, Patel navigates the ideological rifts between himself and other south Asians. It’s his burden, as an Indian American, as a Patel even, to put some distance between his demographic at large and those whose views or prejudices he doesn’t share.Kash Patel, the FBI director whom the comic refers to as Trump’s brand of DEI (“dick-eating Indian”), is a prime target.Patel – Nimesh, that is – is also compelled to clock and respond to a rise in anti-Indian sentiment, which he tells me he’s witnessed in videos and online commentary coming from Canada and the US. The situation reared its head just over a week ago whenBo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner,posteda viral photo on X of students celebrating the University of Texas’s college football win against Ohio State University. A number of the joyful students in the photo appeared to be of south Asian descent. French, in that post and a subsequent post,decriedthat foreigners were displacing Americans. On Saturday, after my conversation with Patel, the US Department of Education’s X account seemed to piggyback on French’s sentiments,postinga photo of the crowd at a University of Texas game with the slogans “make college football great again” and “make education great again”.“Most of those students are probably Indian American,” says Patel. “Those kids likely represent some of the best students in Texas. And they are Americans. They’re rooting football on. They’re drinking beers. What could be more American than that?”Nish Kumar: Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy review – enraged and extremely funnyRead morePatel then plays devil’s advocate, speaking directly to the folks who are mad at the sight of Indians, whose anti-immigrant fury is stoked by partisan politics without self-reflection.“The H-1B program in America was signed into law by [George] Bush, the first one,” says Patel, demanding they address the root cause instead of the symptom. “Corporatists taking over the country wanted cheaper labor that was beholden to the visa. These companies hire people who effectively have a gun to their heads, because if they don’t work, they can just be shipped back.“I don’t agree with not letting people in at all. Every place is richer and better because of immigrants and what they bring to the countries that they go to. But if you have a problem with immigrants –and you shouldn’t have problems with immigrants – you should be addressing the people on both sides that foster that situation in the first place.”Patel than takes a step back, turns the lens back on himself and his wider audience, and situates the relationship between the two in this conversation about what it means to be American.“[Buy the Dip] is probably the most Indian special I’ve put out. It’s Indian in that everything is rooted in an Indian POV. But it’s also deeply American, and I think very universal. I hope people see the optimism in it and take something special away for themselves.”Buy the Dip is out onNetflixnowExplore more on these topicsComedyNetflixUS televisionTelevisionSaturday Night LiveinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fancy a pint … at Lidl? The bizarre battle over Northern Ireland’s stifled nightlife | Music | The Guardian
description: The country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancing
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: The country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancing
Content: ‘I was shocked at how things were regressing’ … Holly Lester and Boyd Sleator, who are campaigning for reform to Northern Ireland nightlife.Photograph: Niall MurphyView image in fullscreen‘I was shocked at how things were regressing’ … Holly Lester and Boyd Sleator, who are campaigning for reform to Northern Ireland nightlife.Photograph: Niall MurphyMusicFancy a pint … at Lidl? The bizarre battle over Northern Ireland’s stifled nightlifeThe country’s licensing laws mean the supermarket has opened a pub so it can sell alcohol, while campaigners are fighting to help other venues open and get people dancingDavid RenshawTue 22 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt first sight The Middle Ale in Dundonald,Northern Irelandlooks just like any other pub. There is a big TV, an array of seating, and beer pumps behind the bar. Look a little closer, however, and you might ask why there are packets of fajitas and gravy granules on the walls.That’s because the pub belongs to the supermarket chainLidl, but the Middle Ale (like “middle aisle”, get it?) isn’t just a wacky marketing stunt. Northern Ireland has ultra-strict laws around licences to sell alcohol, whether as a shop, pub or nightclub. Lidl tried to get a licence to sell alcohol in its Dundonald store, and was refused, but after a court battle it did manage to get a licence for a pub – which it duly opened next door, selling alcohol to take away as well as serving drinks in the pub itself.It’s an absurd chapter of a much bigger story: local activists have long demanded licensing reform that could invigorate Northern Irish nightlife.The Lidl pub situation exposed “the hypocrisy of everything we’re up against,” says Boyd Sleator. In 2021, Sleator and Belfast-based DJ Holly Lester co-founded Free the Night, a charitable organisation formed in 2021 with the aim of creating a safe and progressive nightlife in Northern Ireland.Research conducted by Free the Night claims that obtaining an alcohol licence in Northern Ireland costs, on average, £75,250, but they say they have heard of sums up to £1m changing hands. This is because the current “surrender principle” means that any new pub or club must buy an existing licence from another establishment, a unique “one-in, one out” law. It must also prove an inadequacy of licensed premises to serve the local community.According to the BBC, The Middle Ale cost Lidl more than £500,000 and took six years of planning, numbers that Sleator and Lester say expose the barriers facing those keen to open new venues in the country. “[That’s] something no local can do,” claims Sleator. “In a way I’m glad they did it because it helps us expose how shit the current system is.”There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Lidl. The company did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Gordon Cruikshanks, managing director for Lidl Northern Ireland, previously told the BBC that the pub “was the best option to be able to provide the community in Dundonald with our full range of products”, but any changes to licensing laws were “for others to continue to discuss”.View image in fullscreenLidl pub The Middle Ale in Dundonald, Belfast.Photograph: Lidl/PAFree the Night is mounting a legal challenge over the minister for communities’ decision to reject a 2025 independent review of liquor licensing conducted by the University of Stirling. Key among Free the Night’s aims is a comprehensive review of alcohol licensing legislation, including the removal of the surrender principle. Northern Irish musicians including Bicep, David Holmes and Max Cooper signed an open letter outlining their demands.In a statement, the Department for Communities told the Guardian: “As legal proceedings are ongoing; it would be inappropriate for the Department to comment.”Lester began work on Free the Night during the pandemic when she lost her DJ gigs and returned home to Belfast. “I was shocked at how things were regressing,” she says. “The nightlife ecosystem seemed to be in a worse position than when I’d left eight years previously.”Lester says she finds the night-time economy in Northern Ireland to be “incredibly restrictive” because there are “basically no venues here”. Strict closing times are also problematic, meaning promoters are “trying to cram everything into this very small time frame”. The knock-on effects mean that promoters are less able to attract international talent while also struggling to give opportunities to local talent.Both point to Ulster Sports Club, a historic venue that closed in 2018 before reopening under new management a year later, as an example of one thriving Belfast venue. Bands including English Teacher and Mary in the Junkyard have played there while its 3am weekend closing time offers an opportunity for late-night partying.Sleator has a background in human-rights advocacy, including work around abortion rights and same-sex marriage. He is used to butting heads with the local authorities and speaks of a culture that cares more about the past than the future. “We’ve got an incredibly divided government who still only care about green and orange [traditional Nationalist and Unionist] issues,” he says. The pair also can’t help feeling that their dream of 24-hour clubbing is a little too utopian for those in government. “There’s an attitude of ‘You shouldn’t be shaking your hips, that’s the devil’s work’,” Sleator says with a grim chuckle.One key aim of Free the Night is to give musicians the spaces they need to thrive. The current lack of these has created a “creative drain”, they say. Their research shows that 70% of creatives had thought about leaving Northern Ireland, with 60% actually making the move.View image in fullscreenAn event at Belfast’s AVA festival.Photograph: The Hype Factory/PRDJ Or:la, who signed Free the Night’s open letter, says she has “harboured a real frustration with the licensing laws and lack of venues across the country” since she was a teenager. She has felt “pushed out” in her bid to pursue a career in music and now lives in Liverpool.“It’s clear that Belfast and Northern Ireland more broadly are not yet seen as nightlife destinations in the way that cities such as Berlin, Amsterdam and others across the UK are,” she says. She adds that while Northern Ireland is “flourishing in many areas” its nightlife “seems to be moving backwards”.‘You can let your inner freak out!’: welcome to Pixelate and the growing craze for internet-culture ravesRead moreA court date originally scheduled for mid-September has been delayed as Free the Night requires extra funds to continue its legal action. Free the Night believes that the authorities are overlooking the opportunities that a thriving nightlife economy could bring.“We see clubs and live music venues as spaces that can break down prejudices,” Sleator says. He cites his time raving in the 90s as proof of how music can bring people together. “There’s a lot of stuff in Northern Ireland which is like, ‘Let’s get Catholics and Protestants into a room together …’ We were just going there organically. I think that that’s where a lot of peace-building happened.”Explore more on these topicsMusicBelfastNorthern IrelandPubsClub cultureDance musicLidlnewsShareReuse this content

title: The truth about Sean Combs: ‘No is not a stopping point for him’ | Sean ‘Diddy‘ Combs | The Guardian
description: Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-ins
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-ins
Content: ‘He lives in different versions for different people, but who is he?’ Combs in at the  Cannes film festival in 2008.Photograph: Eric Gaillard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘He lives in different versions for different people, but who is he?’ Combs in at the  Cannes film festival in 2008.Photograph: Eric Gaillard/ReutersSean ‘Diddy‘ CombsThe truth about Sean Combs: ‘No is not a stopping point for him’Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, was as shocked as anyone when allegations of rape and sexual abuse were made against the music mogul. Then she began digging into his past life. In her first interview, she paints a horrifying picture of lost police reports, repeat behaviours, rumours and run-insAnna MooreTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Cheyenne Roundtree, an investigative reporter at Rolling Stone, the civil lawsuit that dropped on Sean “Diddy” Combs in November 2023 seemed to come from nowhere. Filed by his ex-partner, the singer Cassie Ventura, it alleged that Combs had beaten and raped her, plied her with drugs and forced her into sexual encounters with male sex workers throughout their decade-long relationship.Roundtree, along with much of the world’s media, was shocked. “I’d grown up in the era of Diddy and Cassie and viewed them as this power couple,” she says. “Her hit Me & U was my song. Diddy was this mogul – I knew him for the music – and she was this style inspiration, this beautiful, talented woman living an amazing life.”At first, Combs and his legal teamissuedblanket denials. The lawsuit, they said, had followed an attempt by Ventura to blackmail Combs, and was “riddled with baseless and outrageous lies”. Despite this, they settled it immediately with a $20m sum, but within days more women came forward. A second lawsuit was filed one week after Ventura’s, by Joi Dickerson-Neal, which alleged that, as a student in 1991, she had been drugged and raped by Combs, who had filmed the alleged assault and shared it with other men. Days later came another. In this, Anna Kane alleged that Combs and two others had gang-raped her in 2003 when she was 17. As the cases piled up, Combs’s team continued the denials – describing the lawsuits as “money grabs”. Then a leaked video forced them to change tack. Security footage from a Los Angeles hotel taken in March 2016 showed Cassie Ventura creeping from a room, pursued by Combs, who is wrapped in just a towel. He beats her, kicks her and drags her back.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment’ … Cheyenne Roundtree.Photograph: Maria Spann/The Guardian“His attorneys took it head on,” says Roundtree. “They were saying: ‘We’re going to own the domestic violence, but that happened in the past – all that is locked in the 2010s and he has changed.He has become Lovesince then. [Combs had declared in November 2017 that he was renaming himself Love, or Brother Love.] He’s a new person, a father figure.’ But all these other lawsuits were telling a completely different story.”Roundtree started digging through the archives, finding stories, interviews and police reports lost to time, often because they weren’t online. Over the next three years, she spoke to people who had known Combs at every stage of his life – as a boy, a teenage intern, a genius producer and the founder of Bad Boy Records, a Grammy-winning artist, a business mogul – and finally as an inmate in a New Jersey prison. The lawsuits led to a federal investigation and, eventually, Combs’s indictment. Now 56, he is serving a 50-month sentence for transporting people across state lines for prostitution.View image in fullscreenCassie Ventura with Combs at her 21st birthday party in September 2007, at the Jet nightclub at the Mirage on Las Vegas Boulevard.Photograph: Denise Truscello/WireImage“To me, he was always ‘Diddy’,” says Roundtree. “When I talk to anyone from New York, he’s Puff or Puffy. Later, he wanted the world to call him Love and now, in this legal sense, he has become Sean Combs. He lives in these different versions for different people, but who is he?” Her book, Bad Boy for Life, attempts to answer this by picking out the patterns and repeat behaviours, the rumours and run-ins that have threaded through every reinvention. It reads like a “making of a monster”, a damning indictment of celebrity culture, where every impulse, however dark, is enabled by yes men. “I never planned to write a book but I was finding so much material, it felt important to preserve all the history in one place,” she says. “I wanted to show how all the little dots on the timeline brought us to this moment.”It begins in Harlem where Combs spent his first years, and where his father, a gangster, was shot dead when Combs was a toddler. His mother, Janice, moved them to Mount Vernon, a suburb of Westchester County, just north of New York City. The Janice remembered by Combs’s childhood friend Tim Patterson cuts a formidable figure – glamorous, determined and ambitious. Patterson describes discipline that goes beyond “tough love”, and wild parties where it was normal to walk in on couples “butt naked”.View image in fullscreenA mugshot of Combs after his arrest by New York Police Department; he was charged in 2001 with possession of a firearm following a shooting at a Manhattan nightclub.Photograph: Donaldson Collection/Getty Images“His childhood leaves questions that only Combs and Janice can answer,” says Roundtree, “but the sources from that time said that being exposed to sexual things quite young, parenting style and growing up in Harlem meant that, by the time he was a teenager at Howard University, you’re seeing that something had manifested.”Janice Combs has complained of “lies” and “inaccuracies” in how she and her son’s upbringing have been portrayed.At Howard, studying business, Combs was well known – for his drive, his style and his legendary parties. Years later, he also described falling in love at Howard, in an ill-fated Romeo and Juliet-style affair. In a magazine interview, Combs said his girlfriend’s parents disapproved because her grades had dropped from As to Bs. They pulled her from Howard, allowing her back only if she ended the relationship. “That hurt so bad. It’s one of those things in life that everybody goes through, but the pain was so intense it was hard for me to handle,” he said.Former classmates remember it differently. In their accounts to Roundtree, Combs was jealous and abusive. His girlfriend’s parents intervened, they said, only after Combs had shown up at her dorm, called her outside, whipped her with his belt and dragged her by her hair, while students watched horrified from their windows.“The way he romanticised all that, and talked about her as if they were destined by the stars but forces kept them apart, was exactly how his attorney talked about Cassie decades later,” says Roundtree. “In the trial last year, the attorney called Combs’s relationship with Cassie ‘a great modern love story’.”The pages of Bad Boy for Life are packed with allegations, many involving women who have since launched civil suits. (Up to 70 lawsuits are believed to be moving through the system.) There are common features: one-night encounters where drinks are spiked, a woman is raped, and the alleged abuse is filmed, and others that tell how Combs would single out a woman and pursue her relentlessly using any means necessary. (“No is not a stopping point for Combs,” says Roundtree.) He was known for his untamed rage. Many former friends and colleagues describe witnessing his assaults on girlfriends – and on any men deemed rivals.View image in fullscreenCombs in a recording studio in 1997.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesRoundtree also shines a light on other criminal activities in his orbit, from long-forgotten police reports to the notorious murders of his protege Biggie Smalls and Biggie’s rival, Tupac Shakur. Again, she picks out parallels. In 2001, after a shooting inside a Manhattan nightclub, Combs was charged with thepossession of illegal weapons and attempted bribery(it was alleged that he had offered his driver $50,000 to take the blame). By then, at 31, Combs was already a multimillionaire with a record label, a fashion brand and a celebrity girlfriend, Jennifer Lopez. “His team conducted – and won – that early case in just the same way they fought the trial in 2025,” says Roundtree. “The smooth PR, the publicists who would talk to journalists and the crowds outside rooting for him.”In that 2001 case, the jury acquitted Combs but his co-defendant, rapper Jamal “Shyne” Barrow, who had been with him on the night, was convicted, sentenced to 10 years, then deported to Belize, his birth country. Combs didn’t attend Barrow’s sentencing, quietly dropped Barrow from his record label and changed his name from Puff Daddy to P Diddy to mark his fresh start. (Barrow later described Combs as “someone who destroyed my life”.)In every chapter of the book – and Combs’s life – people around him are shot, assaulted, imprisoned and broken, and careers are destroyed, yet he remains A-list, ascending to icon status. How? “That’s the biggest question,” says Roundtree. “How is someone with so many incidents around him, so much ruin in his wake, able to just keep doing better and better?“I think part of it was his personality. The media loved him because he played into the spectacle – he wasn’t afraid to be larger than life. He was also building something people really believed in. His record company was everywhere in New York, and he was giving opportunities to young people, straight out of school. He’d created a living legend in Biggie, who died so early. His clothing line was cool. His fragrance was great. His parties were epic. All these things played into a figure so big and so tangible, people think they can see it all right in front of them. So why look any further?”View image in fullscreenBiggie Smalls, Nate Dogg, Snoop Dogg and Combs, circa 1995.Photograph: Nitro/Getty ImagesVentura’s lawsuit was a pulling back of the curtain. “She was the first to let people into that world,” says Roundtree. “It’s really rare to see the inner workings of a public couple, but she laid it all out there, through her lawsuit, her trial testimony with all those photos on screen and text messages that she was asked to read, in front of the jury, in front of the world. She bared it all.”Ventura had signed to Combs’s record label when she was 19, a model turned singer. She had a hit, Me & U, a 10-album deal, and so much promise ahead. The book describes Combs’s focused pursuit of her, despite the 17-year age gap. (One of his personal assistants recalls Combs describing her as “very mouldable” and saying: “I got her right where I want her. She’s young.”)Combs’s inner circle and Ventura’s testimony describe the control he had over every part of her life – her diary, clothes, hair, nails. Even her medical records went directly to Combs’s email and he tracked her menstrual cycle. Her career stalled. Though Ventura recorded hundreds of tracks, her boss – Combs – didn’t release them. “She was his ‘wife partner’ for 10 years publicly,” says Roundtree. “One of the most surprising things to see was that, behind the scenes, she never lived with him, she never spent Christmas with him.”The relationship described by Ventura was dominated by “freak-offs” – coerced, multi-day-long, drug-fuelled sexual encounters with male sex workers, held in hotel rooms. Every aspect was micromanaged, choreographed, directed, watched and filmed by Combs. According to Ventura, she was 22 when Combs first raised the idea, and she “had no concept of how it would be a turn-on”. But she wanted to please him. After the first, she felt “dirty” but glad Combs was “happy” with her, that she “did something right”.Hundreds more took place around the world with unvetted men she didn’t know. Ventura says she felt “disgusting”, “humiliated”. When she attempted to leave Combs, he threatened to share the videos. (In one exchange between them, she talks of showing the world photos of her beaten face and body. “Release the videos also,” Combs shoots back.) Her life became preparing for “freak-offs”, enduring them and recovering afterwards. (“That’s why nothing gets done,” she wrote in one message to Combs, in 2017, their final year together. “Always healing.”)Ventura officially separated from Combs in 2018 and filed her lawsuit five years later. When federal investigators subsequently approached her to build a criminal case, she handed over phones, iPads, video material, the names of sex workers and other witnesses to help corroborate her claims.The US has no federal laws around coercive control and offences such as rape and assault carry statutes of limitations – legal time limits after which prosecution is not possible. But Combs was charged with racketeering conspiracy,sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, and transportation to engage in prostitution.“Those laws were developed to bring down the mafia, to dismantle criminal networks,” says Roundtree.View image in fullscreenCombs performing at Howard University’s Yardfest in 2023.Photograph: Thaddaeus McAdams/WireImageCombs’s 2025 trial lasted seven weeks, with the prosecution arguing that Combs used his business empire as a front for a criminal operation, relying on close associates to force and intimidate women into freak-offs and transport and supply drugs to keep them compliant. The defence argued successfully that what took place did not constitute a formal criminal enterprise.Ultimately, he was acquitted of most charges. “He was only found guilty of the clear examples where he paid for the male escorts to travel across a state line,” says Roundtree. “If they’d stayed within their states, they couldn’t have charged him with that.”The music industry, says Roundtree, is yet to have its “#MeToo fallout”. “Hollywood had this reckoning; music never really has.” R Kelly is the only other high-profile musician now in prison because of abuse uncovered in the me-too fall out. Others have been untouched by swirling rumours and mounting accusations. “Maybe it’s because an artist is so singular,” says Roundtree. “Actors have this whole machine around them, procedures to go through, people to answer to. And we love our music. Those songs are our fondest memories, they take us right back to a place or a time or a person and it’s hard to give that up, to separate the art from the artist. Sean Combs was a producer. Do we give up every song he touched? So we can’t listen to Biggie any more? It’s not realistic.”Combs’s release date is set for early in 2028, and he has multiple civil cases still to answer, although on Thursday it was reported that his attorneys areno longer acting for himin a dispute over months of unpaid legal bills. What lies beyond this? “He’ll definitely want to try to tell his story and make a comeback,” says Roundtree. “He has had a microphone in his hand since he was in his early 20s and I don’t think that desire to be loved and validated has gone away. There’ll be a next chapter for Sean Combs.”Bad Boy for Life: The Rise and Fall of Sean Combs by Cheyenne Roundtree (Simon & Schuster, £25) is out on 29 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). title: ‘Good music is good music, and most music is not!’ As he hits 90, master minimalist Steve Reich looks back | Steve Reich | The Guardian
description: At 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern living
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: At 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern living
Content: ‘I haven’t quite got there yet’ … Steve Reich at 89.Photograph: Jennifer TaylorView image in fullscreen‘I haven’t quite got there yet’ … Steve Reich at 89.Photograph: Jennifer TaylorSteve ReichInterview‘Good music is good music, and most music is not!’ As he hits 90, master minimalist Steve Reich looks backFlora WillsonAt 14, he heard Stravinsky and resolved to be a composer. As Reich approaches his 10th decade, the man revered by the likes of David Bowie reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern livingTue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Reich is not yet 90 but the celebrations have already begun, with the world premiere of his new piece for large ensemble,In All Your Ways, at the Edinburgh festival last month and alate-night concert at the BBC Proms. But when I ask this most supremely influential of living composers how he feels about becoming a nonagenarian on 3 October, Reich is coy. “I haven’t quite got there yet,” he says. “I don’t want to dot the i before I even get there. I’ll let you know in due course …”Born in New York in 1936, Reich has spent the last six decades producing music that has changed the soundtrack of modern life in Europe and North America, and inspired superlatives from a wide array of music critics. The New Yorker has called him “the most original musical thinker of our time”.Hyperbole? Absolutely not. Alongside his US contemporariesPhilip Glass,Terry RileyandLa Monte Young, Reich was one of the pioneers of musical minimalism. Its repetitive licks, driving rhythms and tonal-ish harmonies have since become the lingua franca of new waves of contemporary classical music, electronic dance music, film soundtracks and more. Reich dislikes the label but explains minimalism to me as “an intuitive movement towards whatwewanted to hear. We loved Stravinsky and Bartók and jazz – and were appreciating Bob Dylan and listening to African and Indian music.”double quotation markWe loved Stravinsky and Bartók and jazzNo wonder Reich’s influence has reached so far. His music has been sampled on records byDavid Bowieand chill-out merchantsthe Orb. Radiohead guitaristJonny Greenwoodhas recorded Electric Counterpoint, a work originally written for American jazz musicianPat Metheny. Twenty years ago, UK pop station BBC Radio 1 celebrated Reich’s 70thbirthday with a remix competition. His is a musical language familiar to millions, whether or not they know his name.Today, Reich may be more conscious than usual of his mortality. He is at home outside New York City when we talk, recovering from a recent fall. He broke a rib and has damaged his wrist. The former “seems to mend itself”, he marvels, but the latter is causing problems because he uses the piano as he composes. “You don’t have to be a great pianist, but you do have to be able to move around. I can do it for a minute or two and then it’sreallypainful.” He has “a few little sketches” for something and is frustrated to be slowed down. But he’s also grateful “that all these wonderful things are happening” for his birthday. “I’m not just laying on my back doing nothing,” he cackles. As if anyone who has met him could imagine that.Reich appears far younger than his 89 years. He joins our video call wearing his trademark black baseball cap and spends the next 90 minutes speaking rapid-fire New York-ese, abandoning long words partway in the scramble to communicate. The composer who once said ofPicasso’s Guernicathat,“as a work of art, it’s a towering masterpiece. As an effective political tool, it’s an absolute waste of time”seems as reluctant as ever to be drawn on his own work’s relationship to politics. But on myriad other aspects of music, sound and listening he is expansive, delivering answers in long paragraphs full of enthusiastic diversions.View image in fullscreen‘Look Ma, no electronics!’ … Reich in his studio in Manhattan studio, New York, in 1989.Photograph: Jack Vartoogian/Getty ImagesHe also cracks self-deprecating jokes, calls me “kid” when I ask him about his younger colleagues, and gleefully mocks me when I don’t catch the name of a major 20th-century composer he references: “Béla Bartók. He’s considered rather important. You might have heard of him …” He recommends an early piano piece by John Cage, In a Landscape – “you hear it and you say, ‘Is this a minimalist and we don’t know his name?’” – and at the end of our call, he wishes me a happy birthday in return, although “I don’t know when your birthday is”. If his reputation for being a“slightly stern”interviewee was ever fair, it’s obsolete in 2026.Yet the pleasure Reich takes in music is rooted in total seriousness. He doesn’t often listen to his own older works but “felt like I’d better brush up”, so he went back to his seminal 1971 percussion piece Drumming a couple of days before we talk. He recorded it in 1974 with his ensemble,Steve Reichand Musicians. “And I thought to myself, this is incredible! I mean, we were young, we were intense …” He recalls the fabulous acoustic – “it was a pop studio in Hanover” – and dives briefly into the minutiae of the recording process.double quotation markI don’t deny for a moment that opera is great music. But it’s not for meMoments later, Reich is talking me through the “two basic kinds of time” in Music for 18 Musicians, the 1976 work widely credited as one of his finest. Bowie hailed it as “a tonetrack into the future”. Fifty years since its premiere, Reich still is excited to demonstrate how it works: the constant rapid chugging of mallet instruments versus the “human breath” of the clarinets functioning “like waves washing over the grid”.This, unmistakably, is the same composer who turned away from the self-conscious “difficulty” of musical modernism – the serialist works that had “no rhythm that you could tap your foot to and no clear key centre that you could hear”. Instead, Reich announced in 1968: “I want to be able to hear the process happening throughout the sounding music.” Most radically of all, he wanted it to be audible to others, too, insisting that even when “everyone hears what is gradually happening, there are still enough musical mysteries to satisfy all”.View image in fullscreen‘I would move and the tape recorder would stay put’ … Reich, the pioneer of the musical phasing technique, in 1982.Photograph: Nancy R Schiff/Getty ImagesReich remains an energetic, acute thinker. He delivers impromptu lectures ranging across 900 years of music history and sings me some pastiche 12th-century polyphony. He speaks admiringly of fellow musicians from arch-modernist composer-conductorPierre Boulez– “he actually helped me indirectly” – to composersNico MuhlyandCaroline Shaw. He softly declaims lines by William Carlos Williams, his favourite poet, who gave a reading at Cornell University that the composer attended as an undergraduate. “He’d had a stroke and had to work at it,” Reich recalls. “It was a very moving experience.”Only names now prove occasionally elusive. “Approaching 90 means your memory is almost vanished,” he mutters at one point. But many anecdotes trip straight off his tongue. I bring up the much-repeated story of his first encounter withStravinsky’s The Rite of Springas a teenager, which he immediately reiterates was “completely life-changing – literally, I mean, my decision to be a composer really starts at the age of 14.” Alongside Stravinsky, the other musical forces at work on him then wereJS Bachand jazz megalithsCharlie ParkerandMiles Davis(“and then later John Coltrane,” he prompts).Has he experienced other equivalent watershed moments since? There is a rare pause in the torrent of ideas. Reich doesn’t think so. “If it was something on that scale, I wouldn’t have to fish around to try to remember it,” he laughs.Music critics and historians may beg to differ. His postgraduate studies with Italian experimental music giantLuciano Berioin the early 1970s clearly had their own significance. Reich arrived at their initial meeting with his own first (and last) 12-tone work, which Berio looked over before suggesting – Reich mimics this gleefully in a thick accent – “If you want to write tonal music, why don’t you write tonal music?”By then, Reich had already played in the world premiere of Terry Riley’s In C, one of the foundational contributions to what would soon be branded minimalism. He’d also bought two Wollensak tape recorders and created his first compositions from looped samples of recorded speech, It’s Gonna Rain (1965) and Come Out (1966). Those led to his development of what he called “phasing” technique.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jennifer Taylor“When I did Piano Phase” – Reich’s landmark 1967 piece for two pianos – “I made a tape loop on the tape recorder, sat down at the piano, and played against the tape recorder. I could count on the tape recorder to stay put,” he laughs. “And I would move – and that’s how the phasing process was discovered, with the interface of a human being versus a machine. When you ask a human pianist to be the machine, it turns out anything but mechanical, because the person who’s moving is like an organic force and you want to join them …”Phasing underpinned all of Reich’s music until he wrote Drumming. So surely its discovery was another big moment for him? “That playing of Piano Phase by myself and the tape recorder? Huge. Playing it with [pianist] Arthur Murphy and myself? Enormous. I just felt like, ‘Oh right,thisis music. Look ma, no electronics!’”A percussionist as well as a composer, Reich was once the driving force behind most performances of his music. As he put it in 1970, “There’s only one person in the world taking care of my music. If I don’t, who will?” These days there are many answers to that question. But no one is more active in promoting Reich’s music than Scottish percussionistColin Currie, who is headlining many ofthis year’s Reich at 90 events.View image in fullscreen‘I hate you – you’re better than my ensemble!’ … the Colin Currie Group performing Reich’s Drumming in 2011.Photograph: Robin Little/RedfernsThey met 20 years ago when the composer attended a performance of Drumming by the newly formedColin Currie Group. “I was completely knocked out,” Reich says. “Afterwards I just embraced him. I said, ‘You know, this is fantastic on the one hand. On the other hand, I hate you because you’re better than my ensemble and I don’t want to be upstaged!’” He grins before looking suddenly serious again. “But that’s exactly how it should be. I sure wish other people would get involved because I’m not going to be around for ever. Not a lot of things are clear in life, but that is.”Reich has a robust sense of his music’s importance and legacy. But he is also quick to own up to his “closet full of failures”. He has mixed feelings about most of his orchestral works (“Three Movementsis not a bad piece. It’s not a great piece”) and about opera as a whole: “I don’t deny for a moment that it’s great music, but it’s not for me.” His two video-operas,The CaveandThree Tales, created in collaboration with his wife, artistBeryl Korot, contain “great material”, he reckons, but “whether they sustain that for the full length of the piece … maybe they do, maybe they don’t”.Ultimately, Reich is clear about his measure for success. “Good music is good music, and most music is not,” he says emphatically. And what makes good music good? “Can you play it next to Charlie Parker? Can you play it next to Johann Sebastian Bach? Does it still sound worthwhile? If it does – hey, you got something!”Steve Reich at 90 festival is at theGlasshouse, Gateshead, from 2-4 October; Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians is performed by theParaorchestra at the Southbank Centre, London, on 27 September; the Barbican Centre’sSteve Reich at 90celebrations begin with the Colin Currie Group on28 OctoberThis article was amended on 22 September 2026. The Colin Currie Group were not performing Steve Reich’s Drumming in a picture as a caption said.
