title: Control Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomena | Games | The Guardian
description: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safe
Content: New York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentView image in fullscreenNew York state of mind … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentGamesReviewControl Resonant review – save New York from paranormal phenomenaPlayStation 5, Xbox, PC; RemedyA surprisingly conventional game from a famously weird developer, this sequel to 2019’s Control is accomplished but safePhil IwaniukTue 22 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is an arthouse action game from Finnish developer Remedy, masters of exactly this type of thing. It’s a sequel, however, so not only must it clear the high bar that its strikingly distinctive predecessor has set – it must also ideally arrive with a bushel of new ideas. There are clear and valuable strengths here in character progression and the lustrous presentation of its paranormal world, but Resonant doesn’t feel as enjoyably recondite or expansive in its influences as 2019’s Control did. As you wander New York brandishing supernatural abilities against glowing orange foes, the sad sense creeps in that you might be playing any number of games.As paranormal event survivor Jesse Faden, your journey through the original Control was like a sequence of playable Twilight Zone episodes, battling prosaic household objects with supernatural properties that teased and twisted reality inside an endlessly fascinating supernatural government bureau called the Oldest House. You’d navigate architecturally impossible spaces bridging the subconscious and the bricks-and-mortar world, in order to defeat a malevolent fridge. That’s broadly true again in Resonant, albeit with diminishing returns. This time you’re playing as Jesse’s brother Dylan, waking up after years of containment in the Oldest House to find its contents have escaped into downtown Manhattan. So you head out of the interesting place, and into a setting you’ve explored before inMarvel’s Spider-Man,The Division,Max Payne, and others ad infinitum.It’s disappointing because being bewitchingly strange has historically been Remedy’s great strength. It’s not unusual for games to give a reverent nod to Twin Peaks now and then, but this studio is the alpha and omega of interactive Lynchian nightmares. It’s been refining that skill since 2001’s Max Payne, and at this point there’s really nobody better at nonlinear storytelling or unnerving dream sequences.View image in fullscreenInception-like gravitational spins … Control Resonant.Photograph: Remedy EntertainmentRemedy’s take on New York has an exhilaratingly free-form structure that lets you take on enemies, missions and places in roughly the order you want. The main missions are fairly rigid, but you can engage with the rest however and whenever you want. You fight a malevolent paranormal force with an imaginative collection of supernatural kung fu moves, whose power and combo potential level up satisfyingly. Your shapeshifting weapon can take many forms, from a dagger-like blade to a scythe or a hammer. Secondary attacks, ranged weapons and passive abilities lend more interest to fights against paranormal entity the Hiss as time goes on, but compared to something like the surgically precise swordplay of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, battles feel a bit blunt here.Your ultimate tests come in the form of the Resonants themselves, a series of bosses lying in wait throughout Manhattan. Remedy’s knack for otherworldly horror comes to the fore in their visual design, which I won’t spoil, and like so much of the game they can be hunted down in any order. Beware, though – beating them changes other enemies’ presence, strength and behaviour afterwards.Dylan’s movement is more imaginative and enjoyable than his arsenal. Here, trading off a fascinating indoor setting for more outdoor space starts to make sense, as you triple-jump your way across rooftops and shift your gravitational grounding to walk on streets that have been bent upwards vertically à laInception. It’s playful about it, too – soon after gaining that latter ability, your bureau handler pumps some EDM down the radio to soundtrack your run through a multistorey car park whose levels fold and distort at impossible angles.It is the little moments like this, not the grand story beats, that prove the most memorable and gratifying. Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.Control Resonant is out now; £49.99Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamesAction gamesGame playPlayStation 5XboxreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Amar Kanwar review: unflinching Indian artist dares you to step into the darkness (literally) | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Making lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missed
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Making lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missed
Content: ‘An atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility’ ... Amar Kanwar’s Such a Morning, 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.View image in fullscreen‘An atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility’ ... Amar Kanwar’s Such a Morning, 2017.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.Art and designReviewAmar Kanwar review: unflinching Indian artist dares you to step into the darkness (literally)Serpentine North, LondonMaking lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, Kanwar focuses on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missedBen EasthamTue 22 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 07.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe exhibition begins in darkness. A darkness so complete, in fact, that I’m forced to wait at the threshold while my eyes adjust to it. To my left, images flash up on screens that seem to float in the gloom: a peacock preens its wet feathers; dried flowers in a wooden bowl; sunlight scatters on water. When the room has resolved to the point that I can identify a chair to sit on, I realise that these pictures are combined with snippets of text telling stories like parables: about a landlord punished for breaking a promise to a beggar; about two friends who survive a massacre because they are down by the river, arguing over the moon.Welcome to the world of Amar Kanwar: if you want to find beauty and truth, you must be prepared to step into the darkness. Over 40 years making increasingly lyrical films about stories ranging from the collapse of empire to endemic sexual brutality, the Indian artist has developed a method that neither reproduces the violence of these histories as spectacle nor glosses it over. Instead he trains his focus on those parts of the story that normally escape attention: the shadows, the neglected, the blind spots. He does not find revelation there, at least not of the kind that suddenly lights up the world and makes sense of it. But there are enough flashes of light to guide us through the darkness.This idea finds its most literal expression in Such a Morning, a feature-length film installed within one of the enclosed spaces that make this old gunpowder store so well suited to Kanwar’s play with darkness and light, secrets and disclosure (the whole exhibition is superbly staged). It tells the story of a mathematics professor who retreats into an artificial darkness in the hope of finding another way to understand the world around him. Through a characteristic combination of exquisite images – a woman sits in a rattan chair clutching an antiquated rifle as her house is dismantled around her – with overlaid text and a trancelike piano soundtrack, the film conjures an atmosphere of commingled crisis and possibility.View image in fullscreenAmar Kanwar’s 2023 film The Peacock’s Graveyard.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Marian Goodman Gallery.Like much of Kanwar’s work, Such a Morning makes demands on your patience. Anyone attempting to make simple sense of the film is likely to sympathise with the professor groping blindly around in the dark. But it is worth putting in the time, because Kanwar’s commitment to doubt as a precursor of knowledge carries a political charge in the present. If you are inclined to feel, on reading the news, that we have recently entered a new dark age, then Such a Morning proposes that we have been blinded by the lights. Overwhelmed by images masquerading as reality and opinions posing as fact, we might follow the professor’s example and commit to a period of reflection on what we choose to see and how we interpret it. He comes to a simple conclusion: we must all learn to attend to the darkness if we are to change the course of “self-destruction” on which humanity is presently set. It’s a lesson worth heeding.The degrees of darkness the professor identifies are represented by illuminated paper screens that protrude from the wall like torches. It’s a brilliant piece of theatre design that leads you through the prevailing gloom to the final work in the show, another film to combine archive footage with fragments of text. The subject of the evocatively titled The Charcoal Man is the 1947 partition of India. Events from the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi to the mass migrations are told from the perspectives of people who might seem incidental to the action: an absent-minded window maker, a boy who dreams of becoming a drummer.The tension here is between forgetting and remembering, both of which are figured as essential to reconciliation, and The Charcoal Man suggests they might be fused through various kinds of alchemy or transference. In one story, for example, a father instructs his son to remove the circuit boards from the computers in his shop and, through a complex chemical process, to aggregate the gold they contain into a bracelet that could be pawned in the event that he needs at short notice to flee. Memories of a violent past are by these means transformed into insurance against the future. Is this what art might do?The same narrator inherits from his grandfather, a professional photographer, an archive of images documenting the violence of Partition. The seemingly paradoxical condition of the bequest is that these photographs should be conserved for ever but never shown. Instead they might continue to exist in the shadows, alluded to (but never revealed) by the kind of stories that preserve the horrors of the past without restarting the cycles of violence. These, after all, are the kind of stories that Amar Kanwar tells.Amar Kanwar is at Serpentine North Gallery from 23 September 2026 until 31 January 2027Explore more on these topicsArt and designArtSerpentine GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea’: a hike along Andy Goldsworthy’s epic art trail in Haute-Provence | France holidays | The Guardian
description: A long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and art
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and art
Content: Sentinel by Andy Goldsworthy, one of three cairns the artist built without using mortar or cement.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyView image in fullscreenSentinel by Andy Goldsworthy, one of three cairns the artist built without using mortar or cement.Photograph: BIOSPHOTO/AlamyFrance holidays‘To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea’: a hike along Andy Goldsworthy’s epic art trail in Haute-ProvenceA long-distance walking route in the south of France devised by the celebrated land artist offers intrepid hikers an opportunity to immerse themselves in nature and artClaudia CasperTue 22 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 02.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 69, I had never hiked with a backpack and I had no idea what land art was. Nonetheless, when my friend Jackie, a nature documentary film-maker, invited me to join her and her friends Wendy and Sasha on a hiking trip toRefuges d’Artin the mountainous countryside of Haute-Provence, I said a resounding “yes”. We would be sleeping alongside sculptures by the renowned land artistAndy Goldsworthy.First, I watchRivers and Tides, a documentary on Goldsworthy’s work, and discover he has built exquisite ice sculptures and stone cairns in my own country, Canada. His work seems to speak to an older part of the soul. Then, I start walking up hills, gradually adding weights to my backpack until I can comfortably carry 9kg (20lb).We meet in Digne-les-Bains, a bustling mountain town in the centre of theUnesco geopark of Haute-Provence, and the starting point for a 10-day, 150km (93-mile) hiking route that includes the possibility of staying overnight at seven reservable but free off-grid sleeping cabins. Goldsworthy worked alongside local teams to restore the abandoned shepherd huts, farmhouses, chapel and stone shelters, and created a site-specific artwork for each one. Over four days, we will visit three of these refuges and hike about 45km (28 miles).double quotation markOn the first day, we encounter one of three sentinels that sit like giant mysterious eggs watching over the routeOur first stop in Digne-les-Bains isMaison Alexandra David-Neél, a museum dedicated to the adventurous, peripatetic life of a woman who, in 1924, disguised herself as a beggar to become the first western woman to enter the Forbidden City of Lhasa in Tibet. The keys to the refuges are kept here, no doubt, to inspire hikers for the adventures that lie ahead.On the first day, we encounter one of three sentinels that sit like giant mysterious eggs watching over the route. These 2 to 3-metre tall cairns were made by Goldsworthy without mortar or cement and rely on fitting the right shapes and weights of the stones.View image in fullscreenLa Forest by Andy Goldsworthy, illuminated by natural light.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyJackie has told us the trail is mostly flat and indeed, we start on even gravel, chatting and laughing, getting used to the weight of our packs. After 5km, she says we should look for a path leading up the hill on our right. She checks her satnav and points to a goat path going straight up the rocks. I panic. My backpack suddenly feels extremely heavy. In desperation, I check further down the road and, to everyone’s relief, find a path marked with white and red horizontal lines signifying agranderandonnée, a trail certified by the French government.We begin our ascent, pausing to photograph curlicued and wispy plants right out of Dr Seuss, yellow, scarlet and blue wildflowers, an orange moth sitting on purple brush. Spanish broom perfumes the air. We lift our gaze and see multiple valleys and unique geological formations. It’s easy to imagine our ice-age ancestors walking these trails 15,000 years ago and it’s gratifying to be travelling under our own steam, as they did.We arrive at the first refuge,La Forest, as the sun is setting. The key unlocks the door. Inside, the air is cold. Our eyes adjust to the dark. A table and benches stand in front of us. To the left, a stairway leads to sleeping platforms. To the right, a doorway into a dark, empty room. From its depths glows a cylindrical obelisk, light falling on one large stone where someone could sit. It’s concave, constructed of light grey stone ending in a porthole to the sky. It’s illuminated by natural light and changes with the time, the weather, the season. This art is living and feels sacred.double quotation markIn the flickering orange light, the sculpture comes to life, looking like one of Plato’s eternal formsThat evening, we eat freeze-dried mushroom risotto in the flickering candlelight, play cards, eat chocolate, laugh and share stories. Sasha, who works in film in Germany, teaches us two words:der salzlose– someone who is bland and without flavour; andextrawurst– someone who always demands more. Neither apply to our group. The camaraderie and conviviality bring pure pleasure.We climb the stairs to the sleeping platforms. Wendy and Sasha have brought sturdy sleeping mats on Jackie’s recommendation. We lay them out and say goodnight. The quiet is complete. Then, a tidal wave of sound erupts. Wendy and Sasha have rolled over. The friction on the technical fabric of their sleeping mats is deafening. The price of comfort has been revealed; they must lie like mummies.View image in fullscreenClaudia and friends Jackie and Sasha (left to right) in Le Vieil Esclangon art refuge.Photograph: Wendy ReevesThe next day, we descend, picnic by a river on crackers, avocados and cheese, then start climbing again. Sasha and I subversively agree that it’s psychologically better to be told something is going to be hard and then it turns out easier. I console myself that climbing with a backpack is good for bone density and way less boring than lifting weights.The next refuge,Le Vieil Esclangon, is in a mountain-top meadow. A majestic fan of lifted rock shines across the wide valley. Everywhere we turn there are more mountains and valleys. The first floor of the refuge is a large dark room split in two by a massive fireplace. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms look out on to a sunlit verge. Across from the fireplace, a tall serpentine shape made of dried mud loops back and forth like a meandering river, ending at the top in the source.The wind picks up and the temperature drops. We gather wood and light a fire. In the flickering orange light, the sculpture comes to life, looking like one of Plato’s eternal forms. We eat our freeze-dried pad thai, the art and the hikers transient and temporary but together in this warm and cosy moment.Later, we sleep to the sound of wind and rain, woken only by a mouse rave in the middle of the night.View image in fullscreenLa Ferme Belon, where ‘huge interlinked semicircular stone arches look like a dragon’s body swimming through earth’.Photograph: B WarluzelWe arrive at the third refuge,La Ferme Belon, in time for a late lunch. In the basement, huge interlinked semicircular stone arches look like a dragon’s body swimming through earth. Upstairs, the sleeping platforms are lovely except for one small detail. A colony of bats hang above. I can feign nonchalance because I know Wendy, who is quietly uber-capable, will find us a delightful B&B for the night. Over pizza and cold rosé, Sasha and I confess to Jackie that we would have rather known how challenging the hikes were going to be. “But you wouldn’t have come if I’d told you,” she answers with a twinkle in her eye.Andy Goldsworthy said: “To me there is a tremendous difference between works of art that we observe in a museum just for a few minutes and works of art in which we live for a short while, in which we sleep. To sleep in a sculpture is a wonderful idea.”In Digne-les-Bains we return the keys and soak our stronger bodies in the town’s hot springs. We’ve already said yes to Jackie’s next adventure, sight unseen.Claudia Casper’snovelThe Mercy Journalswon the Philip K Dick award for distinguished science fiction in 2017(Arsenal Pulp Press)Explore more on these topicsFrance holidaysWalking holidaysSculptureEurope holidaysWalkingAdventure travelProvence holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The secret to making jackfruit curry that actually tastes of something | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Jackfruit is a blank canvas that absorbs flavour brilliantly – it’s all about seasoning it generously and giving it enough time for the aromatics and spices to do their work
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Jackfruit is a blank canvas that absorbs flavour brilliantly – it’s all about seasoning it generously and giving it enough time for the aromatics and spices to do their work
Content: You won’t find anything bland inMeera Sodha’s jackfruitkhanom chin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food Styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones. Photo assistant and retouching: Sophie BronzeView image in fullscreenYou won’t find anything bland inMeera Sodha’s jackfruitkhanom chin.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food Styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones. Photo assistant and retouching: Sophie BronzeKitchen aideChefsThe secret to making jackfruit curry that actually tastes of somethingJackfruit is a blank canvas that absorbs flavour brilliantly – it’s all about seasoning it generously and giving it enough time for the aromatics and spices to do their workAnna BerrillTue 22 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve just made yet another disappointing jackfruit curry.Any tipsfor making it more flavourful?Sally,by email“The trick with jackfruit is not to rush it,” says Eroshan Meewella, founder of Sri Lankan street-food jointAdoh!in central London. “It absorbs flavour brilliantly – spice, curry leaves, coconut milk, tamarind – so you just need to give it time.” Don’t be shy with those flavours, either, because, as Sally has discovered, jackfruit is something of a blank canvas. Sanjana Modha, author ofModern Masala, suggests treating it a bit as you would tofu: “You really have to build flavour around it. Think of jackfruit as a sponge that’s going to absorb your masala. And I cannot emphasise enough how you’ll need more onions than you think.” And she ain’t kidding: for a curry to feed four to six, Modha uses “at least” four large onions. “You must spend time caramelising them properly, so start by getting those onions really golden by frying them with a couple of cinnamon sticks, cloves and cardamom pods.” That will take a good 45 minutes. “Then add ginger, garlic and chillies – don’t be afraid to season generously with all your ground spices.” You’ll want some acidity, too: “Lemon, lime or tamarind towards the end to balance everything.”On to the jackfruit itself, which Luke Larsson, head chef atKhao Birdin London, always uses fresh from an Asian supermarket: “It’s just a hundred times better [than tinned], and it’s such a delicious fruit when fresh.” Modha, meanwhile, tends to go for tinned young green jackfruit in brine: “Drain and rinse it really well, then pat it completely dry using kitchen towel.” She fries it first in neutral oil (rapeseed, sunflower), until golden and slightly caramelised: “This gives it much more flavour, then I marinate it in ground spices and a spoonful of mustard oil for a few hours, or even overnight, before adding it to my curry.”Once the jackfruit is in the curry, Modha would be inclined to cook it in a pressure cooker: “That makes the jackfruit beautifully tender and gives all those flavours time to penetrate.” But make sure you let that curry “really reduce, rather than leaving it wet”, Meewella adds: “That’s when the spices and coconut get right into the jackfruit and you develop that deep, rich flavour.” For a final hit, Modha stirs in a dollop of hot mango pickle right at the end. A curry is all about “big flavours”, after all, she says.As we head into autumn, chestnut mushrooms are good seasonal friends for jackfruit. “It feels really comforting as the weather starts to cool down, but it’s still bright and fresh,” Modha says. Start by frying the mushrooms and drained, dried jackfruit until golden, then marinate them in spices (cloves, cardamom, turmeric, fennel, say). “For the curry, I build a proper masala with onions, ginger, garlic, dried red chillies and ground spices, then add tomatoes, coconut milk, and the marinated jackfruit and mushrooms.” Again, get that in a pressure cooker and “the jackfruit becomes meltingly tender and takes on all the flavour of the masala”. Finish with a squeeze of lemon, some mango pickle and fresh coriander, and serve with rice, roti or paratha, of course.Got a culinary dilemma? title: Sumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipe  | Food | The Guardian
description: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken and onion on flatbread, with tahini yoghurt and a simple, textured salad
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: A rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken and onion on flatbread, with tahini yoghurt and a simple, textured salad
Content: Sami Tamimi’sfattet musakhanwith cucumber and avocado salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’sfattet musakhanwith cucumber and avocado salad.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianFoodSumac roast chicken and bread bake: Sami Tamimi’s fattet musakhan with cucumber avocado salad – recipeA rich Levantine fusion dish of sumac-spiced roast chicken, onion and flatbread with tahini yoghurt, and a simple, textured saladSami TamimiTue 22 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 01.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFattet musakhan, a celebration of two beloved Palestinian dishes, takes centre stage here, bringing together crisp bread, creamy yoghurt, sumac-spiced onions, tender chicken and fragrant olive oil in one rich and comforting dish. Alongside, the salad brings a welcome freshness, with crisp cucumber, creamy avocado and bright acidity cutting through the richness of the chicken. Together, they make a beautifully balanced meal, bringing the generous, communal spirit of Palestinian cooking to the table.Fattet musakhanFattet musakhan is a fusion of two dishes – sumac chicken, and crisp flatbread with tahini and yoghurt – brought together into one generous meal.Prep10 minCook1 hr 10 minServes44 pitta(160g), cut into 5cm chunks75ml olive oil,plus extra for servingSalt and black pepper1½ tsp ground cumin1½ tbsp sumac, plus extra for sprinkling¼ tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground allspice800g boneless skinless chicken thighs2 tbsp lemon juice30g pine nuts1 large red onion, peeled and thinly sliced (250g net)5g flat-leaf parsley, roughly choppedFor the yoghurt sauce400ggreek-style yoghurt, to serve40g tahini1garlic clovepeeled and crushed2 tsp lemon zest2 tbsp lemon juice¾ tsp saltHeat the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5. Put the pitta on a tray lined with greaseproof paper, add a tablespoon of olive oil and an eighth of a teaspoon of salt, and mix well. Spread the bread out in one even layer and roast for 10 minutes, turning once halfway, then remove and leave to cool. Turn up the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.Put all the spices in a small bowl and mix well. Put the chicken in a large bowl with two tablespoons of oil, half the spice mix, the lemon juice, a teaspoon of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Mix well, then spread out on a second paper-lined baking tray. Roast for about 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Remove from the oven and set aside – keep any juices that have collected in the tray (pour these over the finished dish). When the chicken has cooled slightly, shred the meat into long strips and return to the tray.Meanwhile, put the remaining two tablespoons of oil in a large saute pan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for two to three minutes, until golden. Transfer to a bowl lined with kitchen paper, leaving the oil in the pan.Put the onion and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt in the hot oil left in the pan and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 15 minutes on a medium heat, until the onions are completely soft and pale golden (but not caramelised). Mix in the remaining spice mix and some black pepper, until the onions are completely coated.To make the yoghurt sauce, mix all the ingredients in a medium bowl.To assemble the dish, arrange the pitta in one layer on a large platter or in a deep bowl. Spoon half the yoghurt sauce on top, scatter over half the chicken pieces, followed by half the onions. Repeat with the remaining yoghurt, chicken and onion, then pour all the tray juices around the bread. Garnish with the pine nuts, parsley, a good sprinkle of sumac and drizzle of olive oil.Cucumber and avocado saladView image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s cucumber and avocado salad.Fresh, simple and wonderfully refreshing, this brings together avocado and cucumber for a lovely contrast of textures. The bright dressing adds freshness and acidity, making it the perfect accompaniment to rich dishes. I love salads like this, because they’re uncomplicated yet full of character.Prep10 minCook15 minServes43 ripe avocados(350g),peeled and stoned3 tbsp lemon juice300g cucumber(about 4-6 mini cucumbers or 1 large cucumber)1 little gem lettuce, cut into large chunks3-4 spring onions(70g), trimmed and thinly sliced3 tbsp olive oilRed chilli flakes, or your favourite hot sauce, to serve (optional)Cut the avocado flesh into 1cm cubes and put in a large bowl. Add the lemon juice and stir gently.Peel the cucumber in alternating strips, then cut into bite-size pieces and put in the avocado bowl.
